title: Two for One: Privileged Learning for Resource-Constrained Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.29126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning systems are often developed under data-rich conditions but deployed when only incomplete information is available. A natural example arises in colour fundus photography (CFP), where both eyes are commonly imaged because they can provide complementary information for ocular disease assessment. Prior approaches that exploit bilateral information either fuse both eyes in a single model or use knowledge distillation to compress a dual-eye teacher into a lightweight student that still requires both images at test time. However, bilateral acquisition may not always be feasible. We thus propose a privileged learning framework in which a teacher model has access to bilateral CFP images during training and learns representations informed by information from both eyes, while the student is trained to transfer this knowledge from the bilateral teacher using only a single-eye image as input. At inference, the student operates exclusively on this single-eye input and does not require the contralateral image. Experimental results show consistent improvements in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over conventional monocular training, with the largest gains observed for left-eye images for the detection of age-related macular degeneration (0.931 vs. 0.966) and diabetic retinopathy (0.789 vs. 0.836).%, while requiring only a single-eye image at inference. By enabling models to benefit from bilateral information during training while requiring only a single-eye image at inference, our approach may support more reliable deployment in resource-constrained clinical and screening environments.

title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
description:
arXiv:2610.28878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, \delta$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.

title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.

title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.28947v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.

title: Fixed vs random effects in Python, and what a Hausman test result actually tells you
description:
Most panel data tutorials stop at "run the Hausman test, and if p < 0.05 use fixed effects." That rule is fine as a starting point, but it hides a few things that matter once you look at real output. So here is a small worked example you can run yourself, with the numbers I got.

The setup

I used the wage_panel dataset that ships with linearmodels: 545 individuals observed over 8 years, with log wages as the outcome. The regressors are experience squared, marital status and union membership.

bash
pip install linearmodels
python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS, RandomEffects
from linearmodels.datasets import wage_panel

df = wage_panel.load().set_index(["nr", "year"])
y = df["lwage"]
X = df[["expersq", "married", "union"]]

the RE model needs an intercept, the FE (within) model does not

X_re = X.copy()
X_re.insert(0, "const", 1.0)

fe = PanelOLS(y, X, entity_effects=True).fit()
re = RandomEffects(y, X_re).fit()
The two sets of estimates
variable fixed effects random effects
expersq 0.0037 0.0032
married 0.1073 0.1316
union 0.0828 0.1035

The random effects numbers for married and union are noticeably larger. That gap is what the Hausman test formalises. If the unobserved person-level effects (ability, motivation, whatever drives wages and also correlates with marrying or joining a union) are correlated with the regressors, the RE estimator picks that correlation up as if it were an effect of the regressor, and the coefficients drift upward.

Computing the Hausman statistic by hand

linearmodels doesn't ship a one-line Hausman test, but the statistic is short:

python
cols = fe.params.index
b = fe.params - re.params[cols]
V = fe.cov - re.cov.loc[cols, cols]

stat = float(b @ np.linalg.inv(V) @ b)
p = 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(stat, len(cols))
print(f"Hausman chi2 = {stat:.3f}, df = {len(cols)}, p = {p:.4f}")

Output on this data:

Hausman chi2 = 112.118, df = 3, p = 0.0000

A clear rejection. The RE assumption (effects uncorrelated with the regressors) doesn't hold here, so the fixed effects estimates are the ones to report.

Three things the textbook rule skips

A rejection is evidence against RE, not a proof that FE is right. FE only removes confounding that is constant over the sample window. Anything that changes over time and correlates with both wages and marriage is still in your error term.

You pay for FE with the time-invariant variables. The within estimator can't estimate the effect of anything that doesn't change for a person (education at entry, say, or a fixed demographic). I left those out above for exactly that reason. If they are the point of your study, FE alone won't answer your question, and a Mundlak or correlated random effects specification is worth a look.

The classic Hausman test assumes homoskedastic errors. With clustered standard errors, which is the usual choice in applied work, the difference of covariance matrices isn't the right object anymore. A regression-based version (the Mundlak approach: add the group means of each regressor to the RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.

If you'd rather not write code

For a quick check, or to hand something to a colleague who doesn't use Python, there is a panel data regression online tool that fits fixed and random effects models in the browser. Full disclosure: I'm connected to that site. For anything you plan to publish, I'd still keep the script above so the analysis is reproducible.

Curious whether people go Mundlak, or just default to FE and move on.RE model and test them jointly) works with robust errors.

title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
description:
arXiv:2610.29090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.

title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
description:
arXiv:2610.28773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.

title: Railway Says Some Customer Secrets May Have Been Decrypted. What Should Teams Do?
description:
A platform can encrypt a secret at rest and still face a serious incident if an attacker reaches a path that exposes its decrypted value. Railway's October 21 security notice says an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and obtained the decrypted contents of some of them.[1]

Railway has not said that every customer was affected. Its initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset, while its precautionary recommendation applies to all users.[1] This is an evolving incident, so check Railway's notice and status page before acting on older summaries.[2]

What Railway has disclosed

Railway says the affected systems store customer environment variables. Those values can include API keys, database access, or credentials for private registries.[1] The company also says it believes the incident is part of a broader series of attacks against platform companies intended to reach AI inference providers. That is Railway's assessment, not a publicly described attack chain.[1]

Railway paused builds and deployments while investigating.[1] Its status updates on October 22 added response guides, including credential rotation and checks for unusual usage at connected services.[2] At 02:19 UTC on October 22, Railway said builds were still offline and some remediation steps requiring a redeploy would have to wait.[2]

The public notice does not explain how the third party gained access, how many accounts were affected, or which specific variables were exposed.[1] Railway says it will contact customers it confirms were affected.[1] Avoid treating either the possible subset or the platform-wide precaution as a confirmed count. The first is Railway's initial assessment; the second is its response advice.[1]

Rotate credentials at the service that issued them

Changing a value in a hosting dashboard does not necessarily invalidate the old credential. A leaked API token can remain usable until its issuing provider revokes it. A database password remains valid until the database accepts a new one and the old one is disabled.

For each secret stored in Railway, identify the system that issued it, then replace it there. Update the corresponding Railway variable when the platform allows it, and revoke the old value. Railway recommends rolling all environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials.[1]

For database credentials, coordinate the change with the database itself. AWS defines rotation as updating the credential in both the secret store and the database or service that accepts it.[4] Changing only one side can leave the application or database using an outdated value.[4]

Prioritize credentials that can create bills, expose customer data, or grant broad access. Include AI provider keys, cloud access, database passwords, source-control tokens, and private package credentials if they were stored in the affected platform. Railway's notice explicitly includes environment variables and private registry credentials in its recommendation.[1]

Keep a short record of each credential: owner, issuing service, affected application, replacement status, and old-key revocation status. AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3]

Check for use you do not recognize

Review the logs at the service that issued each credential, as Railway recommends reviewing service logs for unusual activity.[1] Look for requests, deployments, access locations, or usage patterns the team cannot explain. Railway's status page has published service-specific guides, including checks for unusual activity at AI providers, cloud accounts, databases, and other connected services.[2]

A lack of suspicious entries does not prove that a credential was not accessed. Logs may have limited retention or may not capture every relevant action. Treat log review as one part of the response, alongside replacement and revocation.

Plan for a paused deployment pipeline

A rotation is not complete if the running application still depends on the old value. But during Railway's response, teams could not deploy new versions while builds were paused. Railway's status page said some remediation steps required a redeploy and had to wait for builds to return.[2]

That creates an operational tradeoff: revoke an old credential immediately and risk breaking the live service, or keep it active while waiting to deploy the replacement. There is no universal answer. For a credential with clear signs of misuse, containment may outweigh availability. For a production database password with no safe way to update the running app, coordinate the change with the database and platform status, and use Railway's service-specific guidance.[2] Avoid making a rushed change that locks out the application without actually revoking the old credential.

The lesson is about the full secret lifecycle

Encryption at rest is important, but it is not the whole security boundary. Applications and platforms must eventually retrieve usable credentials to connect to databases, cloud accounts, registries, and APIs. The important questions are also who can access those values, how access is monitored, and how quickly a credential can be replaced and revoked.

AWS recommends limiting access to secrets, monitoring their use, and rotating credentials as part of secret management.[3] These controls cannot prevent every breach. They can reduce the number of systems a stolen credential can reach and shorten how long it remains useful.[3]

For developers, keep a secret inventory. Record which service issued each key, what it can access, how to revoke it, and which deployment depends on the replacement. AWS's guidance on limiting access and monitoring secret use supports planned secret management.[3]

Railway's disclosure is still developing. Treat its published guidance as the source for the platform response, and check the incident page for new updates before redeploying.[2]

Sources

[1] Railway, Security Disclosure: Wednesday October 21st
[2] Railway, Platform incident updates
[3] AWS, Secrets Manager best practices
[4] AWS, Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets

title: What a Scrape Plus Embed Pipeline Looks Like — Auditable Retention Boundaries
description:
Short answer: a scrape plus embed pipeline looks like five accountable steps end to end: search or list sources, fetch each canonical page, extract and chunk readable text, embed the chunks, then upsert them with the source URL. Each stage can fail independently. An internal knowledge-base bot therefore needs a retry boundary, an observable count, and an audit record at every handoff; the least complex trustworthy design keeps the URL beside every vector and treats a nightly crawl as a reconciliation job, rather than as an opaque batch that either “worked” or did not.

For an edtech market-research team, grounding is the product requirement: an answer about a competitor's course catalog is useful only if a reviewer can follow its citation back to the page that was indexed. The important optimization is therefore not the cheapest embedding call. It is reducing duplicate fetches and retained copies without destroying that chain of custody.

Infrai fits one specific boundary here: the nightly schedule, web acquisition, and vector operations can use one credential, one base URL, and one bill. Its public discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules and exposes the schemas needed to construct requests without guessing. A specialist crawler or vector database remains the better choice when that component's controls dominate the design.

What is the bill actually made of?

Model the run before choosing a vendor. Let S be discovered URLs, U the canonical URLs left after deduplication, B the readable bytes fetched, C the chunks produced, and V the vectors retained. A useful first-pass cost equation is search(S) + fetch(U, B) + embed(C) + store(V) + schedule(runs). The dominant term is the one multiplied by unnecessary repetition; if aliases make U larger than the set of unique canonical pages, every downstream term grows with it. Deduplicating after indexing is late because the fetch, extraction, and embedding work has already been paid for.

Count each boundary separately: URLs discovered, canonical URLs accepted, fetches attempted, pages extracted, chunks emitted, embeddings completed, and vectors upserted. A single “documents processed” counter cannot tell an operator whether a smaller index reflects intentional filtering, a scrape failure, or an embedding retry still in flight. Reconciliation should assert relationships such as embedded chunks <= emitted chunks and account for every difference with a terminal or retryable state.

Count first.

Retention has its own equation: raw page bytes + extracted text bytes + chunk text bytes + vector bytes + audit metadata. The deliberate reduction is to stop keeping redundant rendered copies and intermediate aliases once the configured investigation window closes, while retaining canonical URL metadata and stage-level counts. The cost is real: after that window, a disputed extraction cannot be replayed byte-for-byte from the old input; it must be fetched again, and the page may have changed.

What Does a Scrape Plus Embed Pipeline Look Like?

The boundary begins with source discovery, not with vector search. A search result is a candidate, a fetched page is evidence, extracted text is an interpretation of that evidence, and a vector is a retrieval aid. Conflating those objects makes deletion, replay, and citation review ambiguous.

Canonicalization belongs before fetching. Record the discovered URL as an alias if it matters to research provenance, but key the fetch decision by canonical URL. After extraction, create a deterministic chunk identifier from the canonical URL, the extraction version, and the chunk position; an upsert retry can then replace the same logical record instead of multiplying it. This is an exactly-once outcome built over retryable work, not a claim that the network delivers exactly once.

The source URL must survive in vector metadata. Without it, a retrieved passage may sound grounded while remaining unauditable, and neither a reviewer nor a deletion workflow can reliably connect the answer to its origin. The original RAG paper describes retrieval as supplying external knowledge to generation; production grounding adds the operational obligation to identify which external item supported the output.

URLs are evidence.

How should retries preserve an audit trail?

Use an append-only transition record around mutable indexes. The following runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery surface, authenticates from an environment variable, retries a rate limit with bounded exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, checks error responses, and verifies that the schedule and scrape capabilities advertised for this pipeline are available. It deliberately reads the live schemas rather than inventing write payloads absent from this article.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    ID        string `json:"id"`
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func discovery(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 5 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body, err := discovery(key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    var manifest Manifest
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    wanted := map[string]bool{
        "/v1/cron/create": false,
        "/v1/web/scrape": false,
    }
    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if _, ok := wanted[capability.Path]; ok && capability.Available {
            wanted[capability.Path] = true
            fmt.Printf("%s %s available=%t\n", capability.Method, capability.Path, capability.Available)
        }
    }
    for path, available := range wanted {
        if !available {
            panic("required capability unavailable: " + path)
        }
    }
}

A worker may execute an event more than once. The deterministic key makes that retry recognizable, while the URL makes its effect inspectable. Persist the attempt, response classification, and resulting count before acknowledging work; do not treat a successful scheduler invocation as proof that vectors were written.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a team that wants the nightly schedule and the scrape-to-vector handoff behind one credential and one bill: its verified surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules, and idempotency is a documented platform convention on 171 of 294 capabilities. In this flow, the scheduler can be created through POST /v1/cron/create, while page acquisition uses POST /v1/web/scrape; both sit under the same base URL and Bearer key. That removes separate credential grants between the scheduler and crawler, and its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which is useful when generating the concrete calls rather than freezing guessed payloads in an article.

This consolidation has a cost: one vendor becomes the trust boundary, the bill boundary, and an outage surface shared by the run. Keep the stage ledger portable.

Choosing a boundary, not a logo

A direct stack of cron, Scrapy, and Pinecone means three signups, three credential sets, and glue that passes scheduled work into the crawler and then maps extracted chunks into vector upserts. It offers sharper component substitution, and Scrapy is the better fit when crawl behavior itself requires a mature specialist framework. Pinecone is a stronger direct choice when the vector database is the architectural center and its dedicated controls justify another operational boundary.

Option Boundary it owns Good fit Limit to plan around
Infrai Schedule, web acquisition, and vector operations behind one API key A small platform team prioritizing one auditable HTTP boundary Concentrates trust and operational dependency in one provider
Scrapy + cron + Pinecone Separate scheduler, crawler, and managed vector index Teams wanting specialist crawl control and component-level substitution Three credential domains and custom handoff code
Apify + Qdrant Managed web automation plus a separate vector database Dynamic-site collection paired with an independently operated index The extraction-to-index contract remains yours
Weaviate Vector database with a broader retrieval-oriented platform Teams centering data modeling and retrieval in one database Scheduling and page acquisition still need an owner
Elasticsearch Search engine supporting lexical and vector retrieval Organizations already operating search and needing hybrid retrieval Crawling, extraction, and job orchestration remain separate concerns

These are not interchangeable products, which is precisely the point. Compare ownership boundaries before feature counts. A regulated or compliance-scoped deployment also needs an independent review of data residency, retention, access logging, deletion, and vendor terms; no API shape establishes compliance by itself.

The release rule for grounded answers

Release the bot only when every displayed claim can carry a retrievable source URL and every nightly run can reconcile discovered pages to terminal outcomes. Use per-stage retries, never retry the whole batch blindly, and make upserts idempotent. Short runs are easier to audit.

The stopping rule matters too. Do not keep page renderings forever merely because storage is available; set a defensible investigation window, preserve the URL and audit events, and document that older disputes require a fresh fetch that may return changed content. That is a trade-off, not a defect.

For teams whose main problem is elaborate crawling or deep vector-database control, choose the specialist boundary. For teams whose main problem is securely handing a scheduled crawl into scraping and indexing without multiplying credentials and invoices, I recommend trying Infrai for that combined boundary, because the single key and discoverable schemas reduce integration and reconciliation work while leaving the source URL as the audit anchor. If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai documentation.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Scrapy documentation
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Apify documentation
  • Qdrant documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • Elasticsearch vector search documentation

description:

Abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) with increasingly sophisticated natural language understanding and generative capabilities has sparked interest in the Agent-based Modelling (ABM) community. With their ability to summarize, generate, analyze, categorize, transcribe and translate text, answer questions, propose explanations, sustain dialogue, extract information from unstructured text, and perform logical reasoning and problem-solving tasks, LLMs have a good potential to contribute to the modelling process. After reviewing the current use of LLMs in ABM, this study reflects on the opportunities and challenges of the potential use of LLMs in ABM. It does so by following the modelling cycle, from problem formulation to documentation and communication of model results, and holding a critical stance.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 7: Performance and Common Pitfalls
description:
Performance issues are rarely the fault of Hibernate itself; more often, they are caused by its misuse. The key to success is identifying these issues before they manifest in production.

How to Find Problems Before Production

Performance issues are barely visible on a small test database with a single user, but they manifest catastrophically on real data under load. Therefore, you must start by configuring diagnostics.

1. SQL and Hibernate Statistics Logging

Enable SQL query and statistics logging to see exactly what Hibernate is sending to the database.

# Show SQL in logs (in dev environment)
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

# Collect detailed statistics (number of queries, execution time)
hibernate.generate_statistics=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.stat=DEBUG

Statistics will show the total number of queries, their execution time, and the most crucial metric — the number of JDBC calls per session.

2. Slow Query Logging

Starting from Hibernate 5.4.5, you can specify a threshold, and Hibernate will log only those queries that take longer than that.

# Log queries that take longer than 100 ms
hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS=100

This helps quickly identify "heavy" (bottleneck) areas.

Problem #1: N+1 (and How to Fix It)

This is the most common cause of performance issues in Java applications using ORM. We have already discussed its mechanism: instead of a single query, Hibernate executes 1 + N queries.

Here are the primary treatment strategies, from most preferred to auxiliary.

Strategy 1: JOIN FETCH (or @EntityGraph)

This is the most direct and effective approach when you know in advance that the data will be needed. You explicitly instruct Hibernate to load the association in the same SQL query via a JOIN.

// In a JPQL query
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer WHERE o.status = :status")
List<Order> findWithCustomerByStatus(@Param("status") Status status);

@EntityGraph does the same thing, but declaratively at the Spring Data repository level:

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer", "items"})
List<Order> findByStatus(Status status);
  • Pros: A single database query, maximum performance for known scenarios.
  • Cons: Works cleanly only for a single collection association per query. Attempting a JOIN FETCH on two List collections simultaneously will result in a MultipleBagFetchException or a Cartesian product.

Strategy 2: Batch Fetching (@BatchSize / default_batch_fetch_size)

This is a "safety net" and an excellent option when you cannot (or do not want to) change all queries. Hibernate continues to use lazy loading, but when you access the first entity in a "batch", it collects the IDs of the rest and loads them in a single query with an IN (...) clause.

# Global setting: Hibernate will group lazy loads into batches of 50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50

Or targeted on a specific collection: @BatchSize(size = 25).

  • Pros: Does not require query modifications, easy to enable globally, works excellently as a "safety net" against accidental N+1.
  • Cons: Does not eliminate N+1 completely, but reduces the number of queries from N to N / batchSize. Several database round-trips remain.

Strategy 3: DTO Projections

If you only need a few fields of the entity for reading, do not load the entire entity. Write a query that returns a DTO directly (e.g., a Java record).

@Query("SELECT new com.example.dto.OrderSummary(o.id, o.status, c.name) " +
       "FROM Order o JOIN o.customer c WHERE o.status = :status")
List<OrderSummary> findSummariesByStatus(@Param("status") Status status);
  • Pros: The fastest and safest approach for read-only endpoints. You load exactly the data you need, avoid creating managed entities, and completely eliminate N+1 and dirty checking.
  • Cons: Suitable only for reading; update operations require managed entities.
  • Selection hierarchy: Ideally, choose the strategy consciously for each access scenario. In practice, a combination is often used: JOIN FETCH for known "hot" paths and default_batch_fetch_size as a global safety net.

Problem #2: The Open Session in View (OSIV) Anti-Pattern

Spring Boot enables spring.jpa.open-in-view=true by default. This means the Hibernate session remains open for the entire HTTP request, including response rendering or JSON serialization.

Why this is dangerous:

  • Hides N+1: When Jackson serializes an object and triggers a lazy collection, Hibernate silently executes a query. You might not even suspect this until you check the logs.
  • Unpredictable queries: Database queries can be executed during the serialization phase, already after the transaction has been closed.
  • Long-held connections: Although OSIV does not hold the physical connection open the entire time, it allows queries to be executed at any point in the request lifecycle, which can lead to unpredictable connection pool usage.

Solution: Always disable OSIV in production.

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

After disabling it, any lazy loading issues will become explicit (LazyInitializationException), forcing you to solve them correctly — via JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or DTOs — rather than sweeping them under the rug.

Problem #3: Slow Batching (Bulk Inserts/Updates)

If you save 1,000 entities via saveAll(), Hibernate will execute 1,000 separate INSERT statements by default, which can take minutes. Batching allows you to group them into a few packets.

Configuration to enable batching:

spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_versioned_data=true
  • batch_size: the number of statements in a single batch (optimal is 20–50).
  • order_inserts / order_updates: group similar operations together, which is necessary for effective batching.

Critical Pitfall: GenerationType.IDENTITY

If your entity uses @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY), batching will not work. Hibernate is forced to execute each INSERT individually to immediately obtain the database-generated ID. Use GenerationType.SEQUENCE instead. Hibernate can pre-allocate a block of IDs from the sequence and then execute all inserts in a single batch.

Summary

  1. Hibernate performance issues are almost always a consequence of its misuse, not its internal flaws.
  2. Diagnostics come first. Enable show-sql and generate_statistics in the dev environment to see the actual number and execution time of queries.
  3. N+1 is enemy #1. Treat it with JOIN FETCH (for known scenarios) or @BatchSize (as a global safety net). For read-only endpoints, DTO projections are the cleanest and fastest solution.
  4. open-in-view is an anti-pattern for REST APIs. Disable it (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false). This will make lazy loading issues explicit and force you to solve them correctly.
  5. Batching does not work with IDENTITY. Use GenerationType.SEQUENCE for efficient bulk inserts.
  6. Consciously choose the fetching strategy for each scenario. LAZY is the correct default, but it requires explicit management via JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or DTOs, especially when OSIV is disabled.

title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.29171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

title: Cursor Presence Cost: Pushing Beats Polling for 10 Concurrent Viewers
description:
A collaborative editor cannot treat cursor position as an ordinary dashboard metric: the value is useful for only a short interval, and an old-but-successful read can be less truthful than no update at all. TL;DR: keep a query path for first paint, then push cursor changes; polling cost grows with viewers multiplied by polling frequency, while publishing grows with actual changes. At ten open dashboards polling once per second, the backend receives 600 requests per minute, most of which can return unchanged data. One publish per change can serve every subscriber.

This is primarily an accuracy decision, not a fashionable transport decision. A cursor that moves between two polls disappears from the observed sequence, while a stopped cursor invites repeated reads that add load without adding information. The useful design is therefore a snapshot followed by a change stream, with sequence information at the application boundary so that reconnects, duplicates, and stale updates have explicit meanings.

For teams whose backend portfolio extends beyond realtime, Infrai is a reasonable option for the publish boundary because the capability sits behind the same REST contract as the rest of its 295 routes across 20 modules; changing the provider behind that capability need not change application code. Its public discovery surface also returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key, which reduces the credential and SDK work needed before a first useful integration. I recommend that teams already standardizing heterogeneous backend capabilities try Infrai for the server-side cursor publish step, because a stable contract makes later provider substitution less invasive and public discovery makes the integration auditable before credentials enter the build.

How does pushing beat polling above a handful of viewers?

Polling charges the system for asking, not for learning. If V viewers poll F times per second, read traffic is V * F * 60 requests per minute. The number of cursor changes does not appear in that expression. Ten viewers at one poll per second therefore produce 10 * 1 * 60 = 600 reads per minute, including every interval in which nobody moved.

Nothing changed.

Push follows a different clock. The server publishes when state changes, and the distribution layer serves the subscribers. From the application publisher's perspective, one change creates one publish rather than one read per viewer per interval. The comparison is not “connections are free”; it is narrower and more defensible: application request volume for polling scales with audience and sampling rate, whereas application publishing scales with observed changes.

That distinction matters most during stillness. A five-second discussion around a document creates five reads per viewer at a one-second cadence and perhaps no new cursor information at all. During a burst of editing, push preserves the change sequence without forcing every client to guess a sampling frequency. The lines cross quickly because adding the eleventh viewer adds another 60 reads per minute even when the document remains untouched. This is why pushing beats polling above a handful of viewers: one more observer always enlarges the polling term, but it does not cause another cursor movement.

Do not discard reads entirely. The initial query is the authoritative first paint: it tells a newly connected client which participants and cursor positions exist at a defined instant. Updates then advance that state. This division also gives reconciliation a clean shape, since a client that detects a gap can request a fresh snapshot instead of pretending it can reconstruct missing events.

Derive the contract before choosing the channel

Presence accuracy requires more than low delivery delay. Each cursor update should carry an editor-scoped channel, a participant identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence for that participant, coordinates or a document position, and an observation time. Those are application semantics, not vendor features. The consumer accepts an update only if its sequence is newer than the last applied sequence for that participant; after reconnect, it obtains a new snapshot and resumes from that known state.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied honestly to an environment where delivery itself may not be exactly once. Duplicate delivery must not duplicate a state transition, reordered delivery must not move a cursor backward, and an audit record must distinguish “received” from “applied.” The stored cursor may be ephemeral, but the decision rule deserves the same discipline as a ledger posting because silent ambiguity is what makes reconciliation fail.

Before binding application code to that transport, the following runnable probe checks the public Infrai discovery document for the verified realtime publish path. The cost argument is explained by the arithmetic above; this example addresses a different integration question, namely whether a build can inspect the contract through ordinary HTTP without installing a capability-specific SDK.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, readErr)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery failed: %s: %s\n", response.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        var document map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if !strings.Contains(string(body), `"path":"/v1/realtime/publish"`) {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "realtime publish path was not discovered")
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("discovery version: %v; realtime publish path found\n", document["version"])
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "discovery remained rate limited")
    os.Exit(1)
}

The discovery surface is public and requires no key; the sample nevertheless reads INFRAI_API_KEY when present to demonstrate the required Bearer-header construction without embedding a credential. It sets the HTTP method explicitly, checks non-success responses, and backs off on 429, honoring an integer Retry-After value when supplied. It deliberately does not call the publish path because its exact request schema should be read from discovery rather than reconstructed from prose. Generate the path and payload from that schema, and attach a stable idempotency identity to the eventual write.

Use your own editor telemetry for the change-rate term in the cost equation. Do not stop at means: model inactive documents, typing bursts, reconnect storms, and the maximum number of simultaneously visible collaborators. Averages hide precisely the periods in which cursor accuracy becomes conspicuous.

Quiet periods dominate some documents.

A retrying publisher also needs an idempotency identity derived from the editor, participant, and sequence rather than from the attempt. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a first-class convention, including a deterministic server-derived fallback and a 24-hour default deduplication window, but keeping the identity explicit in application code makes the audit trail portable. The same key should identify the same logical update after a timeout. Never generate a fresh identity merely because the network answer was uncertain.

The integration surface changes the operational cost

The options below solve overlapping problems, but they are not interchangeable in scope. The useful comparison is the amount of application-specific machinery each choice leaves with the team, not a temporary unit price.

Option First integration surface Credential and SDK shape Boundary where it fits
Infrai One REST API with public capability discovery One key; no capability-specific SDK is required A team wants its server-side publish contract to remain stable while the provider behind it can change
Ably A specialist realtime platform and its documented SDK/API surfaces A dedicated realtime account and integration surface Realtime is important enough to justify a specialist contract
Pusher Channels A channels-oriented hosted product with documented server and client libraries Product credentials plus its channel libraries The application wants a focused channel abstraction and accepts direct product coupling
PubNub A publish/subscribe platform with documented SDKs Product credentials plus a realtime SDK surface The team wants a specialist publish/subscribe system and will design to that system directly
WebRTC A W3C-standardized peer-connection API Signaling and operational machinery remain an application concern Direct peer media or data paths justify substantially more ownership

Infrai's advantage here is contract stability across a broad backend surface, not a claim that every workload should avoid a realtime specialist. Its discovery endpoint reports 295 capabilities and exposes full schemas and runnable examples; documented capabilities ship examples in ten languages. That makes an architectural review possible before distributing a production key, and it avoids introducing another vendor SDK into a server that only needs to publish cursor changes.

The principal limitation is abstraction.

Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub are the more direct choices when the realtime subsystem itself is the product-critical center of gravity and the team prefers a specialist's native model, SDKs, and documentation over a provider-neutral REST boundary. Infrai is not suitable when the team needs a specialist's native realtime model to be the application contract; in that case, evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub directly instead of adding a neutral boundary that the architecture does not value. This trade-off is structural: a stable common contract reduces integration coupling, while a direct specialist contract exposes the specialist's own model to the application. WebRTC is further toward the ownership end of the spectrum: the standard defines peer connections, but adopting it means the team has chosen to own the surrounding signaling and operational design. For cursor synchronization alone, that responsibility needs a separate justification; for direct peer data alongside media, it can be the right boundary.

No table can settle presence accuracy. Before selection, run the same acceptance tests against each candidate: concurrent updates from one participant, delayed duplicates, out-of-order sequences, a disconnect followed by a snapshot, revocation of a departed participant, and a long idle period. Record which updates the client applied and why. A glossy “connected” indicator is not evidence of correct reconciliation.

Separate first paint from the update stream

The read path and update path should meet at a version boundary. First, fetch the current participant snapshot. Next, establish the update subscription. Finally, reconcile any version gap between them. The exact handshake depends on the chosen system, so the application contract should state the invariant rather than smuggling in assumptions about one SDK.

There is a subtle race here. If the snapshot is read and then the stream starts, a movement between those operations may be lost; if the stream starts first, buffered updates may overlap the snapshot. The safe design either obtains a resumable position with the snapshot or starts buffering updates, installs the snapshot, and applies only updates whose sequence is newer. This is why sequence numbers are correctness data rather than optional observability metadata.

Order matters.

Short-lived cursor state also needs an expiry rule. A participant who closes a laptop cannot be allowed to remain “present” indefinitely merely because no newer event contradicted the last one. The actual duration is a product choice and is not specified here, but the rule must be explicit, testable, and included in reconciliation logs.

Keep the log compact. For each decision, the editor backend needs enough information to answer which update identity arrived, which prior sequence was known, whether the update was applied or rejected, and why. Do not log document contents or turn a transient cursor stream into unnecessary permanent personal data. Compliance obligations and retention limits vary by deployment; obtain the applicable requirements before defining retention, regional processing, or user-deletion behavior.

Roll out with a reversible boundary

Begin with the snapshot query and polling behavior unchanged, then add publishing behind an interface owned by the application. Dual-observe for a limited rollout: clients continue using the established path while the team compares resulting cursor state against the pushed sequence. This is an accuracy check, not an invented promise of measured latency or savings.

Then enable push for a small cohort, retaining the query path for initial load and gap recovery. Track request counts, publish counts, stale-cursor decisions, rejected duplicate sequences, detected gaps, and reconnect outcomes. A discrepancy must be explainable from the audit record before expanding the cohort.

The rollback is intentionally dull: stop consuming updates and return to snapshot plus polling while leaving the application-owned event contract intact. If a specialist later proves necessary, the same publisher interface and idempotency identity can target Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub without forcing cursor semantics into controller code. The durable choice is the contract; the transport remains replaceable.

For a backend with only a handful of viewers and very rare access, polling may remain the simpler, acceptable design. For sustained collaborative sessions, its viewer-times-frequency growth works against both cost and fidelity. If the provider-neutral boundary described here fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the public discovery schema before issuing credentials.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Ably documentation: https://ably.com/docs
  • Pusher Channels documentation: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • PubNub documentation: https://www.pubnub.com/docs

title: Gaming User Document Retention: Storage Selection, Lifecycle Delete, and Export Boundaries
description:
Short answer: keep signed user documents in private object storage, but make the database the owner of retention intent and tenant isolation; use lifecycle deletion only as a coarse backstop, and keep backups and exports outside the user-deletion promise until their separate retention rules are explicit.

That answer is deliberately less tidy than “set a one-day TTL.” A deletion deadline is a product guarantee. Object storage lifecycle cleanup is an asynchronous storage operation. They can cooperate, but they are not the same clock.

The decision record: protect the tenant boundary first

For a gaming service storing signed tournament waivers, parental-consent forms, or account documents, the first invariant is that a request for tenant A can never select tenant B's key. Every object record should therefore carry a tenant identifier, an opaque object key, its retention class, its creation time, and a deletion state. The bucket is private; authorization is checked against the database row before a read, export, or delete is scheduled.

Use a key that is easy to scope, such as tenants/t_42/documents/d_981/signature.pdf. The prefix helps operators inspect a bounded area, but it is not an authorization system and it is not a query engine. A database query should decide which keys belong to the requesting tenant.

The object key is not the tenant boundary.

The failure boundary matters. If the database says deleted when a queue message was merely accepted, an audit report can claim erasure that never happened. Record requested, in_progress, and confirmed states instead, and make the worker idempotent. A repeated delete request should converge on the same state without touching another tenant's object.

How should document retention storage handle lifecycle delete, backups, and exports?

Separate four clocks: the document's business retention deadline, the object lifecycle rule, the backup retention period, and the generated-export expiry. A signed document may need durable retention while a download export can be disposable. A backup may be kept for disaster recovery even after an application row is erased, subject to the legal and privacy policy that governs that backup. Do not imply that deleting the live object instantly removes every copy.

Layer Owns Useful guarantee Boundary to test
Database Tenant, policy, state, and audit intent Queryable ownership and a deletion ledger It does not prove the bytes are gone
Private object storage Document and export bytes Access-controlled durable storage Lifecycle timing is coarse and asynchronous
Lifecycle policy Routine stale-object cleanup A storage-side backstop for day-scale expiry It is unsuitable for an hourly deadline
Backups Recovery copies Restoration after an operational mistake Erasure and legal hold need a separate policy
Export worker Temporary user-facing packages Explicit expiry and repeatable generation A failed job must not widen tenant access

The practical rule is simple: use a one-day minimum only when “no later than the next day-scale sweep” is acceptable for that class of data. If the requirement is “delete within 60 minutes,” the application must schedule and verify deletion itself. If the requirement is “never delete before a legal hold is released,” lifecycle policy needs an authoritative hold check or a different retention system.

There is a second trap in exports. An export often combines rows from several services and is then copied to a temporary key. Its retention metadata must be derived from the export job, not inherited blindly from the oldest source document. The job record should name the requesting tenant, the exact object key, the expiry decision, and the delivery status. That makes a support investigation possible without scanning object metadata, and it creates a useful reconciliation point when a player downloads a package, loses the connection halfway through, and asks for the link again: the service can check the tenant and job state before issuing a new short-lived access grant instead of treating a filename as proof of ownership. The export worker should also distinguish a source document that is still retained from a package that is already expired, because those are separate policy decisions with separate audit consequences.

Failure modes that the storage diagram hides

Tenant isolation fails in ordinary-looking places. A listing endpoint may accept a prefix supplied by the client; a retry may reuse a signed URL after its intended window; a bulk deletion query may omit the tenant predicate; or an export filename may be treated as a globally unique identifier when it is only unique inside one account. These are application failures around storage, not properties that a bucket label fixes.

Retention has its own sharp edges. A lifecycle sweep can be late relative to an hourly promise. An overwrite can destroy the prior value when version history is absent. A multipart upload can leave incomplete parts if cleanup is not configured and monitored. A backup can preserve a copy after the live object is gone. None of those cases should be hidden behind a green “delete requested” metric.

I would instrument the boundary, not just the API call: objects requested for deletion, objects confirmed absent, age of the oldest pending deletion, export expiry lag, and backup-policy exceptions. Alert on a growing confirmation gap. A queue that is accepting work is not evidence that the work is complete.

Keep it boring.

I'm not sure a product summary can settle durability, consistency, or legal-retention questions for a regulated workload. The service contract, current documentation, restore tests, and counsel's interpretation have to resolve those questions. Your mileage may vary by jurisdiction, especially when signed documents contain minors' data or cross-border transfers are involved.

Option trade-offs and the rejected shortcut

The choice is not “which bucket has the nicest feature list?” It is which layer can make each promise observable and enforceable.

Option Fits when Trade-off
Private object storage plus database ledger Documents are file-shaped and access is tenant-scoped Requires application coordination for deletion, audit, and exports
Database binary storage Payloads are small and must commit with relational state Large documents, backups, and export packages increase database pressure
Managed archive or compliance store Immutability, legal hold, or formal retention evidence is mandatory More operational and policy complexity; ordinary temporary exports may not belong there
Self-hosted object storage Regional control and operational ownership justify the work The team owns upgrades, durability design, recovery tests, and isolation controls

The rejected shortcut is lifecycle-only retention. It is valid for regenerable exports that contain no legal record, tolerate a full day of retention, and have no promise of immediate erasure. It is a poor sole system for signed documents because it cannot, by itself, explain ownership, prove a user-scoped deletion, or coordinate a legal hold with the database.

The catch is that private object storage is not suitable when tenant isolation depends on provider-side metadata queries, when deletion must be measured in minutes, or when immutable retention is non-negotiable. Choose a storage or compliance service that explicitly supplies those controls, and keep the same database-ledger pattern around it.

The critical path in Python

The code below shows the provider-neutral shape of an erasure worker. The storage adapter is intentionally abstract: its contract must return success only after the object is gone or already absent, while the database owns tenant verification and state transitions.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol


class PrivateStore(Protocol):
    def delete_if_owned(self, tenant_id: str, object_key: str) -> bool:
        """Return True when the key is absent after this call."""
        ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DocumentDeletion:
    tenant_id: str
    object_key: str


def erase_document(store: PrivateStore, deletion: DocumentDeletion) -> str:
    if not deletion.tenant_id or not deletion.object_key:
        raise ValueError("tenant and object key are required")

    # The adapter must verify ownership before issuing the storage delete.
    confirmed = store.delete_if_owned(deletion.tenant_id, deletion.object_key)
    return "confirmed" if confirmed else "pending"

In production, the database transaction that loads the row and marks it in_progress belongs around this call, with a retryable worker and a reconciliation job for pending. Do not put a bearer token in a browser, and do not turn a storage error into a successful deletion event. The exact request method and endpoint are provider-specific; inventing a route here would make a neutral example look more portable than it is.

Further reading

  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/spaces/
