title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
description:
arXiv:2610.28943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose
description:
arXiv:2610.29318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.

title: Near-Duplicate Support Tickets 2026: Go Vector Threshold Review
description:
At 03:07, the page says that answers over the logistics support archive have started citing the same incident repeatedly. The on-call opens one trace and sees three PDF tickets about a delayed container, all admitted as separate evidence even though two are near copies created by an email export. The least complex useful response is a similarity gate with three outcomes: accept a clearly new ticket, suppress a clear duplicate, and send the uncertain middle to review. Do not turn one similarity threshold into an automatic delete button.

TL;DR: normalize and embed each ticket with the same pipeline, search only within an operationally meaningful candidate set, and treat similarity as a ranking signal rather than truth. Keep both sides of every decision, the model and preprocessing version, the score, the chosen boundary, and the reviewer outcome. Page on user-visible retrieval damage or sustained decision drift, not on a lone high score.

This matters before generation. Retrieval-augmented generation combines retrieved external material with generation; if duplicated tickets occupy several retrieval slots, the evidence presented downstream is narrower than the result count implies. The pager should therefore fire on the consequence: repeated evidence, missing distinct incidents, or a review queue that can no longer meet its service objective.

Quiet is not healthy.

What should have fired before the answer repeated itself?

The earlier signal is a change in the gate's decisions, segmented by the dimensions that can alter ticket language: carrier, route, document template, language, and ingestion version. A global average can stay calm while one newly deployed PDF template strips spaces or repeats headers, moving an entire cohort across the review boundary. Dashboards are weak evidence here. I want the page to name the affected cohort, the first bad deployment or corpus window, and a few decision identifiers that can be replayed without exposing ticket text.

A useful event is compact but reconstructable. Record a content hash for exact-copy handling, stable identifiers for the candidate pair, the embedding and normalizer versions, similarity, gate outcome, and timestamp. Keep the raw PDFs under the archive's existing access and retention controls; telemetry does not need their contents. Exact hashes catch byte-identical exports cheaply, while vector similarity handles paraphrases and formatting changes. Those are different mechanisms and should have separate counters.

Track the distribution, not merely the mean. Counts entering new, review, and duplicate, plus reviewer reversals for each outcome, expose a threshold that has drifted. A rise in duplicate decisions may be legitimate after a bulk import. The same rise paired with reviewers repeatedly splitting those pairs is evidence of bad suppression.

How should Go dedupe near-duplicate support tickets for review?

Cosine similarity for nonzero vectors is the dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes. Higher scores mean the representations point in a more similar direction; they do not prove that two tickets describe the same operational event. Two reports can share every phrase about a delayed shipment yet refer to different containers, days, or customers. Conversely, an update may add a resolution while still belonging to the original incident.

No score proves identity.

The gate below uses explicit lower and upper boundaries. It assumes the vectors were produced by one pinned embedding pipeline and rejects dimension mismatches and zero vectors instead of manufacturing a score. The policy compares a new ticket only with candidates selected by metadata such as tenant and a bounded event window; comparing every shipment with the entire archive creates plausible but operationally irrelevant neighbors.

package dedupe

import (
    "errors"
    "math"
)

type Decision string

const (
    New       Decision = "new"
    Review    Decision = "review"
    Duplicate Decision = "duplicate"
)

type Policy struct {
    ReviewAt    float64
    DuplicateAt float64
}

func Cosine(a, b []float64) (float64, error) {
    if len(a) == 0 || len(a) != len(b) {
        return 0, errors.New("vectors must have equal, nonzero dimensions")
    }

    var dot, aa, bb float64
    for i := range a {
        dot += a[i] * b[i]
        aa += a[i] * a[i]
        bb += b[i] * b[i]
    }
    if aa == 0 || bb == 0 {
        return 0, errors.New("cosine is undefined for a zero vector")
    }
    return dot / (math.Sqrt(aa) * math.Sqrt(bb)), nil
}

func (p Policy) Decide(score float64) (Decision, error) {
    if p.ReviewAt < -1 || p.DuplicateAt > 1 || p.ReviewAt >= p.DuplicateAt {
        return "", errors.New("invalid policy boundaries")
    }
    switch {
    case score >= p.DuplicateAt:
        return Duplicate, nil
    case score >= p.ReviewAt:
        return Review, nil
    default:
        return New, nil
    }
}

There are deliberately no universal numbers in that policy. A copied subject line, boilerplate carrier disclaimer, or OCR artifact can change the score distribution, as can any change to chunking or embeddings. Boundaries belong in versioned configuration and must come from labeled pairs that resemble current traffic. The upper boundary should reflect the cost of hiding a distinct logistics incident; the lower one should reflect the cost and capacity of human review.

This approach has limits. It is not suitable as the sole decision mechanism when regulations or contractual controls require a human to preserve every report, when the archive is too small to produce representative labeled pairs, or when exact business identifiers already determine identity without ambiguity. In those cases, deterministic matching or mandatory review is the better boundary. The trade-off is plain: a wider review band protects recall but spends analyst time and delays indexing, while a narrow band lowers latency by accepting more classification risk.

Do not compare isolated chunks and then discard the document relationship. A PDF header can be nearly identical across thousands of tickets. Build the decision from ticket-level evidence, preserve identifiers such as shipment or case references as structured features, and give reviewers both complete documents with the matching passages highlighted. A vector match proposes a case; an auditable workflow decides it.

Calibrate with incidents, not convenient examples

Start with labeled pairs sampled from the same path production will use. Include exact exports, paraphrased reports, follow-up messages, shared templates, OCR damage, and hard negatives: similar wording attached to distinct shipment identifiers. Split calibration and evaluation by time or incident group so revisions of one ticket do not leak into both sides and make the gate look cleaner than it is.

Then sweep candidate boundaries and count operational errors. A false duplicate can remove the only evidence of a separate lost shipment. A false new decision consumes index space and may crowd retrieval results. A review decision costs analyst attention and adds latency. Those costs are asymmetric, so a single aggregate accuracy number cannot choose the policy.

Use a replay set when the normalizer, PDF extraction, chunk construction, or embedding version changes. Run the proposed pipeline beside the current one, compare transitions among all three outcomes, and inspect the pairs that cross a boundary. Deploy the decision version with the indexed vectors; mixing new queries with old vectors produces a test you did not design. If either pipeline cannot reproduce its own stored decision from the retained inputs and version metadata, rollback and replay are guesses.

The review interface needs two distinct actions: confirm the same incident, or keep both and record why. That reason can become a future evaluation slice, for example same_template_different_container. Reviewers also need an escape hatch for linked but nonduplicate tickets, because a follow-up report may be valuable retrieval evidence even when it belongs to the same incident family.

Keep both.

Instrument the action path

After the noisy page, add instrumentation where a decision changes the corpus, not only where similarity is computed. The trace should connect PDF ingestion, exact-hash lookup, candidate selection, vector scoring, gate outcome, reviewer action, index mutation, and the retrieval result that later feeds an answer. One correlation identifier across those stages lets the on-call move backward from a repeated citation to the exact gate decision.

The service should fail closed around irreversible actions. A vector timeout can route a ticket to retry or review; it should not silently label the ticket new or duplicate. Invalid vectors and mismatched versions are errors. Queue age deserves an alert when it threatens the promised review latency, while individual review-band matches are normal work and should not wake anyone.

A compact operational record might look like this:

type GateEvent struct {
    DecisionID        string
    IncomingTicketID  string
    CandidateID       string
    ContentHashMatch  bool
    NormalizerVersion string
    EmbeddingVersion  string
    Similarity        float64
    Outcome           Decision
    ReviewedOutcome   Decision
}

Keep metric labels bounded. Ticket IDs belong in trace events or protected logs, not metric dimensions. Metrics can safely aggregate by policy version, outcome, source format, and a controlled cohort vocabulary. The page then links to sampled decision IDs, while the chart remains usable under load.

The decisive checks are end to end: the proportion of retrieved results occupied by one duplicate family, distinct incident coverage in a labeled query set, reviewer reversal rates, and review age. Generation quality cannot repair missing evidence. If deduplication suppresses a distinct ticket before retrieval, the answerer never sees it.

The threshold can create its own incident

Move the upper boundary downward and apparent duplicate removal rises, but so does the chance of hiding separate events that happen to use the same logistics template. Move it upward and reviewers or retrieval results absorb more copies. Widen the middle band and decision quality may improve while latency grows. There is no free setting.

For rollout, shadow the new policy, inspect boundary crossings, then canary it on a defined cohort with a rollback condition tied to reviewer reversals and retrieval coverage. Preserve suppressed documents rather than deleting them, and make the index mutation idempotent so replaying a decision does not create another copy. The runbook should say which decision version to disable, how to drain pending reviews, and how to restore suppressed ticket references.

The false-positive cost deserves the final word. An aggressive threshold can make a quiet dashboard by erasing the disagreement that should have reached a human, and in logistics that disagreement may be the difference between two similar complaints and two separate shipments needing action. A useful page fires when the system is losing distinct evidence or cannot process uncertainty in time. Everything else is a graph to inspect after breakfast.

Pages need consequences.

Further reading

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: Node.js GDPR Log Retention: 4 Boundaries to Delete User Data Safely
description:
A nightly media pipeline needs searchable failure evidence, but replay and rollback can quietly restore data that an erasure job already removed. That constraint changes the design: keep direct user identifiers out of application logs, separate the lookup needed for erasure from the log records, and make deletion state survive every rollback.

TL;DR: Treat log retention and user-data erasure as two different controls. Retention limits how long records exist. Erasure handles records that must disappear sooner. In Node.js, emit a versioned pseudonymous subject token, keep the reversible mapping outside the log system, delete that mapping and matching records through an auditable job, then test that a rollback cannot revive either one.

This is less convenient than logging an email address. Good. Convenience is how identifiers leak into exception strings, queue payloads, and copied debug fields.

How should GDPR log retention handle deleted user data?

The GDPR question is often phrased as a retention-period question: how long should application logs stay searchable, and how does the right to be forgotten apply? For an EU startup, the sharper operational question is where user data can return from after a valid erasure request. The log index is rarely the only copy. A media pipeline may read a nightly manifest, enqueue transformations, retry failed items, export an archive, and retain a replay input. Deleting a user's indexed events while leaving their identifier in any replayable input means the next run can emit the same data again. Good logging practices therefore start before retention: minimize fields at ingress, preserve a narrow lookup path for deletion, and enumerate every store or replay source that can reproduce an event. The legal basis, scope, exceptions, and response duties need qualified review for the actual service; an engineering design cannot decide those questions. It can make the resulting policy enforceable and testable.

The failure is temporal. Deployment version 42 removes a mapping and scrubs current records. A rollback to version 41 restores code that still logs raw ownerEmail, while an old queue message waits for retry. The software rollback worked; the privacy operation did not.

That is the risk.

Deletion state must move forward even when application code moves backward. Put tombstones and schema compatibility outside the application release artifact. An older release must either understand the current privacy envelope or refuse to process it. Never let it guess.

For the media pipeline, I would define four boundaries:

  1. Ingress replaces the account identifier with a scoped subject token before work reaches the queue.
  2. Workers log an allowlisted event shape, not arbitrary request objects or media metadata.
  3. Search storage and cold archives share an erasure manifest, including completion status.
  4. Replay checks the tombstone set before reading historical input or emitting fresh events.

Four is not a universal number. It is the smallest useful model for this pipeline because each boundary owns a different way deleted data can return. Schema version 2 in the example is also a local contract, not an industry standard.

Build the smallest logging surface

Start with types. A logger that accepts Record<string, unknown> is quick to ship and expensive to police. It lets every caller invent fields, so deletion becomes a hunt through unknown shapes.

The following TypeScript keeps the useful operational dimensions: pipeline run, stage, outcome, duration, and a scoped subject token. It deliberately omits filenames, URLs, free-form exception messages, and media captions. Those values can contain user data even when their field names look harmless.

import { createHash, randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type PipelineStage = "ingest" | "transcode" | "index" | "publish";
type Outcome = "ok" | "retry" | "failed";

type PipelineEvent = Readonly<{
  schemaVersion: 2;
  eventId: string;
  occurredAt: string;
  runId: string;
  subjectToken: string;
  stage: PipelineStage;
  outcome: Outcome;
  durationMs: number;
  errorCode?: string;
}>;

const subjectToken = (tenantId: string, userId: string, secret: string): string =>
  createHash("sha256")
    .update(`${secret}:${tenantId}:${userId}`)
    .digest("hex");

export function pipelineEvent(
  input: Omit<PipelineEvent, "schemaVersion" | "eventId" | "occurredAt">
): PipelineEvent {
  return {
    schemaVersion: 2,
    eventId: randomUUID(),
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    ...input,
  };
}

Hashing is not deletion, and a plain hash of a predictable user ID is weak pseudonymization. The secret scopes the token, while a separately controlled mapping or derivation-key lifecycle provides the erasure handle. The token remains personal data whenever it can still be linked back to a person, so do not treat this transform as an exemption from privacy controls.

Keep errors boring. Map known failures to stable codes such as SOURCE_UNREADABLE or TRANSCODE_TIMEOUT; send the original exception to a restricted diagnostic path only after applying the same field policy. A stack trace can carry request values. A generic serializer cannot know which substring matters.

Make erasure a state machine, not a delete button

A one-shot delete call gives weak evidence. The worker can time out after removing hot records but before updating an archive. Retrying must be safe, and operators need to distinguish “accepted” from “complete.”

I use an explicit state transition in the design, even if the first implementation has only one storage backend:

type ErasureState =
  | { status: "requested"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "tombstoned"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "purging"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string }
  | { status: "verified"; subjectToken: string; requestId: string };

interface LogStore {
  deleteBySubject(token: string): Promise<void>;
  countBySubject(token: string): Promise<number>;
}

async function purgeAndVerify(
  state: Extract<ErasureState, { status: "tombstoned" }>,
  stores: readonly LogStore[]
): Promise<ErasureState> {
  for (const store of stores) await store.deleteBySubject(state.subjectToken);

  const remaining = await Promise.all(
    stores.map((store) => store.countBySubject(state.subjectToken))
  );
  if (remaining.some((count) => count !== 0)) {
    return { ...state, status: "purging" };
  }

  return { ...state, status: "verified" };
}

Do not log the erasure request's raw identity from this code. Record its opaque request ID, state transition, policy version, and target-store result in a separate audit stream with its own access rules. Otherwise the mechanism designed to remove an identifier writes a new copy of it.

Retention still matters. It caps exposure and storage volume, but one global duration is usually a blunt instrument. Set periods by event class and documented purpose, then apply the shortest period that still supports the job. Security audit events, pipeline performance samples, and content-level diagnostics do not need identical fields or lifetimes.

The limitation is search fidelity. Removing free-form context makes novel failures slower to investigate, tokenization adds key-management work, and full-store verification can delay completion. This approach is not suitable when a team cannot inventory every replay source or keep old workers compatible with new tombstones; in that state, pause historical replay until the lifecycle is controlled. That is an explicit availability trade-off, not a hidden promise. It also does not determine which records a particular GDPR request legally requires a controller to erase. Policy owners must supply that decision, and the implementation must encode it without broadening the data collected.

Sampling does not solve this problem either. Head sampling decides before an operation completes; tail sampling can decide after observing more of the trace. Both reduce retained telemetry, but neither guarantees that a particular person's records were excluded or erased. Use sampling for signal volume. Use minimization, retention, and erasure for data lifecycle.

Test the rollback, not just the happy path

The valuable test begins after deletion. Seed two subjects across the live index, archive, retry queue, and replay input. Erase one. Then deploy the previous compatible worker version, replay the old batch, and assert three things: the erased token has zero searchable records, no new record is emitted for it, and the other subject remains searchable.

Fail closed on unknown schemas. If version 41 cannot interpret a version 42 tombstone, the queue item should park for review instead of running through legacy logging code. This costs availability for a narrow class of replay. I take that trade because a delayed media job is recoverable; resurrected personal data is much harder to contain.

Benchmark the controls separately. Measure ingestion overhead from tokenization, erasure completion latency across every store, replay throughput with tombstone checks, and query usefulness after fields are removed. Publish the test fixture and percentile method internally. A single average hides the exact tail where nightly batches and deletion jobs collide.

There is one nasty edge: key rotation. If token derivation changes without a version marker, the erasure job may search for today's token while old logs contain yesterday's token. Include a non-secret token version in the schema and retain only the key material needed by the active erasure window. Test every supported version.

What I would change at scale

At small volume, synchronous deletion across a few stores is understandable and easy to verify. At larger volume, use a durable erasure manifest, idempotent workers per storage class, and a final verifier that cannot mark completion until all required targets report zero matches. Partition work, but preserve one request-level state machine.

I would also move from per-event tombstone lookups to a local, frequently refreshed deny set with a strict freshness budget. That improves replay throughput, but introduces a delay between a request and enforcement at each worker. The acceptable budget is a policy decision, not a cache default.

Search quality will drop when raw filenames, URLs, and messages disappear. Compensate with stable enums and bounded dimensions, not a larger bag of strings. For this pipeline, stage, outcome, errorCode, runId, and duration buckets answer the operational questions without turning the index into a shadow user database.

The decision rule stays plain: a release is rollback-safe only when older compatible code cannot recreate erased telemetry from queues, archives, or replay inputs. Verify that property before optimizing ingestion or search. No dashboard can repair a broken lifecycle.

Sources and References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Sampling”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/

title: How to launch an 8-GPU RTX PRO 6000 instance on EcoHash
description:
An eight-GPU instance in EcoHash's Atlanta region gives you a whole node: eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with 96 GB of VRAM each, 200 vCPUs, 1,352 GB of RAM, and up to 5,260 GiB of temporary local scratch space. You can start with an EcoHash container image or bring the stack you already use.

This walkthrough covers the choices that matter before you launch, how to connect afterward, and where to put files you need to keep. Open GPU Instances in the console to follow along. You will need an account with enough credit for the configuration you select.

Choose Atlanta and all eight GPUs

Click Launch Instance, give the instance a name, and select atl for Atlanta. Under GPUs per Instance, choose 8x.

The configuration summary now shows the whole node dedicated to this instance. The eight GPUs provide 768 GB of total VRAM, with 96 GB on each GPU. That is memory distributed across eight devices; your serving or training software must support using multiple GPUs to take advantage of it.

Selecting eight GPUs allocates the whole node. Check the resource summary for your chosen region.

Pick a container for the work you want to run

The EcoHash Images tab offers several starting points. Their names include the installed software versions, so check the dropdown rather than relying on a tag from an old tutorial.

Use the inference image for vLLM, Jupyter for notebooks, or a base image for your own stack.

  • GPU Inference: vLLM configured for the RTX PRO 6000. This is the starting point for serving an LLM. It is a large image, so the first launch on a node may spend several minutes downloading it.
  • GPU Base: a CUDA and PyTorch environment for installing your own software. Choose the CUDA version your workload needs.
  • CUDA Bare: a CUDA 13.0 image without a framework, for building your environment from a smaller starting point.
  • GPU Jupyter: JupyterLab and an ML environment for browser-based notebook work.

The optional Startup Command runs when the instance starts. Use it to launch your application or model server. If you leave it blank, the image's default command applies. Make sure that command keeps the container running.

Bringing your own image

Open Images under Registry and click Add Image. Enter a display name and the full image reference, including its tag. For example, registry.example.com/team/eval:v1.0 is the format; replace it with your real registry and image.

A public image needs only its reference. Private images also need credentials with pull access.

For a private registry, provide its username and a read/pull access token. The form displays guidance for the registry you enter. AWS ECR login tokens expire after 12 hours and cannot be saved for this workflow; use a public ECR repository or arrange for EcoHash's account to have pull access.

Before saving the image, check these requirements:

  • Architecture: build for linux/amd64. On an Apple Silicon Mac, include --platform linux/amd64 in your docker buildx build command.
  • CUDA: use CUDA 13.0 or earlier for the configuration described here.
  • GPU support: your framework and CUDA extensions must support Blackwell sm_120. Check the specific build you are using, especially if you compile extensions yourself.
  • SSH: EcoHash configures SSH automatically for Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine-based images. Include OpenSSH yourself for other base distributions.

Save the image, return to the launch form, and select it under Custom / Registry.

Set up SSH and an HTTP endpoint

Enable SSH access and add your public SSH key in the launch form. Keys are applied when the instance starts, so do this before launching. Keep the matching private key on your own computer.

If you want to call a model server or another HTTP application, enable Expose a public service URL and enter the port your application listens on inside the container, such as 8000.

The endpoint forwards to the HTTP port inside your container.

Your application must listen on 0.0.0.0, not only on 127.0.0.1. A process bound to localhost can run normally inside the container while remaining unreachable through the public URL.

Choose the runtime and attach storage

Select No end time if you want the instance to run until you terminate it. The form explains the credit hold and hourly deductions. This setting does not keep an instance running after the account runs out of credit.

Alternatively, choose a fixed estimated duration if you want an automatic end time. Read the billing summary before launching; it changes with the number of GPUs and the duration you select.

Attach persistent storage before starting work you need to keep.

A cloud drive attaches to one instance at a time. A shared filesystem can be attached to several instances. Both are retained after the compute instance ends. Choose a cloud drive for files used by this instance, or a shared filesystem when several instances need the same datasets, weights, or results.

Treat /workspace as temporary. Its local scratch data is erased when the instance ends, including when it stops because your account balance runs out. Write results you need to keep to an attached cloud drive or shared filesystem.

Review the GPU count, image, SSH keys, service port, duration, and storage attachments. Then click Launch. Allow extra time for the first download of a large container image.

Connect and check your application

Once the instance is running, its detail page shows the SSH command, the public URL if you enabled one, and a web terminal you can open in the browser. Copy the SSH command from that page rather than constructing the hostname or port yourself.

In the terminal, run:

nvidia-smi

For this configuration, the output should list eight RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Check that your application can see all eight before starting a long job.

The public URL requires your console login or an EcoHash API key. To call it from a script, send the key in an Authorization: Bearer header. Paths after /service pass through to your application: /service/v1/models reaches the container as /v1/models.

For a vLLM server exposing that route, copy the instance's public URL and test it with:

export ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL="https://api.ecohash.com/gpu-instances/INSTANCE_ID/service"
# Set ECOHASH_API_KEY in your environment before running this request.
curl --fail-with-body "${ECOHASH_SERVICE_URL%/}/v1/models" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ECOHASH_API_KEY}"

Replace INSTANCE_ID with your instance ID, or use the full URL copied from the console. A ready vLLM server should return a model list. For another application, use one of its own HTTP routes instead.

If the request fails, check that the application has finished starting, listens on 0.0.0.0, and uses the same port you entered in the console. Also confirm that your request includes a valid API key.

Before ending the session, confirm that your outputs are on persistent storage. Terminate the instance when you are finished to stop compute charges.

Open GPU Instances to configure a node, or read more about launching an instance and container images.

title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
description:
arXiv:2610.28898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\omega+1,1+\sqrt{T\Omega}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $\Omega$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\mu+1,1+T^{1/3}V_\mu^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_\mu=\sum_t W_2(\mu_{t+1},\mu_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.

title: A Guide to Realtime APIs — Node.js Connection Recovery for Sports Feeds
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API for live delivery, but make the durable score store and a cursor-based backfill endpoint the authority after every reconnect. A serverless function should publish events and issue access, not hold an open connection for the lifetime of a match.

That boundary matters in a B2B sports operations product. The score feed is durable business state. Typing indicators are disposable presence signals. Read receipts sit between them: useful across a reconnect, but rarely important enough to block a score correction. Treating all three as the same kind of event makes recovery harder than it needs to be.

For a small team, Infrai is worth trying for the publish side of this workflow when plain HTTP is the desired integration boundary. It exposes a REST API, so a Node.js function can call it without installing or maintaining a vendor client library. Infrai also uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. In this sports product, adding a related backend capability can reuse the existing credential and billing boundary instead of creating another secret-distribution path or another invoice-reconciliation job. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, which lets a build check read the current request and response schemas before a deployment instead of relying on a stale hand-copied payload.

How should a Node.js sports score feed handle realtime serverless connection limits?

Start by separating connection ownership from event production. Browsers or another long-lived client connect to the realtime provider. A serverless function validates an upstream change, commits the new scoreboard state, and makes a short outbound publish request. It can finish immediately; it doesn't pretend to be a socket host.

The durable record needs a stable match ID, an event ID, and an ordered recovery cursor generated by your own application. Those are design requirements for the score system, not claims about a provider's payload schema. A returning client sends its last cursor to your backfill endpoint, applies every missing durable event, and only then resumes live updates. If a live event arrives during backfill, hold it briefly and reconcile by ID. Duplicates become boring.

Use a different policy for collaboration signals. A typing indicator can expire and disappear; replaying “Alex is typing” ten seconds later is actively misleading. A read receipt should carry a stable application identifier so the client can collapse repeats, but the UI can update it after the critical score state is current. Authentication, subscription state, and business events should be visible as separate stages in logs and traces. Otherwise a denied subscription can look exactly like an idle match.

This is the key split: realtime transport reduces freshness delay, while backfill restores truth.

Put the publish boundary in one small function

The minimal Infrai integration below calls the verified POST /v1/realtime/publish route. The exact request schema is intentionally not guessed: put a payload validated against the public discovery schema in INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD. That keeps this example runnable while leaving channel and event fields to the current schema rather than freezing an invented shape into application code.

The idempotency key should be derived from the stable application event ID and reused for every retry. The sample also gives a 429 response breathing room, honors Retry-After, and surfaces any other non-success body. It uses Node's built-in fetch, so there is no realtime SDK version to babysit.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const eventId = process.env.SCORE_EVENT_ID;
const rawPayload = process.env.INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD;

if (!apiKey || !eventId || !rawPayload) {
  throw new Error(
    "Set INFRAI_API_KEY, SCORE_EVENT_ID, and INFRAI_PUBLISH_PAYLOAD",
  );
}

const payload: unknown = JSON.parse(rawPayload);
const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const value = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (!value) return 500 * 2 ** attempt;

  const seconds = Number(value);
  if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);

  const date = Date.parse(value);
  return Number.isNaN(date) ? 500 * 2 ** attempt : Math.max(0, date - Date.now());
}

async function publishScoreEvent(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": eventId,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      await sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Publish failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }

    return body ? JSON.parse(body) : null;
  }

  throw new Error("Publish retry budget exhausted");
}

publishScoreEvent()
  .then((result) => process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`))
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    process.stderr.write(`${error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}\n`);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

Keep database commit and publication as two observable steps. If an execution ends after the commit but before publication, an outbox worker can retry the same event ID; the fixed idempotency key prevents a retry from double-applying at the publish boundary. The client still deduplicates because delivery and processing are separate concerns. This sounds fussy until a score correction, a reconnect, and a repeated event occur within the same few seconds. Then it is the whole system.

Don't publish before the authoritative write. A subscriber could display a score that the recovery API cannot return yet, leaving a reconnect to move the UI backward. The safer sequence is validate, commit, enqueue or record the outbox item, publish, and mark that item complete. Exact transaction machinery depends on the database and queue already in the stack; I'm not sure there is one right choice without knowing those constraints.

Compare the boundary, not the demo

Most realtime demos look convincing on one laptop. The useful comparison is less glamorous: who owns the socket, where history lives, how authorization is refreshed, and what a client does with duplicate delivery. Provider choice follows from that boundary.

Option Sensible fit Boundary to verify before committing
Infrai A serverless publisher that benefits from a plain HTTP surface and no required client SDK Validate the current publish request schema through discovery; keep durable history and recovery cursors in the application
Ably A team evaluating a specialist managed realtime product Confirm connection, history, ordering, and token-renewal semantics against the product's current documentation
Pusher Channels A product already designed around the Channels ecosystem Confirm reconnect behavior, authorization flow, and retained-history expectations for the selected plan
Supabase Realtime A team whose data and access model already live in Supabase Confirm how database changes, presence, and application-managed backfill divide responsibility
Cloudflare Durable Objects A team willing to own more coordination logic on Cloudflare Confirm object lifecycle, placement, persistence, and client recovery behavior for match rooms

This table is a shortlist, not a synthetic benchmark. No latency or uptime numbers are implied. Run the same match script against each serious candidate: connect late, drop the network, refresh authorization, deliver one event twice, and reconnect while a correction is being written. Record which component answers each step. A lower median delivery time can't rescue a design that has no defined recovery source.

Stick with Ably or Pusher when a specialist realtime product's documented connection model is the center of the architecture and your team accepts its client integration. Supabase is the more coherent candidate when the source data and authorization model are already there. Durable Objects deserve evaluation when per-match coordination logic is valuable enough to operate explicitly. Infrai is not suitable as a substitute for the application's durable event history; its fit here is the HTTP publication handoff.

Make reconnect and partial failure ordinary

A clean reconnect flow has a small state machine: disconnected, authenticating, subscribed, backfilling, and live. Expose those states rather than compressing them into a green or red connection dot. The UI can then say “catching up” while it applies missing scores, suppress stale typing signals, and queue read-receipt updates behind the score recovery. A subscription expiry is an authentication event. It should not erase the last confirmed scoreboard.

Test at realistic latency, including a delayed backfill response racing a fresh live event. Also test a duplicate with the same stable ID, a gap in cursor order, an expired credential, and an authorization denial for the wrong customer or match. 401, 403, and 429 are different facts and should land in different counters. Don't turn them into one “realtime failed” alert.

Partial failure is normal. A publish request can be rate-limited while the score commit remains valid; the outbox retains the handoff and retries it. A browser can lose its connection while other subscribers remain live; only that browser backfills. A read receipt can lag while the score is correct; the product stays useful. These distinctions keep a transient transport condition from becoming a fabricated business incident.

The read path deserves the longer test because it carries recovery. Seed a match with a known ordered event set, connect a client after event 20, interrupt it after event 27, and write events 28 through 35 while that client is offline. Reconnect with 27 as the last applied cursor, but deliberately delay the backfill response while event 35 also arrives over the restored live connection. Deliver event 31 twice. Expire the old credential during the same run, issue a valid replacement through the normal application flow, and verify that the subscription resumes without resetting confirmed state. Now make an operator type a correction note before the disconnect and stop before reconnecting; the old typing indicator must not reappear. Send the note's read receipt twice and confirm that its stable application ID collapses the duplicate without delaying the scoreboard. At the end, compare the client's materialized score with the authoritative snapshot, not with the order in which callbacks happened to fire. Each stable event ID should apply once, the cursor should reach 35 without a gap, and current presence should be the only presence shown. This is not a provider benchmark, and it proves no universal latency claim. It is a contract test for the boundary your product owns, with enough overlapping events to expose an accidental assumption that reconnect and backfill happen in a tidy sequence.

An operational checklist that stays useful

Before launch, write down the owner of every transition in the connection state machine. Confirm that logs distinguish token issuance, subscription establishment, publication, backfill, and client reconciliation. Attach the stable match ID, event ID, and request ID where each system exposes one, but never put secrets in log fields.

Then rehearse expiry and reconnect under load representative of an actual match. Check that the retry budget is bounded, Retry-After is honored, and an idempotency key survives a new serverless invocation. Verify that a cold client can rebuild state without receiving any live event at all. Finally, make the dashboard show backfill gaps and authorization failures separately from ordinary disconnects.

Ship the boring path first.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Ably documentation: https://ably.com/docs
  • Pusher Channels documentation: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • Supabase Realtime documentation: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime
  • Cloudflare Durable Objects documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/

Further reading

The W3C WebRTC Recommendation is useful when the product needs peer media or data channels rather than a server-published business event stream: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/. If the HTTP publication boundary described here fits your system, start with the current discovery and authentication guidance at https://docs.infrai.cc.

title: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?
description:
arXiv:2610.28619v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.
