title: My Dashboard fetches two things at once — and cancels both on unmount
description:
My Dashboard page needs two things: the stats for the cards, and the five most recent users for the table underneath. Here's exactly how it loads them:

useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;

  async function load() {
    try {
      const [statsRes, usersRes] = await Promise.all([
        client.get('/dashboard/stats'),
        isAdmin ? client.get('/users', { params: { per_page: 5 } }) : Promise.resolve(null),
      ]);
      if (cancelled) return;
      setStats(statsRes.data);
      if (usersRes) setRecentUsers(usersRes.data.data ?? []);
    } catch (err) {
      if (!cancelled) setError(err.response?.data?.message || 'Failed to load dashboard data.');
    } finally {
      if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
    }
  }

  load();
  return () => {
    cancelled = true;
  };
}, [isAdmin]);

Three decisions in here that I reuse on every page of the kit:

One: parallel fetches with Promise.all. The stats call and the users call don't depend on each other, so they go out together. The recent-users fetch only runs for admins — everyone else resolves null and the table section never renders. No separate loading states to juggle, one loading flag for the whole page.

Two: the cancelled flag. Every setState after an await is guarded. If the user navigates away mid-fetch, the cleanup flips the flag and the late responses are dropped silently. No "state update on an unmounted component" warnings, no stale data landing on the wrong page. It's five extra lines and it makes every page feel solid.

Three: honest loading and error states. Loading is a centred spinner (animate-spin with an indigo top border). Failure is a rose-coloured box with the API's own message, or a fallback string. No skeletons pretending the data is almost here, no silent empty tables.

And one small human touch: Welcome back, {user?.name} at the top. Dashboards are cold by default; a name costs nothing.

This same shape — Promise.all, cancelled flag, spinner, error box — is copy-pasted into my Users page too. A starter kit teaches by repeating one good pattern until it's muscle memory, not by showing three clever ones.

This Dashboard page ships in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — the React frontend wired to a real Laravel + Sanctum API: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
description:
arXiv:2610.29225v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

title: Beyond Correct Answers: How Compositional Cues Shape Visual Judgments
description:
arXiv:2610.28843v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.

title: Evolving Semantic Indexes for Generative Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2610.28568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) casts search and recommendation as autoregressive generation of discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs). SID design largely determines GR quality, but its discrete, interdependent components (SID construction, collision handling, decoding, and training) cannot be optimized end-to-end with gradients and remain largely hand-designed. We introduce a framework that improves these components through LLM-driven evolutionary program search, to our knowledge the first application of this approach to GR. A locally served, open-weight 31B model mutates executable GR components, so no proprietary LLM API is used, and a 1M-parameter proxy decoder provides fast feedback in place of repeatedly training the 1B target generator. Across 21 SID programs on NQ320K, proxy and target Recall@100 show strong rank correlation (Spearman $\rho = 0.90$). Guided by this proxy, evolution improves the seed GR on NQ320K, MSMARCO300K, and a multilingual e-commerce dataset under a fixed training recipe. On NQ320K, jointly evolving SID construction and collision handling improves Recall@1 from 55.8% to 59.3% and Recall@100 from 85.8% to 90.6%. A component study shows that proxy reliability depends on what is evolved: improvements transfer reliably for the semantic index but not for the generator's training objective or the full pipeline. LLM-driven evolutionary search is thus a practical tool for GR design, provided proxy reliability is established for the chosen search space.

title: GBase Database Silent Installation FAQ: 5 Common Questions Answered
description:
Silent installation makes it easier to automate GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment across multiple servers. By using a response file to supply installation parameters, administrators can reduce repetitive input and improve configuration consistency.

If you're preparing to automate a GBase Database installation, these five frequently asked questions cover the basics.

Q1: What's the Difference Between Silent Installation and CLI Installation?

The main difference is how installation parameters are provided.

  • CLI installation: Uses a command-line interface and may still require interactive input, depending on the installer and installation mode.
  • Silent installation: Reads predefined parameters from a response file and runs without interactive prompts.

For example, a silent installation command may look like this:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

This approach is useful when the same installation procedure needs to run repeatedly across multiple servers.

Q2: How Do I Generate a Silent Installation Response File?

A response file stores the parameters required by the installer, such as installation settings and selected components.

Depending on the installer version, you may be able to generate a response file with a command such as:

./ids_install -r /opt/bundle.properties

Alternatively, check whether the installation media includes a sample response file that you can copy and customize.

Before using the file in a deployment batch, verify that its syntax and parameter names match the documentation for your installation package. Test the completed file on a single server first.

Q3: Why Is LICENSE_ACCEPTED Required?

A silent installation cannot pause to ask the administrator to accept the license interactively. License acceptance must therefore be supplied in advance when required by the installer.

For example:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Some installation packages also accept the setting as a command-line parameter:

-DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Follow the syntax supported by your installer and make sure you have reviewed and accepted the applicable license terms before proceeding.

Q4: Can I Use GBase Database Immediately After Silent Installation?

Not necessarily. Completing the software installation does not automatically mean that a usable database instance is running.

Depending on the installation package and selected workflow, additional steps may include:

  • Configuring the required environment variables.
  • Reviewing the instance's onconfig configuration.
  • Checking the connection settings in sqlhosts.
  • Initializing the database instance when initialization has not already been performed.
  • Starting the instance and validating connectivity.

For a manual installation, instance initialization may be a separate step performed by the gbasedbt user. Other installation workflows may handle some configuration or initialization tasks automatically.

Always check what the selected installation procedure has already completed before running additional initialization commands.

Q5: When Should I Use Silent Installation?

Silent installation is particularly useful in three scenarios.

Batch deployment: Install GBase Database across multiple servers using a standardized response file and deployment procedure.

Automation and CI/CD pipelines: Integrate database software installation into a repeatable operational workflow, with prerequisite checks and logging.

Consistent environments: Reduce differences caused by repeated manual input when development, testing, staging, or production environments require standardized installation parameters.

Silent installation does not guarantee identical environments by itself. Operating system packages, directory permissions, disk space, and port availability can still differ between servers. Validate these prerequisites before running a batch.

Final Thoughts

Understanding the response file, license acceptance, instance initialization, and deployment prerequisites makes GBase Database silent installation easier to manage.

Start with a tested response file, verify the installation on one server, and then expand to batch deployment. This approach improves repeatability while reducing the risk of spreading a configuration error across multiple machines.

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Control domain

Vercel controls

Deployment governance

Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC

Access governance

Vercel Passport, Deployment Protection, and Vercel Firewall

Integration and data governance

Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

Model and token governance

AI Gateway, including US-only inference and budget controls

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

Contact sales to learn more about enterprise governance on Vercel and get a custom demo of the platform.

title: What the eMudhra certificate compromise means for your apps
description:
On October 19, 2026, Cloudflare learned that private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, according to Cloudflare's write-up. Anyone who holds those keys can forge a certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate a server. Browsers shut this down quickly. According to InfoQ, most other software that relies on the web's certificate system has no way to block a single bad intermediate. That software stays exposed until its list of trusted certificates is updated and redeployed. Your servers, containers and API clients are in that second group.

The background you need

When your app opens an HTTPS connection, the server sends a certificate. A certificate is a signed statement that a public key belongs to a domain name. Your app checks the signature to decide whether it is really talking to that domain. This check stops a man-in-the-middle attacker, someone sitting between you and the server, from pretending to be the server.

The signatures come from certificate authorities (CAs). CAs are arranged in a chain:

  • A root CA is a certificate your software trusts directly, with no further proof.
  • An intermediate CA is a certificate signed by a root. It does the day-to-day signing of website certificates. Anything an intermediate signs inherits the root's trust.
  • The trust store (also called a root bundle or cacerts file) is the list of roots your software accepts.

An analogy: think of roots as national governments and intermediates as passport offices they authorize. A border guard (your app) accepts any passport from an authorized office. If one office's official stamp is copied, every forged passport carrying it looks genuine.

Here is where the analogy breaks. A real passport office can only issue passports for its own country. A CA can issue a certificate for any domain on the internet. InfoQ notes that a typical bundle holds hundreds of CAs, plus thousands of intermediates that inherit trust. Any one of them can create a legitimate-looking certificate for your domain.

The web PKI (public key infrastructure) is the name for this whole system of public CAs and trust stores.

Your trust store is not one file. Depending on the code path, it may come from:

  • the operating system (a ca-certificates package on Linux)
  • a language runtime or library that ships its own copy, such as Python's certifi
  • a bundle baked into an app or a container image
  • a custom configuration someone wrote years ago

Revocation means telling software to stop trusting a certificate before it expires. Browsers have a fast version of this. Chrome's is called CRLSets: a blocklist pushed to the browser in the background, which can target one specific intermediate. Most servers, command-line tools and HTTP libraries have nothing like it. Their only lever is editing the trust store itself, and that takes a package update, a rebuild and a restart.

What actually changed

What is new. According to InfoQ, the eight private keys were not stolen. There is no evidence eMudhra was breached. Instead, the keys appear to have been generated by an insecure mechanism. Each key was all zeros except the final byte. A private key should be a huge random number. These could be found by simply trying every possible value, and once someone matched them to public keys used by live CAs, they counted as compromised.

InfoQ reports that six of the eight were TLS certificates trusted by the Apple, Chrome, Microsoft and Mozilla root programs. The other two were for code signing and trusted by Microsoft.

What was already true. Any trusted CA could always vouch for any domain. Non-browser software could never quickly distrust a single intermediate. This incident did not create those weaknesses. It exposed them.

How people responded. Browsers used their blocklists. Cloudflare says it patched critical services before public disclosure. It also updated shared trust stores and base images, and released new versions of its WARP / 1.1.1.1 clients and cloudflared. Cloudflare says its review has not identified active exploitation on Cloudflare services.

According to InfoQ, many projects could not block just the intermediates. So they removed the whole emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their trust stores. InfoQ says that removal is causing collateral damage for legitimate certificates chained to that root. Cloudflare's post does not discuss the root removal. It focuses on patching and on not disabling verification when errors appear.

InfoQ lists updated ca-certificates packages in Arch, Debian, Gentoo, Fedora and Ubuntu, plus updates in Electron, Go, pip, Python certifi, rustls-webpki, Rust webpki-roots and uv.

What it means if you deploy and run apps

The key fact is the gap between browsers and everything else. A clean browser test tells you almost nothing about your backend. Cloudflare says plainly that a successful browser test does not prove a background service is protected. A curl test does not prove it either if your app uses a different verifier.

What to do:

  1. Map your verification paths. For each service that makes outbound HTTPS calls, find which trust store it uses. Cloudflare warns that an API client may hand verification to an HTTP library, the runtime, the OS or a custom config: "Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy."
  2. Update the right layer. Patch the OS ca-certificates package, bump bundled roots like certifi, and check indirect dependencies in your dependency tree, as Cloudflare advises.
  3. Rebuild and restart. Cloudflare says updates need reloads, restarts or redeployments to take effect. An updated package in a registry does nothing for a container image built last month.
  4. Hunt for buried bundles. InfoQ warns that many applications carry a cacerts file inside them that will keep trusting the compromised CAs. End-of-life systems that no longer get patches stay vulnerable.
  5. Check mTLS. With mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate. If your mTLS endpoint accepts web PKI certificates, InfoQ quotes SSLMate founder Andrew Ayer warning that attackers can simply mint a certificate and authenticate, with no network attack needed.

If you use Cloudflare, upgrade the Cloudflare One / 1.1.1.1 clients to the versions Cloudflare lists (for example 2026.8.2115.0 on desktop). Cloudflare also says Containers users should review their images. Turning on HTTPS egress interception moves certificate checks to Cloudflare's infrastructure, and containers with it enabled are already protected, according to Cloudflare.

After patching, some legitimate connections may fail, partly because some projects removed an entire eMudhra root. Fix those by updating the trust configuration or the server's certificate. Cloudflare explicitly warns against disabling verification, because that removes the protection the updates restore.

What to watch next: how fast your base images and runtimes pick up the new trust stores, and whether services you call start failing because their certificates chain to the removed root.

What we don't know yet

  • Exploitation elsewhere. Cloudflare only says it found no active exploitation on its own services. Neither source says whether forged certificates were used anywhere else.
  • How the keys were made. InfoQ says the keys appear to come from an insecure generation mechanism. The exact cause is not established in the reports.
  • Propagation time. InfoQ says updates will take some time to reach every place they need to go. Nobody can say how many apps carry stale embedded bundles.
  • Collateral fallout. How many legitimate sites break from the root removal, and what their owners must do, is not covered.
  • Code signing. The two code-signing certificates trusted by Microsoft get little detail in either report.

Originally published at pickuma.com. Subscribe to the RSS or follow @pickuma.bsky.social for new reviews.

title: Single-Image Food Mass Estimators Do Not Transfer Their Gram Scale Across Datasets
description:
arXiv:2610.29025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating food mass from a photograph is central to image-based dietary assessment, but whether trained models transfer to new cameras and foods is unclear. We fine-tuned DINOv2-base on 2,253 weighed Nutrition5k dishes to predict mass from one RGB photograph and compared it with a zero-shot vision-language model, Qwen3-VL-32B, on Nutrition5k and three external datasets: ASA24 studio portions, ECUSTFD whole foods and Food Portion Benchmark meal trays. In domain, the fine-tuned model's mean absolute error was 24.8 g, less than half of Qwen's. On external datasets it did not beat Qwen. For a food it had never seen, it ranked portions by size, but no better than a count of food pixels. Its gram scale was wrong in two ways: it changed with how much of the scene the photograph showed, and it was off by a different factor for each food. Training on other foods or trays from the tested dataset cut the external error by 38 to 65%. DINOv2-large, a larger backbone trained on the same dishes, did not reduce the external error. One labeled photograph of the same food cut the model's ASA24 error to 28.3 g, better than that photograph achieved alone. Prediction intervals that held the true mass for 90% of Nutrition5k dishes held it for at most half of external photographs. Nutrition5k often photographed the same plate several times, so a random test split shared near-identical photographs with training and overstated accuracy. Single-image mass estimators therefore need labeled photographs from the setting where they are used.

title: Sandboxing Python: RestrictedPython vs Docker vs Pyodide
description:
Running "untrusted Python" means executing code you did not write, a user's formula, an AI agent's generated script, or a plugin, without letting it read your files, open network connections, or seize the machine. It matters because Python was designed for trusted developers, so the interpreter offers no security boundary and the isolation has to be built deliberately around it.

Key takeaways

  • The classic exec() with stripped builtins is not a sandbox: Python's introspection lets any object walk up to a class that still holds import.

  • RestrictedPython's own maintainers state it "is not a sandbox system or a secured environment": it stops accidents and casual mischief, not a determined attacker.

  • Pyodide gives strong isolation for pure computation in WebAssembly, but its Python-to-JavaScript bridge has been the route of real production escapes.

  • Docker with a seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem suits broadly trusted code; adversarial code needs gVisor or a microVM because containers share the host kernel.

  • Pick the boundary from the threat model, and never rely on interpreter-level tricks as the only layer.

Every few months a team learns this the expensive way: a "run user code" feature ships with exec() and a trimmed builtins dict, a researcher spends an afternoon on it, and the postmortem reads like a magic trick. Python looks sandboxable because you can see the dangerous names. The trap is that those names are never the whole attack surface.

Why can't you just use exec() with restricted builtins?

The naive sandbox looks like this:

exec(user_code, {"builtins": {}})

Emptying builtins feels thorough. It is not. Python's introspection gives every object a ladder back out: ().class reaches tuple, .base reaches object, and .subclasses() lists every loaded class (opencomputer.dev). From there the code picks a class whose module kept normal builtins, reaches through init.globals to grab import, imports os, and calls system, all without naming anything your filter blocked.

Here is the uncomfortable fact stated plainly: CPython was never designed to run hostile code inside its own process. Audit hooks and resource limits each close one hole, but the introspection surface is too large to close hole by hole (opencomputer.dev). Any defence that lives inside the interpreter is playing whack-a-mole against the language's own object model.

So the security boundary has to move somewhere the interpreter cannot reach: out to the operating system, the browser, or the hardware. That is what the three serious options do, each at a different layer.

What does RestrictedPython actually guarantee?

RestrictedPython, maintained by the Zope Foundation, compiles a restricted subset of Python by rewriting the abstract syntax tree at compile time. Attribute access to names starting with underscores is blocked, dangerous builtins are removed from the namespace your code sees, and imports go through a guard you control. The official example shows both sides:

from RestrictedPython import compile_restricted
from RestrictedPython import safe_globals

Harmless code runs fine

source = """
def example():
return 'Hello World!'
"""
byte_code = compile_restricted(source, '', 'exec')
namespace = {}
exec(byte_code, safe_globals, namespace)
print(namespace'example') # 'Hello World!'

Hostile code is stopped at the import

evil = """
import os
os.listdir('/')
"""
byte_code = compile_restricted(evil, '', 'exec')
exec(byte_code, safe_globals, {})

ImportError: import not found

In production you layer more on top: a custom getattr guard and a vetted import hook that only allows the modules your use case needs. It powers formula fields and scripted templates in systems like Plone, where semi-trusted users extend an application the operator controls.

Now the honest part, in the maintainers' own words: RestrictedPython "is not a sandbox system or a secured environment, but it helps to define a trusted environment and execute untrusted code inside of it" (PyPI). It stops accidents and casual mischief: a user who writes a bad formula gets an error, not your filesystem. It was never designed to hold a hostile expression, and treating it as a security boundary against untrusted code is a misuse. Against an adversary, it is at most one layer, never the wall.

Does Pyodide provide real isolation?

Pyodide is CPython compiled to WebAssembly, running in the browser or Node.js. For pure computation the isolation is genuinely strong: WebAssembly modules have no ambient access to the host and receive only the capabilities you grant them.

The catch is the foreign function interface between Python and JavaScript, which is the whole point of embedding Pyodide in a page. Through the js module, Python code can reach JavaScript objects, and by default it sees the host runtime's global scope. One real escape (blog.barrack.ai, CERT VU#414811) is instructive: the sandbox handed Python a mock document built as a plain object literal, and because every such object inherits from Object.prototype, the payload walked .constructor.constructor to the Function constructor, evaluated "return globalThis", and landed in the real global scope. In Node.js that means process, require, and child_process.

This was not a one-off. Researchers disclosed CVE-2025-68668 against n8n's Pyodide-backed code node: n8n blocked risky functions by patching names, but two bypasses worked anyway, one using ctypes to call libc's system() directly, the other using _pyodide._base.eval_code() where the patches did not apply (cyera.com). The proof of concept was two lines. Earlier, Grist disclosed a CVSS 9.1 escape in its Pyodide formula engine (GHSA-7xvx-8pf2-pv5g), fixed in Grist 1.7.9 by running Pyodide under Deno: a real process boundary outside the interpreter.

The pattern is consistent: Pyodide has never claimed to be a security boundary, and the escapes happen at the bridge the embedder built, not in WebAssembly itself. For a browser playground, it is an excellent zero-server-cost choice. On a server, treat the JavaScript globals configuration as the actual security surface: anything reachable from Python is reachable by the attacker.

// Pin a version you have tested; the snippet below is illustrative
const pyodide = await loadPyodide();
// Runs in the visitor's browser: no server, no bill, no shared state
const result = await pyodide.runPythonAsync(
def fib(n):
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(n):
a, b = b, a + b
return a
fib(30)
);
console.log(result); // 832040

Is Docker enough for hostile code?

Containers move the boundary to the operating system: Linux namespaces and cgroups give the code its own filesystem view, process tree, network stack, and resource limits. For code you broadly trust, Docker with a hardened configuration is the workhorse answer:

docker run --rm \
--cap-drop=ALL \
--security-opt=no-new-privileges \
--security-opt seccomp=default.json \
--read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid \
--network none \
--memory 256m --cpus 0.5 \
--pids-limit 64 \
--user 1000:1000 \
python:3.13-slim \
python /app/user_code.py

Each flag closes a real door: no Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation through setuid binaries, a seccomp filter on syscalls, a read-only root filesystem, no network, and hard caps on memory, CPU, and processes so a fork bomb is a billing event rather than an outage.

The caveat is architectural: containers share the host kernel, so a kernel-level exploit escapes the container. For code you broadly trust, that risk is acceptable with a seccomp profile and a read-only root filesystem. For adversarial code, the boundary must move again: gVisor interposes a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls, and microVMs such as Firecracker add a hypervisor, so an escape must defeat virtualisation rather than a single kernel bug (opencomputer.dev).

Production systems rarely bet on one layer. Cohere's Python interpreter documents a defence-in-depth stack: untrusted code runs in a WebAssembly sandbox, inside a Node.js process, inside a Docker container, inside cloud infrastructure, with network egress and the filesystem locked down at every level (Cohere North security docs). No single layer is trusted.

Which one should you use?

Start from the threat model, not the tool. The question is never "which sandbox is best" but "who is writing the code, and what happens if they turn malicious?"

  • Semi-trusted users extending your app (formulas, templates, workflow expressions): RestrictedPython fits: friendly errors instead of breaches, and fast in-process code your test suite can exercise. Still run the whole application in a container, since RestrictedPython is the guardrail, not the wall.

  • Public playgrounds and tutorials: Pyodide in the browser is hard to beat. Execution happens on the visitor's machine, so there is no server to attack and no compute bill. Keep the JavaScript bridge minimal and never expose Node.js globals server-side.

  • Customer or agent-generated code on your servers that you broadly trust: Docker with the hardening flags above, plus timeouts and output limits. This is the standard answer for a reason.

  • Adversarial or multi-tenant code: containers alone are not enough. Use gVisor or a microVM per execution, and treat the container image as untrusted input too.

Much of what remains unknown is operational: sandbox overhead depends on your workload, and public benchmarks measure different things, so treat vendor numbers as directional. What is settled is the principle every story here converges on: CPython cannot sandbox itself, so the boundary must live outside the interpreter. Choose the layer that matches your adversary, stack more than one, and test the configuration the way an attacker would.

title: Issue no.15: The state of design
description: AI-powered tools and workflows are fundamentally changing the way we design.

title: Enhancing analytical photon transport in turbid media through physics-guided neural network corrections
description:
arXiv:2610.26917v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1\% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87\% and 93\% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.

title: PhyMo: Learning Physical Dynamics with Accurate and Continuous Motion from Multi-View Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.29107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.

title: ER-Chord: Spatially Consistent One-Step Image Editing via Equal-Energy Reliability Redistribution
description:
arXiv:2610.29248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step generative models enable fast text-guided image editing, yet they often introduce unintended changes to regions that should remain unchanged. Temporal aggregation stabilizes editing fields across noise levels, but leaves their spatial allocation insensitive to local variations in reliability. Consequently, temporal stability alone does not ensure spatially consistent editing. To address this lim- itation, we propose ER-Chord, a training-free and inversion-free framework for reliability-guided spatial redistribution. Our key insight is that agreement between editing fields at neighboring noise levels provides a local reliability signal for allocating editing strength. We formulate this allocation as an equal-energy op- timization that redistributes control energy according to local reliability while preserving the original editing directions and total control energy. This formu- lation admits a unique global solution that can be efficiently computed using existing field evaluations, requiring no additional denoiser calls. Experiments on two benchmarks, PIE-Bench and TEdBench, demonstrate improvements over state-of-the-art one-step editing baselines, achieving superior source preservation alongside consistent gains across multiple generative backbones.The project page is at https://github.com/Peizeli1/ER-Chord.

title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.29339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.

title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29136v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.

title: I built SiteScope, a free technical SEO audit tool that ranks what to fix first
description:
For my college course I built SiteScope (vikramyadav.me), a free technical SEO audit tool. You enter a site, it crawls every page it can reach, and it tells you what to fix first. No sign-up needed to run an audit. If you want, you can create an account to have your sites re-audited daily or weekly.

The problem

Two things bugged me about free SEO checkers.

First, most test a single URL and hand back an unordered list. SiteScope follows internal links and the XML sitemap and checks every page it finds (up to 300 per audit). Then it ranks issues with one rule:

priority = severity × share of pages affected

A missing alt text on every page outranks a broken link on one page; a 5xx on half the site outranks both.

Second, a lot of sites load their content with JavaScript. SiteScope reads raw HTML, the way most AI crawlers do, so you can check whether your content needs JavaScript to show up. The tool itself uses no JavaScript framework. Every page, including the report, is server-rendered, because a tool that talks about JavaScript SEO should be readable by a crawler that runs none.

It also checks broken links, duplicate and near-duplicate pages (SimHash), the internal link graph (click depth, PageRank, orphan pages), titles, meta descriptions, H1s, canonicals, noindex and more. Reports download as PDF or JSON, and re-running an audit shows what was fixed and what is new since last time.

Tech stack

  • FastAPI (Python 3.12) with Jinja2 templates; audits run as FastAPI background tasks
  • PostgreSQL 16, where each finished result is one JSONB column
  • Docker Compose with an Nginx reverse proxy and Certbot
  • Azure VM: one small VM (2 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM) running two containers
  • Cloudflare for DNS and proxying
  • httpx + asyncio for crawling, BeautifulSoup for parsing, NetworkX for the link graph

What I learned

  • A URL fetcher is an SSRF hole. If a stranger can type any URL, they will try the cloud metadata service or localhost. The guard refuses private, loopback and reserved addresses, checks every redirect hop, and connects to the exact IP it checked, so DNS rebinding can't swap the address in between.
  • Don't trust a header anyone can send. My per-IP limit read Cloudflare's CF-Connecting-IP, but anyone hitting the server's IP directly could send that header with a new value each time. Now it only believes that header when the connection really comes from Cloudflare's IP ranges, and the limit lives in Postgres so a restart doesn't reset it.
  • Keep dependencies small on a small VM. NetworkX's PageRank pulled in numpy and scipy, so I wrote my own PageRank and tested it against the reference. The scheduled re-audits run as a background task inside the app, with no cron, Celery or Redis.
  • Severity alone gets the order wrong. Multiplying by the share of pages affected fixed it.
  • An SEO tool shouldn't create thin pages. Report pages send noindex and are disallowed in robots.txt.
  • DNS moves need care. Switching nameservers to Cloudflare replaces the whole zone, so I recreated the existing records first and issued SSL before turning on the proxy.

What's next

Some things are still open: score-drop emails are waiting on an SMTP provider, and external link checks stop at 200 links per audit.

Try it at vikramyadav.me and see the code on GitHub. Feedback welcome!

title: FoundPDE: A generative foundation model for data-driven symbolic discovery of partial differential equations
description:
arXiv:2610.26963v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observed data is a central inverse problem in computational science and engineering: the goal is not only to predict trajectories, but to identify interpretable symbolic laws that can be analyzed and reused. Existing PDE discovery methods often depend on hand-designed libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or per-equation symbolic search, making them fragile under sparse observations, noisy data, broad equation families, and unseen symbolic compositions. Here, we introduce FoundPDE, a pretrained data-to-symbol foundation model for PDE discovery. FoundPDE maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories to symbolic equations with a transformer, uses Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative augmentation to expose complementary trajectory information, refines numerical coefficients, and supports downstream extension with improved generalization through few-shot fine-tuning and hierarchical discovery. On a clean in-domain benchmark spanning 20 PDE families, our model reaches 97.50% type recognition. Under coefficient shifts beyond the training support, type recognition remains 90.53%; under multiplicative Gaussian noise on the model input, it is 94.43% at a 2% noise level but falls to 52.09% at 10%. For unseen composite equations, few-shot fine-tuning reaches over 90% exact recovery on four held-out families, and we further develop a hierarchical discovery algorithm that recovers two-term composites without fine-tuning FoundPDE. By amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families, FoundPDE shifts PDE discovery from per-dataset search toward a reusable pretrained model that extends to new physics with limited additional data, a step toward foundation models that uncover interpretable governing laws directly from scientific data.

title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams
description:
arXiv:2610.28405v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.

title: SimHack: Predicting the onset of detectable reward hacking before RL training
description:
arXiv:2610.28707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When training LLMs to code with reinforcement learning, reward hacking is often detectable but difficult to prevent, since (a) environment hardening is increasingly difficult as training environments grow more complex; and (b) training-time interventions incentivize models to obfuscate hacking behavior to bypass detection.
  We instead study whether we can predict when detectable reward hacking becomes dominant before executing an RL run, enabling us to select lower-risk recipes in advance. We find that the initial hacking rate alone does not determine onset, which varies substantially across training recipes and repeated runs. We thus formulate this problem as predicting the distribution of the reward hacking onset step under a target training recipe.
  We introduce SimHack, a simulator that learns reward hacking training dynamics from a handful of smaller-scale reference RL runs and generates counterfactual simulation runs of unseen target recipes without costly retraining. Across unseen target recipes, SimHack predicts the median onset to a relative error of 11.3% and achieves across-recipe rank correlation of 0.85, while generalizing to differences in model scale, curriculum, number of rollouts, and learning rate between reference and target recipes. As an application, we show that SimHack can guide training decisions by screening candidate RL curricula, discovering curricula over the same set of scenarios that train for 96.6% longer without hacking.

title: GBase Database Installation Methods Compared: Which Is Most Efficient?
description:
Choosing the right installation method for GBase Database(GBase 8s) depends on more than installation speed. Interaction requirements, component customization, repeatability, and deployment scale all affect operational efficiency.

GBase Database supports several installation approaches, including one-click, typical, manual, and silent installation. Each serves a different purpose.

1. Comparing Four GBase Database Installation Methods

Installation method User interaction Component customization Batch deployment Best use case
One-click installation Low Medium Medium Quick environment setup and validation
Typical installation Very low Low Low Fast testing and basic validation
Manual installation High High Low without additional automation Customized production installation
Silent installation None during installation Medium to high, depending on the response file High Repeatable, automated batch deployment

The ratings above are relative and assume a standard installation workflow. Actual efficiency depends on the installation package, configuration requirements, and automation already available in your environment.

2. One-Click Installation: Quick Setup

One-click installation is useful when you need to establish a GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment quickly.

It reduces manual configuration steps and is suitable for initial validation, demonstrations, and basic environment checks.

However, convenience comes with trade-offs. Default parameters may not match production requirements, so review settings such as the installation path, character set, and database port before using the environment for more demanding workloads.

Choose one-click installation when speed and simplicity matter more than fine-grained control.

3. Typical Installation: Minimal Configuration

Typical installation is designed for users who want to get a basic environment running with minimal interaction.

It works well for quick tests, compatibility checks, and preliminary validation without extensive component selection.

The main limitation is customization. If your environment requires specific components or carefully controlled configuration, a typical installation may not provide enough flexibility.

Choose typical installation when you need a basic test environment with minimal setup effort.

4. Manual Installation: Maximum Control

Manual installation gives administrators more control over the installation process.

You can select components, specify installation paths, and make decisions that align with the target environment's operational requirements.

This flexibility is particularly useful for production deployments that require explicit configuration decisions. The trade-off is time: administrators must understand the installation steps and validate the resulting environment.

Manual installation can also be automated with additional scripting, so it is not inherently unsuitable for batch deployment. Without that automation, however, repeated manual installations require more effort and create more opportunities for configuration drift.

Choose manual installation when customization and direct control are the primary requirements.

5. Silent Installation: Consistency at Scale

Silent installation is the natural choice when deploying GBase Database across multiple servers with a standardized configuration.

Instead of answering installation prompts on every machine, you provide the parameters through a response file.

For example:

./ids_install -i silent \
  -f /opt/bundle.properties \
  -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

The response file makes installation parameters repeatable and easier to manage. Combined with deployment scripts, silent installation reduces repetitive interaction and helps maintain consistency across nodes.

It does not eliminate the need for validation. Target servers may differ in available disk space, dependencies, permissions, or port availability. These prerequisites should be checked before starting a batch deployment.

The efficiency advantage becomes more significant as the number of servers grows. There is no universal threshold at which silent installation becomes faster, but the time saved on repeated interactions and configuration checks can outweigh the initial effort of preparing and validating the response file.

Choose silent installation when repeatability, automation, and batch deployment are the main priorities.

6. How to Choose the Right Installation Method

For GBase Database deployment, a practical decision framework is:

  • Need a quick test? Use one-click or typical installation.
  • Need detailed control over a single production environment? Use manual installation.
  • Need consistent configuration across multiple servers? Use silent installation with a validated response file.
  • Need repeatable deployment at scale? Combine silent installation with prerequisite checks, logging, and incremental rollout.

These methods are not mutually exclusive. A team can validate a configuration with a simple installation first, refine the production settings through a controlled installation, and then automate repeated deployments using silent installation.

Conclusion

The most efficient GBase Database installation method is the one that matches your deployment requirements.

One-click and typical installation reduce setup effort. Manual installation provides greater control. Silent installation makes standardized, repeatable deployment easier to manage across multiple servers.

Rather than choosing one method for every situation, build a workflow around the strengths of each. Validate early, standardize the configuration, and automate only after the installation process is understood and tested.

title: Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.29034v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one-layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre-specified follow-ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono-initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre-specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition-dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.

title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
description:
arXiv:2610.28958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.

title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
description:
arXiv:2610.28484v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
description:
arXiv:2610.29073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.

title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
description:
arXiv:2610.29378v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.

title: Comparing satisfies, type annotations, and assertions through compiler output
description:
Use satisfies when a configuration value should meet a type while its individual properties remain convenient to use. Two common shortcuts are misleading, though: that it can never affect inference, and that it always rejects extra keys.

The comparison uses the same object under a type annotation, satisfies, and as, with emitted declarations and diagnostics as evidence. For this display configuration, the differences were:

Form Type when reading ready Missing waiting
: Notices `string number[]`
satisfies Notices string Error
as Notices `string number[]`

Inspect declarations as well as editor hints

The experiment ran on September 11, 2026, with macOS arm64, Node.js 24.15.0, and TypeScript 7.0.2. The compiler used strict: true, target: ES2022, module: ESNext, and moduleResolution: Bundler, with type checking and declaration emit. The display values are synthetic test data.

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
export const annotated: Notices = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] };
export const checked = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] } satisfies Notices;
export const asserted = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1, 2] } as Notices;
console.log(checked.ready.toUpperCase());

checked.ready.toUpperCase() passed and printed READY. Calling the same method on annotated.ready produced TS2339 because the property could also be an array.

The emitted declarations explain that difference:

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
export declare const annotated: Notices;
export declare const checked: {
    ready: string;
    waiting: number[];
};
export declare const asserted: Notices;
export {};

checked retains the types of individual properties. The other two variables have the annotated Notices type. This makes satisfies useful when a configuration needs a shared compatibility check without requiring extra narrowing wherever a particular value is used. The TypeScript 4.9 documentation describes this use of compatibility checks while retaining a useful expression type.

An assertion can leave a missing property undetected 

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
const value = { ready: "Ready" } as Notices;
console.log(value.waiting);

This code passed type checking and printed undefined. Changing the assertion to satisfies Notices produced TS2741 for the missing waiting property. An assertion does not create that property.

This also does not mean every possible assertion is accepted. TypeScript can reject an assertion based on the relationship between the types. The finding here is narrower: it accepts this particular object despite the missing required key. As the official explanation of type assertions states, assertions do not validate or convert runtime values.

Context can affect inference 

export const plain = { enabled: true, count: 1 };
export const checked = { enabled: true, count: 1 } satisfies { enabled: boolean; count: number };
export const frozenType = { enabled: true, count: 1 } as const;

In the emitted declarations, plain.enabled was boolean, while checked.enabled was true. Both count properties were number. Context from the target type means literal inference is not necessarily identical.

With as const, frozenType.enabled became a readonly true, and frozenType.count became a readonly 1. This does not freeze the object at runtime either. If a configuration will be modified later, decide whether that property should remain the literal true or accept both boolean values, including false.

Extra keys are not always rejected

Writing { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1], typo: 1 } satisfies Notices directly produced TS2353 for the extra typo property. Assigning that object to a variable first changed the outcome:

type Notices = Record<"ready" | "waiting", string | number[]>;
const input = { ready: "Ready", waiting: [1], typo: 1 };
const value = input satisfies Notices;
console.log(value.typo);

This passed and printed 1. A value can satisfy the required structure while retaining additional properties. Restricting the keys of external data requires a runtime check separate from these type constructs.

For the local configuration in this experiment, use satisfies to catch mistakes while retaining operations specific to each value. Use an annotation to specify the type the variable should expose. Reserve as for places where other evidence supports the asserted type.

The T02 cases in the reproduction code and the execution record include both accepted declarations and deliberately invalid inputs. Do not assume diagnostic numbers or inference remain identical across compiler versions; compare declaration output when upgrading.
