title: Rate-Limited Job Queues with Fixed Concurrency, Batch Publishing, Retry, and Idempotency
description:
For rate-limited job processing, a queue and a fixed-concurrency worker are safer than adding another cron run. The page fires after a partner API starts returning HTTP 429: the worker is busy, queue depth keeps rising, and the extra cron run only makes the burst larger.

Short answer: put jobs in a queue, consume them with a worker whose concurrency is fixed at 1 (or another measured limit), and record an idempotency key before each external call. Batch publishing improves the producer path; retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue protects the downstream service.

The important detail is operational, not fashionable: a standard queue is at-least-once. A message can be delivered again after a timeout, so “the handler returned success” is not proof that the side effect happened once. Treat every delivery as a possible duplicate. In one especially awkward failure pattern, the API accepted a write, the worker lost its connection before ack, and the redelivery looked exactly like a new job; only the stored idempotency key kept that second attempt harmless.

The alert-to-action trace

Start with the alert a responder can act on. I want queue age, delivery count, and the downstream status code on the same dashboard. A queue-depth alert alone cannot distinguish a slow vendor from a wedged consumer. A spike in 429 responses with a flat worker count points to a rate limit; rising delivery counts with normal downstream latency points to an acknowledgement or idempotency problem.

Work backwards from that page. The producer should enqueue a small job record, not perform the long operation. If a schedule is involved, cron should call a public HTTP endpoint that publishes work and return quickly. Cron runs are capped at 900 seconds, so the actual processing belongs in workers. Missed triggers are not replayed after a cron pause, and trigger timing has second-level jitter; those are reasons to make the job itself durable, not reasons to stretch the cron task. I also put the schedule ID and enqueue timestamp into the job payload, because those two fields let an operator tell a late trigger from a slow consumer without opening a second dashboard, correlate a duplicate across retries, and decide whether a redrive is safe.

Then change the instrumentation. Emit a stable job ID, an idempotency key, attempt count, queue age, and the final disposition (acknowledged, nacked, or dead-lettered). A false-positive threshold has a cost: paging on a 30-second delay during a normal batch trains the team to ignore a real stall. Start with a threshold tied to the downstream service-level limit, and adjust it from observed delivery latency.

Small signals. Big difference.

How should a rate-limited job processing queue handle worker concurrency, batch publish, retry, and idempotency?

Use the queue as a shock absorber. Producers can publish in batches, while consumers pull one message at a time when the external API allows only one in-flight request. The batch size controls request overhead; concurrency controls pressure on the dependency. They are separate knobs.

Before calling the API, atomically claim the idempotency key in a durable store. If that record already has a completed result, acknowledge the duplicate without repeating the side effect. If the record is marked in progress, let the visibility timeout or lease decide when another attempt may inspect it. Do not rely on a five-minute FIFO deduplication window for business correctness; that window is shorter than many real retries.

Here is a compact worker core. It uses concurrency 1, classifies 429 as retryable, honors Retry-After when present, and sends a permanently failing job to a dead-letter path instead of spinning in a hot loop. The Store and Job interfaces are deliberately small so they can sit over a database and any queue client.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    ID       string
    Target   string
    Attempts int
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string) (alreadyDone bool, err error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(ctx context.Context) (Job, error)
    Ack(ctx context.Context, job Job) error
    Nack(ctx context.Context, job Job, retryAfter time.Duration) error
    DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, job Job, reason string) error
}

func publishBatch(ctx context.Context, baseURL, key string, body []byte) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/queue/publish_batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil { return err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("publish_batch returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return nil
}

func publishFromEnvironment(ctx context.Context, body []byte) error {
    return publishBatch(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), body)
}

type APIError struct {
    Status      int
    RetryAfter  time.Duration
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("downstream status %d", e.Status) }

func callDownstream(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    // Replace this with the vendor call; return APIError with its status and Retry-After.
    return nil
}

func run(ctx context.Context, q Queue, s Store) error {
    for {
        job, err := q.Receive(ctx)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        key := "job:" + job.ID
        done, err := s.Claim(ctx, key)
        if err != nil {
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
        }
        if done {
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        err = callDownstream(ctx, job)
        if err == nil {
            if err := s.Complete(ctx, key); err != nil {
                return q.Nack(ctx, job, 30*time.Second)
            }
            if err := q.Ack(ctx, job); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        var apiErr *APIError
        if errors.As(err, &apiErr) && apiErr.Status == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := apiErr.RetryAfter
            if delay <= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(1<<min(job.Attempts, 6)) * time.Second
            }
            return q.Nack(ctx, job, delay)
        }
        if job.Attempts >= 5 {
            return q.DeadLetter(ctx, job, err.Error())
        }
        return q.Nack(ctx, job, time.Duration(job.Attempts+1)*10*time.Second)
    }
}

func min(a, b int) int { if a < b { return a }; return b }

The example keeps one receive loop, so its effective concurrency is one. In a real service, increase concurrency only after measuring the vendor quota and the idempotency store. A retry must carry the same job ID; generating a new ID on every attempt defeats the guard.

Picking a queue without hiding the trade-offs

The right comparison is about delivery semantics and operating surface, not a feature-count contest. These are materially different choices:

Option Useful fit Delivery and retry shape Where it is a poor fit
Amazon SQS Managed buffering and FIFO ordering Standard queues are at-least-once; visibility timeout and redrive policies handle retries Not a workflow engine; replay and multi-consumer-group analytics need other services
RabbitMQ Teams that need routing exchanges and self-hosting control Acknowledgements, nack, and dead-letter exchanges are explicit Cluster operations and capacity planning become your responsibility
BullMQ Node.js applications already running Redis Attempts, backoff, and rate limiting are close to the job model Redis durability, failover, and large queue history need careful design
Infrai queues A small HTTP-first backend surface across several services Queue operations use one REST convention; keep consumer-side idempotency for at-least-once delivery No DAG or join primitive, no native debounce/throttle, and no Kafka-style replay or consumer groups

Infrai's practical advantage here is the plain REST API, so any worker that can send HTTPS can publish or consume with no SDK version to babysit. Infrai also offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, letting a scheduler, queue, and notification path share credentials and conventions instead of growing three client stacks, three rotation procedures, and separate invoices. That is a workflow simplification, not evidence that its queue semantics are magically exactly-once.

Keep the boundary visible.

Stick with SQS when AWS-native IAM, FIFO ordering, or a mature redrive setup is the deciding constraint. Choose RabbitMQ when routing topology is the product. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already a first-class dependency and the team wants a Node.js-native API. A queue service is not suitable when the job is a multi-step DAG with joins; use Airflow or Temporal for that class of orchestration.

Retry policy, limits, and the boring edges

Nack transient failures and redrive them later. Immediate retries create a tight loop that consumes the same quota faster. Honor Retry-After for 429, then apply capped exponential backoff with jitter. Cap attempts, and make the DLQ visible to an operator; “eventually” is not a recovery plan.

Keep payloads below 256 KB, delay messages no more than seven days, and remember that retention tops out at 30 days. Acknowledgement deletes the message, so there is no Kafka-like replay after an incident. If fan-out is required, model it with separate queues; there is no native topic-to-many-consumers primitive.

Your mileage may vary on the exact backoff values. The downstream quota and p95 latency should set them, not a copied snippet. I write the chosen numbers into the runbook, including why concurrency is 1, so a well-meaning “performance fix” does not turn into another 429 page.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/dags.html
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.28703v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where we represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single optimization loop that leverages continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To achieve scalability to millions of degrees of freedom (DoF), we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains that are distributed across multiple GPUs. To control peak GPU memory usage, we further slice each subdomain into smaller regions whose loss gradients are evaluated sequentially and accumulated to update the NN parameters. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. For validation, we first evaluate the proposed framework on various 2D stress-constrained benchmarks and compare our results to a conventional finite element-based approach, showing that SNTO produces super-resolution designs with sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions. We then consider large-scale 3D problems with up to eight million collocation points and distribute the training over up to eight GPUs.

title: Supabase: The Open Source Firebase Alternative
description:
A New Approach to the Problem

Supabase addresses the need for a scalable, open-source backend solution that rivals proprietary offerings like Firebase. By leveraging PostgreSQL, it provides developers with a robust database solution that supports various application types, from web to mobile to AI applications.

What is it and How it Works

Supabase is a Postgres development platform designed to offer Firebase-like functionality using open-source tools. It features a hosted Postgres database, authentication and authorization, auto-generated APIs (both REST and GraphQL), real-time subscriptions, file storage, and an AI + Vector/Embeddings Toolkit.

Architecture

Supabase operates as a hosted platform that can be accessed without installation. It can also be self-hosted for those who prefer local development. Key components include:

  • Postgres: A reliable object-relational database with extensive capabilities.
  • Realtime: An Elixir server that listens to database changes and broadcasts updates via websockets.
  • PostgREST: Transforms the PostgreSQL database into a RESTful API.
  • GoTrue: A JWT-based authentication API.
  • Storage API: Manages file storage and permissions.
  • pg_graphql: Exposes a GraphQL API.
  • postgres-meta: Manages Postgres instances through a RESTful interface.
  • Envoy: A high-performance edge and service proxy.

Key Capabilities & Developer Onboarding

Supabase offers a range of features that simplify the developer experience:

  • Auto-generated APIs: Automatically creates REST and GraphQL endpoints from your database schema.
  • Authentication: Simplifies user management with built-in JWT support.
  • Real-time subscriptions: Allows apps to receive updates instantly as data changes.
  • File storage: Easily manage files with permissions tied to Postgres roles.
  • AI toolkit: Facilitates the integration of AI and vector embeddings for advanced applications.

To get started, developers can sign up at the Supabase dashboard or clone the repository. The installation commands will depend on the chosen setup method, either hosted or self-hosted.

Who Should Use It & Integration Scenarios

Supabase is ideal for developers looking for a scalable backend solution without the constraints of proprietary services. It's particularly well-suited for:

  • Startups needing rapid development of web and mobile applications.
  • Teams looking to integrate real-time features into their applications.
  • Developers who prefer open-source tools over commercial alternatives.

However, it may not be suitable for teams requiring extremely high customization or those deeply embedded in other proprietary ecosystems.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Despite its strengths, community feedback indicates some pain points. One notable issue was raised in Issue #26785, where developers reported problems with the API Gateway and PostgreSQL logging during local development. This highlights a potential area for improvement in the local development experience, which remains a challenge for some users.

Should You Try It?

Supabase stands out as a compelling alternative to Firebase, especially for developers seeking open-source solutions. Its recent updates, including the introduction of Supabase Pipelines in public alpha and support for ChatGPT authentication, reflect its commitment to evolving in response to community needs. If you need a robust backend for your applications, Supabase is worth considering.

Originally published on GitTrending — Explore daily architectural deep-dives and quality scores for trending open-source GitHub projects.

title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
description:
arXiv:2610.28886v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

title: Doob-Based Generative Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.28990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob's $h$-transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies.

title: Shipping a Mac app without a $99 Apple Developer account
description:
I build Kopi, a free, open-source (MIT) clipboard manager for macOS and Windows. It's written in Rust with Tauri 2 and React, and it's in alpha.

This post is about one decision that took more thought than any feature: how to ship a Mac app without paying Apple $99 a year. I wrote it up as a decision record in the repo (ADR 0006), and this is the longer story behind it.

The problem: $99 a year to open without a warning

On macOS, an app downloaded from the internet opens without a Gatekeeper warning only if it is signed with an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. Getting that certificate means joining the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 a year.

For a commercial app that's a normal cost of doing business. Kopi is free and open source, and I decided it won't pay that fee every year. So the question became: what's the best Mac experience I can ship without it?

Why "just don't sign it" doesn't work

My first thought was the obvious one. Skip the paid certificate, sign the app ad-hoc (which is what you get by default when you build locally), and tell people to click through the warning.

That falls apart because of what Kopi does. A clipboard manager needs two macOS permissions:

  • Accessibility, so it can paste into the app you're using.
  • Pasteboard access ("Paste from Other Apps"), so it can see what you copy.

macOS doesn't remember these grants by app name. It ties them to the app's designated requirement, a rule baked into the code signature that says "this is the same app." For an ad-hoc signature, that requirement includes the build's own hash. Every new build has a new hash, so every new build looks like a different app to macOS.

In practice that meant my alpha testers lost both permissions on every update. Paste stopped working, history stopped recording, and they had to dig into System Settings and re-grant everything. For an app that ships frequent alpha updates, that's not something I could ask people to put up with.

The fix: a self-signed certificate that never changes

The key insight is that the designated requirement doesn't have to mention the build's hash. If you sign with a real certificate, even a self-signed one, the requirement can be based on the bundle identifier and the certificate instead.

So I created a self-signed code-signing certificate and stored it in the repository's secrets. Every release is signed with it. The resulting designated requirement looks like this:

identifier "in.devanshuverma.kopi" and certificate leaf = H"…"

That's the bundle identifier plus the hash of the certificate's leaf. Neither changes between builds. To macOS, version N+1 is the same app as version N, so the Accessibility and pasteboard grants carry over.

This doesn't make Gatekeeper happy. A self-signed certificate isn't trusted by Apple, so the app is still blocked on first open. But it solves the much worse problem of permissions resetting on every update.

You can check this yourself on any signed app:

codesign -d -r- /Applications/Kopi.app

One snag with Tauri

Tauri's bundler can sign macOS builds for you if you hand it a certificate through the APPLE_CERTIFICATE environment variable. The catch: its import only finds Apple-issued certificates, and it refuses to build a release without one. A self-signed certificate isn't Apple-issued, so that path doesn't work.

The workaround is to have the release workflow import the certificate into the keychain itself, then let the build sign with that identity.

Accepting the first-open block, and making it painless

With a self-signed certificate, Gatekeeper will block Kopi the first time someone opens it. I decided to accept that and put the effort into making the first launch as painless as I could, in three ways.

An install guide. INSTALL_ALPHA.md walks through it step by step. On macOS 15 Sequoia and later, you allow Kopi in System Settings → Privacy & Security. On macOS 14 Sonoma, you Control-click the app and choose Open. The guide also explains each permission and what happens if you don't grant it.

A .dmg background that shows the steps. Most people never read install docs, but everyone sees the disk image window when they drag the app to Applications. So the .dmg background itself shows what to do after the first block.

A one-line Terminal install. For people comfortable with Terminal, there's a script:

curl -fsSL https://kopi.devanshuverma.in/install.sh | bash

It downloads Kopi, verifies the download, and copies the app to Applications. The script doesn't quarantine the app, so Gatekeeper doesn't block the first launch.

Piping a script into bash from the internet deserves some care, so the script has a guardrail: it only installs a Kopi that is signed with Kopi's certificate. If the signature doesn't match, it doesn't install. As always, you can read the script before running it.

Updates: blocked once, never again

The first install is the only time Gatekeeper gets in the way. After that, Kopi updates itself with the Tauri updater.

The updater signs updates with its own key, separate from the code-signing certificate. It installs updates without quarantine, so Gatekeeper doesn't block them. And because every build carries the same designated requirement, the permissions survive too.

So the full experience for a tester is: one "Open Anyway" on day one, grant two permissions, and then updates just arrive. Kopi checks every few hours and installs in the background, and you can turn automatic updates off in Settings.

The options I rejected

Here's what else I considered and why I didn't go with it:

Option Why not
Developer ID + notarization Removes the first-launch warning, but costs $99 every year.
Ad-hoc signing only Free, but Accessibility and pasteboard permissions reset on every update.
Mac App Store Needs the same paid program, and Kopi can't run in the App Sandbox.
Homebrew cask The official tap disabled casks that fail Gatekeeper on 2026-09-01, and --no-quarantine is gone. A personal tap could work, but it would have to clear the quarantine flag itself. Deferred unless testers ask for it.

The honest trade-offs

This approach is not free of costs. They just aren't monetary.

Every new user has to find "Open Anyway". It lives in System Settings, and macOS 15 made it harder to get to than the old Control-click → Open trick. The install guide, the .dmg background and the Terminal script all exist to soften this, but it's still a step a notarized app wouldn't need.

Some people won't install an app macOS warns about. That's a reasonable instinct, and I'm not going to argue anyone out of it. Kopi being open source means you can read the code and build it yourself, but I accept that some people will close the warning and move on.

The certificate's private key has to be guarded. Anything signed with that key is something macOS will treat as Kopi, including inheriting the permissions people granted. That's why it lives in the repo's secrets. If it were ever lost, I'd have to create a new certificate, and every user would have to re-grant their permissions once.

For a free, alpha-stage app, I think that's the right trade. If Kopi grows to the point where the first-launch warning is the main thing holding people back, I'll revisit it. That's what the decision record is for.

Try Kopi

Kopi is open source under the MIT license and in alpha on macOS (14 Sonoma or later, Apple silicon or Intel) and Windows 10/11. It keeps your clipboard history locally with no account, filters out password-manager content, and has optional end-to-end encrypted sync over your local network.

  • Website: kopi.devanshuverma.in
  • Repo: github.com/code-devanshu/kopi

If you try it, I'd love to hear what breaks. Issues on GitHub are the best place for bug reports, and Windows feedback is especially welcome right now.

title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
description:
arXiv:2610.28871v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.

title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.

title: Trace a Java service on EKS with one annotation, zero code changes
description:
Getting traces out of a Java service usually means a ticket to the app team; in this build, one EKS deployment annotation injects the OpenTelemetry Java agent with no code change and no image rebuild. I’ll start with a plain Java service that has no tracing, then add the Operator, an Instrumentation resource, and a Collector until spans show up with service.name=orders-java.

The same image stays in place: eclipse-temurin:17.0.13_11-jdk. In my run, the instrumented rollout finished in 85 seconds.

I work a lot with observability agents inside Kubernetes clusters, so I want this kind of change proven from cluster output, not only from a diagram.

Here's how it works, and how to build it yourself.

TL;DR

  • What you get: an EKS cluster where a plain Java service emits OpenTelemetry traces without source edits or an image rebuild.
  • The trick: the OpenTelemetry Operator watches one pod-template annotation and injects the Java agent plus OTEL environment variables.
  • The proof: same image before and after, rollout finished in 85s, Collector received 4 Java client spans with service.name: Str(orders-java).
  • Time and cost: my reproduced run took 23.6 minutes total including cluster creation; the README says the EKS control plane takes about 10 minutes and the run costs well under 1 USD.

Why a healthy Java pod can still produce no traces

A service can serve traffic and still be invisible to tracing. In the baseline run, /orders returned HTTP 200s, but there was no Java agent, no OTEL environment, no init container, and no Collector.

== Evidence of the gap
-- Tracing-related env vars in the app container (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS / OTEL_*):
(none)
-- Init containers on the pod:
(none)
-- Java agent mentions in app logs:
count=0
-- OpenTelemetry CRDs / collector in the cluster:
opentelemetry CRDs installed: 0

That is the platform-team problem: the app is up, but nothing is creating spans and nothing is receiving them.

The trick: mutate the pod template, not the Java code

The OpenTelemetry Operator adds a Kubernetes Instrumentation resource. That resource tells the injected agent where to export traces and which defaults to use.

Then this annotation on the Deployment pod template turns on Java auto-instrumentation:

instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-java: "true"

On rollout, the Operator adds an init container, copies the Java agent into the pod, sets JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, sets the OTLP endpoint, and gives the service a name. In this lab, that name is orders-java.

Build it yourself in 5 steps

Step 1: Create the EKS lab cluster (about 10 minutes for the control plane)

This creates a VPC, an EKS cluster, and two self-managed t3.medium worker nodes joined with nodeadm.

git clone https://github.com/Abhimanyu9988/Abhimanyu9988.github.io.git
cd Abhimanyu9988.github.io/labs/trace-a-java-service-on-eks-with-one-annotation-zero-code
export AWS_REGION=eu-central-1 LAB_NAME=otel-java TF_VAR_lab_name=otel-java
terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve
./reproduce.sh

reproduce.sh waits for nodes, applies k8s/app.yaml, starts the load generator, and prints the before-state evidence.

If your clone only has main.tf, add a small Terraform file with the variable declarations and provider wiring the README calls out. Set permissions_boundary to null if you do not use one.

variable "region" {
  type    = string
  default = "eu-central-1"
}

variable "lab_name" {
  type = string
}

variable "permissions_boundary" {
  type    = string
  default = null
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.region
}

Step 2: Keep the app Deployment plain on purpose

The sample app lives in k8s/app.yaml. It mounts Java source from a ConfigMap and runs it with the JDK image. For your own service, the annotation still belongs under spec.template.metadata.annotations.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-java
  namespace: demo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-java
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-java
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: eclipse-temurin:17.0.13_11-jdk
          command: ["java", "-Xmx256m", "/app/Main.java"]
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            tcpSocket:
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 200m
              memory: 384Mi
            limits:
              memory: 768Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: src
              mountPath: /app
      volumes:
        - name: src
          configMap:
            name: orders-java-src

Change the image, command, ports, and probes for your service. Keep the pod-template location for the annotation.

Step 3: Add a Collector that proves spans in logs

The Collector manifest is k8s/collector.yaml. It uses the debug exporter so the proof stays inside Kubernetes logs instead of depending on a tracing backend.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: observability
---
apiVersion: opentelemetry.io/v1beta1
kind: OpenTelemetryCollector
metadata:
  name: otel
  namespace: observability
spec:
  mode: deployment
  replicas: 1
  config:
    receivers:
      otlp:
        protocols:
          grpc:
            endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
          http:
            endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
    processors:
      batch: {}
    exporters:
      debug:
        verbosity: detailed
    service:
      pipelines:
        traces:
          receivers: [otlp]
          processors: [batch]
          exporters: [debug]

In a real cluster, keep the OTLP receiver and replace the debug exporter with your tracing backend exporter.

Step 4: Point Java auto-instrumentation at the Collector

The Instrumentation resource is k8s/instrumentation.yaml. It points Java agents in the demo namespace at the in-cluster Collector service and turns off metrics and logs for this tracing-only lab.

apiVersion: opentelemetry.io/v1alpha1
kind: Instrumentation
metadata:
  name: java-auto
  namespace: demo
spec:
  exporter:
    endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4318
  propagators:
    - tracecontext
    - baggage
  sampler:
    type: parentbased_always_on
  env:
    - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL
      value: http/protobuf
    - name: OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER
      value: none
    - name: OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER
      value: none

Change the endpoint if your Collector runs in a different namespace or you send directly to an external endpoint.

Step 5: Install the Operator and add the one annotation

fix.sh installs the pinned Operator Helm chart 0.71.2, applies k8s/collector.yaml and k8s/instrumentation.yaml, patches the Deployment, waits for rollout, and prints Collector logs.

./fix.sh
kubectl -n observability logs deploy/otel-collector --tail=-1

The patch it applies is the only app-side change: instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-java: "true".

The proof: same image, injected agent, Collector received spans

Stage What changed Evidence
Before App deployed with no tracing no JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, no init containers, OpenTelemetry CRDs installed: 0
Operator OpenTelemetry Operator installed chart opentelemetry-operator-0.71.2, app version 0.110.0
Collector OTLP receiver created service exposed 4317/TCP,4318/TCP inside the cluster
Annotation Deployment patched rollout finished in 85s, image still eclipse-temurin:17.0.13_11-jdk
Trace proof Java agent exported spans 4 spans received, service.name: Str(orders-java)

After rollout, the new pod showed the auto-instrumentation init container and Java agent startup line:

== Injected pod: orders-java-578744fdb4-lxj4j
-- init containers:
opentelemetry-auto-instrumentation-java
-- agent image:
ghcr.io/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-operator/autoinstrumentation-java:1.33.5
-- app log head:
Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS:  -javaagent:/otel-auto-instrumentation-java/javaagent.jar
[otel.javaagent 2026-10-19 18:15:24:512 +0000] [main] INFO io.opentelemetry.javaagent.tooling.VersionLogger - opentelemetry-javaagent - version: 1.33.5
orders-java listening on 8080

The Collector excerpt is cut, but it shows the important path: Java agent to OTLP HTTP to Collector debug output.

2026-10-19T18:15:40.063Z    info    ResourceSpans #0
...
     -> service.name: Str(orders-java)
     -> telemetry.sdk.language: Str(java)
InstrumentationScope io.opentelemetry.java-http-client 1.33.5-alpha
Span #0
    Name           : GET
    Kind           : Client
...

The 4 spans in this run are outbound Java HTTP client spans from the /orders to /inventory call. The build proves the Java auto-instrumentation and Collector path; it did not capture inbound server spans for /orders in this run.

Use it for services you do not want to rebuild

  • Platform-owned rollout: create the Operator, Collector, and Instrumentation resource once per namespace, then let teams opt in with the pod-template annotation.
  • Service naming: accept the deployment-derived OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, or set resource.opentelemetry.io/service.name on the pod template if your naming standard is different.
  • Backend swap: keep the same app annotation and Instrumentation shape, but replace the debug exporter with the exporter your tracing platform needs.

Clean up (the EKS cluster and EC2 nodes cost money while they run)

Remove the Kubernetes objects first, then destroy the AWS resources.

./cleanup.sh
terraform destroy -auto-approve

What I didn't test

  • I did not send these spans to a production tracing backend; I used the Collector debug exporter only.
  • I did not capture inbound server spans or parent/child links in this run.
  • I did not test private subnets, managed node groups, Fargate, IRSA, Node.js, .NET, or Python auto-instrumentation.

Every file in this lab

Everything above runs from these files. Open any of them to copy it, or clone the repo as shown:

  • README.md
  • cleanup.sh
  • fix.sh
  • k8s/app.yaml
  • k8s/collector.yaml
  • k8s/instrumentation.yaml
  • main.tf
  • providers.tf
  • reproduce.sh
  • evidence/: the raw output of my run

Sources

  • OpenTelemetry Operator for Kubernetes
  • OpenTelemetry automatic instrumentation with the Operator

I built this in a disposable AWS lab. The lab code and raw output are in the repo. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by me.

title: Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first
description:
This is part 1 of the series "Protect Your Own Service Yourself — Self-Defense Security in the Age of AI." Do the checks you can yourself; when it's hard, EarthLink Network can run the assessment for you, and fix the gaps you can't fix on your own.

Series contents

  1. Anyone can attack now, with AI — check your own site first (this article)
  2. What attackers now hold: when AI runs the attack itself (coming soon)
  3. Before you start: test only what is yours, without breaking production (coming soon)
  4. Testing from the outside (1): setup and the first run (coming soon)
  5. Testing from the outside (2): attack tools and legitimate scanners find different things (coming soon)
  6. Checking the code you wrote: static analysis (coming soon)
  7. Checking the parts you depend on: libraries and packages (coming soon)
  8. Checking your infrastructure settings for gaps (coming soon)
  9. Collect every result in one place and decide what to fix first (coming soon)
  10. How to fix what you found: three ways (coming soon)
  11. When you cannot fix it yourself: a maintenance contract (coming soon)
  12. Keep checking automatically every day — from building to protecting (coming soon)

In the summer of 2025, a free attack tool called Villager went up on a public site where developers share code. You tell it "look into this site," and an AI decides on its own where to look, what to try, and what to do next. In about two months, before the press picked it up, it was downloaded roughly 10,000 times.

That is the starting point for this series. Attack tools like this are now free and available to anyone. The people who attack already have them and are already using them. So instead of finding out after a break-in, check your own service yourself first, find the weak spots, and fix them. That is the most reliable defense you have.

Security is no longer only a problem for companies big enough to be targeted. Even if nobody has heard of you, machines now try every site on the internet, one after another. This part explains why that matters now, and what the series will do.

All 12 parts of this series

Here is the plan, up front.

  1. Part 1 (this one): why do this now. The thinking behind it, and how the series runs.
  2. Part 2: what tools attackers hold today, and what it means for an AI to run an attack by itself. Not how to get them, but what such an opponent can do.
  3. Part 3: what to decide before you start testing. Test on a separate copy of your setup so you do not break the live service your customers use, and never look into anything that is not yours.
  4. Part 4: testing from the outside. Setup and the first run.
  5. Part 5: the results of testing from the outside. We compare what attack tools find with what legitimate security scanners find.
  6. Part 6: checking the code you wrote by reading it without running it (static analysis).
  7. Part 7: checking the parts you depend on (libraries and packages) for known weaknesses. This is where findings tend to pile up.
  8. Part 8: checking your server and cloud settings for gaps.
  9. Part 9: collecting the scattered results in one place and deciding what to fix first, including the risk from partners and parts you are connected to.
  10. Part 10: how to fix what you found. There are three ways.
  11. Part 11: when you cannot fix it yourself, the option of a maintenance contract.
  12. Part 12: keep the checks running automatically every day. From building things to protecting them.

The service we test is promptflow, a service our own company builds and runs.

October 2026: breach announcements kept coming

In October 2026, data breach announcements did not stop. In the US, the count of people affected by the 2025 breach at Oracle's health division (formerly Cerner) rose to about 20 million. Heart monitor maker iRhythm disclosed that data on about 8.2 million people had been stolen. In the UK, online retailer ASOS disclosed a leak of customer data, and Frontline Education, which makes software for schools, disclosed a leak of school staff data. In Japan, the parcel carrier Yamato Transport announced a leak of 5.31 million records of personal data, and one count found more than 40 breach announcements there in about a month.

Ransomware is an attack that locks or steals a company's data and demands payment to give it back. Worldwide, according to the security company Bitdefender, the criminals behind it named 790 organizations as victims in September alone, the month before, 30% more than in September a year earlier.

Numbers like these can feel like someone else's problem. What caught my attention was who the victims were: a parcel carrier, an online store, health care companies, school administration. Ordinary companies, with no special reason to be targeted.

The victims were not special companies

Reading the reports, I noticed something else. The way in was not special either. A partner's server. Setting mistakes in an API (the set entry point that other systems and apps use to request data from a service) or in an admin screen. An old bug in a piece of software. A password that someone reused and that leaked elsewhere. Put them side by side, and these are ordinary paths that many companies have right now.

Take the reused password. Some other service, nothing to do with you, leaks a list of email addresses and passwords. The attacker enters those pairs, one after another, into hundreds of unrelated sites. Wherever someone reused the password, the login goes through. Nobody broke into your site. A password that leaked from some other service, and that your user had reused, simply worked on it. A machine does this nonstop, not a person. So even if your own password handling is solid, someone can get in because of what happened on the user's side.

Attacks also work in a different order now. A human attacker chose a target first, with a motive, and spent time on one company. Automated attacks go through the whole internet mechanically, site after site, and pick up whatever happens to have a hole. Whether your service is famous or large does not matter. If it is public and has a hole, that is enough. So "nobody would bother with a small business like us" does not hold. You are not being targeted; everything is being checked at once.

Attacks no longer need special skills

This is the biggest change. Until recently, attacking took real skill: a person had to work out for themselves where to look and what to try next.

Think of a door lock. The common pin tumbler lock, where you insert a key and turn it, could be picked by a skilled person with thin metal picks, setting the pins one at a time by feel. Few people could do that, and that was part of the protection. Then came devices you simply hold against the lock: press a button, and the lock turns. No skill needed. That is why people moved to locks that are harder to copy and pick, such as dimple keys, with rows of small dents on the surface.

The same thing is happening in security right now.

AI now plans the steps of an attack

Since around the summer of 2025, tools that hand the planning of an attack to an AI have been given away for free.

Villager, from a Chinese company, is the example I opened with. Part 2 covers what it does in detail.

Villager is not the only one. Several tools like it, where AI runs the attack by itself, sit on public code-sharing sites and have been copied many times. How far have they spread? One has about 7,700 copies (forks, where someone copies the project to keep their own version), another about 4,700, another about 2,900. When one gets attention, hundreds of similar copies spread right away. That is how free software works. It is not something anyone can stop.

Some of these are legitimate tools built for defenders, presented as a way to "find and fix the weaknesses in your app." In this series we use both kinds on our own service, because you only learn where someone can really get in by checking the way attackers do it. Then we show how their findings differ.

My point here is not about good or bad. It is a fact: the skill barrier has dropped to almost zero. One short instruction, and anyone, in theory even a child, can move an attack forward. The time when skill itself was the protection is almost over.

Small companies are the least likely to have checked

Small companies are the most exposed to these automated attacks. Large companies have security staff who test their systems regularly, and budget for outside firms. Sole proprietors and companies of a few people have neither. So the businesses that have checked the least are probed by these automated scans just as often as everyone else. They have not checked, so they do not know they have weak spots, and they learn about it only after the leak.

This is why I care about tools that run with one click. If a tool does the planning, a small company without security staff can still run a check at least once. As long as checking takes expert knowledge, people stop at "I know it matters, but we can't." The same thing that lowered the barrier to attack has lowered the barrier to checking. Not all of this is bad news.

Hiding information only hurts the defenders

Whenever I write like this, I get the same pushback: "Don't name those tools. You're giving attackers a lead." I think that idea is backwards.

Attackers do not learn about tools from honest articles like this one. They got them elsewhere, long ago, and that is why they are attacking right now. The pile of breaches in October 2026 is the proof. Keeping quiet did not prevent any of them.

So who is hurt when information is hidden? Only the people with no other way to find it: the defenders. Attackers already know which tools are out there and what they can do; only the defenders do not. They do not even know where they are exposed. That is the most dangerous state to be in.

Defenders benefit from this being public. Once it is known which weakness a tool goes after, software makers can fix it quickly and users can review their settings. If it were hidden, nobody could fix anything, and attackers would quietly keep using it.

It was the same with locks. Keeping a lock's design secret does not help if the lock is weak. A strong lock is strong because it holds even when everyone knows how it works. Software security is the same: do not protect it by hiding, build it to hold up when it is known. That is why, in this series, I name the tools, say what they do, and show the results of checking our own service, without hiding any of it.

First, check your own service yourself

What to do is simple. Take the same tools attackers use, run them against your own service first, find the weak spots, and fix them. If a key that works on almost any lock is on sale, first see whether it works on your own door. If it does, switch to a stronger lock. That is all.

We limit the target to our own service, promptflow, for two reasons. Because it is ours, we decide how far to test, and we can make sure the test copy does not reach real users or outside services. And we are the ones best placed to fix its weak spots. Doing the whole loop of testing, finding, and fixing on something we own seemed the most honest and useful way to show it.

promptflow is a service we build and run for working with AI. Users log in, it holds data, and it connects to other systems through APIs. It has the same kinds of entry points used in the October 2026 breaches, which makes it a good subject. If we find a weak spot in ours, the same spot may be weak in yours. We show the steps exactly as we run them, so you can check the same things on your service.

"Is it safe?" is a call a person makes after testing

I believe that from now on, people's job is to make decisions: AI does the drafting, and people make the final call. "Is my service safe?" is exactly this kind of decision. And a decision needs facts from real testing. Saying "it's probably fine" without testing is not a decision. It is a hope.

Until recently, attackers had the advantage: their attacks were automated, while defenders checked by hand, one thing at a time. Now defenders can use the same automation. If attackers can try with one click, so can we. There is no reason not to use it.

What we will actually do in this series

From Part 4, we test promptflow for real. Here is the approach, without the specific steps yet.

We check from two directions.

  1. From the outside, the way an attacker would: we try the service from outside, just as attackers do. The login screen, the API entrances, the admin screen, files we never meant to make public. We list those entry points, check that each lets in only who it should, and confirm whether a weakness we found can really be reached from outside. Something that is risky in theory and something that can actually be touched from outside are different things.
  2. From the inside, by reading: with your own service, you can see the inside too. The code you wrote, the parts you use (libraries and packages), and your server and cloud settings. We read these three without running them and check for known weaknesses and setting gaps.

Protecting only your own service is not enough. If a partner you connect to, or a system you share with other companies, is broken into, attackers can come in from there; in the October 2026 breaches, one way in was a partner's server. So we also map what your service connects to and which parts and outside services it relies on, and count those risks in the results. That does not mean testing anyone else's site. It means collecting the connections and the known weaknesses in them.

Checking only from outside, or only from inside, leaves gaps. Collect both sets of results in one place, decide what to fix first, and fix it. What you cannot fix yourself, hand to someone who can. That is one full round.

AI tools can chain these checks together without a person giving every instruction. You do not need an expensive AI model or an expert; a cheap model run many times gets you a long way, which is exactly how attackers work too. So even a first-timer can realistically run the whole thing once. From Part 4, I go through it step by step with the promptflow screens.

Checking is also not something you do once. A service keeps changing, and new weaknesses keep being found. If attackers retry automatically, defenders should re-check automatically too. New weaknesses in the parts you use are found almost every day, so the most reliable way is to run the code and library checks automatically every day. Testing from the outside is not a daily job, and it runs against a separate copy, not your live service. The last part of the series shows that setup.

Will testing break my own service?

The natural worry is: "If I use an attack tool on my own service, will it break?" Honestly, depending on how you do it, it can put a load on the service. So Part 3 explains how to test on a separate copy of your setup, or on a copy of the source code, instead of the live service your customers use, and where to draw the line so you do not push too hard. Choose where you test and how hard you push, and there is no need to be afraid. Running your live service without ever checking it is far more dangerous.

Never use these on anyone else's site

One last warning. The tools and ideas in this series are for checking services you own. Never use them on someone else's site, or on any system you do not have the rights to. It breaks the law, and it is the exact opposite of what this series is for. Only check what is yours.

Where the information in this article comes from

What I wrote here about attack tools is based on news reports and public information. The results of testing our own service start in Part 4, with real, unedited screenshots: where we found weaknesses, where we found none, and what was reported as a weakness when it was not.

Next time

Next time, we look inside the tools attackers hold. What does it actually look like, step by step, when an AI runs an attack by itself? As a defender, what should you assume? Again, I will not explain how to get them. The goal is to know what this opponent can do, so you can calmly check your own service.

In this series, in an age when attack tools are free and one click away for anyone, I show step by step how to check your own service yourself and close the gaps before someone else finds them. The target is always our own service; the series does not cover attacking anyone else's site.
If running the checks yourself is hard, EarthLink Network can do the assessment for you. Found a gap you can't fix? We'll handle the fix. Feel free to reach out.
If this was useful, please like and follow.

Our products are listed at https://www.eln.ne.jp/products

EarthLink Network builds its own products to run the whole company on AI — each one born from a need along the way. See the full index of what we build:

title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
description:
arXiv:2610.27026v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.

title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.28693v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 6: Transaction Management and Locking
description:
Hibernate and Spring ensure data integrity during concurrent operations. It is crucial to understand two key mechanisms here: transactions, which define the boundaries of a unit of work, and locks, which resolve conflicts during concurrent access.

Transaction Management in Spring and Hibernate

At the core is the @Transactional annotation, which wraps a method in a transaction via Spring AOP (proxies) and decides when to commit or roll it back.

Key point — Rollback Rules:
By default, Spring rolls back a transaction only for unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error). For checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception, but not RuntimeException), the transaction commits by default. This is a frequent source of errors: a developer throws an IOException and expects a rollback, but the data is partially saved.

// Explicit rollback management
@Transactional(
    // rollback for checked exceptions
    rollbackFor = { IOException.class, PaymentGatewayException.class },
    // commit for RuntimeException (e.g., to retry later) 
    noRollbackFor = { OptimisticLockException.class } 
)
public void processOrder(Order order) throws IOException {
    // ...
}

Important: A rollback will only trigger if the exception "escapes" the @Transactional method. If you catch it inside the method, Spring will not know about it, and the transaction will commit.

Isolation Levels:
Spring allows you to explicitly specify the isolation level (Isolation.READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, etc.). By default, it uses Isolation.DEFAULT, which relies on the underlying database's default settings. This can be dangerous if different environments (e.g., staging and production) use different databases with different default levels — the code's behavior will become unpredictable.

Propagation:
Defines how a method's transaction relates to an existing one. For example, Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW always creates a new transaction, suspending the outer one. This is useful for operations that must be committed independently (e.g., audit logging).

Locking: Conflict Resolution Strategies

Hibernate, like JPA, offers two fundamentally different approaches to locking: optimistic and pessimistic.

Optimistic Locking

Based on the assumption that conflicts are rare. Transactions do not lock data during reads, but before committing, they check if anyone else has modified the data since it was read.

It is implemented via a field annotated with @Version (a number or Timestamp). On every update, Hibernate executes SQL like UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If no rows satisfy the WHERE condition (because the version changed), an OptimisticLockException is thrown.

  • When to use: For most web applications and scenarios with rare conflicts. It is a scalable and performant approach.
  • LockModeType modes: OPTIMISTIC (version check on commit) and OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT (forced version increment even without actual changes).

Pessimistic Locking

Based on the assumption that conflicts are likely. Data is locked at the database level for the duration of the transaction, preventing other transactions from modifying or reading it.

It is implemented via LockModeType (e.g., PESSIMISTIC_WRITE), which translates to SQL SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

  • When to use: For critical operations with high contention (e.g., deducting money from an account), where rollbacks and retries are undesirable or too costly.
  • Risks: Locks are held until the end of the transaction, which can lead to deadlocks and reduced throughput.

Typical Mistakes and Pitfalls

  1. Misunderstanding rollback rules: Expecting a rollback for a checked exception, or conversely, committing after a RuntimeException that was caught and swallowed inside the method.
  2. "Poisoned" session: After an exception (e.g., DataIntegrityViolationException), the Hibernate session may be marked as rollback-only. Subsequent operations in this transaction will fail. The solution is to use Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW to isolate the failing operation.
  3. Spurious OptimisticLockException: Can occur when using orphanRemoval and complex object graphs, where Hibernate attempts to update an already deleted entity. Sometimes em.flush() followed by em.clear() helps to synchronize the state.
  4. Mixing strategies: The presence of @Version (optimistic locking) does not bypass the version check even when using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic locking). If another transaction modified the data, an OptimisticLockException will still be thrown upon update.
  5. Long transactions: Holding a pessimistic lock or an open session during user interaction (e.g., via OpenSessionInView) is a direct path to connection pool exhaustion and deadlocks.

What to Use and When

Feature Optimistic Locking Pessimistic Locking
Principle Conflicts are rare. Check before commit. Conflicts are likely. Lock in the DB.
Implementation @Version LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)
When to use Most web apps, CRUD, rare updates. Critical operations with high contention (finance, reservations).
Risks OptimisticLockException on conflict (requires handling/retry). Deadlocks, reduced throughput, long-held locks.

Summary

  1. Spring rolls back only RuntimeException and Error by default. For checked exceptions, rollback must be explicitly specified via rollbackFor.
  2. The exception must "escape" the @Transactional method for Spring to perform a rollback. Do not swallow exceptions inside the method.
  3. Optimistic locking (@Version) is a version check upon update. It does not lock data, but merely reports a conflict (OptimisticLockException). This is the default choice for most systems.
  4. Pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) is an actual lock at the database level. Use it sparingly, only where its absence would cause a critical data integrity error.
  5. Isolation.DEFAULT can lead to different behavior across environments. For critical operations, specify the isolation level explicitly.
  6. Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW is your tool for isolating failing operations (e.g., logging) that should not affect the main transaction's rollback.

title: Make targets big enough to hit (Web HIG tip #12)
description:
Open your site on a phone and try to tap the "×" that closes a banner, the edit icon in a table row, or the second of three pagination numbers. If you hit the wrong one, or have to zoom in first, the target is too small. People with tremors, limited dexterity, or a phone in one hand on a moving bus miss it much more often.

Web HIG tip #12 (Quick #75 / HIG-A11Y-007): Interactive targets MUST be at least 24×24 CSS px. Primary touch actions SHOULD use 44×44 CSS px.

Why it matters

A target is the area that responds to a click or tap, not the icon you can see:

  • A 16px icon with no padding gives the finger a 16px target, even if the design looks roomy around it
  • Small targets packed side by side turn a miss into a wrong action: delete instead of edit, next page instead of previous
  • Icon-only toolbars, close buttons, table row actions, and pagination links are the usual offenders
  • Pointer users with tremors or limited dexterity are affected too, not only touch users

The full HIG covers this in §5.4, Target Sizes, and it separates two levels on purpose. 24×24 CSS px is the MUST (HIG-A11Y-007, severity error), aligned with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. The WCAG-defined exceptions apply, and the HIG does not redefine them. 44×44 CSS px is a SHOULD, an ergonomic recommendation for primary touch actions. It is not a WCAG AA floor and is not part of HIG-A11Y-007 enforcement, so a 32px secondary button is not a defect. Quick #20 is the companion rule: targets must not overlap in ways that cause mis-taps.

The rule of thumb

Ask: if I tap the middle of the gap between two controls, do I know which one I'll get?

Grow the hit area, not the icon. Padding is usually all it takes.

<button class="icon-button" type="button" aria-label="Close">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" width="16" height="16">…</svg>
</button>

/* 16px icon, 24px minimum target, 44px on coarse pointers */
.icon-button {
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  min-inline-size: 24px;
  min-block-size: 24px;
}

@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .icon-button {
    min-inline-size: 44px;
    min-block-size: 44px;
  }
}

The visible icon stays the same size. The button around it grows, and that is the part that receives the tap.

Do this instead

  • Measure the clickable box, not the glyph. In DevTools, inspect the <button> or <a>, not the <svg> inside it
  • Use padding or min-inline-size / min-block-size to reach 24×24, and aim for 44×44 on primary touch actions such as submit, add to cart, and the main navigation toggle
  • If a control has to stay visually small, keep enough space around it. WCAG's spacing exception covers an undersized target only when a 24px circle centred on it doesn't intersect another target or another such circle
  • Links inside a sentence are covered by WCAG's inline exception. Footer link lists, tag chips, and breadcrumb rows are not sentences, so give them room
  • Put the size on the component (your IconButton, Chip, Pagination) so every use inherits it, and use your spacing tokens rather than one-off pixel values (Quick #63)

Quick check for your app

Open a page on example.com in your browser's device mode, or on a real phone. Inspect each icon button, close control, chip, and pagination link, and read the box size of the element that has the click handler. Anything under 24×24 needs more size or more space around it. Then try the primary actions with your thumb, one-handed: those are the ones that should reach 44×44. A tool can measure boxes, but only trying it tells you whether the controls are easy to hit.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/27
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/make-targets-big-enough-to-hit-web-hig-tip-12-2n50
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mygutvbn5227

title: A loop tempo ramp belongs at the repeat boundary
description:
A practice loop can start below a score's written tempo and rise a little on each pass. The useful boundary is the end of the selected passage: changing speed while notes from that pass are still being scheduled makes the transition harder to reason about.

In Pianory's score player, the sheet UI supplies a five-percentage-point tempo step. The player reaches the end of the selected passage, checks whether it will repeat, then raises the percentage and caps the ramp at 100% of the written tempo. It reports the new percentage and anchors the next pass at the loop's start. A 90% start with a five-point step therefore reports 95%, then 100%, and stops rising.

The passage range resolves to quarter-note positions with an exclusive end event. Notes that cross the passage end are clipped to that boundary before the next pass is scheduled. Those rules let the repeat restart at a defined score position instead of inheriting a note tail past the loop.

One important distinction: 100% is the ramp's destination, not the tempo slider's maximum. The general tempo control permits 25%–125%. The optional ramp is a practice behavior layered on top of that control. It advances at a repeat boundary; it does not measure whether the player performed the passage cleanly.

A focused unit test starts a one-measure loop at 90% with a five-point step and checks callbacks [95, 100] plus the final setting. Timeline tests cover the exclusive range. Those checks do not measure audible note-onset spacing after a tempo change, so I would add an audio-scheduling regression test before claiming that every ramped pass sounds exact in a browser.

This is a narrow implementation lesson: make the repeat boundary explicit, update the tempo once there, and keep the next pass anchored to the selected score range.

AI assisted with drafting this article; I checked its claims against the repository and focused tests. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app used in this example.
