title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
description:
arXiv:2610.28799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.

title: PW-Pruning: Phase-Aware Expert Selection for Speech-Centric Omni-Modal Models
description:
arXiv:2610.26891v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.

title: Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
description:
arXiv:2610.28325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Factual sycophancy, a language model's deference to a user's false beliefs, is usually understood as a bid for the user's approval at the expense of truthfulness. We argue that this framing over-emphasizes the user and propose viewing sycophancy as a failure within the broader and generally useful process of in-context updating, by which models revise their answers based on information supplied during an interaction. We support this view with behavioral and mechanistic evidence. First, models' responses to user claims sit within a broader pattern of source-sensitive updating. They revise their answers in response to information attributed to external sources as well, more so when it appears better supported, and their deference to the user persists even when no user approval is at stake. Second, the internal components that support deference to the user are also causally important for in-context updating more broadly. Our results suggest that factual sycophancy arises when in-context updating gives a user's assertion excessive weight relative to its evidence. Because sycophancy is embedded in this process, reducing it risks reducing useful updating as well, a trade-off that calls for evaluations measuring both behaviors and mitigations that decouple them.

title: Deriving a Ghost theme palette from one accent color
description:
The constraint: Ghost gives you one color

Ghost themes get exactly one brand color from the admin: --ghost-accent-color. That value often needs to carry most of the UI: links, buttons, hovers, subtle backgrounds, borders.

You can add more theme settings, but it is possible to treat that single accent as the source of truth and derive everything else in CSS.

With one custom property in package.json, the theme can generate tints, hover states, borders and soft backgrounds using color-mix() and, where helpful, oklch(). No extra admin fields are required.

Starting point: normalize the accent color

Ghost exposes the accent color as --ghost-accent-color on :root. A simple first step is to mirror it into a small set of semantic tokens so the rest of the CSS never touches the raw accent directly.

:root {
  /* from Ghost admin */
  --ghost-accent-color: #ff1a75;

  /* base semantic tokens */
  --accent: var(--ghost-accent-color);
  --accent-text-on-solid: #fff;
}

--accent is the only color that is really “brand”. Everything else hangs off it with color-mix().

Using color-mix() for hover and focus states

A straightforward use is hover states. For buttons and links you can create a slightly stronger accent on hover without guessing a separate color.

:root {
  --accent-strong: color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 85%, black);
}

.button-primary {
  background: var(--accent);
  color: var(--accent-text-on-solid);
}

.button-primary:hover,
.button-primary:focus-visible {
  background: var(--accent-strong);
}

This works well for mid-range colors, but it can break down at the extremes. A very dark accent mixed toward black barely changes. A very light accent mixed toward black can jump too hard and fail contrast against white text.

Very light and very dark accents

Two cases tend to cause trouble:

  • Almost-white accents, like #fbe9ff or very light pastels.
  • Almost-black accents, like #050505 or deep navy.

With almost-white accents, Ghost often pairs them with dark text, not white. If you always use --accent-text-on-solid: #fff and darken the accent on hover, the background can still end up with too little contrast against white text.

With almost-black accents, mixing toward black on hover does very little visually. The button looks unchanged.

Instead of assuming the accent is a normal mid-tone, it helps to reason about it in oklch().

Using oklch to reason about lightness

oklch() exposes a lightness component that behaves more linearly than srgb. That makes it easier to decide two things:

  • Should text on the accent be light or dark?
  • Should hover move the accent lighter or darker?

First, convert the accent to oklch() in a custom property. Browsers can do this conversion implicitly:

:root {
  --accent-oklch: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 100%, black 0%);
}

Then derive lighter and darker variants by nudging the lightness channel via mixes toward black or white.

:root {
  /* Slightly darker for hover, slightly lighter for subtle backgrounds */
  --accent-strong-oklch: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 90%, black 10%);
  --accent-soft-oklch:   color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 90%, white 10%);
}

These are still oklch-space colors, but the browser returns them as usable CSS colors. For many accents this gives smoother steps than mixing in srgb, especially for saturated colors.

Choosing text color based on accent lightness

Ghost itself decides whether to use light or dark text on the accent in some places, but inside a theme it is useful to have a consistent rule. Accents above a certain lightness can be treated as “light backgrounds” and use dark text on them.

There is no native if() in CSS yet, so a practical approach is to define two modes in the theme, then switch modes based on a class that is set server-side or through a small script that inspects the computed accent color.

:root {
  --accent-text-on-solid: #fff;
}

.theme--accent-light {
  --accent-text-on-solid: #111;
}

A script can read getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--accent'), convert it to oklch() using a helper, and toggle .theme--accent-light if the lightness is above a threshold. Extremely light accents then flip to dark text, and the hover and active colors derived from oklch stay on the right side of the contrast line.

Subtle backgrounds and borders from the same accent

For cards, badges and inline highlights you can use the accent to create a soft background and a slightly stronger border.

:root {
  --accent-bg-soft: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 12%, white);
  --accent-border-soft: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 45%, white);
}

.badge {
  background: var(--accent-bg-soft);
  border: 1px solid var(--accent-border-soft);
  color: var(--accent);
}

For very dark accents, mixing toward white like this keeps the badge readable without turning it into a loud block. For very light accents, the badge is barely tinted; the accent still shows up in the border and text.

The same pattern works for focus outlines:

:root {
  --accent-outline: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 65%, white);
}

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--accent-outline);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

Checking contrast without designing per brand

Because the accent is user-controlled, you cannot guarantee perfect contrast for every possible color. You can only make it harder to get into trouble.

A practical approach is to test a small grid of accent colors locally:

  • Very light pastel
  • Mid-tone brand color
  • Deep saturated color
  • Near-black

For each, check a few key pairs in a contrast checker:

  • --accent vs --accent-text-on-solid
  • --accent-bg-soft vs body text
  • Focus outline vs page background

oklch-based mixes help keep these pairs within acceptable ranges for normal accents. Extremely low-contrast choices from the admin, such as an almost white accent on a white site background, will still be low contrast, but the theme does not make that worse by using the accent for long-form body text.

Fallbacks for browsers without color-mix()

color-mix() is not universal yet, so the theme should keep a basic experience for older browsers.

One pattern is:

:root {
  /* basic fallback */
  --accent-strong: var(--accent);
  --accent-bg-soft: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.03);
}

@supports (color-mix(in srgb, black, white)) {
  :root {
    --accent-strong: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 85%, black);
    --accent-bg-soft: color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent) 12%, white);
  }
}

In browsers without @supports (color-mix), buttons still use the accent, they just do not get a more intense hover color. Soft backgrounds fall back to a neutral tint instead of an accent-tinted one.

Keeping everything wired to one variable

The main benefit of this approach is that the entire palette stays wired to --ghost-accent-color. When someone changes the accent in Ghost admin, links, buttons, cards, focus states and badges all follow without touching the theme settings.

The trade-off is that you have to be conservative: avoid using the accent for long-form text, keep strong backgrounds limited, and lean on oklch and color-mix() to keep hover and subtle states in a safe range.

title: GRaSP: Latency-Aware Optimization for Geo-Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.26938v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, where wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules compete with retrieval quality. Conventional pipelines rank by semantic similarity alone and ignore where content lives, inflating tail latency and cost. We formalize the Geo-RAG Selection Problem (GRaSP), a drop-in re-scoring layer that decays relevance by latency and adds an optional cost penalty under a cardinality budget and per-region caps, with no retraining. We first settle its complexity: the base formulation is a linear objective over a partition matroid, solved optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm, rather than NP-hard as a knapsack framing suggests, with hardness entering only under an additive egress budget. On a five-node CloudLab testbed emulating a four-region WAN over the Natural Questions corpus (2.68M passages), GRaSP's benefit is placement-dependent: under uniform placement it cuts fetch latency at negligible quality cost; under topical (residency-like) placement it traces a recall-latency Pareto frontier that dominates relevance-only, nearest-k, and a latency-budgeted baseline. At a moderate latency setting, GRaSP lowers P90 fetch latency by 41% while retaining 78% of relevance-only's recall, with sub-millisecond selection overhead, stable to 200 queries/s. Findings generalize across four public BEIR benchmarks. In end-to-end question answering, GRaSP reduces context-fetch latency by 43% while remaining within 0.062 absolute EM of relevance-only retrieval.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

title: Realtime Message Order: Node.js Delivery Guarantees Explained for Live Auctions
description:
Short answer: Message order is not delivery order in a live auction: treat the database sequence as authoritative, put that sequence in every notification, and make a detected gap trigger a state refetch rather than a message replay.

The server may commit bid 418 before bid 419, yet a reconnecting browser can observe 419 first because messages take different paths and clients resume at different moments. Infrai fits teams that want realtime publication and jobs/queues capabilities under one REST API, one key, and one bill. Its limitation is the same consolidation that makes it convenient: teams needing a specialist recovery model or client ecosystem should evaluate Ably, Pusher, or PubNub instead.

That choice also controls the real bill. For an auction with 20,000 connected bidders, 40 accepted bid changes per second, and a 90-minute session, the dominant term is fan-out: 40 x 20,000 x 5,400, or 4.32 billion attempted client deliveries before reconnect traffic, presence, and observability. The useful optimization is therefore to publish compact invalidations and refetch canonical state on gaps, not to retain an unlimited event transcript in every delivery layer.

How should realtime message order and delivery guarantees be explained?

An accepted bid has at least three distinct moments: database commit, realtime publish, and browser receipt. Only the first belongs to the transaction that decides the winner. A socket provider can preserve order within one healthy connection and still be unable to impose that connection's history on a browser that disconnected, changed networks, or rejoined through another edge.

This is the trap: engineers often assign semantic meaning to arrival order because the happy path looks ordered. It is not evidence. Two concurrent publishes may traverse different paths, and a reconnect creates a new observation point; as a result, “I received event B after event A” says something about one connection, while “the database assigned sequence 419 after 418” says something about the auction.

Use a monotonically increasing sequence scoped to the aggregate, such as auction_id, and include the current authoritative version in the payload. If a client holding 417 receives 419, the gap is knowable. It should fetch the current auction representation, replace its local projection, and continue from that version. Replaying 418 and 419 is the wrong recovery when those messages are merely hints, because a replay can reproduce obsolete intermediate states while the database already contains the answer.

Sequence numbers detect loss and reordering; they do not make a network exactly once.

Model the operating bill before selecting transport

The workload has four material terms: connection time, publish operations, fan-out deliveries, and recovery reads. Add engineering and control-plane costs: credential rotation, audit evidence, retry behavior, invoice reconciliation, and the storage used for backlogs or logs. A unit-price table captures only part of this system, and it ages quickly.

For the example workload, reducing payload size helps bandwidth, but changing one 300-byte notification to one 150-byte notification does not change the number of delivery attempts. Coalescing invalidations can. If five accepted changes occur while a client is already scheduled to refetch, one auction.changed hint can replace four redundant hints without changing the authoritative result. This is an explicit trade: clients may skip transient price displays, while the winner and current price remain correct because those facts come from the database.

Retention deserves the same discipline. Keep the ledger-grade bid record and its audit trail in the transactional store. Keep enough notification metadata to diagnose a publish and correlate a request, but do not turn the socket system into a second ledger. I would deliberately stop retaining a replayable notification for every client delivery. During an incident, that means losing the ability to reconstruct each bidder's exact animation sequence; it must never mean losing the accepted bid order, winner, or reconciliation evidence.

Put correctness at the database boundary

The write transaction should reject stale commands, allocate the next auction sequence, persist the bid, and append an outbox record under one commit. An idempotency key on the bid command prevents a retried mobile request from becoming a second bid. A worker then publishes the outbox record. Marking that record sent is also idempotent, because a crash between publish and acknowledgement can cause a duplicate.

Clients therefore implement three rules:

  1. Ignore a notification whose sequence is less than or equal to the version already rendered.
  2. Apply the next sequence only when it is exactly current plus one.
  3. On any gap, refetch canonical auction state and replace the projection.

The third rule matters most. Do not wait forever for 418 after seeing 419.

The following Go program publishes one outbox item through the verified realtime route. It uses a deterministic idempotency key, checks error bodies, and honors Retry-After on rate limiting. The queue consumer that supplies item is intentionally transport-independent; its durable source is the application's outbox, so correctness does not depend on a realtime vendor claiming exactly-once delivery.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type OutboxItem struct {
    AuctionID string `json:"auction_id"`
    Sequence  int64  `json:"sequence"`
    Event     string `json:"event"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    item := OutboxItem{AuctionID: "auction-73", Sequence: 419, Event: "auction.changed"}
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "channel": "auction-73",
        "event":   item.Event,
        "data":    item,
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", fmt.Sprintf("auction-73-%d", item.Sequence))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Second << attempt)
            continue
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    panic("publish failed after retries")
}

The notification is disposable; the outbox row is not. That distinction produces an auditable chain from accepted command to database version to publish attempt, without pretending that a browser acknowledgement is a financial commit.

Compare the full stack, not a socket logo

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
Pusher + Amazon SQS Realtime SDK plus queue service Teams already operating AWS queues Two credential sets, two bills, and custom handoff glue
Ably Specialist realtime platform and SDKs Products where connection recovery drives the decision A separate durable-work system may still be required
PubNub Specialist publish/subscribe platform and SDKs Global distribution and client ecosystem needs Transactional auction truth still belongs elsewhere
Infrai REST capabilities under one key A smaller control plane across realtime and queued work One provider becomes a shared trust and outage boundary

Pusher Channels offers a focused hosted realtime product and is attractive when its channel model, client libraries, and operational tooling match the application. Pairing Pusher with Amazon SQS for durable offline work requires two signups, two credential sets, two bills, and glue that maps queue retry and deduplication semantics onto channel publication. SQS standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer still needs idempotency; adding a queue does not promote a socket delivery into exactly once.

Ably provides realtime messaging with documented ordering and delivery semantics, and its integrated history and connection features can be the better choice when detailed connection recovery is central to the product. PubNub likewise offers a mature publish/subscribe network and message persistence features; it deserves evaluation when global realtime distribution and its client ecosystem outweigh the desire for a smaller control plane. Neither product changes the database's responsibility for auction truth.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a team that wants realtime publication and jobs/queues capabilities behind one REST API, one key, and one bill, particularly when credential rotation and month-end reconciliation are meaningful operating costs. Its public discovery surface exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, which supports generating and auditing integrations rather than maintaining another vendor-specific SDK. The recommendation has a boundary: choose a realtime specialist such as Ably, Pusher, or PubNub when its recovery model, protocol features, or client tooling is the deciding requirement.

Consolidation has a cost. One provider becomes one trust boundary, one invoice, and one outage surface for both the durable handoff and live fan-out. A database outbox preserves the option to republish through another transport, but it does not erase that correlated operational risk.

What guarantee should the product promise?

Promise authoritative, monotonic auction state, not ordered screen animations. The server can state that accepted bids receive a durable sequence and that clients converge by refetching whenever they detect a gap. It should not state that every client sees every notification once, or in the same order, because reconnects alone invalidate that promise.

This decision also gives compliance reviewers a clean boundary. The audit record contains command identity, idempotency key, committed sequence, actor, and database result; realtime metadata explains dissemination but does not decide financial truth. Reconciliation compares durable records, never WebSocket transcripts.

The resulting system spends retention on evidence that matters and uses notifications as hints. During a degraded network period, a bidder may miss an intermediate visual transition and perform an extra read. The current price remains correct. That is the guarantee worth buying.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS delivery semantics
  • Ably message ordering
  • PubNub message persistence

If this control-plane boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation.

title: Small SaaS Custom Metrics Dashboard — 4 Push API and Pull Model Boundaries
description:
For a small SaaS evaluating a Prometheus alternative, send each completed game-data batch through an idempotent push API, then expose reconciled custom metrics to the dashboard; do not treat either a successful push or a successful pull scrape as proof that the nightly pipeline produced correct data. The deciding constraint is signal quality: the service needs to distinguish late, duplicated, partial, and invalid batches without turning every log line into a metric, regardless of whether Grafana or another dashboard renders the result.

TL;DR: For a nightly pipeline, push one bounded completion record per batch into a durable receiver, derive low-cardinality metrics there, and retain structured logs as the audit trail. A pull endpoint remains useful for live process health. The two transport models solve different failure windows, so combining them is often clearer than declaring either one the universal winner.

This architecture decision record uses four boundaries: batch identity, acceptance, reconciliation, and publication. They matter more than the choice of dashboard.

Should a small SaaS push or pull custom metrics?

The concrete workload is a gaming pipeline that transforms a night's events into searchable structured logs and a small custom-metrics dashboard. Operators need to answer questions such as: Did every scheduled shard finish? Which game mode produced rejected records? Is the apparent drop in processed events real, or did telemetry arrive late?

Four invariants keep those answers defensible. First, every batch has a stable identifier derived from the scheduled run and shard, not from an individual retry. Second, accepting an observation never silently replaces a conflicting observation for the same batch. Third, aggregate counts can be reconciled against the accepted batch records. Fourth, dashboard publication cannot erase the underlying audit evidence. A beginner may reasonably start with the visible choice between a Prometheus pull model and a custom push API, but that framing omits the harder question: which observation survives long enough to prove what happened after an ephemeral job exits? A Node.js producer, a Go producer, and a shell-launched batch all face the same boundary. Transport syntax changes; the reconciliation obligation does not.

These are exactly-once effects, not a claim that a network transports a message exactly once. Retries happen. A receiver can acknowledge a request just before the client loses the response, and a scraper can miss a short-lived process between intervals. The design therefore makes repeated delivery harmless and exposes uncertainty rather than hiding it.

Keep the labels restrained. environment, pipeline, game_mode, and a bounded result can support operations; player_id, raw error text, and batch_id belong in logs or a lookup store, because their value sets grow with the workload. OpenTelemetry distinguishes metric instruments and their intended semantics, but an instrument does not rescue a poor attribute model. Cardinality is an architectural input.

Noise compounds.

A compliance-minded retention policy also separates the two records. Metrics answer aggregate operational questions, while structured logs preserve the traceable batch decision with access controls and retention appropriate to their contents. Do not copy player identifiers into metric attributes merely because a dashboard query feels convenient.

Decision: split durable batch facts from live health

The critical path is short. At batch completion, the worker submits one summary containing the stable batch key, counts, timestamps, and a checksum of the summarized output. A receiver validates it, applies an idempotency rule, persists the accepted fact, and returns an acknowledgment. A separate projector turns accepted facts into bounded metrics. The dashboard reads those metrics, while investigators search structured logs by batch key.

The worker also exposes pullable process metrics for memory pressure, queue depth, and current work. Those observations describe a running target and can disappear when the target exits; they are not the ledger of completed overnight work. Separating the paths prevents a common category error: process liveness and business completion have different clocks.

Decision point Push completion record Pull live target
Natural clock A batch reaches a terminal state A process is running at scrape time
Main failure boundary Ambiguous acknowledgment and retry Missed samples during target absence
Duplicate control Stable idempotency key plus conflict detection Collector timestamps repeated samples
Best signal here Completed, rejected, and reconciled batch totals Queue depth and worker health
Noise risk One series or event per unbounded identifier Scraping many ephemeral or irrelevant targets
Audit role Durable fact can point to detailed logs Snapshot alone is insufficient evidence

This comparison does not depend on a particular metrics product. OpenTelemetry provides a vocabulary for metric signals and instruments; it does not require the batch fact and the live gauge to use the same delivery path. Likewise, the dashboard is a view, not the system of record.

For a small operation, simplicity means fewer ambiguous states, not necessarily fewer components. One receiver, one durable table, and one projector may be easier to reason about than teaching every ephemeral worker to retain state until an external scraper happens to observe it. The reverse can be true for long-running services whose useful signals already exist continuously in memory. The trade-off is operational ownership: a durable receiver introduces schema evolution, storage recovery, access control, and projector lag. It is unsuitable when the team cannot operate that state correctly or when losing a best-effort counter has no consequence. In those cases, the pull model's smaller failure surface can be the better decision.

Critical path in Go

The following handler illustrates the contract, including the distinction between a duplicate and a conflict. The storage interface must enforce uniqueness on BatchID; an in-memory check followed by an insert would reopen the race.

package ingest

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Completion struct {
    BatchID   string    `json:"batch_id"`
    Pipeline  string    `json:"pipeline"`
    GameMode string    `json:"game_mode"`
    Processed uint64    `json:"processed"`
    Rejected  uint64    `json:"rejected"`
    Finished  time.Time `json:"finished_at"`
}

type Store interface {
    InsertOrCompare(ctx context.Context, batchID, digest string, c Completion) (inserted bool, conflict bool, err error)
}

type Handler struct{ Store Store }

func (h Handler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    defer r.Body.Close()

    var c Completion
    dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 64<<10))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&c); err != nil || c.BatchID == "" || c.Pipeline == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid completion", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    canonical, err := json.Marshal(c)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "cannot encode completion", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256(canonical)
    digest := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])

    inserted, conflict, err := h.Store.InsertOrCompare(r.Context(), c.BatchID, digest, c)
    if err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
            return
        }
        http.Error(w, "temporary ingest failure", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    if conflict {
        http.Error(w, "batch identity conflict", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }
    if inserted {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

Two limits are concrete here.

The 64 KiB body limit is a contract guard, not a throughput claim. A completion summary should remain small; detailed records stay in the structured-log path. The HTTP outcomes also have deliberately narrow meanings: 201 records a new fact, 204 recognizes an identical retry, 409 identifies a conflicting reuse of the batch key, and 503 leaves the client free to retry because no durable acceptance was promised. DisallowUnknownFields makes schema drift visible, although a production evolution policy may instead accept known versioned envelopes. This strictness has a limitation: independently deployed producers cannot add fields casually. A versioned envelope or an explicit compatibility window is required once producer and receiver releases can diverge.

The subtle part is the digest. Replaying an identical body for the same batch_id is success, because the desired effect already exists. Reusing that identifier with different counts is a conflict that should page or enter a review queue; silently choosing the latest payload would destroy the audit trail. Persist the accepted record and its digest in one transaction. Only then may the projector update dashboard-facing aggregates.

A projector can fail after persistence. That is acceptable if it checkpoints progress and can replay accepted records, because the dashboard may briefly lag while the durable fact remains intact. The lag itself should be measured as the age of the newest unprojected record, using a bounded set of attributes. This yields a signal about the observation system without recursively emitting a metric for every failed event.

How do we test signal quality rather than transport success?

Begin with fault cases, since a happy-path request proves little. Send the same completion twice and require one durable fact. Send the same key with altered counts and require a conflict. Cancel the client after the server commits, retry, and require an idempotent acknowledgment. Stop the projector, accept several batches, restart it, and require aggregates to converge without double counting. Finally, terminate a worker before the next scrape and verify that the batch remains visibly incomplete rather than falsely successful.

Reconciliation is the stronger test. For each nightly run, compare the expected shard manifest with terminal batch facts, then compare the sum of accepted processed and rejected counts with the pipeline's output manifest. A dashboard status is complete only after those checks agree. HTTP success means accepted, not reconciled.

Deployment deserves the same caution. Add the completion schema before requiring new fields, deploy the receiver before producers emit the new version, and keep projector rebuilds possible from durable records. An alert should fire on missing expected batches, identity conflicts, projector lag, and reconciliation mismatch. It should not fire once per malformed log line.

Review the noise weekly.

Inspect alert volume, the fraction of signals that led to an action, attribute cardinality growth, and time to reconcile the nightly run. These are decision criteria rather than invented universal thresholds. The acceptable limits depend on the schedule, on-call coverage, and regulatory obligations governing the underlying data. Document those limits beside the ADR and test them as configuration. An easy first assumption is that more labels make the Grafana dashboard more useful; later reconciliation exposes the flaw, because an identifier useful for one forensic search can create a separate metric series for every batch or player. Keep that identifier in the structured logs and link investigations through the stable batch key.

Rejected option and where it still fits

The rejected design exposes only an in-memory Prometheus pull endpoint from each nightly worker. It is attractive because there is no explicit ingestion receiver, and it can be adequate for a long-running service whose metrics describe current process state. For short-lived batch workers, however, absence is ambiguous: the job may not have started, may have completed between scrapes, or may have crashed before exposing a final value. A Grafana dashboard cannot infer which event occurred from a missing target. This is a limitation of the observation boundary in this workload, not a general defect in Prometheus.

The other extreme, pushing every structured log field directly into metric labels, is also rejected. It improves apparent search flexibility at the expense of uncontrolled series growth and muddles two data models. Search belongs over structured records; aggregation belongs over deliberately bounded dimensions. A custom log sink can encapsulate delivery, as the Logback appender documentation demonstrates for that ecosystem, but delivery plumbing does not define the correctness contract.

There is a valid use case for pull alone: stable services with discoverable endpoints, continuously meaningful gauges, and no requirement to prove that a transient batch reached a terminal state. There is also a valid use case for a simple push gateway without a durable fact store: disposable best-effort counters whose loss or duplication cannot affect an operational decision. Neither description matches a nightly gaming pipeline used for reconciliation.

The final choice is architectural, not promotional. Preserve one immutable batch fact, make retries idempotent, project only bounded metrics, and use pull observations for live health. That arrangement gives a small team a dashboard it can trust without asking the dashboard to become an audit database.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • https://logback.qos.ch/manual/appenders.html

title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

title: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates
description:
arXiv:2610.28604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression, the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization, how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz's Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization.

title: The Best Open Source Cloud Providers in 2026
description:
The open source cloud landscape covers a lot of ground. Some platforms give you a full IaaS stack with their own API surface. Others sit on top of existing hypervisors. A few implement the AWS API so your existing tooling carries over unchanged. The right choice depends on what you're replacing, what your team already knows, and whether you can afford to rebuild your operational model from scratch.

This is a practical comparison of the main options in 2026, written from our own vantage point as one of them. We've tried to be honest about where each tool fits and where it doesn't.

OpenStack

OpenStack is the oldest and most battle-tested open source cloud platform available. It covers compute (Nova), object storage (Swift), networking (Neutron), block storage (Cinder), identity (Keystone), and a dozen other services, each maintained as a separate project under the OpenStack Foundation. Telecoms, national research networks, and large enterprises run it in production at serious scale.

The operational complexity is real. Deploying OpenStack on anything other than a managed distribution requires substantial expertise, and keeping it running requires a dedicated team. If you are evaluating OpenStack for a team of five engineers, the maintenance overhead will consume more capacity than the platform returns.

OpenStack has its own API surface. Your AWS CLI, Terraform AWS provider, and eksctl workflows do not carry over. Teams switching from AWS need to learn a new operational model.

Best fit: Large organisations with dedicated infrastructure teams who need maximum flexibility and have no AWS tooling dependency.

Apache CloudStack

CloudStack is a mature IaaS platform originally developed by Cloud.com, open-sourced in 2010, and now under the Apache Foundation. It is simpler to deploy and operate than OpenStack and has been used by several commercial cloud providers as the underlying platform. The API is CloudStack's own, with some AWS EC2 API compatibility that covers basic instance management but not the full surface.

The community is smaller than OpenStack's and development pace has slowed, but the platform is stable and well-understood. For teams that need a proven IaaS layer without OpenStack's operational overhead, CloudStack is worth evaluating.

Best fit: Mid-size organisations building an internal cloud who want something more operationally accessible than OpenStack.

OpenNebula

OpenNebula is a European open source cloud platform with a strong following in HPC, research, and edge computing environments. It manages KVM, LXC, and Firecracker workloads and is designed to run on a lean footprint, making it viable on smaller hardware clusters where OpenStack would be overkill. It has its own API surface and a web interface that is considerably simpler to navigate than OpenStack's Horizon.

OpenNebula's community is smaller than either OpenStack or CloudStack, but the project is actively maintained and the documentation is good. For edge and research deployments where simplicity and low resource usage matter more than breadth of services, it is a credible choice.

Best fit: Research institutions, HPC environments, and edge deployments that need a lightweight IaaS layer.

Proxmox VE

Proxmox is a hypervisor management platform built on KVM and LXC, not a cloud platform in the IaaS sense. It gives you a web interface for managing virtual machines and containers across a cluster, along with Ceph integration for shared storage. It does not give you an API that applications call to provision infrastructure programmatically in the way that AWS, OpenStack, or CloudStack do.

Proxmox's star rose sharply after Broadcom's VMware acquisition triggered 800 to 1,500% price increases for standalone vSphere customers, and it is the most common destination for VMware refugees. The transition from vSphere to Proxmox is relatively straightforward for teams whose operational model is manual VM management through a web interface.

Teams who built their operational model on Terraform, eksctl, and the AWS CLI face a harder transition. Proxmox has no equivalent for those tools.

Best fit: Teams replacing VMware who manage VMs through a web interface rather than programmatically.

Ubicloud

Ubicloud (AGPL-3.0, Ruby, 12,300 GitHub stars) is a managed cloud service running on Hetzner and Leaseweb hardware that offers elastic compute, block storage, managed Postgres, Kubernetes, firewall, load balancer, and AI inference endpoints. Pricing runs 3 to 10x lower than equivalent AWS services, which is the primary pitch.

Ubicloud is a hosted service you access over the internet rather than software you deploy on hardware you own. For teams looking to cut their cloud bill without changing their operational model significantly, it is worth evaluating. For teams with data sovereignty requirements or air-gapped deployments, it is not the right answer because your data still lives on someone else's hardware.

Best fit: Teams on AWS who want to reduce their bill and can tolerate moving to a different hosted provider.

Spinifex

Spinifex (AGPL-3.0, Go, github.com/mulgadc/spinifex) is our product. It implements the AWS API surface — EC2, S3, IAM, EKS, ECS, ECR, VPC, EBS — on standard Linux bare metal, with no external control plane and no internet requirement.

The specific thing Spinifex does that none of the other platforms on this list do is preserve your AWS tooling investment. If your team has Terraform configs written against the AWS provider, eksctl workflows, IAM role structures, and scripts using the AWS CLI, those run against Spinifex with a single endpoint override, meaning far less rework to your operational model.

The performance case is documented in our OnLogic HX401 benchmark: CPU overhead runs 7% (sysbench single-thread: 1,358 events/s guest vs 1,456 bare metal). The docs also cover areas of active improvement.

Spinifex is the right answer for teams in air-gapped or sovereign environments, teams on edge hardware where AWS connectivity is unreliable, and teams with enough AWS tooling investment that rebuilding it on a new API surface is not a viable option. It is not the right answer for teams who need maximum breadth of services, or are primarily doing web-based VM management.

Best fit: Teams deploying to air-gapped facilities, edge hardware, or sovereign environments who have existing AWS tooling they want to preserve.

Choosing between them

The questions that narrow the field fastest:

Do you need AWS tooling compatibility? If your team has significant Terraform, eksctl, or AWS CLI investment, that eliminates OpenStack, CloudStack, OpenNebula, and Proxmox from the running. Ubicloud covers some AWS API surface but is a hosted service. Spinifex covers the core services required to run on hardware you own, with additional AWS service support added regularly.

Do you need to keep data on hardware under your direct control? That eliminates Ubicloud. The on-premise options are OpenStack, CloudStack, OpenNebula, Proxmox, and Spinifex.

Do you need to operate without internet connectivity? OpenStack can run air-gapped with sufficient effort, but it was not designed for it. Spinifex installs from a release tarball with no external dependencies and has no phone-home requirement.

Do you need to replace VMware with something familiar? Proxmox is the most direct path if your team manages VMs through a web interface. If your team provisions infrastructure programmatically, Proxmox does not cover what VMware gave you.

Given the many options for open source cloud providers, we encourage teams to research each option thoroughly to decide which option is best for them.

Full Spinifex documentation is at docs.mulgadc.com. For the other platforms: openstack.org, cloudstack.apache.org, opennebula.io, proxmox.com, ubicloud.com.

The quickest and easiest way to tell if Spinifex is the best option for you is through our hosted sandbox, which gives you 72 hours to try Spinifex without getting your own hardware involved. Sign up here: https://mulgadc.com/signup

title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces
description:
arXiv:2610.28801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224x224, JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.

title: Map pointer coordinates into the canvas drawing buffer
description:
Convert the pointer position into drawing-buffer coordinates before drawing a marker on a resized canvas. The event reports viewport coordinates, while the drawing buffer has its own width and height.

For a canvas displayed at half its buffer width, one CSS pixel covers two buffer pixels. Subtracting the canvas position gives a local CSS coordinate. Multiply that value by the buffer-to-display ratio before drawing a marker or choosing a crop boundary.

function canvasPoint(canvas, event) {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (rect.width === 0 || rect.height === 0) return null;
  return {
    x: (event.clientX - rect.left) * canvas.width / rect.width,
    y: (event.clientY - rect.top) * canvas.height / rect.height
  };
}

This example assumes an axis-aligned canvas with no CSS border or padding and no rotation or skew. Put a decorative border on a wrapper. The bounding rectangle includes border and padding, so those would need separate handling if placed on the canvas itself.

The returned coordinates describe the canvas buffer. If the drawing context has a transform, or if the photo is letterboxed inside that buffer, mapping into the photo requires another step. Reject clicks outside the displayed photo before calculating a crop.

Check the mapping near both corners after resizing the page. If a marker follows the pointer near the upper-left corner but drifts near the lower-right, check the scale conversion. Read the current rectangle for the interaction; a rectangle saved before a layout change can be stale.

Reference: MDN

title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
description:
arXiv:2610.28601v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

title: Data-Driven Glyph Positioning for Handwritten Music Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.28899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesised data is a common strategy to address the lack of annotated handwritten music scores in Optical Music Recognition (OMR). Smashcima is a recent synthesis framework that assembles pages of handwritten scores by sampling glyph images from MUSCIMA++ and positioning them with hard-coded rules. In this work we ask whether these rules are grounded empirically and whether a learned model for context-dependent positioning can further improve synthesis quality. We extract inter-glyph distributions from around 285 thousand annotated relationships across MUSCIMA++ and OmniOMR, finding that several key parameters deviate systematically from real handwriting. Replacing these constants with empirical means reduces positioning RMSE by up to 60%. We then train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) on the Music Notation Graph structure to predict context-dependent offsets, achieving an additional 50 to 85% RMSE reduction on stems and beams by modelling how neighbouring glyphs constrain placement. Cross-dataset analysis shows that spacing differences between the two corpora are explained by note density (3.3), not style, and that duration-proportional spacing does not hold in handwriting (R2 = 0.001). In downstream evaluation, a YOLOv8 detector pretrained on GNN-positioned synthetic data achieves +30% mAP50 over the baseline and +11% over empirical means when fine-tuned on 200 real handwritten staves, showing that positioning accuracy matters for downstream OMR.

title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

title: TEMPL: A Resource-Efficient and Transparent Model-Free Framework for Pseudo-Label Generation in Material CT Scans
description:
arXiv:2610.28974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scarcity of large annotated datasets limits deep learning (DL) segmentation in material CT analysis. DL-based pseudo-labeling can help, but it is often computationally expensive and hard to interpret. We introduce a multi-stage, model-free framework that generates pseudo-labels directly from grayscale CT scans. It combines thresholding, morphological dilation, and a custom breadth-first search region-growing algorithm to produce polygonal annotations without pre-trained weights, labeled data, or a GPU. We compare it against the zero-shot Segment Anything Model (SAM), a fully supervised 3D U-Net, and classical baselines. On a dendrite dataset with ground truth, our method reaches 63.19% IoU versus 10.74% for zero-shot SAM, with four times the instance recall at 0.5 IoU (33.3% versus 8.3%). The supervised 3D U-Net serves as a reference ceiling that requires expert labels. On a silica sand specimen, YOLO models trained on our labels performed comparably to models trained on SAM labels in a qualitative comparison. Across 1,053 extracted grains, the median equivalent diameter was 163.8 micrometers, near the specimen's known 106 to 150 micrometers sieve range, compared with 219.5 micrometers for SAM, whose labels merge adjacent particles and add spurious detections. A sensitivity analysis shows a stable operating range for the key threshold and a sharp, predictable failure point linked to phase contrast. Our method needs 15s per image on a standard CPU versus 28s for SAM on a GPU. These results support our transparent approach as a tool for annotation bootstrapping and microstructural quantification in resource-limited settings.

title: "File size too small": hitting a KB range instead of just a ceiling
description:
Most upload forms only set a ceiling: "under 50 KB". Some set a range instead, like a signature "between 10 KB and 20 KB". That catches people out in the other direction. A clean, tightly cropped signature resized to the requested pixels often comes out at a few KB, and the form rejects it as too small.

The usual instinct is to make the image worse or bigger until it weighs more. Neither is a good idea, and there's a cleaner option built into the JPEG format.

Why a clean signature is tiny

JPEG stores an image in 8 x 8 pixel blocks. A block that's flat white costs almost nothing. A signature is black strokes on a mostly white background at a small pixel size, so most of the image is cheap blocks. At a sensible quality it ends up at a few KB, and that's the correct result for that picture.

To check, I drew a simple black stroke on a 300 x 120 white image and saved it at JPEG quality 90. It came to 2,609 bytes.

Ways people push the size up, and why I wouldn't:

  • Raising pixel dimensions. If the form specifies a pixel size, you've now broken that rule instead.
  • Quality 100. Helps a bit. My test image went from 2,609 to 4,224 bytes, still nowhere near 10 KB.
  • Adding noise or a grey background. Makes the size go up and the signature look worse. Forms that ask for black ink on white paper want it to look like that.

JPEG comments: bytes that don't change the picture

A JPEG file is a list of segments, each starting with an FF marker byte. One of them is the comment segment, marker FF FE. Decoders skip over it. It was meant for text notes, and one comment segment can hold up to 65,533 bytes (its 2-byte length field maxes out at 65,535 and counts itself).

So you can raise a JPEG's file size without touching a single pixel: insert a comment segment of the right length.

Here's a small Python script that does it. It puts the comment straight after the start-of-image marker:

import sys

src, dst, target = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
data = open(src, "rb").read()
assert data[:2] == b"\xff\xd8", "not a JPEG"

need = target - len(data)
if need > 4:
    payload = b" " * min(need - 4, 65533)
    com = b"\xff\xfe" + (len(payload) + 2).to_bytes(2, "big") + payload
    data = data[:2] + com + data[2:]

open(dst, "wb").write(data)
print(len(data), "bytes")

python3 pad_jpeg.py signature.jpg signature-padded.jpg 11264   # 11 KB

The 4 extra bytes are the marker plus the length field. On my 2,609 byte test image this produced a file of exactly 11,264 bytes. ImageMagick's compare -metric AE between the original and the padded file reported 0 different pixels, identify still read it as a normal 300 x 120 JPEG, and Pillow opened it without complaint.

If the target is more than about 64 KB above the current size, one segment isn't enough; the script caps the padding at one segment, so check the printed size.

If you'd rather not write code, exiftool -Comment="..." can add a comment too, but you have to build a string of the right length yourself.

Aim inside the range, not at the edges

Ranges have two edges and both can be ambiguous.

The top edge. "20 KB" might mean 20,480 bytes (1 KB = 1024) or 20,000 bytes (1 KB = 1000). A file of 20,300 bytes passes the first reading and fails the second. Staying a little under the limit avoids the question.

The bottom edge. Padding lands exactly on the number you give it. If a validator checks "more than 10 KB" instead of "at least 10 KB", a file of exactly 10,240 bytes could fail. I don't know which validators do which, so I pad to about 1 KB above the stated minimum. That's why the example uses 11 KB, not 10.

Will a portal strip the comment or complain?

I don't know of one that does, but I can't promise none will. The padding is standard JPEG structure, not a change to the image data. If a portal re-encodes uploads on its side after the size check, the padding just disappears, which doesn't affect you.

The gotcha: pad last

Order matters. Any resize or recompression after padding re-encodes the image, and the size moves again. In my test, ImageMagick and Pillow both kept the comment when I resized the padded file slightly, but the ImageMagick result still shrank from 11,264 to 10,973 bytes, under the 11 KB I'd aimed for. Other editors and phone apps may drop comments entirely.

So do the crop, the pixel resize and any compression first. Pad last, then check the exact byte count in file properties before you upload.

I built ToolOcean, a set of browser-based file tools. Its exact-size image pages have an "Optional minimum (JPEG padding only)" field that adds this kind of comment padding when a JPEG comes out under the minimum, and the result note says how many bytes are padding. The image stays in your browser tab: https://toolocean.co/compress-image-to-50kb

title: Our AI agent bought an eSIM for its owner, then got the money back. Every step is on chain.
description:
On 15 October the owner of ARGUS, our personal AI agent, wrote to it in Telegram: buy me the cheapest eSIM for Turkey. A few seconds after the owner said /yes, the QR code was in the chat. Thirty-four minutes later the owner asked for a refund, and 0.31 USDC came back to the agent's wallet.

Nothing in the run was simulated. A real eSIM was issued by a real wholesaler and then cancelled, and both payments are transactions on Base you can open. Three things in it are worth telling: the agent refused the first request, the eSIM's secret never passed through the model, and the agent never touched ETH.

It refused the first request

The first message was "buy it and refund it right away". ARGUS did not do that. Buying something only to return it at once looks like a test or a mistake, and it asked what the owner actually wanted: buy and keep it, buy nothing, or a refund for a real reason. The owner chose to buy. The refund came later, as a separate request with its own reason ("I did not install it").

Both the purchase and the refund waited for the owner's /yes. ARGUS has four eSIM tools: esim_offers, esim_buy, esim_status and esim_refund. The two that move money match built-in approval patterns (*buy* and *refund*). A config file can add patterns but never remove them. A hard cap of 1 USDC per eSIM was checked against the seller's own payment terms before anything was signed.

The secret skips the model

The activation code is the traveller's secret: whoever has it can install the eSIM. So it goes from the seller to the owner's chat through the tool's code, around the language model. The model sees the profile number, the price and the transaction. The QR code and the activation code are not in its context, not in ARGUS's memory, and not in its purchase ledger. If no Telegram channel is connected, ARGUS says so and sends nothing.

No ETH, one signature

ARGUS paid over x402: the seller answered the order with 402 Payment Required and its terms, and ARGUS signed one EIP-3009 transfer authorization for exactly that amount. Coinbase's x402 facilitator put it on chain and paid the gas. The refund went the same way in the other direction: the seller node checked with the wholesaler that the eSIM had never been installed (0 bytes used), cancelled it, and signed the transfer back.

Step Transaction From → to USDC
Purchase 0x617efd7a…3ae0 ARGUS → seller 0.31
Refund 0x6dcfb7f0…ed4b seller → ARGUS 0.31

The agent's wallet started with 0.50 USDC and ended with 0.50 USDC. The wholesaler's balance ended where it started.

Then without a hint: found through a marketplace

In the first run ARGUS was pointed at a private seller. In the second, it was given nothing. It searched the modelmarket.dev hub for an eSIM seller, got the offers through the hub, and paid the seller directly. For the test we switched our public seller node from demo to selling, at cost, for 52 minutes, and back to demo right after.

The first attempt ended without a purchase, and that was the agent being right. The node's quote said demo: false, but the node was still called "modelmarket.dev demo seller", and ARGUS would not pay a seller with "demo" in its name. We renamed the node by its mode and labelled every offer [SELLS] or [DEMO] from the seller's own answer, with a rule that the label decides, never the name. The second attempt bought and refunded within 26 seconds (purchase, refund).

Two agents, one seller, and a hub that counts

A marketplace that only lists sellers cannot tell one that delivers from one that takes the money: the payment goes straight from the buyer to the seller. So the seller node now signs a receipt for every delivery and every refund, and the buyer may bring it to the hub with the transaction. The hub checks the signature against the key the seller's listing published, checks the transfer on Base, and counts a confirmed delivery. It keeps no amounts and no addresses in the clear, and a buyer can keep its purchases private.

We tested it in a nine-minute selling window with two different buyers. A coding agent in the owner's terminal ran the kit's one-command example buyer, and three minutes later ARGUS bought the same plan in Telegram. Both refunded. The seller's listing ended with {"confirmed": 2, "distinct_buyers": 2, "refunded": 2}.

What broke along the way

  • Telegram approvals could never succeed. The bot's update loop waited for each task to finish, so a task waiting for /yes never received it, and every approval timed out as a "no". The loop now keeps reading while a task runs.
  • The demo name. Above. The fix was to trust the seller's answer, not its name.
  • The hub's privacy filter blocked the quotes. A data allowance of 104857600 bytes looked like a national ID number to the hub's personal-data check. Integer byte counts are now treated as machine values.

Try it, or sell eSIMs to agents yourself

  • ARGUS, the agent: github.com/alexar76/argus. The full case with every transaction is in docs/use-case-esim-purchase-refund.md.
  • The seller's side, an eSIM operator kit with x402 payments, automatic refunds and signed receipts: github.com/alexar76/esim-operator-kit, with the cases page.
  • Our node at esim.modelmarket.dev is back in demo mode: it quotes and refuses orders. Selling needs an operator with a wholesale account, which the kit sets up with one command.

We build ARGUS and the eSIM operator kit. Every purchase in these tests was at cost, by us, and refunded; no customer was involved.

title: Policy-Mask: Budget-Aware Adaptation of Diffusion Features to Discriminative Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.28889v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-$\Sigma$ and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.
