title: Cloudflare's Rust TypeScript (tsrs) vs tsgo: The 8x Claim Is Closer to 3x
description:
Microsoft spent most of 2025 explaining why the native TypeScript compiler would be written in Go and not Rust. TypeScript 7.0 (tsgo) shipped on July 8, 2026. On October 20, Cloudflare published tsrs, a port of TypeScript to Rust, and says it is "up to 8x faster" than TypeScript 7.0 with "~70% less memory". The fairest comparison in the published numbers puts it closer to 3x.

So we now have two native TypeScript compilers, and only one of them is tsc. I've read the Cloudflare post, the tsrs repo and its benchmark file, Microsoft's announcements and the 207-comment Hacker News thread. My view after all that: both companies picked the right language for their own problem, your CI gate should stay on tsgo, and the thing that worries me is tsrs turning into a second tsc.

What tsrs actually is

The tsrs repo lives under the Oxc project. It describes itself as a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 type checker, meant as a drop-in replacement for the TypeScript 7 compiler and language server, with "100% conformance" as the goal. A few facts that matter more than the headline number:

  • The README credits Max Schwenk with the port, and Owner.com sponsored the initial work. Cloudflare and VoidZero are backing it, and Cloudflare says Theo Browne's tsc-rs will be merged with it into one package.
  • It tracks the main branch of microsoft/TypeScript (the benchmarks use a 7.1-dev commit) and is aiming for a stable release against TypeScript 7.1. Releases so far are 0.x: v0.18.0 landed on GitHub on October 19, and npm ships it as 0.18.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929.
  • License is Apache-2.0. The README says it is not affiliated with or endorsed by Microsoft.
  • Pull requests are closed. Issues with minimal repros are welcome.
  • There's a Wasm build, @tsrs/wasm, targeting wasm32-wasip1.
  • Known gaps: --init and --showConfig aren't supported, and the benchmark file flags at least one real tsrs bug (same error count as tsgo on drizzle-orm, different locations).

Cloudflare's post insists "we are not forking TypeScript". It also says "frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days" and that it will apply the same process it uses for Vinext, where the Next.js test suite runs against Vinext every night, to keep tsrs in sync with upstream, with an agent reviewing upstream changes each morning and opening tracking issues. That's the whole maintenance plan: agents and a test suite.

Why Microsoft picked Go

Ryan Cavanaugh's "Why Go?" discussion from March 2025 is still the best primary source. The main reasons:

  • The new codebase had to stay "as compatible as possible, both in terms of semantics and in terms of code structure", because the team would maintain both codebases for a while.
  • "Idiomatic Go strongly resembles the existing coding patterns of the TypeScript codebase."
  • Go offers "excellent control of memory layout and allocation", and "the downsides of a GC aren't particularly salient in our codebase."
  • The admitted weakness: "Go's in-proc JS interop story is not as good as some of its alternatives."

That plan worked. The TypeScript 7.0 announcement reports VS Code going from 125.7s on TypeScript 6 to 10.6s on TypeScript 7, and 8x to 12x speedups on full builds generally. 7.0 is built to match 6.0's type-checking and command-line behavior, which is exactly what you want from a compiler that so many CI pipelines depend on.

Why Cloudflare picked Rust

Cloudflare's argument for Rust is mostly about Wasm: "When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go's garbage collector along with it." Rust's memory management model "enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host." If you want a type checker inside a Worker, inside a browser playground, or inside Oxlint as a library, that is a real difference.

The most important comment in the HN thread comes from Daniel Rosenwasser of the TypeScript team. "We even did our own Rust vibe port", he wrote, and the team suspects "a lot of the speed does not just come down to language choice." Some of what makes TS 7.1 faster "actually comes from optimizations discovered in tsrs": work done more lazily, changed allocation patterns, experiments with struct layouts. Cloudflare's post says the same thing from the other side: some 7.1 optimizations "were upstreamed from tsrs".

So the Go vs Rust argument is mostly a proxy war. Go was the right call for a faithful port by the people who own the language. Rust is the right call if you want to embed the checker somewhere a GC is a liability.

tsrs vs tsgo benchmarks: where 8x becomes 3x

These are the published figures. None of them are mine; each row comes from the source named in it.

Source Project tsgo (TS 7.x) tsrs
Cloudflare blog, same worker count general claim baseline (7.0) up to 8x faster, ~70% less memory
Cloudflare blog TS 7.1 beta vs 7.0 up to 2.5x faster n/a
bench/RESULTS.md, defaults, 16 vCPU vscode 11.10 s, 7.48 GiB 0.82 s, 2.10 GiB
same mui-docs 12.66 s, 7.39 GiB 0.75 s, 1.60 GiB
same, watch mode, 8 vCPU vscode edit-to-report ~1.2–1.8 s ~31–34 ms
HN, quoting the blog charts vscode vs TS 7.1 nightly 5.28 s 1.73 s

The 13.55x vscode result in RESULTS.md runs tsgo at its default 4 checkers and tsrs at 16 threads on a 16-vCPU box, compares against typescript@7.0.2 while tsrs ports a 7.1-dev commit, and uses tsrs's PGO-optimized build. When Cloudflare equalizes worker counts, the claim drops to "up to 8x". When you compare against the 7.1 nightly instead of 7.0, the VS Code gap is about 3x. That's still a big result, and 3x is the number I'd quote.

The watch-mode number is the one I'd actually care about. Edit-to-diagnostic in tens of milliseconds instead of over a second is something you feel in an editor all day. A 12-second CI check becoming 1 second mostly isn't, and commenter pier25 has a point: for most projects tsgo is "already plenty fast."

What breaks in TypeScript 7 and in tsrs

tsgo (TypeScript 7.0) ships without a programmatic API. The announcement says so directly: "it does not ship with an API." typescript-eslint, Volar, Vue, Svelte, Astro and MDX tooling still need 6.0. Microsoft's workaround is @typescript/typescript6, which gives you a tsc6 binary and the old API. A new, different API is expected in 7.1.

tsrs has no stable release, only 0.x builds against a 7.1 dev snapshot. --init and --showConfig aren't supported. The README also warns that tsgo itself can produce diagnostics and traces in a different order depending on parallel parse, resolution and check order, so a naive diff between the two will be noisy even when both are right. tsrs canonicalizes some of that by default; tsgo doesn't. And keeping a port in sync with agents that track upstream is a plan nobody has seen survive a major TypeScript release yet.

What to put in CI today

My recommendation for a real project in October 2026:

# 1. The gate stays official
npm install -D typescript@7

# 2. Keep the 6.0 API for typescript-eslint and friends
npm install -D typescript6@npm:@typescript/typescript6

# 3. Before chasing another compiler, tune the one you have
npx tsc --noEmit --checkers 8

# 4. Try tsrs as a non-blocking job and compare results
pnpm add -D tsrs
pnpm exec tsrs --noEmit --checkerAssignment go --noLazyMembers

The two tsrs flags in step 4 are the ones its README recommends for the closest comparison with tsgo. If the error lists match on your codebase for a few weeks, you have a fast pre-check. Your merge gate should stay on tsc.

Oxlint, Biome, swc: who gets type-aware linting

Oxc wins, obviously. Cloudflare names type-aware lint rules in Oxlint as a use case, and the repo lives under oxc-project. Rust linters have spent years approximating types without a real checker, and an in-process Rust type checker fixes that for whoever gets to link against it.

Neither Biome nor swc is mentioned in the Cloudflare post. If tsrs ends up as a crate with a clean API that Biome, swc, Rolldown and anyone else can depend on, the whole Rust JS toolchain gets real types. If it ends up as "the oxc type checker" with its own CLI, its own LSP and its own subtly different diagnostics, we get the Babel-vs-tsc split all over again, this time at the type level, where differences hurt more.

My take is that tsrs is good news as a library and bad news as a rival tsc. The CLI and LSP are what make it look like a rival. The Wasm build and the embeddable checker are the parts I'd want, and I hope that's where the effort goes.

Did Microsoft get it right with Go, or did Cloudflare just prove Rust was the better call all along? And would you put a community port in your CI gate if it were 3x faster? Tell me why I'm wrong.

Sources

  • Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust (Cloudflare)
  • oxc-project/tsrs README and bench/RESULTS.md
  • Hacker News discussion
  • Why Go? (microsoft/typescript-go #411)
  • A 10x Faster TypeScript (Microsoft, March 2025)
  • Announcing TypeScript 7.0 (Microsoft)

title: Two Android ML tests that could never fail, and a TFLite check that can
description:
Two tests in my Android app could never fail. One only counts the labels; the other compares the output with an
answer file that holds no answers. And both of them look at this picture:

The app runs a Keras model exported to LiteRT, the new name of TensorFlow Lite. This post is about one rule: a check
proves something only if you have seen it fail. Here is how mine could not, and the check I would build instead.

Two tests that could not fail

The classification test asks only this of the result
(ClassificationE2ETest.kt, line 66):

assertTrue("Expected top-5 results",
    success.output.size in 1..5)

Any five labels pass, including the five least likely ones the app shows
(part 1
explains why it shows those).

The detection test looks better. It reads a golden file, the saved answer a test compares against, and matches each
expected box by its label and its overlap. Here is the golden file
(detection_golden.json,
its note cut to fit):

{
  "_note": "Golden generation skipped: ...",
  "model": "ssd_mobilenet_v1_detect.tflite",
  "image": "images/test_image.jpg"
}

The note in full reads "Golden generation skipped: No module named 'ai_edge_litert'". No boxes. The match loop runs
once per expected box, so with none it checks nothing, and the size check becomes "at least zero"
(DetectionE2ETest.kt, lines 130 to 131).
The script that should write the answers wrote this placeholder and carried on.

The check that can fail

1. Get the notebook's answer

Start from a real photo with a known answer. KerasHub's own example uses a California quail, and "quail" is class 85
in ImageNet, the label set these classifiers use
(imagenet_utils.py).
Its example downloads the photo with keras.utils.get_file, and on 22 October 2026 Wikimedia answered
403 -- Forbidden. That photo is CC BY-SA 3.0, too, not public domain. So I downloaded a public-domain one from the
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
cropped it square, and loaded it from disk. With my exported preset in the example's place:

image = keras.utils.load_img("california_quail.jpg")
classifier = keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier.from_preset(
    "mobilenet_v3_small_100_imagenet",
    activation="softmax",
)
preds = classifier.predict(np.array([image]))
top_labels = keras_hub.utils.decode_imagenet_predictions(preds)

predict() runs the preset's own preprocessing, so this is the answer the model was built to give. On a computer's
CPU it gave quail 10.30, partridge 3.94, prairie chicken 3.77, black grouse 3.57 and ruffed grouse 3.43. One surprise:
those are raw scores. Despite activation="softmax", the 1,000 scores summed to 162.5, not 1.

2. Check the .tflite file in Python first

Run the .tflite file on the array the Keras model sees after preprocessing (KerasHub's hint is
model(model.preprocessor(x))), with the interpreter code from the
keras.io guide. Then compare the two outputs the way KerasHub's own export
tests do
(test_case.py):

abs_diff = np.abs(keras_val - litert_val)
mean_abs_diff = np.mean(abs_diff)
max_abs_diff = np.max(abs_diff)

On the quail photo they agreed: max_abs_diff 1.1e-05 and mean_abs_diff 1.9e-06 over the 1,000 scores, with the
same five labels in the same order and quail at 10.31 in both. If the file disagrees with the notebook here, the phone will too, and the bug is
in the export, not the app.

3. Hold the phone to the saved answer

Save the five labels and scores as the golden file, or for detection the boxes as label, score, x1, y1, x2,
y2: the keys my detection test already reads. Push the same photo to the phone and keep the test's matching rule:
the same label, and a box overlap of 0.5 or more, measured as IoU (the area two boxes share divided by the area they
cover together). Two guards make it a test that can fail:

  • An empty or missing golden file fails. It never counts as a pass.
  • The same pixels go in. The preset crops the photo to a square before it resizes it, and my app stretches it. Use a square photo, or crop it first.

Here it is failing

I copied my app's preprocessing into Python (resize to 224 by 224, then the preset's numbers) and fed the same file
the same square photo. Quail still came first, at 10.11 instead of 10.31, but prairie chicken and partridge swapped
places. A check that compares the ordered five labels fails right there, with the right numbers in the sidecar: what
is left is the resize step. That is the rule working, on a computer's CPU; I did not run the phone for this post.

What I have not solved

How close is close enough? My app's resize alone moved the top score by 0.2 and swapped two labels, before any
quantization (weights stored in fewer bits to make the file smaller). KerasHub's thresholds are set by hand, per model
and per output, and I do not have a rule for picking one. If you have one, I would like to read it.

The two tests are still in the repo as they were at commit b8d3e2f (3 July 2026). The scores and differences above come from a run
on 22 October 2026 with keras 3.15.1, keras-hub 0.32.0, litert-torch 0.10.0 and ai-edge-litert 2.3.0.

Next: five ways the export itself breaks, each with its public record →

title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
description:
arXiv:2610.28578v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
description:
arXiv:2610.29212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.

title: Building an AI Shirt Agent with Spring AI and Tool Calling
description:
Why a Shirt Recommender Is a Good First Spring AI Project

Most tutorials that introduce large language models to Java developers start with a chatbot that answers questions. That is a useful starting point, but it hides the part that makes LLM features valuable inside a real application: the model has to take an action that your code controls. A chatbot that only produces text is a demo. An agent that looks something up in your own system and returns a structured result is a feature.

This article walks through shirts-agent, a small Spring Boot and Spring AI example that makes the idea concrete. A user sends an item and a color to a REST endpoint. An AI agent calls a Java method that searches an in-memory catalog, and the service returns a structured shirt recommendation. The whole project fits in a few classes, which makes it a good way to see how the pieces fit together before you build something larger.

The project uses Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5.6, Spring AI 1.1.8, OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini model, and Maven. The complete source is available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

The Problem: Language Models Do Not Know Your Data

A language model is trained on public text up to a certain date. It does not know what is in your product catalog, your inventory, your customer records, or your internal APIs. If you ask it "which shirt do you recommend in red?" without any extra help, it can only guess, and a guess is not a recommendation a shop can sell.

There are several ways to connect a model to your data:

  • Stuff the data into the prompt. This works for small datasets, but it wastes tokens, grows with your catalog, and leaks everything to the model on every request.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). You search a vector store or index for relevant documents and include them in the prompt. This is the right tool for unstructured text such as manuals or policies.
  • Tool calling (function calling). You describe a set of Java methods to the model. When the model needs information or wants to perform an action, it asks for one of those methods to be executed. Your code runs the method and returns the result, and the model uses that result to finish its answer.

shirts-agent uses tool calling. The data is structured (a catalog of shirts with a color and a name), the question has a clear shape (find a shirt of this color), and the answer must come from your system rather than from the model's imagination. Tool calling is a natural fit.

The Architecture in Four Steps

The request flow is short and easy to follow. According to the project documentation, ShirtController receives the HTTP request, ShirtService validates the input, and ShirtAgent asks the model to find a shirt. The model then calls ShirtCatalogTool.findShirtByColor and returns a structured Shirt object. Invalid input is rejected with HTTP 400 before the model is ever called.

That last point deserves emphasis. Every call to a hosted model costs money and adds latency. Validation belongs in ordinary Java code, in front of the model, so that obviously bad requests never reach it.

The layers look like this:

  1. Controller. Exposes POST /api/shirts/recommend and maps the JSON body to a request object.
  2. Service. Checks that item and color are present and well formed. Rejects bad input with a 400 response.
  3. Agent. Wraps the Spring AI chat client. It builds the prompt, tells the model what it is allowed to do, and converts the model's final answer into a Shirt.
  4. Tool. A plain Java class with a method annotated with @Tool. This method is the only place where the model touches your data.

Keeping these responsibilities separate pays off quickly. You can test the validation logic without a model, test the tool against the catalog without a model, and swap the model provider without rewriting the business logic.

Defining the Tool

In Spring AI, a tool is an ordinary Spring bean with a method that the model is allowed to call. The @Tool annotation provides a description that the model reads to decide when the tool is useful. The parameter names and descriptions matter, because the model relies on them to fill in the arguments correctly.

An illustrative version of such a tool looks like this. It is a simplified sketch to show the shape of the code, not a verbatim copy of the repository:

@Component
public class ShirtCatalogTool {

    private final ShirtCatalog catalog;

    public ShirtCatalogTool(ShirtCatalog catalog) {
        this.catalog = catalog;
    }

    @Tool(description = "Find a shirt in the catalog by its color")
    public Shirt findShirtByColor(
            @ToolParam(description = "The color of the shirt, for example red or blue") String color) {
        return catalog.findByColor(color)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No shirt found for color: " + color));
    }
}

Notice what the tool does not do. It does not decide which shirt is best, it does not format prose, and it does not call the model. It takes a color, looks it up in a deterministic source of truth, and returns a typed result. The model is responsible for the conversation and the final wording. Your code is responsible for the facts.

This separation is the most important design habit when working with tools. Keep the tool small, deterministic, and easy to test. Put the intelligence where it belongs: in the orchestration of the model, not inside the data access.

Keeping the Output Structured

A recommendation that comes back as a paragraph of text is hard to use in an application. A frontend needs fields. A test needs assertions. A downstream service needs a predictable shape.

Spring AI can ask the model to return its answer as a Java object. The agent declares the target type, the framework converts the model's response into that type, and your service receives a Shirt rather than a string it has to parse. This is what the project means by "returns a structured Shirt."

Structured output reduces an entire category of bugs. You no longer depend on regular expressions over free-form text, and a change in the model's phrasing cannot silently break your parsing code. If the model returns something that does not fit the expected type, the failure shows up as an error you can handle rather than as wrong data that reaches a user.

Validation Before the Model

The service layer is where you protect both your budget and your users. In shirts-agent, the service checks the request before the agent is invoked. A missing item or color results in an HTTP 400 response, and the model is never called.

This pattern is worth copying into any LLM-backed feature. Ask yourself which inputs can be rejected with plain Java. Length limits, required fields, allowed values, and basic format checks all belong in front of the model. Each request you reject locally is a request you do not pay for, and a failure you can explain to the caller in a clear message.

Validation is also a security measure. Free-form text sent to a model can contain instructions that try to change its behavior. You do not eliminate that risk by validating input, but you reduce the surface area. Constrain what the model is asked to do, and constrain what the tool can return.

Running the Project Locally

The project is intentionally easy to run. You need JDK 21 and Maven 3.9 or later. Clone the repository, export your OpenAI key, and start the application with Maven:

git clone https://github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.git
cd shirts-agent
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
mvn spring-boot:run

Then send a request to the endpoint on port 8080:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/shirts/recommend \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"item":"playera","color":"red"}'

The unit tests run with mvn test, and they do not call the model. That detail matters. Testing an LLM application should not depend on a live API call for every build. Test the controller, the service validation, and the tool logic in isolation, and reserve live model calls for a small number of integration checks.

What the Project Deliberately Leaves Out

A good example is honest about its boundaries. shirts-agent has no database. The catalog is an in-memory list of four shirts, which is enough to demonstrate the pattern and nothing more. There is no messaging layer, no event stream, and no cloud deployment. There is no Dockerfile or compose file. The application runs on port 8080 and depends on the OpenAI API.

Each of these omissions is a useful discussion point. In production you would replace the in-memory catalog with a repository backed by a real database, perhaps with caching for frequently requested colors. You would add authentication to the endpoint, rate limits to protect your model budget, timeouts around the model call, and observability so you can see latency, token usage, and tool invocations. You would also decide how to handle a color that is not in the catalog: return a friendly message, suggest the closest available color, or ask the user to try again.

The point of the example is not to be production-ready. The point is to show the smallest set of moving parts that still demonstrates a real agent calling a real tool.

Lessons for Java Teams Adding LLM Features

Several practical lessons come out of a project this small.

Start from the data, not from the model. Identify the facts your feature needs and where they live. If the answer depends on your catalog, your orders, or your policies, the model should retrieve those facts through a tool rather than generate them.

Make tools boring. A tool should be a deterministic method with clear inputs and outputs. The less cleverness you put inside a tool, the easier it is to test, reason about, and trust.

Validate in code before you call the model. Use the programming language you already know to reject bad input, enforce limits, and protect your budget.

Prefer structured output. Typed results are easier to test and integrate than free-form text. Let the framework handle the conversion, and fail loudly when the shape is wrong.

Test without the model where you can. Most of your application logic should run in unit tests without network calls. Reserve live calls for integration tests that you run deliberately.

Keep the model replaceable. Spring AI abstracts the chat provider behind common interfaces. Keep your domain logic and tools free of provider-specific details so that changing models is a configuration decision rather than a rewrite.

Where Spring AI Fits in the Java Ecosystem

Spring AI brings the patterns Spring developers already know to LLM applications. Dependency injection wires the chat client and the tools. Configuration properties select the model and its settings. Auto-configuration sets up the common parts so that you can focus on your domain. The result feels familiar to any team that already builds Spring Boot services, which is the main reason to consider it for enterprise Java work.

This matters for teams in regulated or long-lived systems. The question is rarely whether a model can answer a question. The question is whether the feature can be built, tested, deployed, monitored, and maintained by the same engineers who maintain the rest of the platform. Using familiar tools reduces the cost of answering yes.

Extending the Example

If you want to take this project further, there are several natural next steps that keep the same architecture.

First, add more tools. A real shop needs to check stock, look up sizes, and calculate prices. Each of these can be another annotated method with a clear description. The model decides which tool to call based on the request, so give each tool a name and description that make its purpose obvious.

Second, add a second data source. Imagine a product search over a vector index for descriptions and reviews, combined with the exact catalog lookup you already have. Retrieval handles the fuzzy part of the question, and tools handle the exact facts. This hybrid approach is one of the most useful patterns in production LLM systems.

Third, add evaluation. Create a set of requests with expected outcomes and run them regularly. When you change a prompt, a model, or a tool description, the evaluation tells you whether the behavior got better or worse. Without evaluation, LLM features drift in ways that are hard to notice until a user complains.

Fourth, add observability. Record which tools were called, how long each step took, and how many tokens were used. This information is essential for controlling cost and diagnosing unexpected answers.

Conclusion

shirts-agent is a small project with a big lesson. A language model becomes useful in an application when it can call your code, and your code remains the source of truth. A controller accepts the request, a service validates it, an agent coordinates the model, and a tool returns the facts. Each layer has a clear job, and each can be tested on its own.

If you are a Java developer curious about AI features, this is a good place to start. Clone the repository, run the example, change the catalog, add a second tool, and watch how the model chooses between them. Then ask the question that matters for your own domain: which facts in my system should the model be allowed to ask for, and which rules should my code enforce before the model is ever involved?

The full source code and documentation are available at github.com/josesaid/shirts-agent.

Key Takeaways

  • Use tool calling when a model must answer with facts from your own system.
  • Keep tools small, deterministic, and easy to test.
  • Validate requests in ordinary Java code before calling the model.
  • Prefer structured output over free-form text for application features.
  • Test most of your logic without live model calls.
  • Keep the model provider replaceable through the framework's abstractions.

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

title: Keeping Your Streamlit App Awake with Serverless Functions and a Free Cron Job
description:
You deploy a little Streamlit app on Community Cloud, share the link, and a day later it's showing a sleepy "Zzzz, this app has gone to sleep due to inactivity" page. Anyone who opens it has to click a button and wait for a cold start.

There's no keep-alive switch in Streamlit Community Cloud, and the advice on the forums boils down to "push an empty commit" or "automate a browser". Both work, but both are heavier than they need to be. There's a simpler way: do exactly what that button does, with one HTTP request, on a schedule.

⚠️ This uses an undocumented endpoint that the Streamlit web page itself calls. It can change without notice. Only use it on apps you own, and keep the schedule gentle.

What the "wake up" button really does

If you open dev tools on a sleeping app and click Yes, get this app back up!, you'll see a single request:

POST https://<your-app>.streamlit.app/api/v2/app/resume

It needs two small things besides the POST itself, and neither one is a login:

  1. A CSRF token. The page never stores it anywhere fancy. It simply remembers the x-csrf-token response header from the previous API call and sends it back. The server also sets a matching _streamlit_csrf cookie on that same response.
  2. A machine id. A random UUID sent as x-streamlit-machine-id.

So the whole dance is: ask for the app status, grab the token and cookie, then POST to resume.

Try it with curl

I'm using webpie.streamlit.app here, swap in your own app URL. Save this as wake.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Wake a sleeping Streamlit Community Cloud app.
# Usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app
set -euo pipefail

APP_URL="${1:?usage: ./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app}"
COOKIES="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$COOKIES"' EXIT

# Step 1: any API call hands us a CSRF cookie (saved in the jar)
# and an x-csrf-token response header (we grab it here).
CSRF_TOKEN=$(
  curl --silent --output /dev/null --dump-header - \
    --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
    "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status" \
  | tr -d '\r' \
  | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1) == "x-csrf-token" { print $2 }'
)

# Step 2: the browser also sends a random UUID as a machine id.
MACHINE_ID=$(uuidgen | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

# Step 3: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
curl --silent --include --request POST \
  --cookie "$COOKIES" --cookie-jar "$COOKIES" \
  --header "x-csrf-token: $CSRF_TOKEN" \
  --header "x-streamlit-machine-id: $MACHINE_ID" \
  --header "origin: $APP_URL" \
  --header "referer: $APP_URL/" \
  "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/resume"
echo

# Step 4 (optional): check the status afterwards
curl --silent --cookie "$COOKIES" "$APP_URL/api/v2/app/status"
echo

Run it:

chmod +x wake.sh
./wake.sh https://webpie.streamlit.app

A 204 No Content from the resume call means the request was accepted. The status call at the end shows the app's state; while it's booting, the status number changes. (An app that's already awake just answers normally, so it's safe to run any time.)

Make it run itself

A shell script on your laptop doesn't help while you're asleep too. The nice part is that the logic is just fetch calls, so it runs on almost any serverless platform: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda, Deno Deploy. Pick whichever you already use.

Here's the core logic once, in plain JavaScript:

// Shared logic: wake a Streamlit Community Cloud app.
// Works in Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, Node 18+, anything with fetch.
export async function wakeApp(appUrl) {
  // Step 1: any API call gives us a CSRF cookie and an x-csrf-token header.
  const status = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/status`);
  const csrfToken = status.headers.get("x-csrf-token");
  const cookies = status.headers
    .getSetCookie()
    .map((cookie) => cookie.split(";")[0]) // keep "name=value", drop attributes
    .join("; ");

  // Step 2: this is the call behind the "Yes, get this app back up!" button.
  const resume = await fetch(`${appUrl}/api/v2/app/resume`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      cookie: cookies,
      "x-csrf-token": csrfToken,
      "x-streamlit-machine-id": crypto.randomUUID(),
      origin: appUrl,
      referer: `${appUrl}/`,
    },
  });

  return { ok: resume.ok, status: resume.status };
}

Option A: Cloudflare Workers

worker.js:

import { wakeApp } from "./wake.js";

export default {
  async fetch(request, env) {
    // Optional: stop strangers from poking your endpoint
    const secret = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get("key");
    if (env.WAKE_KEY && secret !== env.WAKE_KEY) {
      return new Response("Nope", { status: 401 });
    }

    const result = await wakeApp(env.APP_URL);
    return Response.json(result);
  },
};

Set APP_URL (for example https://webpie.streamlit.app) and an optional WAKE_KEY as variables in the Worker settings, then deploy with npx wrangler deploy. You'll get a URL like https://wake-streamlit.<you>.workers.dev/?key=<your key>.

Option B: Vercel

Put wake.js in your project root and add api/wake.js:

import { wakeApp } from "../wake.js";

export default async function handler(req, res) {
  if (process.env.WAKE_KEY && req.query.key !== process.env.WAKE_KEY) {
    return res.status(401).send("Nope");
  }

  const result = await wakeApp(process.env.APP_URL);
  res.status(200).json(result);
}

Add APP_URL and WAKE_KEY under Project Settings → Environment Variables and deploy. Your endpoint is https://<project>.vercel.app/api/wake?key=<your key>.

Trigger it with cron-job.org (free)

You don't even need the platform's own scheduler. cron-job.org is free and will call any URL on a schedule:

  1. Create an account and click Create cronjob.
  2. URL: the Worker or Vercel endpoint from above, including ?key=....
  3. Schedule: every 6 hours is plenty. Apps seem to sleep after roughly 12 hours without visitors, so you want to land well inside that window.
  4. Save. Under the job's history you can see each run's status code. 200 means your function ran.

That's the whole setup: cron-job.org pokes your serverless function, the function pokes Streamlit, and your app stays warm. No browser, no Selenium, no fake commits.

Things worth knowing

  • It's unofficial. If Streamlit changes the endpoint, the script breaks. Check the cron history now and then.
  • It's polite use only. One request every few hours for your own app. Please don't hammer it.
  • Waking isn't the same as being busy. This resumes a sleeping app. It doesn't pretend to be traffic, so the app can still go back to sleep later, which is why the schedule keeps repeating.
  • Keep the key secret so nobody else can trigger your function.

If you'd rather stay inside the official lines, the alternative is hosting the app somewhere that doesn't sleep. But for a free-tier hobby app, a 20-line function and a free cron service is hard to beat.

Happy hacking!

title: KIRA: A Full-Stack Reading Screening System with Dual-Pathway Analysis for Children
description:
arXiv:2610.28840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early-grade reading screening is critical for identifying children at risk of reading difficulty. Existing AI-based screeners are often limited in the scope of their analyses and evaluation metrics, or are proprietary systems that lack transparent model specifications and evaluation. We present KIRA, a dual-pathway screening system that pairs word-level fluency scoring with detailed phoneme-level error detection. We adapt pretrained word and phoneme recognizers to children's speech, reducing word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%. Powered by these child-adapted models, we implement Word Reading (WRE) and Oral Reading Fluency (ORF), two foundational tasks in K-2 screening. The system integrates these recognizers with a web-based teacher-facing interface presenting fluency scores alongside phoneme feedback for potential targeted intervention. KIRA brings modern child-speech recognition into a full-stack, deployable, classroom-ready reading screener.

title: B-CARE: Blind Classwise Assessment of Relative Evidence for Stance Error Ranking
description:
arXiv:2610.29350v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stance classifiers make errors that can be costly to identify under limited human-review budgets. Prioritizing potentially incorrect predictions remains challenging, particularly across heterogeneous base models. We introduce B-CARE (Blind Classwise Assessment of Relative Evidence for Stance Error Ranking), a prediction-blind framework for identifying high-risk stance predictions. Given only a target and text, a fixed LLM verifier assigns ordinal evidence scores to all candidate stance labels without observing the base model's prediction or confidence. B-CARE constructs a comparative risk score by contrasting the strongest alternative-class evidence with the evidence supporting the predicted class. The resulting classwise evidence profile can be reused across multiple base models without training a separate error detector or calibrating risk scores. We evaluate B-CARE on four stance benchmarks and three heterogeneous base LLMs, covering 12 dataset-model settings and 5,206 unique test instances. Evaluation includes error-ranking discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC), selective prediction (E-AURC), and review effectiveness (ErrorCapture at fixed review budgets). B-CARE achieves a mean AUROC of 0.735 and a mean AUPRC of 0.524, capturing 41.06% of errors within the highest-risk 20% of predictions. Although B-CARE does not uniformly outperform strong confidence-based baselines, it provides a reusable, complementary evidence signal for prioritizing potentially incorrect stance predictions across heterogeneous models.

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

title: Enhancing Cross-Grade Generalization in Banana Variety Classification via Hybrid CNN-Transformers and Knowledge Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.29008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, automated fruit classification systems have become a more critical component in precision agriculture for efficient yield estimation, quality control, and supply chain optimization. However, they still face significant challenges under varying quality, fruit maturity, illumination, texture degradation, morphological attributes, domain shift, and post-harvest handling conditions. In this study, we address the challenging issue of cross-grade banana variety classification. This is a real-world setting where models that have been trained on specific quality grades must generalize to unseen grades to handle significant domain shift. Under a rigorous Leave-One-Grade-Out evaluation protocol, we present a thorough comparative analysis of CNNs, ViTs, and dual-stream hybrid architectures using a large-scale dataset of 31,678 banana images with three varieties and three quality grades. Specifically, to address the drawbacks of single-paradigm frameworks, we present a dual-stream Swin ResNet hybrid framework enhanced with KL-divergence-based self-distillation to align probabilistic feature representations across the CNN and Transformer streams. Comprehensive experimental analyzes show that the presented hybrid framework with KL-divergence based self-distillation achieves better overall performance, i.e., it attains a mean accuracy of 81.25% and significantly surpasses CNN and Transformer baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the hybrid framework in this study improves discriminative feature transferability, improves attention localization, and stabilizes optimization.

title: One Trip.com URL, Five Pulls, Twelve Hours: 21 Different Hotels, Six Every Time
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads Trip.com: a city, two dates and a guest count in, one row per hotel out, with the live nightly rate for exactly those dates.

Trip.com is the booking channel for most of Asia and it has no public web API, so a scraper is the only way in. The field I expected to cause trouble was the price. It didn't. What caused trouble was something I hadn't thought to check: which hotels the page shows you at all.

The same URL, five times, one day

My QA runs hit a hardcoded list URL so I can diff the output day over day. On 21 October 2026 five of them fired against a byte-identical URL:

https://www.trip.com/hotels/list?city=723&checkin=2026%2F11%2F20
  &checkout=2026%2F11%2F23&adult=2&children=0&curr=USD&locale=en-XX

Bali, three nights, two adults, USD. Pulls at 00:30, 07:48, 07:55, 08:20 and 12:10 — an 11-hour-40-minute span. Twelve hotel rows each, which is one page, 60 rows total.

Those 60 rows contained 21 distinct hotels. Six appeared in all five pulls. Nine appeared exactly once.

Appeared in Hotels Median nightly
5 of 5 pulls 6 $22
4 of 5 3 $30
3 of 5 3 $89
1 of 5 9 $52

Pairwise, the overlap decays with the gap between requests, and it decays cleanly:

Pair Gap Common rows
07:55 vs 08:20 25 min 12 / 12
07:48 vs 07:55 7 min 11 / 12
00:30 vs 07:48 7 h 8 / 12
08:20 vs 12:10 4 h 8 / 12
07:48 vs 12:10 4 h 7 / 12
00:30 vs 12:10 11 h 40 6 / 12

So this is not per-request randomness. Requests minutes apart come back identical or off by one row. Requests hours apart come back half different. That is the signature of a result set that is assembled and cached, then reassembled later — not a ranking you can treat as stable.

It replicates. Three pulls on 20 October against the 19–22 November window: the two fired a minute apart agreed 12 of 12, the one twenty hours earlier agreed 7 of 12 with both. Two pulls this morning, four hours apart, agreed 7 of 12 — a $260 Kempinski vanished, a $283 resort appeared.

What that does to a number you'd actually report

The prices held almost perfectly still. Across the six hotels present in all five pulls, the nightly rate moved in three of them, by exactly one dollar: $34→$35, $10→$11, $28→$27. Kenran Resort sat at $72 in all five, Moonloka at $16. If you track one named property, Trip.com is boringly consistent and this article is irrelevant to you.

Aggregate those same five pulls and the stillness disappears:

Pull Median nightly Mean nightly
00:30 $31.00 $51.60
07:48 $35.00 $62.80
07:55 $31.50 $61.40
08:20 $31.50 $61.30
12:10 $23.50 $39.00

The mean nightly rate for Bali swung from $39.00 to $62.80 — a 61% spread — on one day, from one URL, with essentially no price changing. Every dollar of that swing is sampling. The 12:10 pull happened to miss the expensive tail: no Anvaya at $110, no Kayon Jungle at $281, no ARNA at $90. The 07:48 pull caught all three.

Which direction it biases is not random either. The six properties that never moved are all in the cheap half — $9 to $72, median $22. The nine one-time visitors have a median of $52 and include $86, $98, $106 and $166. Page one has a sticky cheap core and a rotating expensive tail, and a "city average" built on page one inherits whichever part of that tail it happened to catch.

Asking for more rows is a different question, not a bigger answer

The obvious fix is to pull deeper. It works, but not in the way "more data, same answer" suggests. Three runs on Bangkok this morning, 21–24 November, same two adults, minutes apart:

  • 12 rows: median $38.50, mean $45.10
  • a second 12-row run three minutes later: 11 of 12 the same hotels, zero price differences, order reshuffled
  • 48 rows, thirty seconds after that: 48 distinct properties, median $53.50, mean $75.30

Median $38.50 against $53.50 on the same city, the same dates, the same minute. Page one is not a random sample — it is cheap-skewed, and each extra page walks you up the price distribution. The 48-row run also did not contain 2 of the 12 hotels the first run had just returned.

The practical rule I now use: if you want a city-level statistic, fix the row count and never compare two samples of different depth. If you want coverage, run it more than once and union on hotelId — the churn is working for you then, because five pulls of 12 gave me 21 properties, not 12.

import requests, statistics
from collections import defaultdict

TOKEN = "<APIFY_TOKEN>"
seen = defaultdict(dict)

for _ in range(5):  # five pulls, spaced hours apart by a scheduler
    rows = requests.post(
        "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~tripcom-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items",
        params={"token": TOKEN},
        json={"cityId": 723, "cityName": "Bali",
              "checkIn": "2026-11-21", "checkOut": "2026-11-24",
              "adults": 2, "maxHotels": 48, "currency": "USD"},
    ).json()
    for r in rows:
        if r.get("type") == "hotel" and r.get("price"):
            seen[r["hotelId"]] = r          # last write wins, one row per property

print(len(seen), "distinct hotels")
print("median", statistics.median(r["price"] for r in seen.values()))

Note the type == "hotel" filter. The last row of every run is a free notice row with the run's own accounting — rowsDelivered, chargedTotalUsd, timings. The 48-row Bangkok run reports {"rowsDelivered": 48, "chargedTotalUsd": 0.144} and finished in 28 seconds. Leave it in your dataframe and it becomes a hotel with no price.

Two price fields you should not multiply

While I had 451 priced rows from 22 runs sitting on disk, I checked the arithmetic between price (nightly) and totalPrice (the stay).

totalPrice was larger than price × nights in 451 of 451 rows. Median ratio 1.200, range 1.056 to 1.339. Two things are stacked in there: totalPrice is the number Trip.com prints as incl. taxes & fees, and price is rounded to a whole currency unit, which on a $9 room is an 11% rounding step on its own. I am not going to tell you the tax rate, because Trip.com ships a formatted total and a rounded nightly figure and splitting them is guessing. What I will say is that price * nights is never the number the guest pays, and the error is a fifth, not a rounding wobble.

The discount badges have a smaller version of the same gap. 373 rows carried an originalPrice, and it was above price in all 373 — median implied discount 29.4%. On the 364 rows that also carried an "N% off" tag in dealTags, the discount you compute from the two numbers beat the badge in 341 of them, median by 2.7 points: Lloyd's Inn says 61% off with $80 → $28 next to it, which is 65%. Use the badge as a label and compute your own number, and don't expect them to agree to the point.

The Actor is Trip.com Scraper — hotel cards with the live rate for your dates, property details, and the guest reviews off the hotel page, by city ID or by URL.

When this is the wrong tool

  • You need a booking. This reads public pages. There is no availability hold, no rate code and no reservation here.
  • You need every hotel in a city, exactly once. You will get there by unioning repeated runs, not by one run. If you need a guaranteed complete inventory as of a timestamp, Trip.com's page one will not give you one.
  • You need per-room rate plans. Each row carries the one room Trip.com chose to price for your dates — roomName, roomId — not the hotel's full rate table.
  • You need a tax breakdown. You get the pre-tax nightly figure and the all-in total. The split between them is not published as fields, and I'd rather ship two honest numbers than three invented ones.

If you keep one thing from this: before you trust a scraped ranking, pull it twice an hour apart and count the overlap. A field that disagrees with itself is obvious. A row set that quietly swaps half its members is not, and it moves your averages far harder than any price ever will.

title: Media User Reminders: Node.js Cron Webhook Queue Handoffs Past 900 Seconds
description:
Short answer: for a media subscription renewal reminder, let cron call a public HTTPS endpoint that only enqueues work; let a queue worker do the potentially slow send. A 900-second cron ceiling makes “send every reminder in the scheduled request” a fragile design, especially when a billing-date spike arrives.

The mental model is small: cron is the alarm, the queue is the waiting room, and the worker is the person doing the calls. The trigger should acknowledge quickly. The worker can retry a delivery, record an idempotency key, and keep processing after the trigger has returned.

For this boundary, Infrai is worth testing when you want one plain REST API for both the cron admission and queue publish calls. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and includes runnable examples, so a Node.js team can inspect a capability and send HTTP without installing another SDK.

Why a 900-second deadline changes reminder design

Cron is a clock, not a batch runtime. Its single execution limit is 900 seconds. If a publisher tries to look up thousands of accounts, render messages, and call an email provider in one run, the last pages can still be running when the clock closes. A timeout then looks like a scheduling failure even though some messages were already sent.

There is a second boundary that is easy to miss: the cron target must be a public HTTP URL. Push delivery also requires a public HTTPS endpoint. A private service name, localhost address, or VPN-only route isn't reachable from the scheduler. Check the run history for failures, but don't treat its output as your application log; only the first 4 KB is retained, so the trigger and worker should emit their own structured events.

That is the whole fix.

The trigger admits work, and the worker owns delivery. For a renewal due at 09:00, put a stable reminder ID in the message, not a mutable row snapshot. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the send handler must make the provider call idempotent (or record a sent marker under that same ID) before acknowledging the message. FIFO deduplication only covers a five-minute window; it isn't a substitute for consumer idempotency.

Consider a deadline-day spike: 18,000 subscribers become eligible in one hour, but the public handler has only enough time to validate the batch and publish chunks. The worker drains those chunks at the provider's safe rate, records renewal_2026_09_12_1842 before acknowledging, and retries a 429 with backoff. If the process dies after provider acceptance and before acknowledgement, the same ID is seen again and the sent marker suppresses a second message. This is a longer path than a one-shot cron script, but each step has an observable state and a bounded retry; that is what keeps a 900-second limit from deciding which subscribers get contacted.

How should Node.js reminders use cron, a public HTTPS endpoint, and a queue worker?

Start with a public HTTPS route such as /hooks/reminder-admission. Its job is deliberately boring: authenticate the scheduler, accept the reminder batch identifier, publish one message per bounded unit of work, and return a 2xx response. It must not wait for email or SMS delivery. If the endpoint cannot be reached publicly, fix the network boundary or place a small public relay in front of the private worker; do not point cron at an internal hostname and hope retries will repair reachability.

The queue message can carry { reminderId, dueAt, attempt }. reminderId is the idempotency key used by the worker. dueAt lets the worker reject stale work or choose a fresh template, while attempt makes retry policy visible in logs. Keep payloads well below the 256 KB message limit and delay no more than seven days. Retention tops out at 30 days, and acknowledging a message removes it, so copy the fields you need into your own audit store.

Here is the smallest publisher I would keep near the public trigger. It uses an explicit method, an environment key, a client idempotency key, and a bounded retry for HTTP 429. The route and field names come from the scheduling API's discovery surface; there is no SDK to install.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const message = {
  queue: "media-renewal-reminders",
  payload: { reminderId: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842", dueAt: "2026-09-12T09:00:00Z", attempt: 0 },
  idempotency_key: "renewal_2026_09_12_1842"
};

for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(message)
  });

  if (response.ok) break;
  if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === 3) {
    throw new Error(`queue publish failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
  const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
}

The worker then claims a message, checks its own sent-record table with reminderId, sends once, and acknowledges only after the provider confirms acceptance. A network timeout after the provider accepted the message is the classic duplicate-send case; the idempotency record is what makes a retry safe. Your mileage may vary with provider semantics, so verify whether the downstream API offers an idempotency key or use a transactional outbox plus a sent marker.

Which scheduling option fits the boundary?

The right comparison is operational shape, not a leaderboard. GitHub Actions schedules are convenient for repository-owned maintenance, but a media reminder service still needs a reachable handler and a separate worker when volume spikes. RabbitMQ gives mature acknowledgements and consumer controls; it is a strong choice when your team already operates a broker and needs its routing model. Temporal or Airflow are better when the job is a long, branching workflow with durable state and joins. Inngest and Trigger.dev sit between a hosted trigger and a full workflow engine: they suit teams that want managed retries and developer-facing functions, while a plain queue remains easier to inspect with existing worker tooling.

Option Good fit Friction or limit for renewal reminders
A cron trigger plus queue worker A short public admission request and bursty sends You own idempotent consumers and application logging
GitHub Actions schedule Repo-local housekeeping and small, predictable batches Public webhook and worker lifecycle still need design
RabbitMQ Teams needing broker-level acknowledgements and routing More infrastructure and credentials to operate
Temporal or Airflow Multi-step workflows, joins, and durable orchestration Heavier control plane than a single enqueue-and-send path
Inngest or Trigger.dev Managed function retries with a developer-centric workflow surface Another hosted execution model and its event semantics to learn

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the main pain is integration friction: its discovery endpoint describes capabilities and runnable examples, and the same REST convention covers cron and queue calls. Infrai also uses a one key, one bill model across that boundary, which removes a small but recurring credential and invoice reconciliation task. One key can cover those backend capabilities, so a Node.js service can stay with plain HTTP instead of adding another SDK and credential set. I would recommend it for the public admission and queue boundary, not as a replacement for a workflow engine. The concrete advantage is fewer integration surfaces to review: discovery, auth, and request envelopes follow one convention while you swap the downstream sender behind your worker.

The catch is important. Infrai does not provide DAG orchestration, a fan-out/join primitive, native debounce, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. Choose Temporal or Airflow for a renewal process that must wait on several independent approvals, and choose RabbitMQ when you need its richer broker topology. Stick with a direct provider integration when the extra platform boundary would add more review work than it removes.

What should you observe after the handoff?

Track three timestamps: scheduled time, enqueue time, and provider-accepted time. Add the reminder ID, queue message ID, attempt count, and response status to each application log line. The cron run history is useful for spotting a failed trigger, but its truncated output cannot explain a whole batch. A small dashboard that separates “not admitted,” “waiting,” “retrying,” and “accepted” will tell you which side of the boundary needs attention.

Test the awkward paths on purpose: an unreachable public URL, a 429 from the queue API, a worker restart after provider acceptance, and a duplicate delivery inside and outside the five-minute FIFO window. Those tests expose the real contract. A green cron run alone does not prove that a subscriber received a reminder.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the cron and queue reminder guide and verify the request schema before wiring production traffic.

References

  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/inngest-functions
  • https://trigger.dev/docs/documentation/introduction
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.29061v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
