title: GO: Introduction and core syntax
description:
Go (Golang) is Google's statically typed, compiled, cross-platform, open-source programming language that combines efficiency with ease of use. Its features include built-in concurrency via goroutines and channels. It has simple syntax, fast compilation, and a comprehensive standard library. It's popular for microservices, web servers, and cloud-native development.

Installation guide: Getting Started with Go — Install Go

Module One: Go Core Syntax

  • Package declaration and Imports
  • Variables and Types
  • Control Flow and Loops: for loops, range loops, and switch statements

Package declaration and Imports

A Go program is made of packages. Packages in Go are directories containing source files that work together to organize and reuse code. Every Go file belongs to a package, and that package is declared at the top of the file. A package like fmt (for formatted I/O) is one you bring in with an import.

A package can also be defined as a group of files that share one package name, usually in one folder. Every Go file starts with a package line that names it. A Go program starts in a package called main, and its function main is where the program starts running.

A package works like a folder of recipes in a cookbook section. Every recipe card in the folder says which section it belongs to. The section that starts the meal is the one the cook opens first.

// package line
package main
// import line
import "fmt"
func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Expected output: Hello, World!

package main tells Go which package the file belongs to. The main package is special because it's the entry package for a program intended to run as an executable.

import "fmt" makes Go's standard library fmt package available to the file. It is used for formatted input and output, including printing text to the terminal.

func main() declares a function named main. When you run an executable program, execution begins in the main function.

fmt.Println("Hello, World!") calls the Println function from fmt to print text, followed by a new line. The dot accesses an exported name from a package, and the parentheses contain the arguments you're passing to the function.

How to Use Code That Belongs to Another Package (Import Another Package)

Our file often needs code from another package, which is listed in the import line. The import statement makes a standard library package available to the file. After importing, you call its functions using the package name, a dot, and the function name, such as fmt.Println. fmt is the package, and Println is the function inside it.

package main

// Makes the standard library package available to the file.
import "fmt"

// Declares the function where execution begins.
func main() {
    // Creates a variable named name as a string using the short variable declaration.
    name := "Ada"

    // Calls fmt.Println, which lives in the fmt package.
    fmt.Println("Hello", name)
}

Expected output:

Hello Ada

Naming Conventions in Go

As an example, we have fmt.Println("Train Name"). Under fmt, we have the package name, and under Println, we have the function name.

Note: Println starts with a capital letter. In Go, names beginning with a capital letter are exported and can be accessed from another package, while names beginning with a lowercase letter are unexported and can only be accessed within their own package. Go decides what other packages can use based on the first letter of a name.

Unused Imports and Compiler Errors

Go checks imports strictly. If a file imports a package and doesn't use it, the compiler stops with an error. If the file uses a package without importing it, the compiler also stops. The import block is an honest list that shows what a file depends on, and every imported package must be used.

Never use a package you haven't imported yet. Check whether an imported package is needed before importing it. You don't need to use every function inside an imported package, just one.

Incorrect:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
}

Go complains about fmt and strings being imported and not used. It also complains that name is declared and not used, because Go is just as strict about unused variables.

Correct:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    name := "ada"
    fmt.Println(strings.ToUpper(name))
}

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
const name = "Ada"; name := "Ada"
console.log("Hello", name); fmt.Println("Hello", name)

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Every Go file starts with a package line, and package main with the main function is where a program starts.
  2. An import statement brings in another package, and you can call its functions using the package name.
  3. A name starting with a capital letter is exported and can be used from other packages, while a lowercase name remains unexported.
  4. Go returns a compiler error for unused imports.

Variables and Types

A variable is a named storage location in memory used to hold a value of a specific type. It is a named box that holds a value.

In Go, variables are statically typed, meaning their type is known at compile time and cannot change.

Variables are declared using the var keyword, followed by the name, the type, and an optional value. The type says what kind of value the box can hold, and Go checks this. Any value written with the wrong type will be rejected by Go.

Kitchen analogy: There is a labelled jar in the kitchen. The label is the name, the jar's size and purpose are the type, while the contents are the value.

var itemCount int = 3
  • var — keyword
  • itemCount — name
  • int — type
  • 3 — value

Go also infers the type from the value. If you provide a value, you can leave out the type. In that case, 3 becomes an integer (int), 2.5 becomes a float64, "C" becomes a string, and true or false becomes a boolean.

The short assignment operator (:=) is used to declare a variable in Go, with the type usually inferred from the assigned value. It can only be used inside a function. Variables declared outside a function must use the var keyword.

Use var when you want to specify a type that cannot be inferred from the value, or when you want a zero value, which is the default value Go assigns to a variable when no value is provided. Inside a function, the short assignment operator (:=) is the usual choice for declaring a new variable.

Go vs. JavaScript

JavaScript Go
let item = 3; itemCount := 3

Type Inference in Go

Type inference is Go working out a variable's type from the value you give it. Go determines a variable's type from the initial value you assign to it. You don't write the type; Go infers it from the value, and the variable has a fixed type. So, the variable can't later hold a different kind of value. For example, if name is declared as a string using the short assignment operator (:=), assigning 5 to name later would be incorrect because name has already been defined as a string.

Kitchen analogy: A shelf is labelled by the first item placed on it. If the first item placed on a shelf is a book, then it can't also be used to store a banana.

// Type Inference in Go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    // var declares itemCount with the type int and the value 3.
    var itemCount int = 3

    // price := 29.5 declares a new variable. Go infers float64 from 29.5.
    price := 29.5

    // name := "tea" declares a string. The := creates a new name here.
    name := "tea"

    // A plain = assigns to an existing variable. It does not declare a new one, so no := is needed.
    itemCount = itemCount + 6

    // Prints the three values in order: name, itemCount, and price.
    fmt.Println(name, itemCount, price)
}

Expected output:

tea 9 29.5

How does this compare to TypeScript?

If you're coming from TypeScript, this will feel familiar:

let name = "tea";
name = "coffee"; // Valid
name = 5;        // Type error

TypeScript infers that name is a string, much like Go does. The difference is that TypeScript's types disappear once it's compiled to JavaScript, while Go's types are part of the compiled program. Both languages help catch certain mistakes before your program runs. Here's the same thing in Go:

name := "tea"
name = "coffee" // Valid
name = 5        // Compile error

Go Variable Naming Rules

Go variable names can be short, like x and y, or descriptive, like age and price. They must start with a letter or underscore, cannot start with a digit, and can contain only letters, digits, and underscores. Variable names are case-sensitive, cannot contain spaces or be Go keywords, and have no length limit. Multi-word variable names can use camel case (myVariableName), Pascal case (MyVariableName), or snake case (my_variable_name).

Lesson Takeaway

  • The var keyword is used to declare a variable in Go.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) declares a variable with its type inferred from the assigned value.
  • The short variable declaration operator (:=) can only be used inside a function.

Control Flow and Loops

A quick note before we start: the snippets in this section leave out package main and import "fmt" to keep things short. If you want to run one, add those two lines at the top of the file.

for Loops

Many languages have a separate keyword for each loop type, but Go doesn't. It has only for, and what follows it decides the loop shape. The header sits between for and the opening brace, and the body is the code that repeats.

Kitchen analogy: A kitchen timer can count down a set number of minutes. When it reaches zero, it stops and is ready to be turned off. One tool, 3 uses.

func main() {
    // i := 1 happens once, before any check.
    // i <= 3 is checked before every pass, and the body only runs while it's true.
    // i++ adds 1 after each pass.
    for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

1
2
3
  • for — keyword
  • i := 1 — initialises i to 1
  • i <= 3 — condition
  • i++ — increments i by one
  • fmt.Println(i) — body, the code that repeats

A typical for loop has three parts, separated by semicolons.

  1. Initial statement: It runs once before the loop starts and usually creates a counter. 
i := 1;
  1. Condition statement: It is checked before each pass through the loop. 
i <= 3;
  1. Post statement: It runs after each pass and usually changes the counter. 
i++

So, i := 1 starts the counter at one, the loop runs while i is less than or equal to three, and i++ adds one after each pass.

Types of For Loops in Go

There are three major types of loops in Go:

  • Classic loop
  • Condition only loop
  • Infinite loop

1. Classic Loop

We use a classic loop when we want to repeat something a known number of times or track a counter.

for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

A classic loop has three parts: the initial statement, condition statement, and post statement. It runs five times in this example, printing 0 to 4.

2. Condition Only Loop

This works like a while loop in JavaScript or TypeScript.

count := 0
for count < 5 {
    fmt.Println(count)
    count++
}

Note: There's no semicolon in the loop header. It has only a condition and runs while the condition is true.

3. Infinite Loop

You use an infinite loop when you omit the condition. The loop continues indefinitely unless something inside stops it, usually with the keyword break or return.

for {
    fmt.Println("Still running")
    break
}

Note: break stops the loop after the first print. An infinite loop has no condition and runs indefinitely until it is stopped.

Go vs. JavaScript/TypeScript

Purpose Go JavaScript
Counter loop for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { } for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
Condition loop for count < 3 { } while (count < 3) { }
Infinite loop for { } while (true) { }

Main difference: Go does not have a separate while keyword. It uses for for all loop types, and what follows for determines how the loop behaves.

Range Loop

Writing i := 0; i < 5; i++ can honestly be a bit long sometimes. So Go gives us a shorter way to write it using range.

for i := range 5 {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

This gives i values from 0 to 4, printing each value on a new line.

Expected output:

0
1
2
3
4

Note: range 5 iterates five times, producing values from 0 up to, but not including, 5. Ranging over a number like this needs Go 1.22 or newer, so if it doesn't compile, run go version to check what you have installed.

In a loop, continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the whole loop.

func main() {
    for i := range 5 {
        if i == 2 {
            continue
        }

        fmt.Println(i)
    }
}

Expected output:

0
1
3
4

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Go has only one looping keyword, for.
  2. A classic loop has three parts, separated by semicolons: an initialisation statement that starts the counter, a condition statement that is checked before every pass, and a post statement that runs after every pass.
  3. A condition-only loop runs as long as the condition is true.
  4. An infinite loop runs indefinitely unless it is stopped using break or return.
  5. A range loop provides a shorter way to iterate over values, such as for i := range 5, which produces values from 0 to 4.
  6. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one, while break stops the loop.

Route Logic Using Typed Switch Statements

In JavaScript or TypeScript, there is a switch statement or an if-else statement. Go has both too. A switch statement in Go selects and executes one block of code from multiple possibilities based on the value or type of an expression. A switch statement provides a cleaner alternative to multiple if statements. It also supports both value-based and type-based branching.

How does it work?

A switch statement tells Go which values to examine. Then, each case defines a possible value. Go runs the code under the matching case. If no case matches, it runs default.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    day := "Monday"

    switch day {
    case "Monday":
        fmt.Println("Start of the week")
    case "Friday":
        fmt.Println("Almost the weekend")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another day")
    }
}

Expected output:

Start of the week

Go supports two types of switch statements

  1. Expression switch
  2. Type switch

1. An Expression Switch

An expression switch evaluates an expression and executes the matching case block. This is useful when you have several possible options.

// Expression switch: evaluate the value, find a match,
// execute the matching case, and exit the switch.

func main() {
    route := "/profile"

    switch route {
    case "/":
        fmt.Println("Home page")
    case "/dashboard":
        fmt.Println("Dashboard page")
    case "/profile":
        fmt.Println("Profile page")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Page not found")
    }
}

An expression switch can also check more than one value in a single case. Just separate the values with a comma.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case 18:
        fmt.Println("Finally an adult")
    case 25, 30: // two values, one case
        fmt.Println("How's life?")
    case 35:
        fmt.Println("Oldie")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Another age")
    }
}

Expected output:

How's life?

The value in the switch and the values in the case expressions must be comparable under Go's type rules. E.g., an integer variable cannot be compared directly against a string.

func main() {
    age := 25

    switch age {
    case "25": // Error: cannot compare int with string
        fmt.Println("Twenty-five")
    }
}

This code produces a compile-time error because age is an integer (int), while "25" is a string. Go does not allow these incompatible types to be compared directly in a switch statement. The fix is to make both sides the same type, like case 25:.

Go also allows you to omit the value after switch. Each case can then contain a Boolean condition.

func main() {
    score := 75

    switch {
    case score >= 80:
        fmt.Println("Excellent")
    case score >= 60:
        fmt.Println("Passed")
    default:
        fmt.Println("Try again")
    }
}

Go evaluates the cases from top to bottom and executes the first case whose condition is true.

2. Type Switch

A switch checks the value, while a type switch checks what type a value is. This is useful when a variable has an interface type, such as any, and the value inside can be any data type. In Go, any is an alias for the empty interface, and it can hold a value of any type.

func main() {
    var value any = true

    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        fmt.Println("This is a string:", v)
    case int:
        fmt.Println("This is an integer:", v)
    case bool:
        fmt.Println("This is a Boolean:", v)
    default:
        fmt.Println("Unknown type")
    }
}
  • value — a variable of type any.
  • .(type) — the syntax used to inspect the value's type in a type switch.
  • v — a variable declared in the switch that refers to the value inside each case, with its specific type.
  • case string — when the value is a string, v is a string.
  • case int — when the value is an integer, v is an integer.

Expression Switch vs. Type Switch

Feature Expression switch Type switch
What it checks A value or Boolean condition The type of a value
Typical use Routes, selectors, and codes Values whose types may differ
Example switch route switch v := value.(type)
Cases Values or Boolean conditions Types such as string, int, etc.
Matching Executes the matching case Executes the case matching the value's type
Type handling Cases must be compatible with the switch expression's type Go identifies the value's type in each case

Go vs. JavaScript

Feature Go JavaScript
Syntax switch expression { } switch (expression) { }
Case behaviour Exits the switch automatically after a matching case (use fallthrough if you want it to continue) Requires break to prevent fall-through

Lesson Takeaway

  1. Use an expression switch when one value can have several possible outcomes.
  2. Use a type switch when you need to identify a value's type.
  3. Use case to define options and default to handle anything unmatched.

Final Practice Exercise

Create a small program that combines what you've learned.

Your program should:

  1. Declare a variable called status and assign it "pending".
  2. Use an expression switch to print a message for "pending", "approved", or "rejected".
  3. Print "Unknown status" for any other value.
  4. Use a for loop with range 5 to print the numbers zero through four, but skip the number two using continue.

title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
description:
arXiv:2610.28771v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.

title: MINER: Modeling Inter- and Intra-Person Variance for Reidentification
description:
arXiv:2610.28941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clothes-Changing Person Re-Identification (CC-ReID) remains challenging due to drastic appearance shifts across outfits. Most prior works devise biometric signal-extraction heuristics to enhance inter-person variance, e.g., using segmentation masks, while leaving intra-person variance uncontrolled. We present MINER, a simple model-agnostic framework that suppresses garment bias by contrasting hard examples and adaptively balancing dataset-dependent intra- and inter-person variance. Extensive experiments show that MINER improves retrieval across CC-ReID benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and ranking among the leaders in all three tracks of the open TVRID RGB-Depth ReID challenge.

title: Carving Radiology Reports at Their Evidential Joints: Anatomical Region Sets as Generation Units
description:
arXiv:2610.29165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organizing radiology reports into independently generated units offers a way to generate fine-grained clinical content and bind it to visual evidence. However, existing methods typically adopt generation-unit structures not directly specified in natural reports or their annotations, introducing additional modeling compromises. We propose RadCarve, which instead defines generation units directly from the anatomical region sets in existing statement-region correspondences, unifying unit formation with visual evidence selection. RadCarve's planner uses composition-specialized query banks to jointly predict unit existence and region composition from the image, iteratively refining both with regional evidence aggregated according to current membership predictions. The generator independently produces each unit's text conditioned on the joint visual evidence of its predicted region set. Compared with strong baselines, RadCarve improves CXRFEScore by 9.4% in unit generation given region sets and achieves 2.4 times the end-to-end binding F1. It also achieves leading report-generation results on Chest ImaGenome and PadChest-GR, using fewer than one-sixth as many parameters as large-scale baselines.

title: Complexity-Aware Surgical Video Reasoning Segmentation with Digital Twin and Context Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.28776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional surgical segmentation relies on closed-set categories or explicit text queries, which cannot resolve implicit queries that require reasoning about workflows, instrument functions, and temporal relationships. To address these limitations, we propose SurgReasonSeg, a complexity-aware method that brings reasoning segmentation over digital twin (DT) representations to surgical video. Specifically, SurgReasonSeg constructs DT representations from surgical foundation models and trains two low-rank adapters (LoRA) of one large language model with reinforcement learning (RL), each specialized for a different query complexity. A lightweight router, also trained with RL, selects between the two adapters to balance latency against accuracy. SurgReasonSeg also sets the temporal context with an adaptive sliding window conditioned on query complexity and workflow phase, and retrieves relevant historical cases from a surgical context memory by workflow similarity and procedural relevance. We further introduce EndoVis-ReasonSeg, a surgical reasoning segmentation benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal categories. On EndoVis-ReasonSeg, SurgReasonSeg improves J&F over the strongest baseline, ReSurgSAM2, by 0.178, 0.237, and 0.297 on semantic, spatial, and temporal queries, and it also achieves the best results on the Ref-EndoVis17 and Ref-EndoVis18 referring segmentation benchmarks. A backbone-matched attribution protocol separates the contribution of the upstream segmenter from that of the reasoning modules. Our method runs at 18.8 FPS averaged over the query distribution, enabling real-time reasoning segmentation in surgical videos.

title: Don't Stop Long-Context Continual Pre-Training Too Early: An Empirical Scaling Law
description:
arXiv:2610.29352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-context continual pre-training (LCCP) is widely used to improve long-context capability, but how its benefits scale with the number of tokens used for LCCP remains unclear. We investigate this question through modeling, monitoring, and validating the benefits of scaling LCCP. First, we establish an empirical additive power law relating long-context performance to model size and the respective token budgets of short-context pre-training and LCCP. Experiments across five model scales and more than one hundred short- and long-context budget configurations show that the fitted law reproduces the observed trends and extrapolates well to held-out model scales. Second, we introduce \textsc{Constant-Last4}, a training and observation protocol that averages the four most recent consecutive checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate run to enable stable monitoring along a single extensible training trajectory. Under this protocol, the same scaling-law form fits well and accurately predicts the LCCP performance trajectory of a 1.22B-parameter model trained on approximately 100B LCCP tokens. Finally, downstream evaluations along this trajectory show continued improvements in long-context performance, with no clear sign of saturation within the evaluated range. These gains persist after both 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, with benefits extending to long-context understanding and agentic tasks. Together, these results argue for continuing to scale LCCP rather than stopping early: its gains are stably observable along an extensible trajectory, quantitatively predictable, and transferable to downstream tasks.

title: Tuning the Linux Kernel for 10x Traffic: How We Prepared a Modest Cloud Server for the Hug of Death
description:
Somaxconn, SYN backlogs, TCP syncookies, and finding our breaking point with stepped Autocannon load benchmarks.

The alert hit our channel at 11:14 AM on a Tuesday.

Our product had just been picked up on a popular tech newsletter, and inbound traffic surged from our normal baseline of 8 requests per second to over 180 requests per second within three minutes.

On the surface, our 2-vCPU, 4GB RAM cloud instance looked relaxed. CPU utilization hovered around 32%. Memory had nearly 2GB free. Disk I/O was barely moving.

Yet visitors were seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors, and API clients reported connection timeouts:

curl: (35) OpenSSL SSL_connect: Connection reset by peer in connection to api.example.com:443

Why would a server drop incoming web traffic when more than half of its compute capacity was sitting idle?

The answer was not in the application code, the database queries, or the cloud provider firewall. The bottleneck was inside the Linux kernel network stack. Out of the box, Linux distributions ship with network socket limits designed for the hardware realities of twenty years ago. When an unexpected traffic surge hits your front door, the kernel drops incoming TCP handshakes before your reverse proxy or web application even knows they exist.

Here is the exact diagnostic workflow, the kernel parameters we tuned to handle ten times our normal traffic, and the stepped Autocannon load tests we used to find our server breaking point.

The Silent Killer: The Two TCP Queues

To understand why a server with an idle CPU rejects incoming web requests, you have to look at how the Linux kernel handles incoming TCP connections.

Before an HTTP request reaches Nginx, Node.js, Go, or Python, the kernel network subsystem must complete the standard TCP three-way handshake:

  1. The client sends a SYN packet to request a connection.
  2. The server responds with SYN-ACK.
  3. The client replies with an ACK packet.

The connection is now established. Only then does the application receive the socket through the accept() system call.

What most engineers miss is that the kernel maintains two completely separate queues in memory during this process:

The SYN Queue (Half-Open Sockets)

When a client sends a SYN, the kernel creates a lightweight request socket in memory and parks it in the SYN queue (also called the half-open connection queue). The connection stays here while waiting for the client final ACK.

The size of this queue is bounded by the kernel parameter net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog.

The Accept Queue (Fully Established Sockets)

Once the client returns the final ACK, the handshake is complete. The kernel promotes the connection from the SYN queue to the Accept queue.

The connection sits in the Accept queue until your application process calls accept() to pick it up and assign it a file descriptor.

The size of this queue is bounded by the system-wide limit net.core.somaxconn and the backlog parameter passed by your application to the listen() system call.

Here is the problem: on many standard cloud images, net.core.somaxconn defaults to 128 (or 4096 on newer kernels, while application servers still request 128 or 511). And net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog often defaults to 128 or 512.

If a sudden burst of 200 users attempts to connect simultaneously, the Accept queue fills up instantly.

Once the queue is full, the kernel has a stark choice. By default, it silently drops newly arriving ACK packets. The client assumes the packet was lost in transit and attempts TCP retransmissions, creating an artificial latency spike of one to three seconds.

If the queue remains congested, the client connection times out or the server resets it with a RST packet.

Your application never logged an error because the request was killed before user space ever saw it.

How to Prove Your Sockets Are Dropping Packets

Never guess when debugging the Linux network stack. You can inspect queue depths and drop counters directly from the command line.

Inspecting Live Socket Backlogs with ss

The ss command is the modern replacement for netstat. Most engineers know how to use it to check open ports, but few know how to interpret its queue output on listening sockets.

Run this command on your server:

ss -lnt '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )'

You will see output formatted like this:

State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:PortProcess
LISTEN     0      511          0.0.0.0:80        0.0.0.0:*
LISTEN     128    128          0.0.0.0:443       0.0.0.0:*

On an established socket (a live data connection), Recv-Q represents bytes in the receive buffer waiting to be read by the application, and Send-Q represents bytes waiting to be sent over the wire.

On a LISTEN socket, those columns mean something completely different:

  • Send-Q: The maximum backlog capacity of the Accept queue.
  • Recv-Q: The current number of established connections waiting in the Accept queue to be accepted by the application.

Look at port 443 in the sample output above. Recv-Q is 128 and Send-Q is 128.

The Accept queue is completely full. Every single incoming connection arriving at that exact microsecond is being dropped by the kernel.

Checking Kernel Drop Counters with nstat and netstat

To verify whether your server has suffered queue overflows historically, query the kernel SNMP network statistics:

nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops

Or using netstat:

netstat -s | grep -i "listen"

Sample output:

14820 times the listen queue of a socket overflowed
14820 SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped

If TcpExtListenOverflows is greater than zero, your server has dropped real customer connections because the Accept queue was saturated.

If TcpExtListenDrops is incrementing, the kernel had to discard incoming connection attempts because either the Accept queue was full, the SYN backlog was exhausted, or memory pressure prevented socket allocation.

To check if SYN flood protection or queue exhaustion has been triggered recently, inspect the kernel ring buffer:

dmesg -T | grep -i -E "syn|drop|backlog"

If you see messages like TCP: request_sock_TCP: Possible SYN flooding on port 443. Sending cookies. Check SNMP counters, the kernel SYN queue is overflowing.

The Double-Gatekeeper Bottleneck

A common mistake is changing net.core.somaxconn in /etc/sysctl.conf and assuming the problem is solved.

It is not. The Accept queue size is governed by a double gatekeeper:

Effective Accept Queue = min( net.core.somaxconn, application listen backlog )

When an application server initializes a socket, it executes the listen() system call:

int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);

The second argument tells the kernel how large of an Accept queue the application wants. But the kernel caps that request at the value of net.core.somaxconn.

If you raise net.core.somaxconn to 4096, but your application server requests a backlog of 128, your effective queue remains 128.

Conversely, if your Nginx configuration specifies listen 443 default_server backlog=4096;, but your kernel somaxconn is set to 512, the kernel truncates your queue to 512.

Both layers must be configured in unison.

Nginx Configuration

In your Nginx site configuration, explicitly set the backlog parameter on your listen directives:

server {
    listen 80 backlog=4096;
    listen 443 ssl backlog=4096;
    server_name api.example.com;

    # ... rest of configuration
}

Node.js / Express Configuration

In Node.js HTTP servers, the default backlog is 511. You can raise it by passing an options object to server.listen():

const express = require('express');
const app = express();

const server = app.listen({
    port: 3000,
    host: '0.0.0.0',
    backlog: 4096
}, () => {
    console.log('Server running with listen backlog 4096');
});

Python Gunicorn / Uvicorn

If you run Python workloads with Gunicorn, set the backlog parameter in your command line or config file:

gunicorn --workers 4 --backlog 4096 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 app:wsgi_app

The High-Performance Kernel Recipe

To prepare a production Linux host for high concurrency and unexpected traffic surges, create a dedicated sysctl configuration file at /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf.

Here is the exact configuration we deploy across our cloud nodes:

# /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf

# 1. Expand Socket Listen and SYN Backlogs
net.core.somaxconn = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 4096

# 2. Connection Exhaustion and SYN Defense
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries = 2

# 3. Socket Lifecycle and Teardown Acceleration
net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1

# 4. Ephemeral Port Range Expansion
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535

# 5. Network Buffer Allocation (Safe for 2GB - 8GB RAM nodes)
net.core.rmem_max = 16777216
net.core.wmem_max = 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 16777216

# 6. Anti-Spoofing and Path Verification
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

Let us break down why each parameter is set this way and what it changes in practice.

Socket Listen and SYN Queues

net.core.somaxconn = 4096 expands the maximum Accept queue limit from the legacy default to 4096 entries. This gives the application an order of magnitude more headroom during traffic spikes.

net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096 ensures the SYN queue can hold up to 4096 half-open connections while handshakes complete.

net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 4096 governs the incoming packet queue between the physical or virtual network interface card (NIC) and the kernel network stack. When the NIC receives packets faster than the CPU can process kernel interrupts, this buffer prevents packet drops at the driver layer.

SYN Cookies and Handshake Resiliency

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 activates cryptographic SYN cookies when the SYN backlog overflows. Instead of dropping new connection requests, the kernel encodes the connection state into the initial TCP sequence number sent in the SYN-ACK. When the legitimate client responds with its ACK, the kernel reconstructs the socket without having stored anything in memory. This repels SYN flood attacks and absorbs unexpected spikes without degrading service.

net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries = 2 lowers the number of times the kernel retransmits a SYN-ACK packet before abandoning the attempt. The default is 5, which ties up resources for over 30 seconds if a client disappears. Lowering it to 2 reclaims half-open sockets within 7 seconds.

Socket Teardown and TIME_WAIT Recycling

net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15 reduces the time a socket stays in the FIN-WAIT-2 state from the default of 60 seconds down to 15 seconds. When clients disconnect abruptly without completing a clean four-way TCP shutdown, this ensures the kernel frees orphaned sockets four times faster.

net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 allows the kernel to safely reuse sockets in the TIME_WAIT state for new outgoing connections, provided the incoming timestamps are strictly greater than the previous connection. This is vital when running a reverse proxy (like Nginx) that opens and closes high-frequency TCP connections to local backend services.

Ephemeral Port Range

net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535 expands the dynamic port range available for outbound client connections. The default Linux range is 32768 60999, offering approximately 28,231 ports. Setting it to 10240 65535 expands the pool to 55,295 ephemeral ports.

When an Nginx proxy handles 5,000 requests per second against an upstream Node.js application, ports in TIME_WAIT can rapidly exhaust the default range, leading to EADDRNOTAVAIL (Cannot assign requested address) errors. Doubling the port pool eliminates this ceiling.

Applying the Changes Safely

To load the new configuration into the running kernel without rebooting:

sudo sysctl --system

Verify that the values took effect:

sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse

Output:

net.core.somaxconn = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1

Don't Forget the Conntrack Table and File Descriptors

Two additional system limits frequently trip up engineers who tune socket backlogs but leave firewall or file descriptor defaults untouched.

1. The Netfilter Connection Tracking Table

If you use iptables, nftables, or ufw on your server, the kernel tracks every active stateful connection in a table called conntrack.

When traffic spikes, the connection tracking table can fill up completely. When that happens, the kernel drops incoming packets immediately, logging this terrifying message to dmesg:

nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet

Check your current conntrack usage and maximum table limit:

cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max

On a system with 2GB to 4GB of RAM, raise the limit inside /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-tuning.conf:

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 600

Lowering nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established from its default of 432,000 seconds (5 full days!) down to 600 seconds (10 minutes) purges dead tracking entries exponentially faster.

2. Systemd and File Descriptor Ceilings

Every open socket in Linux requires a file descriptor. The default per-process file limit in systemd is often 1024.

If your Nginx worker process hits 1,024 open connections, it logs:

2026/10/21 11:15:02 [alert] 1240#1240: *45100 socket() failed (24: Too many open files) while connecting to upstream

To permanently fix this for Nginx, create a systemd drop-in configuration:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/override.conf

Add these lines:

[Service]
LimitNOFILE=65535

Also add worker_rlimit_nofile 65535; to the top of /etc/nginx/nginx.conf:

user www-data;
worker_processes auto;
pid /run/nginx.pid;
worker_rlimit_nofile 65535;

events {
    worker_connections 8192;
    multi_accept on;
}

Reload and restart:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart nginx

Check the applied limit on the running process:

cat /proc/$(pgrep -o nginx)/limits | grep "Max open files"

Output:

Max open files            65535                65535                files

Real-World Socket Engineering: The Local Port Churn Lesson

When I was building AiroShare, a local DLNA streaming server and high-performance media engine, socket management was one of the earliest friction points I ran into.

In that project, the application broadcasts media manifests to DLNA receivers over SSDP multicast while servicing concurrent media chunk streaming requests over HTTP. During intense chunk streaming, ephemeral sockets opened and closed at an aggressive rate.

Without setting net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 and expanding the local port range, high-concurrency client requests quickly choked on dead sockets sitting in TIME_WAIT. The operating system refused to assign new client sockets, throwing EADDRNOTAVAIL errors even though the machine had negligible CPU load.

The exact same problem happens on cloud servers with reverse proxies. When Nginx proxies thousands of incoming connections to a local backend on 127.0.0.1:3000, it consumes an ephemeral port for every single upstream connection.

If keepalive connections are not enabled between Nginx and the backend, each request opens a new socket and leaves it in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds.

Always configure upstream keepalive pools in Nginx:

upstream backend_cluster {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
    keepalive 64;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl backlog=4096;
    server_name api.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://backend_cluster;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
    }
}

Adding proxy_http_version 1.1 and clearing the Connection header allows Nginx to reuse established TCP connections to your application, slashing socket churn by over 80%.

Stress Testing Live: Finding the Breaking Point with Autocannon

Applying kernel parameters without testing them is wishful thinking. To verify our tuning and find the true breaking point of our 2-vCPU node, we ran stepped load benchmarks using Autocannon.

Autocannon is a fast, Node.js-based HTTP benchmarking tool that supports high concurrency, pipelining, and custom headers.

Instead of hitting the server with a static blast of traffic, we used a stepped concurrency testing model:

  1. Step 1: 10 concurrent connections (moderate baseline load).
  2. Step 2: 25 concurrent connections (medium-high production burst).
  3. Step 3: 50 concurrent connections (extreme saturation test).

We ran tests against two separate endpoints: a heavy SSR/database-backed endpoint and an optimized, lightweight JSON telemetry endpoint.

Test 1: Baseline Load at 10 Concurrent Connections

Command executed:

autocannon -c 10 -d 30 -p 10 https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry
10 connections with 10 pipelined requests

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      78ms     135ms    210ms    245ms    138.4ms   34.2ms    312ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      28       31       38       44       38.2      4.1       25

1.1k requests in 30.05s, 4.2 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

At 10 concurrent connections with pipelining, our server processed 38.2 requests per second at a median latency of 135ms. The CPU remained below 40%. Zero packet drops occurred. Socket errors stayed at zero.

Test 2: Scaling Up to 25 Concurrent Connections

Next, we tested the optimized API endpoint under higher concurrency:

autocannon -c 25 -d 30 https://api.example.com/api/v1/status

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/status
25 connections

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      52ms     102ms    180ms    210ms    105.1ms   28.6ms    260ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      62       68       75       84       75.3      5.8       58

2.3k requests in 30.04s, 8.9 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

On this endpoint, throughput climbed to 75.3 requests per second with a median latency of 102ms.

The contrast was stark. Before our kernel tuning, this exact test triggered TcpExtListenOverflows within four seconds. It dropped over 18% of all connection attempts. With the expanded backlog and tuned TCP syncookies, zero connections were dropped. Not one packet failed.

Test 3: The Latency Cliff at 50 Concurrent Connections

We pushed the 2-vCPU node further to find its ceiling:

autocannon -c 50 -d 30 https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry

Output:

Running 30s test @ https://api.example.com/api/v1/telemetry
50 connections

Stat         2.5%     50%      97.5%    99%      Avg       Stdev     Max
Latency      190ms    450ms    1620ms   1840ms   485.2ms   215.4ms   2410ms

Stat         1%       2.5%     50%      97.5%    Avg       Stdev     Min
Req/Sec      35       38       42       46       41.6      3.2       30

1.2k requests in 30.08s, 4.8 MB read
0 errors, 0 timeouts, 0 non-2xx responses

Look closely at what happened.

Throughput plateaued at 41.6 requests per second. Median latency jumped from 135ms to 450ms. The 99th percentile surged to 1,840ms.

During the test, running pidstat -u 1 on the server showed CPU utilization at 98.4%. The cores were pegged.

This is the classic latency cliff.

Crucially, because the kernel queue parameters were properly tuned, there were still zero connection drops and zero timeout errors (0 errors, 0 timeouts).

The server did not crash. It did not reset connections. Instead, requests queued orderly in the expanded Accept queue until CPU cycles were available to process them.

That distinction matters.

An untuned server crashes under load. It drops users with 502 Bad Gateway errors while CPU sits idle. A hardened server queues the burst gracefully. It trades latency for 100% request completion.

An Interesting Fact About somaxconn

The default value of 128 for somaxconn was not chosen through scientific analysis of modern networking.

It was first hardcoded into the 4.2BSD Unix kernel release in 1983.

At the time, typical Unix workstations had between 2MB and 16MB of total physical RAM. Network engineers feared that allowing more than 128 outstanding socket requests would exhaust kernel mbuf memory and trigger a system crash.

That 128-socket limit remained the default across mainstream Linux distributions for over two decades. Even today, many production cloud images default to conservative backlog values that can be saturated by a single office browser refresh.

My Default Rule of Thumb for High-Concurrency Nodes

When preparing a production Linux server for sudden traffic surges:

  • Match your backlogs: Set net.core.somaxconn = 4096 and net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096 in sysctl, and match them with backlog=4096 in your Nginx or application server.
  • Enable SYN cookies: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 protects you from both deliberate SYN floods and legitimate viral traffic surges.
  • Speed up socket reclamation: Set net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15 and net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 to prevent orphaned sockets from lingering.
  • Double your file limits: Add LimitNOFILE=65535 to your systemd overrides and configure worker_rlimit_nofile 65535; in Nginx.
  • Reuse proxy upstreams: Always configure keepalive in Nginx upstream blocks to avoid ephemeral port exhaustion on 127.0.0.1.
  • Monitor with ss -lnt and nstat: If Recv-Q matches Send-Q on a listening socket, or TcpExtListenOverflows is increasing, your Accept queue is overflowing.

Have you ever experienced an outage where your server was dropping traffic even though CPU and memory were barely breaking a sweat? What turned out to be the bottleneck?

title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.29231v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.

title: GBase Database Batch Silent Installation: How to Troubleshoot Deployment Failures
description:
Batch deployment makes it easier to install GBase Database(GBase 8s) across multiple servers. But when a silent installation fails on several machines at once, a small configuration mistake can quickly become a deployment-wide problem.

The key is to stop the rollout, identify the failure on a single machine, and validate the fix before continuing.

Here is a practical troubleshooting workflow for failed batch silent installations.

1. Stop the Next Batch Immediately

If multiple servers start reporting installation failures, pause the remaining deployment tasks.

Continuing to deploy with the same configuration can spread the problem to more machines and make troubleshooting harder.

Keep a record of which nodes have completed installation successfully, which have failed, and which have not yet been processed. Avoid modifying verified nodes unless there is a clear reason to do so.

2. Reproduce the Failure on a Single Machine

Choose one failed server and rerun the silent installation using the same response file and parameters used in the batch deployment.

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

Capture the complete command output and inspect the installation logs. Identify the first error rather than focusing only on the final failure message.

The goal is to determine whether the problem comes from the installation parameters, the target server's environment, or a conflict with existing files and services.

If the failure cannot be reproduced on the selected machine, compare its configuration with the other failed nodes before making changes.

3. Check Four Common Causes of Batch Installation Failures

Response File or Path Problems

A response file that works on one server may be missing, corrupted during transfer, or stored at a different path on another server.

Check that the file exists and is readable:

ls -l /opt/bundle.properties

If the same response file is distributed to multiple servers, verify that its contents match the intended configuration. Pay particular attention to installation paths, selected components, and other environment-specific parameters.

Missing Dependencies or Environment Differences

Servers in the same deployment batch are not always identical. Differences in installed packages, operating system configuration, permissions, or environment variables can cause the same silent installation to succeed on one machine and fail on another.

Compare a failed node with a known-good node. Use the installation logs to identify missing dependencies or environment-related errors before changing system settings.

Port or Directory Conflicts

An installation may encounter conflicts with existing files, directories, or services on the target machine.

Check whether the intended installation directory already contains files from a previous attempt. Also verify that the configured database port is not already in use.

For example, inspect the installation directory:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

If a port conflict is suspected, check the actual port configured for the target instance and identify the process using it. Do not assume every server uses the same port configuration.

Insufficient Disk Space

A batch deployment may fail only on certain servers because their available disk space differs.

Check the installation filesystem:

df -h /opt

If the installer uses a separate temporary filesystem, check that filesystem as well. Package extraction and temporary files may require additional space beyond the final installation footprint.

4. Fix One Machine Before Resuming the Batch

Once you identify the root cause, correct it on the selected server and repeat the installation or recovery procedure as appropriate.

Before resuming the rollout, verify that:

  • The silent installation completes successfully.
  • The installed files have the expected ownership and permissions.
  • The database instance can be initialized and started using the documented procedure.
  • The configured port and connection settings work as expected.

Remember that successful software installation does not necessarily mean the database instance is ready for use. Validate the relevant instance initialization and connection steps separately.

After the test machine passes these checks, resume deployment in small batches and monitor the results before increasing the rollout size.

5. Make the Next Batch Deployment More Reliable

A repeatable GBase Database deployment process should include a few safeguards:

  • Validate first: Test the response file and installation procedure on a single representative server.
  • Check prerequisites: Verify operating system requirements, dependencies, disk space, permissions, and port availability before deployment.
  • Keep configurations consistent: Use a controlled response file and explicitly document any server-specific differences.
  • Deploy incrementally: Increase batch size only after the previous batch passes validation.
  • Record failures: Keep installation output, relevant logs, and the affected server's configuration for later comparison.

These practices help distinguish problems in the deployment procedure from differences between individual servers.

Final Thoughts

When batch silent installation of GBase Database fails, resist the temptation to rerun the entire deployment immediately.

Stop the rollout, reproduce the error on one machine, identify the first failing step, and validate the fix before proceeding. A controlled, incremental deployment is much safer than allowing the same unknown problem to spread across every server.

The principle is simple: validate one machine, verify one batch, and scale only when the results are consistent.

title: Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.24833v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: As AI agents become increasingly connected through networks and take on tasks that require negotiation and joint decision-making, a systematic approach is needed to assess how their views converge and what information supports their decisions. We present an evaluation framework that treats consensus formation as the evolution of publicly stated positions toward a shared region, using accumulated communication history as context. The framework tracks position trajectories, group dispersion, and information expressed in public messages. Two case studies examine staffing decisions based on distributed facts and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract. Results from 1,872 completed runs associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, while the second task reveals persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers. Membership-change experiments provide a complementary evaluation. By separating convergence among agents from progress toward a task's full-information answer, the framework relates decision accuracy and bounded disagreement to the information available during the exchange.
