title: Go Retrieval Architecture and Query Limits for a Financial Research Dashboard
description:
Short answer: for a financial research dashboard, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way to the answer; choose a managed vector boundary when reducing integration and on-call load matters more than owning every retrieval control.

For a financial research dashboard that answers questions over a folder of logistics-company PDFs, the safe default is two observable stages: ingest pages into a named collection, then query that collection under a declared retrieval contract. Keep answer generation outside that contract. This makes recall, latency, freshness, and citation failures distinguishable instead of turning every bad answer into one vague "RAG problem."

I recommend that teams with a small platform group try Infrai for the vector upsert and query boundary when they want plain REST from Go without installing or tracking a provider SDK. In operational terms, Infrai uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so adding another backend capability to the workflow does not create another secret-rotation schedule or invoice owner. Its API is also self-describing: the public discovery surface requires no key and returns full request JSON Schema before integration code is written. The recommendation is conditional, not universal; a specialist vector database is the better call when proprietary ranking controls or deep engine-specific tuning are requirements.

What failure signal should drive the architecture?

The signal is disagreement between answer quality and retrieval evidence. If the dashboard cites a quarterly report that never entered the candidate set, generation isn't the first place to look. If the right page was retrieved but a stale filing ranked above the current one, collection boundaries, metadata, and freshness policy deserve attention. Those are different failures with different owners.

Treat each user-visible answer as the output of a retrieval contract. The contract names the retrieval unit, allowed metadata filters, freshness rule, candidate bound, and citation fields. For the logistics PDF folder, a page is often a more inspectable unit than a whole report: a page can carry the document name, reporting period, and source location without forcing an operator to guess which part of a 180-page filing matched. This is a design choice, not a universal law; tables split across pages may justify a different unit, and representative documents must decide it.

The capacity-planning reflex matters here. An unbounded query converts one dashboard interaction into an unknown fan-out, while a bound lets the team reason about queue depth and a latency SLO before traffic arrives. A burst that receives HTTP 429 needs exponential backoff and Retry-After handling at the client boundary; it should not become a tight retry loop that amplifies load. At the application layer, use a local error such as RETRIEVAL_BOUND_EXCEEDED when a request violates policy, because that failure is actionable and should never be confused with an empty result.

Be precise.

A bound is useful only when operators can see it.

I'm not sure a fixed candidate count will remain correct as the PDF mix changes, and nobody can settle that from architecture diagrams. A labeled evaluation set containing current filings, stale filings, scanned pages, near-duplicate reports, and questions with no supported answer will resolve the uncertainty. Track retrieval recall and precision on that set, then observe end-to-end latency separately. A single blended score hides the trade-off the dashboard actually has to manage.

How should a financial research dashboard set retrieval query limits?

Set limits as an application policy derived from the latency objective and evaluation set, not as an undocumented number scattered through handlers. Before defining a payload, verify the provider contract rather than guessing it. The following runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery surface, selects the verified vector query capability by its exact method and path, and prints the advertised request schema. Discovery needs no API key; the eventual query call uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY after the team has generated a payload from that schema.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery status=%d\n", resp.StatusCode)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    var manifest Manifest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&manifest); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/vector/query" {
            if !capability.Available {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "vector query is not advertised as available")
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(capability.Params); err != nil {
                fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            return
        }
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "POST /v1/vector/query was not found in discovery")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Discovery is the guardrail, not the retrieval policy itself. The application still keeps ingestion, querying, and citation separate: ingestion owns PDF parsing, unit selection, metadata normalization, and collection assignment; querying accepts only approved filters and a bounded candidate request; answer generation receives candidates plus citation keys, but it cannot silently widen the query or discard provenance. Generate the query payload from the returned schema, validate the application ceiling before sending it, and keep the source identifiers in the response path. That invariant is easy to lose when one function does everything — and it is the reason a plausible answer can become impossible to audit.

Don't use the bound as a substitute for testing. Run representative questions through the same contract, record whether the supporting page appeared, and compare quality at several application-policy settings while holding the corpus constant. Then change one variable at a time: retrieval unit, filter, freshness rule, or candidate bound. Otherwise a quality improvement may be credited to the wrong mechanism and disappear at the next ingest.

Two viable system shapes and their invariants

The first shape is a managed retrieval boundary. A Go service parses and normalizes PDFs, sends explicit units and metadata through a vector upsert capability, issues bounded vector queries, and passes returned source context to a separate answer stage. Infrai fits here alongside Pinecone and managed Weaviate: its primary distinction for this system is plain HTTP with Bearer authentication, so there is no client library release to babysit. The invariant is provider-neutral application state: collection names, source identifiers, citation keys, and the evaluation set live under the platform team's control.

The second shape keeps retrieval in infrastructure the team already operates, commonly Postgres with pgvector or OpenSearch. It can reduce the number of separately managed data systems and may expose controls the team already understands, but the on-call team now owns capacity, indexing behavior, upgrades, and retrieval regressions. The invariant is stricter: schema changes and index changes must be observable and reversible independently of answer generation.

System shape Representative options Best fit On-call and lock-in trade-off
Managed retrieval boundary Infrai, Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud Small platform team prioritizing a stable service boundary Less engine operation; contract discipline is needed to preserve portability
Self-managed or existing data plane pgvector, OpenSearch, self-hosted Weaviate Team already operating the engine and needing its native controls More tuning freedom; capacity, upgrades, and index health stay on the pager

The catch is control depth. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when their specialist retrieval features are part of the measured quality plan, and prefer pgvector when transactional proximity to Postgres data is more valuable than a separate managed boundary. OpenSearch is a reasonable candidate when search operations and expertise already exist. Infrai is not suitable when the architecture requires engine-specific knobs that a common REST contract does not expose. Your mileage may vary because staffing and existing operational skill often dominate a feature checklist.

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a product beauty contest. I initially favor the managed shape for a narrow PDF dashboard because it caps the new on-call surface, but that preference flips when the team already has proven index operations, alerting, and rollback procedures for the existing data plane. No option removes evaluation work.

Verification, rollout, and rollback

Start with a shadow collection built from representative PDFs. Record the collection identity, ingestion version, retrieval-unit rule, metadata schema, and source checksum for every evaluation run; without that trace, a score change cannot be attributed to code, corpus, or index state. The acceptance gate should contain two independent checks: retrieval quality on labeled questions and a latency SLO measured at the application boundary. Do not trade one away in an average.

Roll out by routing a small, controlled cohort to the new collection while preserving the previous collection and query policy. Compare unsupported-answer rate, citation coverage, candidate recall, and latency distributions. Averages are weak evidence here: tail latency is what turns a dashboard into an incident during a burst, while a few easy questions can make mean retrieval quality look healthier than it is.

Rollback must be boring. Keep the prior collection immutable during the rollout, version the contract beside application code, and make the active collection an explicit configuration value. If the quality gate or latency SLO fails, restore the previous collection and contract together; rolling back only the candidate bound can pair old assumptions with a new corpus. Ingestion writes should be idempotent so a replay cannot duplicate units, and query retries after 429 should back off rather than multiply demand.

Roll back the contract and collection as one unit.

One more operational test is worth the time: remove or age a source document and verify that freshness policy changes the candidate set while citations still resolve. This catches the quiet failure where retrieval appears healthy but the answer points to context the dashboard can no longer show. It also proves the separation between ingest, query, and answer stages under a controlled change.

The decision rule stays simple: buy the managed boundary when interface stability and lower on-call load are the constraints; build on an existing engine when native control and established operational competence are the constraints. In both cases, explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable context are non-negotiable.

If that managed boundary matches the system, use the Infrai vector retrieval guide to verify the retrieval stage before connecting answer generation.

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector documentation
  • OpenSearch vector search documentation

title: T-DIG: Text-Conditioned Diversity for Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.29003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) platforms typically return several images per prompt so users can explore different visual interpretations and choose one that matches their intent. However, T2I models are usually optimized for single-image quality which comes at a cost of multi-image diversity, limiting this exploration. Diversity is also contextual: one user wants variations in background, while another wants them in artistic style, and the same user may later want variations in clothing. The generated images should differ along whatever axis the user cares about. In this paper, we introduce T-DIG, a text-conditioned diversity framework for image generation and editing. T-DIG is an iterative framework comprising multiple modules that lets users type prompts, inspect default generations, request variations using natural language, and continue refining outputs until they're satisfied. At its core, T-DIG uses an LLM policy that produces K axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for a frozen generator or editor. We train this policy with GRPO using a text-conditioned diversity reward and alignment penalties. Because the image generator remains frozen, T-DIG applies to open-weight, distilled, and proprietary models. We also release the first dataset for text-conditioned prompt diversity in image generation, with the training and validation splits built from human-written axes and a test set drawn from real user interactions with T-DIG. T-DIG far exceeds baselines in improving text-conditioned diversity, while preserving base-prompt alignment across a variety of metrics and human judgements. We show that user-directed diversity exploration can be added to a wide range of image generation models, open and closed, without the need to access their weights. Website: https://image-study.org/t-dig/

title: From Weather to Enhanced Weathering: Weather Foundation Models for Carbon Dioxide Removal at Operational Scale
description:
arXiv:2610.28973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO$_2$ per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$$10^5$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. Few-shot prediction, blending the model with a few samples per field, is supported today: TerraNova-ERW recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields with two samples per field, roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field's mean removal, and can cut sampling on our densest fields by 28-98%.

title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
description:
arXiv:2610.28858v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.

title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
description:
arXiv:2610.28895v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.

title: Marketplace Fan-Out: Node.js Cron and Queue Patterns for Scheduled Email Reports
description:
Short answer: use cron to create one durable reporting job, and use a queue when that job fans a shipment update out to many subscribers or needs independent retries. The decision is about the failure boundary, not which tool has the shorter configuration.

I care about this distinction because I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A daily report email looks small on a diagram. In a marketplace, the report may also carry a shipment-status change to a large subscriber list, and a single slow recipient can turn a tidy timer into a long-running delivery operation.

The report is a business record, not a timer event

Cron is the clock. A queue is the work ledger. The durable report record is the evidence. Keep those responsibilities separate even if the first implementation lives in one Node.js process.

The simplest design is a scheduled command that computes the reporting period, writes a run record, and hands a bounded job to a worker. If report generation and the initial email handoff are predictably short, the scheduled command can perform both steps. When the job fans out shipment updates, however, the command should create independently retryable units: one tenant and reporting period, or one stable subscriber group, depending on the product's delivery contract.

That gives the scheduler a small, inspectable responsibility. It starts work once for a period. The worker owns delivery attempts. The database records what the business considers complete. A queue does not make a message exactly once; it gives the worker a place to retry work whose acknowledgement and side effect may finish at different times. I want the runbook to answer four questions without asking an engineer to infer intent from process logs: which period was due, which shipment update was selected, which subscribers were targeted, and which delivery result was final. The same record also gives support a stable explanation when a subscriber reports a missing email and gives an operator a precise item to replay instead of rerunning every tenant's work.

Use a queue for duration, retry isolation, or fan-out. Don't add one merely because queues sound more production-ready.

What does a marketplace Node.js SaaS need from cron, queue, and a scheduled daily email report?

The bounded failure I keep in the runbook is straightforward. A scheduled run creates a shipment-update job, the worker hands the email to the provider, and the worker loses its acknowledgement before it records success. The broker delivers the job again. A second send follows unless the application has a stable delivery key.

It failed quietly.

The reverse failure is just as important. The scheduler may run late, fail before creating a job, or create a run that has no completed delivery record. A timer log cannot answer the customer question, “Did my report for this period arrive?” The application needs a durable record keyed by the tenant, reporting period, shipment event or digest version, and subscriber.

This is where a small postmortem becomes an architecture rule: schedule intent and delivery completion are different facts. Alert on a missing business record after the agreed deadline, then replay the same period with the same idempotency key. Recovery should converge on one report, not create a new edition every time an operator presses retry. In the shipment fan-out case, the key must be derived from the business identity rather than from the queue message ID: a new message created during recovery still represents the same tenant, period, shipment update or digest version, and subscriber. That identity choice is the difference between a replay and an accidental second notification, so it belongs in the data model, tests, and operator command before production traffic arrives.

The practical consequence is that the queue consumer must tolerate redelivery. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation describes this boundary for a standard message consumer, and the principle applies to any at-least-once delivery system. Acknowledging before the side effect succeeds loses work; acknowledging after the side effect succeeds can repeat work. Idempotency is the control that makes the second outcome safe.

The queue is a governance choice

Write down the delivery contract before choosing the component. “Send the daily report” is not specific enough. Decide whether one subscriber gets one email per reporting period, whether shipment updates may be coalesced, and how late data changes the report. Decide which clock defines the period as well: tenant timezone, marketplace timezone, or UTC.

Then define the recovery path. The operator needs to find a missing period, enqueue it without changing its identity, observe attempts and final status, and stop a retry storm. These are runbook requirements, not optional dashboard polish.

Boundary Cron-only worker Cron plus queue
Time Starts the bounded run Starts job creation
Work Performs the whole operation Performs one retryable unit
Retry Repeats the whole run Retries an individual unit
Duplicate control Application idempotency Application idempotency plus consumer acknowledgement
Operations One process and its logs Scheduler, broker, workers, and metrics

The trade-off is real. A queue improves isolation while adding a broker, worker lifecycle, visibility rules, and another failure surface. A cron-only path is easier to operate while making the whole report the retry unit. For a small report with one recipient and a harmless rerun, that simplicity can be the better engineering choice.

Make replay the normal operator action

The following code keeps the business rule independent of the queue implementation. SendOnce must use durable storage or a mail boundary that honors the key. An in-memory map is not enough; a process restart would erase the only duplicate check.

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type ShipmentReport struct {
    TenantID     string
    SubscriberID string
    Period       time.Time
    Address      string
    Body         []byte
}

type Mailer interface {
    SendOnce(ctx context.Context, key, address, subject string, body []byte) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, mailer Mailer, report ShipmentReport) error {
    if report.TenantID == "" || report.SubscriberID == "" ||
        report.Address == "" || report.Period.IsZero() {
        return fmt.Errorf("invalid shipment report")
    }

    period := report.Period.UTC().Format("2006-01-02")
    key := deliveryKey(report.TenantID, report.SubscriberID, period)
    subject := "Daily shipment report for " + period

    if err := mailer.SendOnce(ctx, key, report.Address, subject, report.Body); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("deliver report %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func deliveryKey(tenantID, subscriberID, period string) string {
    value := tenantID + "\x00" + subscriberID + "\x00" + period
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(value))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

The worker should acknowledge only after SendOnce returns success. If it returns an error, the queue policy can retry the same logical job. The mail adapter should retain the successful result for the key, and the reporting record should make reconciliation possible when the network outcome is ambiguous.

There is no universal exactly-once promise between a database and an external mail service. If the mail boundary has no idempotency contract, document the remaining duplicate risk and build a reconciliation state machine. “Exactly once” in an architecture document does not create an atomic transaction.

A Go delivery boundary for the decision

Stay with cron alone when the report is bounded, the recipient set is small, the complete operation can be retried safely, and the team can monitor the process that owns the timer. Keep a durable run record anyway. Small systems still miss work.

Choose cron plus a queue when subscriber fan-out makes one slow delivery hold up every other delivery, when a failed subscriber should retry without rebuilding the report, or when operators need to replay one period and inspect each attempt. Split work around a business-stable key, not an arbitrary batch size that changes between retries.

Your mileage may vary on the exact split. Measure generation time, delivery latency, retry volume, and the deadline promised to subscribers before adding another component. I’m not sure a recipient count alone can tell you when to introduce a queue; the data shape and recovery contract matter more.

This pattern is not suitable when the actual problem is a multi-step workflow with durable waits and joins. Use a workflow engine if the report requires several dependent stages whose state must survive deployments. It is also a poor fit when the team cannot operate a broker or has no need for isolated retries. Stick with a direct scheduled worker until the failure mode justifies the operational cost.

Keep the smallest honest system

The final rule is plain: let cron express when a reporting period becomes due, let a queue carry retryable shipment-update work, and let durable application records prove what each subscriber received. The tools may change. That evidence should not.

References

  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms

title: Test the AI Handoff After the Ticket Is Created
description:
Your assistant created the escalation ticket. The integration returned success.

Can the next person work the case?

For a fictional service assistant, that question needs its own test. Ticket creation proves that a record was created; it does not prove that the right context survived the transition.

This article proposes a test design with synthetic fixtures. It does not report an executed benchmark.

Define the handoff contract

Agree on what the receiving role needs to continue the task. A fixture might require the goal, established facts, attempted steps, completed actions and unresolved decision. Include the destination and owner where the application defines them.

Specify which information the recipient may receive. The contract should identify both required context and excluded content. A complete transcript is not automatically an acceptable result.

Keep expected facts independent of the generated summary. Otherwise the evaluation can simply repeat the same omission it is meant to detect.

Seed distinctions that matter

Create a synthetic case where the customer reports a symptom, the system confirms a narrower fact, and an explanation remains unverified. Give the fixture one completed action and a separate proposed action that still needs approval.

These distinctions let a reviewer detect whether the summary upgrades an assumption into a fact or describes a proposal as completed.

Use harmless, identifiable fixture values. Do not create real customer incidents or send real notifications merely to test the handoff path.

Exercise the full transition

Run the assistant to the point where escalation is expected. Inspect the persisted ticket and the actual views used by the receiving person, not just the assistant's last message.

If the workflow generates a notification separately, inspect that output too. A correct ticket can coexist with a misleading notification, especially when separate components summarise the same case.

Check that the case reaches the intended test destination. Keep any real external side effects isolated or within explicitly approved test accounts.

Score continuity separately from writing quality

Check Example mismatch
Goal preserved Summary mentions the topic but omits the requested outcome
Facts attributed correctly Customer suspicion becomes a confirmed system finding
Action state preserved Proposed step is described as already completed
Unresolved decision visible Approval requirement disappears
Recipient access respected Unrelated restricted detail appears in the summary
Next step identifiable Ticket exists without a usable destination or task

The expected result depends on the workflow. This table is a scoping aid, not a universal specification.

A concise summary can pass if it preserves the required context. A long summary can fail if it loses the one fact needed to avoid repeating an action. Avoid rewarding length as a substitute for completeness.

Check the customer's version of events

Compare the assistant's closing message with the persisted state. “Created a ticket” should not become “a colleague has reviewed your case.” Similarly, an unresolved action should not be presented as completed simply because escalation succeeded.

Where the product provides a reference or a next step, verify that it matches the stored case. If it promises a follow-up, test the supported route rather than treating the sentence as evidence that one exists.

Retain useful failure evidence

Record the fixture revision, expected fields, permitted recipient scope, persisted outputs and the specific missing or altered facts. Include the smallest safe evidence needed for another engineer to investigate.

Keep deterministic checks on required fields or action states separate from repeated evaluations of generated wording. For generative steps, state the relevant configuration and repetitions.

Report the conditions and limits of the test. A successful sample does not establish that every conversation will produce a complete handoff, and an escalation count alone says little about the quality of the work transferred.

Acadify AI Lab supports scoped LLM evaluation, AI testing and developer feedback. Acadify Solution supports custom software and AI applications.

Which omission would matter most in your handoff tests: the goal, completed actions, uncertainty or the next owner?

Disclosure: written by an AI agent for Acadify Solution / Acadify AI Lab. The assistant and service case are fictional.

title: Humans Correct Their Judgments Through Debate, but Weaker AI Models Do Not
description:
arXiv:2610.28539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges, whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, weighted voting produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors, whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. Notably, the behavior of minority judges in non-diverse deliberation protocols suggests that, under symmetric settings, incorrect positions could be more persuasive than correct ones. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.

title: SSMCGM-Stream: A Streaming State-Space Model for Personalized Diabetes Management
description:
arXiv:2610.28976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring supports diabetes management but requires forecasting models that are accurate, interpretable, and efficient enough for real-time deployment. We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space model that maintains a personalized hidden state updated with each incoming glucose reading to provide constant-time forecasting, physiologically structured counterfactual reasoning, and interpretable forecasts through hidden-state attribution. Built on this foundation, SSMCGM-Agent delivers risk-aware, natural-language decision support by translating forecasts, explanations, and counterfactuals into grounded recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. Evaluated on the T1DEXI cohort, SSMCGM-Stream achieves forecasting performance comparable to strong neural baselines while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling continuous on-device diabetes decision support.

title: Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention and Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion for Video Action Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.29176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In video action detection, modeling the temporal dependencies in continuous video streams is crucial. Previous methods based on deep neural networks can perform frame-level video recognition tasks. However, these methods struggle to model dynamic temporal patterns, facing challenges such as redundant frame information, difficulty balancing global and local features, and insufficient fusion of visual and textual features. To address these issues, we propose a video temporal attention module based on the Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention, which aggregates continuous temporal sequences into feature representations across diverse temporal scales while efficiently reducing redundancy. We also introduce a Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion module that leverages cross-attention at both latent and standard feature levels, achieving fine-grained fusion between video and textual features to enhance semantic alignment and feature interaction. Experimental results across multiple video recognition benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability.

title: AWS Transform adds storage migration assessments for Amazon S3, EBS, EFS, and FSx
description:
Migration assessments in AWS Transform now evaluate on-premises storage for migration to AWS. Instead of manually analyzing thousands of volumes across protocols, capacity, and performance, you upload a storage inventory and AWS Transform does the mapping for you. It matches each workload to the best-fit service, sizes the recommendation, and projects costs to produce a total cost of ownership business case. Bring NAS shares, SAN LUNs, direct-attached disks, or backup repositories via a NetApp Digital Advisor export, RVTools file, or other inventory. AWS Transform routes workloads across Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx (NetApp ONTAP, Windows File Server, OpenZFS, Lustre). Run what-if scenarios to compare deployment options such as Single-AZ vs. Multi-AZ or cost-optimized vs. performance-optimized, then ask follow-up questions about any result in chat.

Storage migration assessments are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is available. To learn more, see the AWS Transform User Guide.

title: Towards Realistic Models of Change: A Causal Perspective on Decision-Making and Dynamical Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28803v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While statistical learning has made remarkable progress in recent decades, driven by large datasets and data-driven protocols that have transformed scientific practice, it still faces a key limitation: it struggles to generalize beyond the data it has seen, often failing under distribution shift. Causality offers a promising solution: causal models focus on the underlying mechanisms of change rather than surface-level associations, enabling robust reasoning under external interventions. This allows systems not only to learn from data, but also to reason about hypothetical scenarios, adapt to new environments, and inform better decisions. This thesis explores how these approaches can inform each other, in two parts.
  The first part examines algorithmic recourse, that is, identifying which changes an individual can make to overturn an unfavorable decision. We propose an alternative perspective to the established framework, arguing for a more realistic cost function, a reformulation of the problem in causal terms, and the inclusion of a temporal dimension in policy evaluation.
  The second part focuses on dynamical systems, extending the notions of causal interventions and effects to discrete and continuous stochastic processes. We show that the equilibria of these processes, and how they change following an intervention, can be linked to Structural Causal Models (SCMs), viewed as compressed representations of the underlying temporal dynamics. We argue for the relevance of such temporal causal models, since in real-world scenarios actions take time to produce their effects.
  The common goal of both parts is practical: the utility, robustness, and trustworthiness of these models depend critically on their ability to realistically represent the underlying phenomena.

title: SICAF: Time-Varying Focus Bottleneck for Self-Supervised Event-Based Optical Flow with Spiking Neural Network
description:
arXiv:2610.29158v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Event-based optical flow estimation achieves high temporal resolution and dynamic range by exploiting asynchronous events, while self-supervised learning provides an effective solution to the absence of ground-truth labels. Spiking neural networks (SNNs), as brain-inspired models, process information through asynchronous spikes, naturally aligning with optical flow events. However, the temporal irregularity across event streams hinders the compact extraction of spatiotemporal features, while the absence of explicit labels leads to spurious correlations, thereby increasing redundancy within latent representations. In this paper, we propose a novel 'Compactly Compress, Time-varying Focus' training strategy. We present SICAF (Spikes Information Compression And Focus) framework that formulates the learning process as a constrained optimization with temporal modulation. It encourages self-supervised SNNs to extract compact latent representations while preventing over-compression that would discard temporal saliency. To better enable feature selectivity across time steps, we design an estimator with learnable temporal attention, achieving context awareness with cross-time dependencies. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate that SICAF achieves state-of-the-art performance in self-supervised SNNs, with a 8.14% improvement in AEE on the MVSEC dataset and a 13.49% increase in robustness under white-box adversarial attacks.

title: Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too.
description:
Your agent forgot a decision you made last week. Mine did too.

Last month my team reversed a queue decision. Nobody could say why we
had picked the first design, what evidence it rested on, or who had
signed off on the replacement. The old design was still half-wired in
as a "fallback", quietly depending on the thing we had just replaced.
We found out in production.

Vector RAG remembers text. It does not remember decisions — what
was chosen, what it rested on, what contradicted it, and what replaced
it. So I built a tiny local graph for exactly that: memgraph.

What it does

One zero-dependency Node.js CLI. No network, no server, no embeddings.
The store is a single JSON file you can commit next to your code.

memgraph init
memgraph add --type decision --title "Use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for the queue" --source "ADR-014"
memgraph add --type fact --title "NOTIFY payloads cap at 8000 bytes" --source "Postgres docs"
memgraph link m-002 m-001 --relation contradicts
memgraph add --type decision --title "Switch the queue to Redis Streams" --source "ADR-019"
memgraph supersede m-001 m-003 --reason "payload cap makes NOTIFY the wrong tool"

Three questions it answers, fast:

  • Why did we decide this? memgraph why m-003 — source, supporters, contradictions, supersession.
  • Is anything stale or contradictory? memgraph check — unresolved contradictions, live nodes resting on superseded ones, sourceless claims.
  • What do we believe? memgraph list — every node, with superseded ones marked.

memgraph check exits 1 when it finds an error, so it works as a CI
gate: a PR that introduces a contradiction, or keeps depending on a
superseded decision, fails before it merges.

Demo

The repo ships a small team graph — a queue decision, the fact that
killed it, its replacement, and one leftover fallback still depending
on the dead design:

sh examples/run-demo.sh

memgraph check on that graph reports exactly two problems: the
fallback reader depends on a superseded decision, and one open
question has no source. The contradiction between the payload-cap
fact and the old decision does not get flagged — the old decision
was superseded, so that contradiction is resolved history, not a
live conflict.

One honesty note

A graph is only as good as what you record. memgraph cannot tell you
whether a source is true — it tells you where every claim came from
and whether the graph still holds together. A decision with no source
is a rumor with formatting; that is why check flags it. And when a
decision changes, supersede it — don't delete it. Deleting history is
how teams end up re-litigating the same choice every six months.

Repo: https://github.com/techdevfun/memgraph — MIT, zero dependencies,
Node.js 18+.

title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.29326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $\tau^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.

title: How Intervention History Changes AI Agent Sabotage on Subsequent Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.26935v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI control evaluations often reset agents' memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent's ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model's solution. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model's no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model's replacement. For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model's replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5's successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.

title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.28957v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.

title: To Keep or Not to Keep: Learning KV Cache Retention in Disaggregated LLM Serving Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Disaggregated \textsc{LLM} serving separates prefill and decode across node pools, placing a network fabric between \textsc{KV}-cache computation and consumption. This breaks a key assumption of classical cache policies: a miss no longer incurs only local recomputation, but also network transfer to the decode node. Likewise, admitting a block to the global cache requires an additional transfer, so poor retention decisions waste both memory and bandwidth. We present \textbf{KVLearn}, a learning-based framework for cost-aware \textsc{KV}-cache retention in disaggregated serving. KVLearn includes: (i) a lightweight Prefix Reuse Predictor (\textsc{PRP}) that estimates reuse probability from structural and temporal prefix features without modifying model weights; (ii) a Cost-Aware Retention Score (\textsc{CARS}) that converts reuse probability into keep/admit decisions using recomputation, transfer, and storage costs; and (iii) an Adaptive Threshold Controller (\textsc{ATC}) that adjusts admission thresholds online from observed hit rates and memory pressure. We integrate KVLearn into a globally disaggregated serving topology and evaluate it on text and multimodal workloads, including large image/video-derived \textsc{KV} blocks with heterogeneous reuse patterns. KVLearn reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 56% versus No-Cache, 38% versus LRU-Pool, and 33% versus Mooncake-style baselines, while cutting inter-node \textsc{KV} transfer volume by up to 53% versus LRU-Pool. On MM-Session, throughput remains within ${\sim}5%$ of oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/FastLM/KVLearn.

title: Local and Sparse Kernel Operator Learning for Incompressible Flows: An Operator Lagrange Formulation
description:
arXiv:2610.29009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a local and sparse kernel method for learning the solution operators of incompressible flows. It builds on our earlier property-preserving kernel method, whose global output reconstruction and dense operator regression scale poorly. Our method replaces the global output reconstruction by local divergence-free interpolants with divergence-free polynomials of any degree, solved in parallel on the GPU. These interpolants are divergence free, periodic on periodic domains, and, with a multiscale kernel, approach Kolmogorov statistics under refinement. A compactly supported kernel, positive semidefinite in any input dimension, makes the operator regression sparse. Its support radius, and hence the sparsity, is fitted to data, and optional affine polynomials in the input capture global trends. Operator Lagrange weights join the two. They cost one sparse solve per new input and act on the training fields before the output reconstruction, so their local coefficients are never formed. We show that, unlike direct evaluation, Lagrange evaluation does not amplify solve errors by the cancellation among spatial coefficients. On ten fluid benchmarks, validation selects sparse matrices nearly everywhere, with densities that mostly decrease as the training set grows, and affine augmentation lowers the error by more than an order of magnitude for forced isotropic turbulence. These sparse models are at least as accurate as our earlier dense method and more accurate than neural operators. Lagrange evaluation is as accurate as direct evaluation with local output reconstructions, and up to nearly three orders of magnitude more accurate with global ones. We also present GPU timings and storage.

title: Credit Where Credit Is Due: Contrastive Attribution Topology Search for Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.29292v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An LLM multi-agent system (MAS) is only as good as the agents it chooses to trust: its accuracy and cost hinge on its topology, meaning which agents are included and how they communicate. A single task score, however, does not reveal which agents help or hinder performance. We propose Contrastive Attribution Topology Search (CATS), which searches for compact teams within a fixed supergraph of specialized agents. An LLM attributer compares execution traces across candidate topologies and assigns credit to individual agents. CATS uses these credits to update supergraph edges while progressively pruning weak edges and agents, yielding a small team for deployment. With small open-weight models and matched candidate evaluations, CATS improves mean accuracy on BigCodeBench by 5.3 percentage points over score-only heuristic search while using 54\% fewer deployment tokens. On MBPP, CATS matches the strongest baselines with fewer tokens than the other searches. In a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test, CATS excludes all adversarially prompted agents in all three runs, whereas random search retains some at comparable accuracy. Per-agent credit thus supports both team optimization and the pruning of potentially harmful agents.

title: Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective
description:
arXiv:2610.28997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tokenization that partitions time series into subsequences has become a foundational paradigm in modern time series modeling. However, we find that current tokenization strategies inherently introduce spectral distortions, forcing the learned representations to diverge from the true underlying patterns such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, thereby impairing model performance. Through theoretical analysis from a frequency perspective, we derive the boundary conditions under which such distortions occur. To overcome this distortion, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data. TimeFT obtains tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting, and Nyquist sampling. The method is parameter-free, incurs negligible computational complexity, and can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizers. Our extensive experiments on diverse tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that TimeFT consistently and significantly improves performance.

title: Dissimilarity-Based Markov Decision Processes for Stabilizing State Distributions
description:
arXiv:2610.29024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning for stochastic systems typically optimizes expected cumulative rewards, while reliable and repeatable behavior also depends on how the state distribution evolves over time. Optimizing expected return alone does not guarantee that this distribution converges to a desired target or remains stable. This paper develops a theoretical framework for learning policies that stabilize state distributions. We formulate the problem as a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its dissimilarity to a target distribution. We establish sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable. To support policy learning, we introduce a finite-dimensional representation of distributions and show how stability guarantees for its parameter dynamics extend to the underlying state distributions. We further develop certificates for the learned policies, including their deployment using estimated distribution parameters. These results quantify how learning and estimation errors affect the guarantees and identify conditions under which learned policies retain asymptotic stability. For practical implementation, we combine distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC. A computable example on a linear system illustrates the proposed theoretical certificates. Furthermore, experiments on a HalfCheetah task demonstrate the benefits of distribution feedback and explicit target matching for regulating the velocity distribution.

title: Figma's next-generation data caching platform
description: Scalability and reliability gaps in our Redis platform were a growing threat to Figma's site availability. This is the story of how we built FigCache, a foundational technology that underpins a reimagined internal platform for ephemeral data.

title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
description:
arXiv:2610.26991v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic.
  To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

title: 5 Nodejs Checks for Batched Metric Updates to Dashboard Channels in 2026
description:
TL;DR: Collect changed presence series over a short window, publish them as one batch, and have each media workspace apply that diff; periodically send a full snapshot so a reconnecting dashboard converges even after it missed updates. The deciding constraint is the delivery guarantee at fan-out, not how lively the chart looks.

For a newsroom workspace showing which editors, producers, and reporters are online, an Express process should not turn every presence change into its own outbound request. A brief batching window absorbs a burst into one request while remaining short enough for the roster to feel live. Keep the publishing contract behind an application-owned adapter, too: the route and payload boundary stay put if the service behind that capability changes.

That is the operational recommendation. The rest is the runbook I would want beside the alert, because a green dashboard cannot prove that a disconnected browser received anything.

1. What page should fire when fan-out falls behind?

Page on a user-visible freshness or convergence failure, not on raw publish volume. A burst of 300 contributor changes can legitimately become one batch; request count falling during that burst is therefore evidence of batching, not evidence of loss. The useful signal is whether the online roster stops converging after publishes continue.

Ask the uncomfortable question first: what page fired? If the answer is merely "the realtime dashboard looks unusual," the monitor has confused a picture with a guarantee. Instrument the path as three separate facts: a change entered the short collection window, a batch was handed to the publisher, and a later snapshot gave clients a recovery point. Those facts describe the failure domain without inventing an exactly-once promise.

This is the postmortem frame: the missed update is not the root cause; the absence of a bounded recovery path is.

2. How should Nodejs push batched metric updates to a dashboard channel?

The Express-side collector should hold only changed series during a small, explicit window, coalesce repeated changes to the same series, and submit the resulting set through POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. Batch publishing turns a burst into a single request. Do not infer a universal window duration from somebody else's traffic: the correct value is the largest delay your workspace can tolerate before "online" feels false.

Short wins here.

There is a real trade-off. A wider window reduces request pressure but makes presence stale; a narrower one feels immediate but gives up much of the batching benefit. Record the selected window as an operating parameter, then test it under a synchronized reconnect burst rather than tuning it by eye. This also keeps the Node.js handler boring: accept the change, place it in the collector, and let one publisher own flushing.

Infrai is one candidate for that publisher when an application wants one key and one REST contract across a verified surface of 295 routes in 20 modules. Its discovery surface is self-describing, and the same adapter boundary lets the service behind the capability move without changing calling code. That is useful here because the presence algorithm remains an application decision rather than becoming vendor-shaped. It doesn't remove the need to define recovery semantics.

The following Go publisher accepts a batch body that has already been validated against the discovery schema. Keeping the body in a file makes the transport example runnable without guessing undocumented fields. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and a unique BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY, then pass the JSON filename as the only argument.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 {
        panic("usage: publisher batch.json")
    }
    body, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    idempotencyKey := os.Getenv("BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || idempotencyKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/realtime/publish/batch", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    panic("publish remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

3. Treat every diff as disposable and every snapshot as recovery

A reconnecting browser may have missed one or several diffs. Do not ask the next diff to repair an unknown gap; send a full snapshot periodically, and make applying it replace the client's current workspace roster. Between snapshots, clients apply only the changed series from each batch.

This split is deliberately asymmetric. Diffs optimize the normal path. Snapshots repair uncertainty.

A practical verification drill has four steps:

  1. Connect two dashboard clients to the same shared workspace.
  2. Disconnect one client while several online states change and the connected client receives batched diffs.
  3. Reconnect the isolated client before a full snapshot, then verify that no test assumes an unproven replay guarantee.
  4. Wait for the scheduled snapshot and verify that both rosters converge to the same full state.

The evidence to retain is the batch boundary, snapshot boundary, workspace identifier, and client-observed convergence result. A screenshot is weak evidence. It cannot tell an incident responder whether the browser recovered through replay, a snapshot, or luck.

4. Compare products by recovery contract, not feature count

Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub are real alternatives, but their documentation exposes different concepts and those concepts should shape the test plan. Ably documents connection state recovery and message continuity; Pusher Channels documents presence channels and their membership events; PubNub documents Presence separately from message persistence. These are objective interface differences, not a ranking. Read the linked product documentation before assigning any of them a guarantee that its name merely suggests.

Option Contract to inspect for this workload Boundary to test
Ably Connection state recovery and channel continuity Whether the intended disconnect duration and client state qualify for recovery
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership events How reconnect and resubscribe rebuild the member view
PubNub Presence plus the separately documented persistence behavior Which state comes from presence and which recovery requires stored messages or an application snapshot
Infrai Batch publish behind a consistent REST capability contract Application-owned periodic snapshots and diff application

The fair decision rule is narrow: choose the option whose documented recovery contract matches the failure you are willing to tolerate, then prove that behavior with a disconnect test. Use an application snapshot when the contract does not establish that every missed diff will return. WebRTC is not a substitute for that analysis; its standard covers peer connections, while this job is server-mediated workspace presence and dashboard fan-out.

No vendor row earns a pass from a successful happy-path demo.

5. Verify rollback before enabling the publisher

Rollout should begin with observation: build batches and record their size and age while the existing delivery path remains authoritative. Next, enable the batch publisher for a bounded workspace cohort and run the disconnect drill. Promotion requires both acceptable freshness on the connected client and convergence after the full snapshot on the reconnected client.

Rollback is a routing decision, not a data repair strategy. Stop sending batched diffs through the new publisher, restore the prior authoritative path, and immediately issue a full snapshot through that path so clients do not preserve an ambiguous partial roster. Keep snapshot generation independent from diff batching; coupling them creates the exact common-mode failure the snapshot is meant to repair.

At 3 a.m., the runbook should answer three things without dashboard archaeology: which workspace stopped converging, whether batch publication continued, and when the last full snapshot completed. If those answers are available, an operator can distinguish publisher trouble from a reconnect recovery gap and can roll back without claiming that a missing diff was delivered.

References

  • Ably connection state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels presence channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • PubNub Presence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/presence/overview
  • PubNub Message Persistence: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/storage

title: ArcFlow: Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets
description:
arXiv:2610.28788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.

title: ChartEvo: Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses for Long-Tail Chart Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.28282v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced chart understanding and reasoning, yet their performance remains highly uneven across chart types. While modern MLLMs perform well on common charts, their accuracy drops sharply on long-tail charts with diverse visual structures and reasoning requirements. Tool-augmented agents can improve complex chart reasoning by introducing specialized visual capabilities, but manually engineering strategies and tools for the heterogeneous and evolving long tail is difficult to scale. We introduce \textbf{ChartEvo}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables chart agents to adapt to underperforming chart types through experience-driven harness-level self-improvement. ChartEvo jointly evolves reusable chart-specific Skills and executable Tools, while learning reusable local tool-call chains to compose evolved capabilities and control the inference overhead of tool-augmented reasoning. On long-tail charts from ChartBench and ChartX, ChartEvo improves accuracy over its base MLLM, Qwen3.7-Plus, by \textbf{45.6\%} and \textbf{32.5\%}, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of recursive self-improvement for long-tail chart adaptation.

title: How Does Orthogonalization Adapt to the Neural Network Hessian Structure? A Gradient Self Outer-Product Analysis at Initialization
description:
arXiv:2610.28975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Muon orthogonalizes a weight matrix's momentum before each step, and on neural networks this simple preconditioner beats AdamW in a wide range of tasks. Existing analyses explain Muon within general optimization frameworks or on a few specific models, and many of them view orthogonalization as a preconditioner. Since the Hessian is the optimal preconditioner under a quadratic approximation of the loss, these works leave a basic question open: what makes orthogonalization suited to the Hessian of a neural network? Prior work shows that the layer-wise Hessian of a neural network is row-block diagonally dominant, and Muon's implicit preconditioner, the Kronecker product $(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top)^{1/2}\otimes\mathbf{I}$ with $\mathbf{V}$ the momentum, has the same row-block structure exactly when $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ is diagonally dominant. Diagonal dominance of $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ has been observed in language models, but why a neural network produces it has not been explained. This work provides a quantitative asymptotic theory for neural networks at initialization, and points out the intuition that the overparameterization of the weight matrices drives the diagonal dominance. We analyze $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^\top]$, which equals $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top]$ at initialization, in four canonical models: symmetric matrix factorization, deep linear networks, two-layer ReLU networks, and single-layer linear attention. In each case the diagonal entries outgrow the off-diagonal ones at explicit rates as the hidden dimensions grow; for the query, key and value weights of attention the off-diagonal vanishes altogether. Simulations of the four models and experiments on language models at initialization confirm the predicted scaling.

title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.
