title: From Canon to Nikon: Camera Domain Shift and Potential Equity Implications in Retinal AI
description:
arXiv:2610.29104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet access to regular screening remains limited worldwide. AI offers a scalable approach, but its performance can be sensitive to image quality and acquisition conditions. In a Brazilian cohort of 8,524 patients, retinal images acquired with the Nikon NF5050 were more than twice as likely to have inadequate image quality compared with those acquired with the Canon CR-2, despite refurbished Canon systems costing more than twice as much as Nikon systems. This potential cost-quality trade-off highlights an important consideration for the reliability of AI systems deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. Using a frozen pretrained retinal foundation model, we systematically evaluate whether camera-associated performance differences persist across 12 retinal disease classification tasks, four input resolutions, and five downstream classifiers. We find that camera-associated performance differences vary substantially across tasks, and that neither higher input resolution nor classifier choice consistently mitigates cross-camera variation. These findings identify camera platform as a potentially overlooked source of performance variability, with implications for the safety and reliability of retinal AI when deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. We release all source code, evaluation scripts, and per-task results on GitHub to support reproducible benchmarking.

title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
description:
arXiv:2610.28892v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.

title: Building Multi-Tenant SaaS Help Center Retrieval — A 4-Stage Citation Contract
description:
The hard choice in a multi-tenant SaaS help center is not “which vector database is fastest?” It is deciding how much freshness and control your citation contract can tolerate. Short answer: keep a durable, tenant-filtered index for stable content, add a live retrieval path for fast-changing pages, and make both produce the same citation-shaped result. That lets the answer layer remain boring and auditable.

I start with the answer a support user will see, then work backward. A citation must identify the tenant, source document, revision, and the exact text span used. If a result cannot carry those fields, it is not ready for generation, no matter how relevant its embedding looks.

The constraint is a retrieval contract

Write the contract before picking an endpoint. Mine has four invariants: every query is scoped to one tenant; every chunk has a stable source and revision; freshness is explicit; and an answer cites only chunks returned by retrieval. Those rules prevent a surprisingly common failure where a global index returns a plausible paragraph from another customer.

Infrai fits the durable branch when you want one REST API for this vector work and adjacent backend jobs. The public discovery surface is self-describing, so the adapter can inspect the documented method and path instead of baking provider-specific assumptions into each tenant.

The retrieval unit matters too. A whole article is easy to cite but noisy for reranking. A tiny sentence has sharp relevance but loses context. In practice, I use a section-sized chunk with a parent document id, heading path, locale, ACL, and updated_at. Your mileage may vary; chunk size depends on how your help center authors write.

Keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Log tenant id and request id at each boundary, plus candidate count and the selected source ids. Do not log the full customer text by default. That is a compliance decision, not a performance trick.

How should multi-tenant SaaS help center retrieval handle freshness and citation tracing?

There are two viable shapes.

The durable path ingests published content into a tenant-partitioned vector collection. It gives predictable filtering, repeatable evaluation, and a clean revision history. The live path fetches or searches the current help-center source at query time, then ranks those passages alongside durable candidates. It catches an article edited five minutes ago, but it adds network variability and another place to enforce tenant permissions.

Their shared invariant is the citation envelope. A candidate should look conceptually like this:

candidate = {
    "tenant_id": "t_42",
    "document_id": "doc_918",
    "revision": "r17",
    "heading_path": ["Billing", "Invoices"],
    "text": "...",
    "source_url": "https://help.example.test/billing/invoices",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-31T09:20:00Z",
    "retrieval_path": "durable",
}

The answer service accepts only this envelope. It can merge durable and live candidates, deduplicate by document and revision, and attach citations without guessing where a sentence came from. A short-lived live result that lacks a revision should be marked ineligible for citation, even if it helps reranking.

Ship it carefully.

Where a narrow API surface helps

For a team that wants this split without installing an SDK for every backend concern, Infrai is a deliberate option. Its breadth is behind one consistent REST surface: discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and a single key can cover the vector operations alongside other backend capabilities. That can reduce adapter code when the same service also owns notifications or scheduled ingestion.

For the durable branch, the documented vector surface covers collection creation, upsert, query, and deletion. Generate request details from the public discovery document instead of copying assumptions between tenants. The useful advantage here is the uniform contract, not a claim that one index will fit every workload. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so an ingestion worker does not need a new vendor credential when it adds a scheduling or notification step. One REST API means plain HTTP from any language, with no SDK installation required.

This is the small discovery probe I use during startup. It is intentionally read-only; the production writer still validates its tenant metadata before calling a vector write route.

import os
import time
import requests

def load_discovery():
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = requests.get(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
                timeout=10,
            )
            if response.status_code == 200:
                return response.json()
            if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}")
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)

Here is the boundary I keep in code: the provider client returns candidates, while my application owns tenant filters and citation validation.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Candidate:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    revision: str
    text: str
    source_url: str

def citation_ready(candidate: Candidate, tenant_id: str) -> bool:
    return (
        candidate.tenant_id == tenant_id
        and bool(candidate.document_id)
        and bool(candidate.revision)
        and bool(candidate.source_url)
        and bool(candidate.text.strip())
    )

That small check is where cross-tenant leakage gets stopped. It also makes a provider swap less dramatic because the downstream contract does not change.

How do the common alternatives compare?

The comparison is about system shape, not a universal leaderboard. Pinecone is a managed vector index, Weaviate is an open-source and managed vector database, and Elasticsearch combines mature lexical search with vector capabilities. All can participate in a durable path; the surrounding operational model is the differentiator.

Option Durable index fit Live/fresh path Citation-control implication
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with tenant metadata filters Usually an application-owned fetch or re-index step Keep revision and source fields in metadata; validate them before generation
Weaviate Flexible self-hosted or managed collection model Application can combine collection search with source fetch More deployment choices mean more policy to standardize
Elasticsearch Hybrid lexical/vector retrieval in an existing search stack Strong fit when the source is already indexed and refreshed Mapping and analyzer changes become part of the citation audit trail
Infrai vector surface One REST contract for collection create, upsert, query, and delete Pair vector results with an application-owned live fetch Discovery and consistent envelopes simplify the adapter boundary; tenant policy remains yours

No row removes the need for a labeled evaluation set. Before rollout, label a small sample per tenant with the expected supporting passage, then measure recall at the candidate stage and citation accuracy at the answer stage. I once treated a high top-k score as proof of grounding; the first revision-heavy test showed that stale, well-phrased chunks can still win. That was a design correction, not a model problem.

Roll out the two paths without losing the audit trail

Start durable-only for a narrow set of published articles. Store the retrieval path, revision, and source ids with every generated answer. Add the live branch behind a flag for tenants whose content changes hourly, and compare citation coverage against the same labeled set. Keep a kill switch that selects durable candidates when the live source is unavailable; the answer should then say it is based on the last indexed revision.

The catch is operational ownership. A live fetch is not suitable when your source has strict latency budgets, offline regions, or no stable revision identifiers. Stick with a durable-only specialist such as Elasticsearch when lexical controls and existing cluster operations are the primary constraint. Conversely, a live branch earns its cost when “current policy” matters more than a fixed response time.

If your boundary fits the uniform REST approach, start with the Infrai documentation and confirm the current discovery schemas before wiring ingestion. The decision rule is simple: choose the path that preserves freshness, control, and citation evidence together; combine both when the feature needs durable and live context.

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: AWS RDS Explained: Launch, Secure, and Scale a Managed Database
description:
By Vishal Patil | #vishalcloudjourney

Running a database on your own EC2 instance means you are also the DBA. You patch the OS, schedule backups, set up replication, and wake up when the disk fills. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) takes that operational work off your plate so you can focus on your application. In this hands-on guide, you'll launch a MySQL database on RDS, lock it down, connect from EC2, test automatic failover, and learn how to scale reads.

What Is Amazon RDS?

Amazon RDS is a managed service for relational databases. You choose the engine and size, and AWS handles the heavy lifting.

Supported engines: Amazon Aurora (MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible), MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2.

What AWS manages for you

  • Hardware provisioning and OS patching
  • Automated backups and point-in-time recovery
  • Database software patching during a maintenance window
  • Multi-AZ failover
  • Monitoring through CloudWatch

What you still manage

  • Schema design, queries, and indexes
  • Security groups, network placement, and user access
  • Choosing instance size and storage
  • Cost control

Note: With standard RDS you don't get SSH or OS-level access to the underlying host. That's the trade-off for a managed service.

What You Will Build

  • A security group setup where only your EC2 app server can reach the database
  • A private MySQL RDS instance with encryption and automated backups
  • A connection from EC2 to the database
  • A Multi-AZ standby and a failover test
  • (Optional) A read replica

Architecture:

EC2 app server (ec2-app-sg) → RDS MySQL primary (rds-sg, AZ-a)
                                  ↓ synchronous replication
                              RDS standby (AZ-b), takes over on failure

Key Concepts in 60 Seconds

  • DB instance: The managed database server you pay for.
  • DB subnet group: The subnets (in at least two AZs) where RDS is allowed to place your database.
  • Multi-AZ: A standby copy in another AZ, kept in sync, that takes over automatically if the primary fails. It's for availability, not for read scaling.
  • Read replica: An asynchronously updated copy used to scale read traffic.
  • Automated backups: Daily backups plus transaction logs, kept for 1 to 35 days, enabling point-in-time restore.
  • Snapshot: A manual backup that stays until you delete it.
  • Endpoint: The DNS name your application uses to connect. Always use the endpoint, never an IP.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for RDS, EC2, and VPC
  • A VPC with subnets in at least two AZs (the default VPC works)
  • A running EC2 instance (Amazon Linux 2023) to act as your app server, or you can launch one in Step 4

Cost note: RDS bills while the instance is running, and Multi-AZ roughly doubles the instance cost. Check the current Free Tier terms for your account and follow the cleanup section at the end.

Step 1: Create the Security Groups

Use two security groups so the database is reachable only from your app server.

App security group (ec2-app-sg) attached to your EC2 instance

  • Inbound: SSH (22) from your IP, or use EC2 Instance Connect or Session Manager

Database security group (rds-sg)

  • Inbound: MySQL/Aurora (3306) from ec2-app-sg (select the security group as the source, not 0.0.0.0/0)

This is the single most important RDS security habit: never open your database port to the internet.

Step 2: Check the DB Subnet Group

  1. Go to RDS → Subnet groups.
  2. The default VPC already has a default subnet group covering its subnets.
  3. For your own VPC, create a subnet group and add subnets from at least two AZs.

Step 3: Create the Database

  1. Go to RDS → Databases → Create database.
  2. Choose Standard create and engine MySQL.
  3. Template: Free tier or Dev/Test, depending on what your account shows.
  4. Settings:
    • DB instance identifier: mydb-rds
    • Master username: admin
    • Credentials: choose Managed in AWS Secrets Manager (recommended), or set a strong password yourself
  5. Instance configuration: a small burstable class such as db.t4g.micro or db.t3.micro.
  6. Storage:
    • Type: General Purpose SSD (gp3), 20 GiB
    • Enable storage autoscaling with a sensible maximum
  7. Connectivity:
    • VPC and subnet group: your chosen ones
    • Public access: No
    • VPC security group: rds-sg
  8. Additional configuration:
    • Initial database name: appdb
    • Automated backups: enabled, retention 7 days
    • Encryption: enabled (this must be chosen at creation)
    • Deletion protection: on for anything important
  9. Click Create database. It takes a few minutes to reach Available.
  10. Open the database and copy its Endpoint.

Step 4: Connect from EC2

  1. Connect to your EC2 instance (launch one with ec2-app-sg in the same VPC if you don't have one).
  2. Install a MySQL client: 
   sudo dnf install -y mariadb105
  1. Connect using the RDS endpoint: 
   mysql -h <your-rds-endpoint> -u admin -p

If you used Secrets Manager, open the secret in the console and choose Retrieve secret value to get the password.

  1. Create a table and add data: 
   USE appdb;
   CREATE TABLE visitors (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50));
   INSERT INTO visitors (name) VALUES ('Vishal'), ('AWS Builder');
   SELECT * FROM visitors;

You now have a working managed database that only your app server can reach.

Step 5: Turn On Multi-AZ

  1. Select your database and click Modify.
  2. Under Availability, choose Create a standby instance (Multi-AZ).
  3. Choose Apply immediately and confirm.

RDS creates a standby in another AZ and keeps it synchronized. Your endpoint stays the same.

Step 6: Test Failover

  1. Select the database, then Actions → Reboot.
  2. Check Reboot with failover? and confirm.
  3. Watch the Events tab and the database's AZ. The standby is promoted, and the AZ changes.
  4. Re-run your SQL query. Your data is still there, and the same endpoint works.

Expect a short interruption (typically a minute or two) while DNS flips to the new primary. Your application should retry failed connections.

Step 7 (Optional): Add a Read Replica

  1. Select the database and choose Actions → Create read replica.
  2. Give it an identifier such as mydb-rds-replica.
  3. Once available, point read-heavy queries at the replica's endpoint and keep writes on the primary.

Replication is asynchronous, so replicas can lag slightly behind the primary.

Multi-AZ vs Read Replica

Multi-AZ Read Replica
Purpose High availability and failover Read scaling
Replication Synchronous Asynchronous
Takes traffic normally No (standby only) Yes (reads)
Automatic failover Yes No (manual promotion)

Security Best Practices

  • Keep Public access set to No and place the DB in private subnets.
  • Allow access only from application security groups.
  • Use Secrets Manager for credentials and rotate them.
  • Enable encryption at rest (KMS) and enforce SSL/TLS connections.
  • Turn on deletion protection and automated backups.
  • Use IAM to control who can modify or delete DB instances.

Cost Tips

  • Pick the smallest instance that meets your needs and resize later.
  • Use Multi-AZ for production, but not for throwaway labs.
  • Stop or delete dev databases you aren't using. (A stopped RDS instance is automatically started again after 7 days.)
  • Delete old manual snapshots you no longer need.
  • Consider Reserved Instances for steady, long-running databases.

Common Issues and Fixes

Problem Likely cause Fix
Connection times out rds-sg doesn't allow 3306 from your app's SG Add the inbound rule with ec2-app-sg as source
Can't connect from your laptop Database is private (public access: No) Connect through EC2, a bastion, or Session Manager
Access denied for user Wrong username or password Re-check credentials or the Secrets Manager value
Unknown database Initial DB name wasn't set Run CREATE DATABASE appdb;
Storage full warnings Autoscaling off or limit reached Enable storage autoscaling or increase size

Clean Up

To avoid charges:

  1. Delete the read replica first (if you created one)
  2. Turn off deletion protection, then delete the DB instance
  3. Decide whether to keep a final snapshot (it costs storage) and whether to delete automated backups
  4. Delete leftover manual snapshots
  5. Delete the security groups and the EC2 instance if no longer needed
  6. Delete the Secrets Manager secret if you created one just for this lab

Conclusion

Amazon RDS lets you run production-grade relational databases without managing servers, patches, or backups by hand. With private networking, Multi-AZ, and automated backups, you get a secure and resilient foundation in minutes. Next, try adding a read replica, enabling Performance Insights, or moving to Aurora to see how far managed databases can go.

If you found this helpful, let's connect and keep learning together.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: vishalpatil-devops-aws
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS

title: LIFT: Scoped Constraints for Evaluating and Training Instruction Following
description:
arXiv:2610.28819v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the ability of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be verified programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints, pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-access, and cannot be easily extended. We present Lift-Bench, an IF benchmark that asks a model to draft a document given a topic and a structured outline. Constraints are scoped to certain document sections, providing finer control over constraint density. Lift-Bench includes both verifiable and judged constraints, as well as a training counterpart, Lift-Train. Importantly, Lift-Bench provides both main task and instruction-following constraints, mitigating shallow reward hacking. On experiments with multiple models, we find that frontier models struggle with the harder subsets of our benchmark and analyze model performance along multiple axes. We also find that training on Lift-Train is much less susceptible to reward hacking than training on the common IFTrain. Lift-Bench and Lift-Train are publicly available, as well as the data generating pipeline.

title: Hyva Went Free, PWA Studio Wound Down: The Magento Frontend Bet for 2026
description:
Open the network tab on a stock Magento storefront and count the JavaScript. You'll find jQuery, RequireJS pulling in dozens of small AMD modules, and Knockout.js wiring up the cart and checkout, all before a single product image finishes loading. That's the Luma theme, and it's been the default face of Magento for a decade. It's also the reason so many Magento stores quietly fail Core Web Vitals.

For years the escape hatch cost money. Then, in a short stretch of late 2025, the whole frontend question shifted under everyone's feet. Hyva, the server-rendered theme that had become the community's favorite way off Luma, relicensed itself free and open source. And Adobe, meanwhile, let PWA Studio settle into maintenance while it poured its energy into something else entirely. If you're speccing a Magento build for 2026, the menu you're choosing from is not the menu you knew in 2023.

What actually changed in late 2025

Two things happened, and they point in different directions.

Hyva went free. On November 10, 2025, Hyva announced it was relicensing its Theme under OSL-3.0 and AFL-3.0, the exact dual license Magento Open Source itself uses. In their words: "like Magento Open Source, our Theme can be used free of charge and redistributed under commercial licenses." Before that, the Hyva Theme was a paid license, reported by the community at roughly 1,000 euros (a bit over a thousand dollars) per store. That price tag was the single biggest thing keeping teams on Luma out of inertia. Overnight, it was gone.

Adobe moved on from PWA Studio. Not with a funeral, not with a deprecation notice, just with where the roadmap went. Adobe's frontend attention shifted to Edge Delivery Services, and PWA Studio slid into the same maintenance-mode existence Luma has lived in for years. More on exactly what "maintenance mode" means below, because the internet loves to overstate it.

So the free option got better and the Adobe-official option changed identity. Both of those change the answer to "what do I build my storefront on."

Why Luma was always the problem

To understand why Hyva took off, you have to understand what it's running away from. The classic Luma frontend is built on four technologies that all made sense in 2015 and none of which you'd pick today: Knockout.js for data binding, RequireJS for module loading, jQuery for DOM work, and LESS for styles.

The problem isn't that any one of them is terrible. It's the compound weight. RequireJS fetches a long waterfall of tiny JavaScript modules. Knockout stands up an entire MVVM layer to keep the cart and minicart in sync. jQuery sits underneath all of it. The result is a storefront that ships a large JavaScript bundle and does a lot of work on the main thread before the page is interactive, which is precisely what Largest Contentful Paint and Interaction to Next Paint punish you for. Agency migration write-ups routinely describe a Luma product page pulling well over a megabyte of JavaScript across a couple hundred files. You can tune it, you can lazy-load, but you're fighting the architecture the whole way.

Here's the shape of a typical Luma interaction, wired through Knockout's declarative bindings:

<!-- Luma: Knockout binds the DOM to a view model, RequireJS loads the component -->
<div data-bind="scope: 'minicart'">
    <span data-bind="text: getCartParam('summary_count')"></span>
</div>
<script type="text/x-magento-init">
    { "[data-block='minicart']": { "Magento_Ui/js/block-loader": "..." } }
</script>

To make that span update, the browser has loaded RequireJS, resolved the Magento_Ui module graph, instantiated a Knockout view model, and bound it to the DOM. For a number in a corner.

Hyva's bet: ship almost no JavaScript

Hyva made one architectural decision and built everything around it: render on the server, and send the browser almost no JavaScript. It throws out Knockout, RequireJS, jQuery, and LESS entirely, and rebuilds the storefront on just two things: Tailwind CSS for styling and Alpine.js for the small amount of interactivity a page genuinely needs.

Alpine is the key. It's a tiny library that lets you sprinkle behavior directly into markup, no build-time module graph, no view models. That same minicart counter becomes a few attributes on an element:

<!-- Hyva: Alpine holds a little state right in the markup, no module loader -->
<div x-data="{ count: 0 }" @update-cart.window="count = $event.detail.count">
    <span x-text="count"></span>
</div>

No RequireJS waterfall, no Knockout instance. The page arrives fully rendered from the server, and Alpine hydrates the handful of interactive bits. The reason Hyva wins on performance isn't a clever trick, it's subtraction: there's simply far less JavaScript to download, parse, and execute. Teams that migrate consistently report their storefronts moving from failing Core Web Vitals to passing them, and the mechanism is exactly what you'd expect from cutting the main-thread work by an order of magnitude.

Now, the honest part about "free," because it's not quite all-you-can-eat. What went open source is the Hyva Theme and its compatibility modules. Hyva Checkout, Hyva Enterprise, and Hyva Commerce stayed commercial, and the UI kit was split out into its own paid product. So a store built on the free Hyva theme is genuinely free; a store that also wants Hyva's dedicated checkout is still writing a check. That's a fair deal, and it's still a categorically different world than "a thousand dollars per store before you render a single page."

PWA Studio didn't die, it stopped being the plan

Let's be precise here, because this is where hot takes go wrong. PWA Studio, Adobe's React-based headless storefront (the magento/pwa-studio repo and its Venia storefront), is not dead, deprecated, or archived. The repo still gets commits. It's still shipping point releases, with v14.5.1 landing in May 2026. There is no official Adobe end-of-life notice, and if you're running it in production it isn't going to stop working.

What happened is subtler and, for planning purposes, more important: it stopped being where Adobe invests. The releases are compatibility and security work, PHP version bumps, dependency updates, the maintenance you do to keep the lights on, not major new capability. The community consensus, which Adobe hasn't contradicted, is that active feature development wound down and the strategic focus moved elsewhere. In other words, PWA Studio now sits roughly where Luma sits: supported, functional, and not the future.

That's the framing that matters when someone pitches you a new PWA Studio build in 2026. It'll work. But you'd be adopting Adobe's yesterday, not its tomorrow.

Adobe's actual 2026 answer: Edge Delivery Services

Adobe's tomorrow is Edge Delivery Services, the same tech behind its AEM sites, now aimed at Commerce. The pitch is a storefront assembled from Commerce drop-in components (prebuilt, customizable pieces like product details and cart) plus content authored as documents, served from Adobe's edge. Adobe markets it as the path to "the fastest storefronts on the web," and there's a real official starting point: the hlxsites/aem-boilerplate-commerce template repo.

It genuinely is fast, because the model is edge-served and light by design. But go in clear-eyed about the tradeoff, because it's a big one. EDS is a fundamentally different way to build. The document-authoring model, the block-based component system, and the AEM lineage mean your team isn't writing a Magento theme anymore, they're learning a new platform with its own mental model and its own gravity. Adobe presents EDS as its strategic direction rather than publishing a literal "this replaces PWA Studio" statement, but the direction of travel is not subtle.

So what do you actually build on in 2026?

Here's the decision, stripped down.

Luma is legacy. Pick it only if you're maintaining an existing store and a re-theme isn't on the table. It works, it's supported, and it will keep quietly costing you Core Web Vitals. Don't start something new here.

Hyva is the pragmatic default now, and going free is what makes that true. It's server-rendered, it ships almost no JavaScript, the performance story is real, and, crucially, it's still just a Magento theme. Your existing Magento developers can work in it, you can hire for it, and you're not betting the store on a new platform paradigm. For the large majority of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source builds in 2026, this is the boring, correct answer.

Edge Delivery Services is Adobe's bet on the future and the best raw performance ceiling, but it asks the most. Choose it if you're aligned with Adobe's roadmap, you have a team willing to learn the EDS/AEM model, and top-end speed is a hard business requirement worth a steeper build. It's the strategic pick, with strategic-sized costs.

And if you're a composable shop that wants a fully custom head, the fourth door is still open: build your own frontend (Next.js or Nuxt against Magento's GraphQL API), or use Alokai, the commerce frontend platform that used to be Vue Storefront before its 2024 rebrand. More freedom, more to own.

The through-line is that the cheap, sensible middle finally exists without an asterisk. For years the good answer to "how do I get off Luma" had a thousand-dollar-per-store price attached, and plenty of teams stayed stuck because of it. That barrier is gone. If you're still shipping Knockout and RequireJS to your customers' phones in 2026, the reason can't be budget anymore. It's just habit.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration
description:
Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration

Introduction

In this rapidly evolving era of Artificial Intelligence, I wanted to go beyond simply learning about AI and start understanding how it works in real-world applications. My goal is to dive deeper into the world of AI, explore its workflows, understand how Large Language Models (LLMs) operate, and learn how AI agents can reason, use tools, and solve practical problems.

As technology continues to advance, I believe the best way to grow as a developer is to challenge myself by building real-world applications, experimenting with new technologies, and learning from the problems I encounter along the way. I wanted to push my boundaries, strengthen my AI engineering skills, and contribute to the growing AI ecosystem through practical implementation.

That motivation led me to build AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration.

The idea was to create more than a traditional chatbot. I wanted to explore how an AI assistant could interact with external tools, retrieve relevant information, and respond to different user requests through a single conversational interface.

In this article, I'll share my journey of building this project, the technologies I explored, how tool integration works, the challenges involved, and the lessons I learned while developing my practical AI skills.

Project Links

Explore the project and its source code:

  • Live Demo: AI Chat Assistant
  • Frontend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Frontend
  • Backend Repository: AI Chat Assistant Backend

Feel free to explore the code, try the live application, and share your feedback. I'd love to hear your thoughts and suggestions!

1. The Problem: An AI Model Alone Is Not Enough

LLMs are powerful at understanding natural language, generating responses, summarizing content, and explaining technical concepts. However, a standalone model has limitations.

For example:

  • It may not know the latest news or current weather conditions.
  • Its training data may not include recent technical information.
  • It cannot automatically access external services without an integration.
  • It needs additional application logic to interact with APIs and handle errors.

I wanted to solve these limitations by building an assistant that could select the appropriate tools when answering different types of questions.

For example, when a user asks, "What is the weather in Chennai?", the assistant should use a weather service rather than simply generate an answer from its language model.

Similarly, when a user asks a programming question, it can use a relevant technical information source when appropriate.

This led me to explore agentic AI and tool calling.

2. What Is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work toward a goal by choosing actions, using tools, and incorporating the results into their responses.

A traditional chatbot typically follows a straightforward pattern:

User input → LLM → Response

An agentic assistant can follow a more flexible workflow:

User input → Understand the request → Select a tool → Execute the tool → Process the result → Generate a response

For example, consider this request:

"Find recent technology news and summarize the important points."

The assistant can identify that the user needs current information, invoke a news or search tool, process the returned results, and generate a concise summary.

The LLM handles language understanding and decision-making, while external tools provide capabilities that the model does not have on its own.

An important distinction is that the LLM does not magically gain access to external services. The application must explicitly provide the tools, their descriptions, and the code needed to execute them.

3. Project Architecture

I designed the application around a frontend, a backend API, an LLM integration, and a collection of specialized tools.

The main components are:

Frontend

The frontend provides the conversational interface where users submit questions and view assistant responses.

Backend API

The backend receives requests, manages the conversation flow, coordinates model interactions, executes tool calls, and returns the final response.

LLM integration

The language model interprets user requests, determines when a tool may be useful, and generates natural-language responses from the available context.

Tool integrations

Individual tools connect the assistant to external information sources and services, such as weather, news, web search, Wikipedia, movie information, Stack Overflow, and Notion.

Supporting services

The application also uses supporting infrastructure such as a database and Redis, depending on the feature and workflow, for data persistence and caching.

The overall flow looks like this:

              User
               |
               v
        Frontend Chat UI
               |
               v
          Backend API
               |
               v
          LLM / Agent
               |
        Selects a tool
               |
               v
       Tool Execution Layer
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |       |        |
     Weather  Search   News
       |       |        |
       +-------+--------+
               |
               v
        Tool Result
               |
               v
        LLM Generates
        Final Response
               |
               v
          Frontend UI

This architecture separates the user interface, orchestration logic, and external integrations, making the application easier to extend and maintain.

4. Integrating Multiple Tools

One of the most interesting parts of the project was connecting different capabilities through a single assistant.

Each tool has a specific responsibility.

Weather

The weather tool retrieves weather information for a requested location. This allows the assistant to answer questions that require current or forecast data.

Web Search

The web search tool helps retrieve information from online sources when a question requires information beyond the model's built-in knowledge.

News

The news integration provides access to recent news information, helping the assistant respond to requests about current events.

Wikipedia

Wikipedia provides reference information about people, places, organizations, and general topics.

Movie Information

The movie tool supports queries about films and related information, demonstrating how a specialized API can extend an assistant's capabilities.

Stack Overflow

This integration helps retrieve programming-related discussions and technical information that may be relevant to developer questions.

Notion

The Notion integration connects the assistant to a productivity and knowledge-management platform, where supported operations can help users work with information in their workspace.

The key idea is that these tools are not interchangeable. Each one has its own inputs, outputs, API requirements, and possible failure conditions.

The assistant needs enough information about each tool to select it appropriately.

5. How Tool Calling Works

A tool-enabled LLM workflow generally consists of several steps.

Step 1: Receive the request

The backend receives the user's message and prepares the relevant conversation context.

Step 2: Ask the model to determine the next action

The model evaluates the request and can return either a normal response or a structured tool call, depending on the framework and tool definitions.

Step 3: Execute the selected tool

The backend validates the requested arguments and calls the corresponding function or external API.

Step 4: Return the result to the model

The tool output is passed back into the conversation so the model can interpret it.

Step 5: Generate the final answer

The model converts the available information into a response that is understandable to the user.

Conceptually, a tool definition might look like this:

def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """
    Retrieve weather information for a city.
    """
    # Call the configured weather API here.
    # Validate the response and handle API errors.
    return {
        "city": city,
        "temperature": 28,
        "condition": "Partly cloudy"
    }

This is a simplified example showing the shape of a tool function, not the complete implementation of a production weather integration.

In a real application, the function would retrieve actual weather data, validate the location, handle timeouts, and report errors appropriately.

The LLM should not invent tool results. It should base its answer on the returned information and communicate when reliable data is unavailable.

6. Technology Stack

The project combines frontend development, backend engineering, AI integration, and external services.

The main technologies include:

  • Next.js and React: Building the frontend experience.
  • FastAPI: Exposing backend endpoints and coordinating application logic.
  • Python: Implementing backend functionality and tool integrations.
  • LLM providers: Powering natural-language understanding, reasoning, and response generation.
  • LangChain and related agent tooling: Supporting model and tool integration where configured.
  • PostgreSQL: Providing relational data persistence.
  • Redis: Supporting caching and other appropriate fast-access operations.
  • External APIs: Providing specialized information and capabilities.

Each technology addresses a different part of the system. The frontend handles interaction, the backend coordinates execution, the model processes language, and external APIs provide information or actions.

The exact model, API provider, and available operations depend on the configured integrations.

7. Challenges I Had to Consider

Building an AI assistant involves more than connecting a model to an API. Several engineering concerns become important as the number of tools increases.

Choosing the right tool

Similar user requests can require different tools, and vague questions can be difficult to interpret.

Clear tool descriptions, well-defined parameters, and appropriate model instructions help improve tool selection.

Handling API failures

External services can return errors, enforce rate limits, or respond slowly.

The backend should handle timeouts, validate responses, and return useful error messages rather than allowing one failed integration to break the entire conversation.

Managing API keys

Third-party API credentials should remain on the server and be loaded through environment variables or a suitable secrets-management system.

They should never be exposed in frontend code or committed to a public repository.

Keeping responses grounded

When a question requires current information, the assistant should use the relevant external source instead of presenting unsupported information as fact.

It is also important to distinguish retrieved information from the model's own explanation.

Maintaining a modular architecture

Adding more tools can make backend logic difficult to maintain if every integration is implemented inside a single large function.

Separating tool implementations from orchestration makes it easier to add capabilities, test individual integrations, and handle failures independently.

These considerations helped me understand why reliable AI applications need thoughtful backend engineering in addition to a capable language model.

8. Security and Reliability Considerations

An AI assistant that can access external services needs appropriate safeguards.

Some important practices include:

  • Validate tool arguments before executing them.
  • Apply authentication and authorization to protected endpoints.
  • Use request timeouts and controlled retry policies.
  • Limit tool permissions to the operations the application actually needs.
  • Avoid passing secrets or unnecessary sensitive data into model prompts.
  • Sanitize external content and treat retrieved text as untrusted input.
  • Apply rate limits and usage controls where appropriate.
  • Log useful operational information without exposing credentials or private conversation content.

For integrations that can modify external data, such as creating or updating records, additional permission checks and confirmation steps may be necessary.

These controls help make tool-enabled AI systems safer and more predictable.

9. What I Learned

This project helped me understand how LLMs can become part of a complete software system rather than functioning as isolated text-generation components.

Some of my main takeaways were:

LLMs need reliable tools. A language model becomes more useful for current or specialized questions when it can access appropriate external information.

Backend design matters. Tool orchestration, validation, error handling, authentication, and API integration are essential parts of an AI application.

Modularity improves extensibility. Keeping integrations separate makes it easier to introduce new capabilities without rewriting the entire application.

AI responses need grounding. A polished response is not necessarily a correct one. Reliable results depend on tool quality, context, validation, and clear handling of uncertainty.

Full-stack development and AI engineering complement each other. Building a useful assistant requires frontend interaction, backend APIs, model integration, and operational reliability to work together.

10. What's Next?

There are several ways to improve a multi-tool assistant as it evolves:

  • Add streaming responses for a more interactive experience.
  • Improve conversation memory and context management.
  • Introduce retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for private or domain-specific knowledge.
  • Add structured evaluation to measure tool-selection accuracy.
  • Improve observability with tracing, latency metrics, and error monitoring.
  • Introduce more granular permissions for tools that can modify external data.
  • Explore standardized tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where appropriate.

These improvements can help move an experimental AI assistant toward a more reliable and maintainable application.

Conclusion

Building an AI Chat Assistant with Agentic LLMs and Multi-Tool Integration was an opportunity to explore the intersection of full-stack development and modern AI engineering.

The project demonstrates how a conversational interface, an LLM, a backend orchestration layer, and external tools can work together to answer different types of questions.

More importantly, it reinforced an important lesson: building a useful AI application is not just about choosing a powerful model. It is about designing the systems around that model so it can access reliable information, use tools appropriately, and communicate results clearly.

I'm continuing to explore LLM engineering, agentic workflows, and practical AI integrations, and I'm looking forward to applying these lessons to more complex projects.

If you're building an AI assistant yourself, I'd be interested to hear what tools you're integrating and what challenges you've encountered.

Thanks for reading!

Opt tools in by adding them to the experimental_webMcp object:

Then load the script from your MCP endpoint with the ?webmcp-script parameter:

The script registers those tools with the page and proxies each call back to your MCP server as the signed-in user, so authenticated tools work without a browser-side OAuth flow.

title: The Hidden Dangers of Free Proxies: A Deep Dive into Security Risks and Building Secure Alternatives
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

For many developers, the allure of a "free proxy list" is a quick fix for bypassing geo-restrictions, scraping public data, or masking an IP address during early-stage testing. However, in the world of networking, there is no such thing as a free lunch. When you route your traffic through a server you do not control and that is provided for free, you are essentially handing the keys to your data stream to an anonymous third party. This article explores the underlying mechanisms that make free proxies dangerous and provides a technical blueprint for implementing secure, self-hosted alternatives.

  • The Architecture of a Proxy
  • The Threat Model of Free Proxies
  • Common Attack Vectors
  • The Economic Incentive: Why are they Free?
  • Building a Secure Alternative with Squid and WireGuard
  • Production Best Practices for Proxy Infrastructure
  • Frequently Asked Questions

The Architecture of a Proxy

To understand the risk, we must first understand the flow. A proxy server acts as an intermediary gateway between a client (your application) and a destination server (the API or website you are accessing).

In a standard request flow:

  1. The client sends a request to the proxy server.
  2. The proxy server forwards that request to the destination server.
  3. The destination server responds to the proxy.
  4. The proxy forwards the response back to the client.

From the perspective of the destination server, the request originated from the proxy's IP, not the client's. While this provides anonymity from the destination, it creates a single point of failure and a total point of visibility for the proxy operator. If the proxy is "transparent" or "anonymous," it may or may not hide your original IP via the X-Forwarded-For header, but the operator of the proxy server always sees the raw TCP stream.

The Threat Model of Free Proxies

When using a free proxy, your threat model expands significantly. You are no longer just worried about the destination server or the ISP; you have introduced a malicious actor into the middle of your request-response cycle.

The "Man-in-the-Middle" (MITM) by Design

A proxy is, by definition, a Man-in-the-Middle. While legitimate proxies use this for caching or filtering, a malicious free proxy uses it for interception. Because the proxy terminates the TCP connection from the client and initiates a new one to the server, it has full access to the payload of every unencrypted packet.

TLS Termination and SSL Stripping

Many developers assume that HTTPS (TLS) protects them from proxy risks. While TLS provides end-to-end encryption, a sophisticated proxy can attempt SSL Stripping. In this attack, the proxy intercepts the initial HTTP request and prevents the upgrade to HTTPS, serving the client a plaintext HTTP version of the site while maintaining an HTTPS connection with the actual server. If the developer's code doesn't strictly enforce HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) or validate certificates, the proxy can read every password, API key, and session token in plaintext.

Common Attack Vectors

1. Packet Sniffing and Data Exfiltration

Free proxy operators often run packet sniffers like tcpdump or Wireshark on the proxy interface. Any data sent over HTTP, FTP, or SMTP is captured in real-time. Even with HTTPS, metadata (DNS queries, destination IPs, packet timing) is leaked, which can be used for fingerprinting the developer's infrastructure.

2. Payload Injection

Because the proxy controls the response body before it reaches the client, it can inject malicious code. For a web scraper, this might mean the proxy modifies the HTML to include a malicious script or redirects a download link to a malware-infected binary. For an API client, the proxy could modify JSON responses to trigger vulnerabilities in the client's parser (e.g., injecting oversized strings to cause a buffer overflow).

3. IP Reputation Poisoning

Free proxies are often shared by thousands of users, many of whom are using them for botnets or DDoS attacks. When you use these IPs, your traffic is associated with a "dirty" IP. This often leads to your legitimate requests being flagged by WAFs (Web Application Firewalls) like Cloudflare or Akamai, resulting in permanent IP bans for the proxy range and potential flagging of your own account if you are authenticated.

The Economic Incentive: Why are they Free?

Maintaining servers and bandwidth costs money. If a service is free, the data is the product. Proxy operators monetize their infrastructure through:

  • Selling Data: Logs of user activity, headers, and intercepted credentials are sold on dark-web forums.
  • Ad Injection: Injecting banners or scripts into HTTP responses to generate ad revenue.
  • Botnet Recruitment: Using the proxy as a distribution point for malware to infect the clients connecting to it.
  • Traffic Rerouting: Sending your traffic through other "partner" proxies to artificially inflate traffic numbers for certain sites.

Building a Secure Alternative with Squid and WireGuard

Instead of relying on public lists, developers should build a private proxy cluster. The most secure approach is to combine a VPN (WireGuard) for transport security and a Caching Proxy (Squid) for request management.

Prerequisites

  • A VPS (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS recommended)
  • Root access to the server
  • Basic knowledge of Linux networking

Step 1: Securing the Transport Layer with WireGuard

To prevent the proxy from being exposed to the open internet (and thus becoming a target for open-proxy scanners), we wrap it in a WireGuard VPN. This ensures only authenticated clients can even reach the proxy port.

# Install WireGuard
sudo apt update && sudo apt install wireguard -y

# Generate keys
wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey

Configure /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <Server_Private_Key>
Address = 10.0.0.1/24
ListenPort = 51820

[Peer]
PublicKey = <Client_Public_Key>
AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32

Step 2: Installing and Configuring Squid

Squid is the industry standard for HTTP proxying. We will configure it to listen only on the WireGuard interface, making it invisible to the public web.

sudo apt install squid -y

Edit /etc/squid/squid.conf. We want to disable public access and only allow our VPN subnet:

# Define the WireGuard network
acl vpn_network src 10.0.0.0/24

# Allow access from the VPN network
http_access allow vpn_network

# Deny everything else
http_access deny all

# Change default port if desired
http_port 3128

# Hide the client IP (Make it an anonymous proxy)
forwarded_for off
request_header_access Via deny all
request_header_access X-Forwarded-For deny all

Step 3: Implementing the Client Connection

On the developer's machine, connect to the VPN and then route the application traffic through the proxy IP.

# Start WireGuard client
sudo wg-quick up wg0

# Test the proxy using curl
curl -x http://10.0.0.1:3128 https://api.ipify.org

By using this architecture, you have eliminated the MITM risk from third parties. The traffic is encrypted from your machine to your VPS via WireGuard, and the proxy is not accessible to the public, preventing it from being hijacked by botnets.

Production Best Practices for Proxy Infrastructure

For engineers scaling this to a production environment, consider these advanced configurations:

  1. Rotation via Load Balancer: If you are scraping, do not use one IP. Use a pool of small VPS instances and a load balancer (like HAProxy) to rotate requests across different exit nodes.
  2. Strict TLS Validation: Always use libraries that enforce certificate validation. In Python's requests, ensure verify=True (which is default). Never set verify=False when using a proxy, as this disables the only protection you have against SSL stripping.
  3. Monitoring and Logging: Implement Prometheus and Grafana to monitor proxy latency and error rates. High spikes in 403 Forbidden responses usually indicate that your proxy IP has been flagged and needs rotation.
  4. Avoid Long-Lived Sessions: If you are automating tasks, rotate your proxy identity frequently to avoid pattern detection by the destination server's behavioral analysis engines.

For more architectural patterns on secure networking, check out Tamiz's Insights for deep dives into system design.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can't I just use a SOCKS5 proxy instead of HTTP?
SOCKS5 is more flexible as it handles any TCP/UDP traffic, not just HTTP. However, it doesn't provide the caching or header manipulation capabilities of Squid. The security risks remain the same: if the SOCKS5 server is "free," the operator can still sniff all unencrypted traffic passing through the socket.

Q: Is a commercial "Paid Proxy" safer than a free one?
Generally, yes, because there is a legal contract and a business model based on service availability rather than data theft. However, the operator still has the technical ability to see your traffic. The only way to ensure total privacy is to own the infrastructure (self-hosting).

Q: What is the difference between an Anonymous and an Elite proxy?
An Anonymous proxy hides your IP but tells the server it is a proxy (via the Via header). An Elite (or High Anonymity) proxy hides your IP and pretends to be a regular browser, omitting any proxy headers. While Elite proxies are better for bypassing blocks, they don't provide additional security against a malicious operator.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: Private Exports: Caching Signed Download Links to Reduce Presign Rate-Limit Requests
description:
Short answer: object storage fits private fintech exports, but large-file throughput depends on keeping page refreshes away from the presign path. Cache each still-valid signed download URL in the backend, preserve the export job and object key, and retry presign generation with bounded exponential backoff instead of signing again on every click.

A 4 GB statement archive should spend its time moving from object storage to the customer, not making the application mint another authorization artifact because a browser tab refreshed. The link is control-plane work; the file transfer is data-plane work. Treating both as one request path creates a rate-limit problem that more transfer capacity won't solve.

How should a fintech export page cache signed download URLs under presign rate limits?

Key the cache by tenant, user authorization scope, export job, and object key. Return a cached URL only while it has a conservative validity margin; otherwise, let one backend worker generate the replacement while concurrent requests wait for that result. Don't cache by object key alone. In a fintech system, that shortcut can cross an access boundary even when the underlying object remains private.

The export record is the durable center of the flow. It should hold the job state and object key after generation completes. The signed URL is disposable state layered on top. A page refresh can then read the same completed record and reuse its current link rather than starting a new export or presign call. This separation also prevents an impatient user clicking five times from creating five large archives.

Keep the expiry margin explicit. I'm not sure what margin is right for every workload because it depends on link lifetime, clock skew, and how long a download may sit before it starts; load tests with realistic file sizes and client geography should settle it. The important part is to expire the cache before the URL itself, not at the same instant.

One request wins.

Cache first.

The following Python script calls the verified presign path without inventing a request body or response field. Set INFRAI_API_ROOT to the API's versioned root and pass tenant, user, export, bucket, and key arguments. The example demonstrates scoped cache keys, one in-flight signer per key, a short reuse window, HTTP 429 handling, Retry-After, and jittered exponential backoff. Any other 4xx response is surfaced rather than treated as success.

import json
import os
import random
import sys
import threading
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


class RateLimited(Exception):
    def __init__(self, retry_after: float | None = None):
        self.retry_after = retry_after


API_ROOT = os.environ["INFRAI_API_ROOT"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
CACHE_SECONDS = 30
cache: dict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = {}
locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = {}
locks_guard = threading.Lock()


def lock_for(cache_key: str) -> threading.Lock:
    with locks_guard:
        return locks.setdefault(cache_key, threading.Lock())


def request_signed_link(bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    path = "/storage/object/presign/{}/{}".format(
        quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")
    )
    request = Request(
        API_ROOT + path,
        method="POST",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
    )
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {response.status}")
            return json.load(response)
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        if error.code == 429:
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            raise RateLimited(float(retry_after) if retry_after else None)
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error


def get_link(tenant: str, user: str, export: str, bucket: str, key: str) -> dict:
    cache_key = f"{tenant}:{user}:{export}:{bucket}:{key}"
    cached = cache.get(cache_key)
    if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
        return cached[1]

    with lock_for(cache_key):
        cached = cache.get(cache_key)
        if cached and cached[0] > time.monotonic():
            return cached[1]

        for attempt in range(5):
            try:
                result = request_signed_link(bucket, key)
                cache[cache_key] = (time.monotonic() + CACHE_SECONDS, result)
                return result
            except RateLimited as error:
                if attempt == 4:
                    raise
                base = error.retry_after or min(2**attempt, 16)
                time.sleep(base + random.uniform(0, base * 0.25))

    raise RuntimeError("retry loop ended unexpectedly")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(get_link(*sys.argv[1:6]), indent=2))

For more than one application process, replace the in-memory map and locks with shared equivalents that provide an atomic winner. The cache key might look like tenant_81:user_204:export_991:ledger.csv; the exact identifiers are yours, but every authorization dimension must be present. A cached link should never outlive a permission change without an invalidation strategy. That compliance detail is easy to miss because the URL still works exactly as designed.

Separate presign pressure from large-file throughput

Large-file performance needs two measurements. First, count application requests that reach the presign operation per completed export. Second, measure the actual object transfer independently. If refresh spam raises the first number while bytes delivered stays flat, tuning multipart transfer or adding application workers attacks the wrong side of the system.

Retries can amplify the same mistake. A browser retry, an API gateway retry, and a worker retry can multiply one click into several signing attempts unless they share stable request identity. Presign generation is the narrow operation here, so coalesce identical requests and cap retry attempts. Honor Retry-After when it is supplied; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Fast retry loops are traffic generators wearing a reliability label.

Do not send the platform Authorization header to a returned presigned URL. The signed URL carries its own temporary authorization, and the object must remain private or signed-only. The application should redirect the authorized user to that URL or return it to the client, then get out of the large-file byte path unless policy requires the application to proxy every byte.

The edge case I would test first is refresh during expiry: 30 tabs ask for the same finished export while its cached link enters the safety margin. The correct result is one replacement signing operation, not 30. Also test a permission revocation during that window, a job that has finished but whose link cache is empty, and repeated requests while the export is still running. Those tests expose authorization and state-machine gaps long before a throughput chart does.

Picture the request sequence rather than the average: export export_991 finishes, its private object key is committed to the job record, and a customer opens the page on a slow connection. The first authorized page request signs the object and places the result in a tenant-and-user-scoped cache. The browser refreshes twice, a mobile session opens the same export, and a gateway retries one request. All four follow-up requests should read the same cached result; none should rebuild the CSV, and none should independently hit the presign operation. When the cache enters its early-expiry margin, one shared lock elects a replacement request while the others wait. If that request receives 429, it honors Retry-After or applies bounded exponential backoff with jitter. At every step, the durable job record still points to one object. This is the difference between controlling a burst and merely moving it downstream.

Back off.

How do storage options compare after request amplification is controlled?

The right comparison is not which logo serves a byte fastest in an unspecified region. It is how much provider-specific control the team needs, and whether a shared backend surface is worth the capability boundaries it introduces.

Option Integration shape Best fit Reason to choose something else
AWS S3 Direct provider integration Teams standardized on the S3 control plane A shared interface is more valuable than provider-specific integration
Cloudflare R2 Direct provider integration Teams that have already chosen R2 The workload must also move across several supported storage vendors through one contract
Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct provider integration Teams committed to OSS One application contract across vendors matters more
Tencent Cloud COS Direct provider integration Teams committed to COS One application contract across vendors matters more
Google Cloud Storage Direct provider integration GCS is a hard requirement It is outside Infrai's current vendor coverage
Infrai One REST surface over R2, S3, OSS, and COS A team wants one credential and consistent conventions for multiple backend capabilities Native-only storage controls or an unsupported provider are required

Infrai is a strong option when integration overhead is the constraint: its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so wiring storage starts by reading the operation contract rather than installing another SDK. It also puts multiple backend capabilities behind one key and one bill. For this flow, the relevant verified operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}; discover its live schema before constructing the request, and keep the returned link in the application cache described above.

That advantage doesn't make it the automatic choice. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, or Tencent Cloud COS directly when provider-specific controls are central to the design. Choose Google Cloud Storage when GCS support is mandatory. AWS EFS solves a different problem: it is a managed file system, so it should not be treated as a drop-in answer to a signed object-download workflow.

What capability boundaries change the export design?

Private, expiring downloads are supported, but permanent public links and static-site hosting are not: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. That's a sound boundary for this use case, yet it rules out using the same path as a public image host. Browser-direct uploads also need separate planning because self-service CORS configuration is not exposed.

There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite therefore isn't recoverable through this surface, and financial records that require WORM retention need an external design. There is also no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database transaction. These aren't footnotes for a fintech workload; they determine which records may be placed behind the abstraction.

Operationally, lifecycle expiration has a one-day minimum. That works for daily cleanup, not hour-level deletion. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, metadata cannot be searched server-side because listing only filters by prefix, and accumulated exports require explicit monitoring of bucket usage and object counts. Cross-region automatic replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling are absent. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.

The catch is clear: use this pattern for private export artifacts whose authorization lives in the application and whose cleanup can tolerate daily granularity. It is not suitable for immutable regulatory archives, public asset hosting, GCS- or B2-dependent deployments, self-managed browser CORS, or workloads that require native cross-region replication.

Roll out with counters, state, and cleanup

Start with one export type and preserve the old download path during rollout. Add an export state machine such as requested, running, completed, and expired; save the object key once; then place signed-link reuse in front of presign generation. A stable request identifier should follow a repeated user action through the application so retries do not create duplicate export jobs.

Watch four counters: export jobs created, completed objects, presign attempts, and cache hits. Their relationships matter more than a single total. If page traffic rises but completed objects and presign attempts remain nearly steady, coalescing is doing its job. Your mileage may vary on the cache window, especially for customers who begin multi-gigabyte downloads long after opening the page.

Finally, schedule lifecycle cleanup with the one-day minimum in mind and audit object counts as well as bytes. Rollback should disable link reuse without deleting job state or object keys. That gives the team a compact change surface: the heavy data path stays in object storage while the application gains control over refresh spam, retries, authorization, and expiry.

References

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • AWS EFS managed file system overview: https://aws.amazon.com/efs/

title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
description:
arXiv:2610.28537v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from $3.8$ to $32$B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on \emph{generative} tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about $2.3$ effective bits per weight and retains $89$ to $97\%$ of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses $1.4$ to $30\times$ less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.
