title: Connection Pooling for PostgreSQL Under Real Concurrency
description:
Here's a number worth staring at. In a benchmark Andres Freund ran while working on Postgres connection scalability, one active connection doing simple reads managed 33,457 transactions per second on an otherwise idle server. Add 10,000 connections that do nothing at all, and the same single connection dropped to 14,496 TPS. Nothing else changed. The idle connections weren't running queries. They were just there.

That's the part of connection pooling most teams never think about. They treat pool size as a knob on one service: bump max from 10 to 50 because the API felt slow, ship it, move on. But Postgres doesn't see your services. It sees one flat pile of backend processes, and every service, every replica, every cron job, and every half-finished rolling deploy adds to the same pile.

So let's do this properly. Not "what should max be," but "how do you split one database's real capacity across everything that talks to it, and keep it split when the cluster autoscales at 3pm on a Friday."

What a Postgres connection actually costs

Postgres uses a process-per-connection model. Every client connection gets its own backend process, forked by the postmaster, with its own slot in shared memory and its own row in pg_stat_activity. That's very different from a thread-per-connection database, and it's why the question "how many connections can Postgres handle?" has a more interesting answer than you'd expect.

There are three separate costs, and people usually blame the wrong one.

Memory is smaller than folklore says. You'll read "10MB per connection" in a lot of blog posts. Freund's analysis on the Citus blog measured it properly and found the per-connection overhead is below 2 MiB when the server is configured sensibly, with huge_pages on. That's not free, but it's not the reason your database fell over either. (The shared-memory side is also allocated up front: max_connections sizes the lock tables and process slots at startup, which is one reason changing it needs a restart.)

Snapshots were the real bottleneck, and they got fixed. Every statement takes a snapshot to decide which row versions it can see. Before Postgres 14, building that snapshot meant walking the state of every backend, including the idle ones. In Freund's CPU profile, with one active connection next to 5,000 idle ones, the bottleneck sat squarely in GetSnapshotData(). His fix landed in Postgres 14, and the before/after is dramatic: with 48 active connections and 10,000 idle, throughput went from 369,845 TPS to 1,115,740 TPS on the same hardware (2x Xeon Gold 5215).

Active concurrency is the cost that never goes away. Here's the thing Postgres 14 didn't change and can't change: if 400 connections are all running queries at the same time on a 16-core box, they're fighting over 16 cores, the same buffer pool, the same locks, and the same disk queue. Context switching goes up, cache hit rates go down, lock waits pile on. More concurrent work past the point of saturation doesn't make the database do more. It makes every query slower.

That last point is the whole article in one sentence. Idle connections are now cheap. Active connections are still expensive. Your pooling strategy should be about capping active concurrency at the database, not about hoarding slots.

The formula everyone quotes, and what it really means

The HikariCP wiki's "About Pool Sizing" page is one of the most-cited pieces of writing on this topic, and it opens with a result from Oracle's Real-World Performance group: reducing the connection pool size alone, with no other change, cut application response times from around 100ms to around 2ms. Smaller pool, faster app.

Then it gives its starting-point formula:

connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)

A few details matter here and get lost in the retelling:

  • core_count is the database server's physical cores, not the app server's, and not hyperthreads.
  • effective_spindle_count is how many disk operations can be in flight usefully. On SSD or NVMe, people typically plug in 1 as a starting point. The "extra" connections beyond cores only exist to cover time a backend spends blocked on I/O.
  • The wiki's own example is a 4-core server with one disk: (4 * 2) + 1 = 9, rounded to 10. It claims that setup comfortably serves 3,000 front-end users running simple queries at 6,000 TPS.

And the wiki is explicit that this is a starting point, not a law. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude anchor.

The detail that matters most here: that formula tells you the size of the pool for the whole database. It does not tell you what to put in one service's config. If you have a 16-core database, the formula says somewhere around 33 connections should be actively working at once. If you have eight services each running six replicas, and each replica's pool is sized "by the formula," you've just told the database it should expect 1,584 of them. That's how teams end up quoting HikariCP correctly and still melting their database.

Your real pool size is a multiplication

Let's make it concrete. The following is a hypothetical system, but the shape will look familiar: four workloads on one Postgres primary with 16 physical cores and max_connections = 200.

Workload Replicas (steady) Pool max per replica Connections at steady state
api (Node, pg) 12 10 120
worker (Go, pgxpool) 6 16 96
reporting 2 10 20
cron + migrations + humans with psql varies varies ~5
Total 241

It's already over 200 at steady state, and nothing is misbehaving. Each team picked a reasonable-looking number. Two of those numbers are literally library defaults: pg.Pool defaults max to 10, and pgxpool defaults MaxConns to the greater of 4 or runtime.NumCPU(), so a worker pod on a 16-vCPU node gets 16 without anyone deciding that.

Now add the two things that make this worse at the worst possible moment.

Rolling deploys. A Kubernetes Deployment's maxSurge defaults to 25%. During a rollout, old and new pods coexist, so your 12 API replicas can briefly be 15. That's 30 more connections, and they show up exactly when you're deploying, which is also when you're least prepared to debug FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.

Autoscaling. The HPA scales on CPU or custom metrics. It has no idea your database has a connection budget. When traffic spikes, it'll happily add pods, and each new pod can fill its whole pool as soon as traffic reaches it. The database gets more connections at the exact moment it's getting more load.

And don't forget the slots you can't use. Postgres reserves superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) for superusers, and since Postgres 16 there's also reserved_connections (default 0) for roles granted pg_use_reserved_connections. Those exist so you can still get in and fix things when the app has eaten every other slot. Keep them. Your app budget is max_connections minus those reservations minus whatever replication, monitoring, and migration tooling need.

So the honest formula for a direct-to-Postgres setup is:

sum over services of (pool_max * max_replicas * (1 + surge))
    + ops_and_tooling
    <= max_connections - superuser_reserved_connections - reserved_connections

Notice it uses max_replicas, the HPA ceiling, not today's replica count. If you size against the steady state, the budget holds right up until you need it.

Size each service with Little's Law, not vibes

If the database-wide number comes from cores, where does the per-service number come from? From how long each request actually holds a connection.

Little's Law says the average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times time in the system: L = lambda * W. For a connection pool, L is how many connections are busy on average, lambda is how often the service checks one out, and W is how long it keeps it.

Take a worked example, again with hypothetical numbers. Say one API replica handles 200 requests per second at peak, and each request holds a connection for about 15ms (query time plus the round trips in between, from checkout to release):

busy connections = 200 req/s * 0.015 s = 3

Three connections busy on average. A pool of 10 per replica gives you a lot of headroom for bursts and slow queries. A pool of 50 gives you nothing except the ability to hurt the database when things go wrong.

The useful insight isn't the arithmetic. It's that W is the variable you control, and it's usually the one that's out of whack. If that same service holds a connection for 150ms instead of 15ms, it needs ten times the connections for the same traffic. And the most common reason W balloons isn't slow SQL. It's code like this:

// Looks fine. Holds a Postgres connection across an HTTP call.
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const order = await client.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE', [id]);
  const charge = await paymentGateway.charge(order.rows[0]); // 300-2000ms, network
  await client.query('UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2', ['paid', id]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} catch (err) {
  await client.query('ROLLBACK');
  throw err;
} finally {
  client.release();
}

That transaction pins a connection (and a row lock) for the full duration of a third-party network call. Under load, the pool drains, and every other request queues behind payment latency. Bumping max doesn't fix it. It just moves the queue into Postgres, where it now also holds row locks. Do the external call outside the transaction, and let the database connection live only as long as the database work.

Postgres has a guardrail for the worst version of this: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout terminates sessions that sit idle inside an open transaction longer than the limit. It's off by default. Turning it on per role is cheap insurance.

Configure the client pool like you mean it

Library defaults are tuned for "works on a laptop." Under real concurrency, a few of them bite hard.

In node-postgres, connectionTimeoutMillis defaults to 0, which means no timeout. When the pool is exhausted, pool.connect() and pool.query() just wait. Forever. Your request timeout fires upstream, the client retries, and now you've got two waiters instead of one. Here's a pool that fails fast instead:

db.ts

import pg from 'pg';

export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  host: process.env.PGHOST,
  database: process.env.PGDATABASE,
  user: process.env.PGUSER,          // one role per service, see below
  max: 10,                           // sized from the budget, not from a hunch
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000,    // fail fast when the pool is empty
  idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000,         // the default, stated on purpose
  maxLifetimeSeconds: 1_800,         // recycle so connections rebalance after failover/scale
  application_name: 'api',           // shows up in pg_stat_activity
});

// An idle client can error (e.g. the server restarted). Without a
// listener, that error is unhandled and can crash the process.
pool.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('idle pg client error', err);
});

// Export these as metrics. waitingCount > 0 for long = pool is the bottleneck.
export function poolStats() {
  return {
    total: pool.totalCount,
    idle: pool.idleCount,
    waiting: pool.waitingCount,
  };
}

pool.waitingCount is the most underrated metric in Node database code. If it's regularly above zero, requests are queueing for connections inside your app. That's fine in short bursts; it's exactly where you want the queue to be. If it's pinned high, you've either got a W problem (connections held too long) or a genuinely undersized pool, and the Little's Law math tells you which.

On the Go side, the trap is different. database/sql defaults SetMaxOpenConns to 0, which means unlimited. Nothing in your service stops it from opening one connection per concurrent goroutine that touches the database. If you're using pgxpool directly, set the limits explicitly instead of inheriting runtime.NumCPU() from whatever node the pod landed on:

db.go

cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
cfg.MaxConns = 16                        // explicit: from the budget, not NumCPU
cfg.MinConns = 2
cfg.MaxConnLifetime = 30 * time.Minute
cfg.MaxConnIdleTime = 5 * time.Minute
cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams["application_name"] = "worker"

pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)

The nested-checkout deadlock

One more client-side footgun, and it's a nasty one because it looks like the database is hung. If a single request can hold two connections at once (for example, it opens a transaction, then calls a helper that does pool.query() outside that transaction), then a pool can deadlock itself: every connection is held by a request that's waiting for a second connection that will never come free.

The HikariCP wiki gives the minimum pool size that avoids this: Tn * (Cm - 1) + 1, where Tn is the max number of concurrent threads and Cm is the max connections any one of them holds at once. With 8 threads each holding up to 3, that's 17. The better fix is to not do it: pass the transaction's client down instead of reaching back into the pool.

Give every service its own role

One cheap move pays off in three places. Instead of every service connecting as app, give each one its own Postgres role.

CREATE ROLE api_svc       LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 150;
CREATE ROLE worker_svc    LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 100;
CREATE ROLE reporting_svc LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 20;

-- Per-role guardrails, applied at session start, no app code needed
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE api_svc       SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';
ALTER ROLE reporting_svc SET statement_timeout = '120s';
  1. CONNECTION LIMIT turns the budget into enforcement. A misconfigured reporting deploy can exhaust its own 20 slots and get errors, instead of exhausting the whole database and taking the API down with it.
  2. Per-role settings replace per-connection SET. This matters a lot once PgBouncer's transaction mode enters the picture, because SET doesn't survive there. ALTER ROLE ... SET is applied when the server connection starts, so it works through the pooler.
  3. Visibility. Combined with application_name, you can finally answer "who is using my connections?" in one query: 
SELECT usename, application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY usename, application_name, state
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

If that query shows 180 connections in state idle and 6 in active, you've just learned that your database isn't busy, it's crowded. That's the signal for the next step.

When the math doesn't close: PgBouncer

At some point the budget stops working. You've got too many services, too many replicas, or serverless functions that each want their own connection, and the sum of pools is fundamentally bigger than what Postgres should hold. That's when you put a pooler between the apps and the database.

PgBouncer is the standard answer. It's lightweight (the docs cite about 2 kB of memory per client connection by default), and its key trick is that client connections and server connections are separate numbers. Thousands of app connections can map onto a few dozen real Postgres backends.

The pooling mode decides how aggressively that mapping happens:

  • session (the default): a server connection is assigned for the lifetime of the client connection. Safe, fully compatible, and it barely reduces server connections at all if your app pools hold connections open.
  • transaction: a server connection is assigned only for the duration of one transaction, then returned. This is where the multiplexing actually happens, and it's what you want for the "many services, one database" problem.
  • statement: returned after every statement. Multi-statement transactions aren't allowed. Rarely what you want.

A transaction-mode config for our hypothetical system might look like this:

pgbouncer.ini

[databases]
; per-database cap on real Postgres connections, across all users
appdb = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=appdb max_db_connections=60

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000        ; app-side connections PgBouncer will accept
default_pool_size = 20        ; server connections per (user, database) pair
reserve_pool_size = 5         ; extra server conns under load...
reserve_pool_timeout = 3      ; ...after a client waited this many seconds
max_prepared_statements = 200 ; protocol-level prepared statements in txn mode

query_wait_timeout = 30       ; client waiting for a server conn gives up
server_idle_timeout = 600
server_lifetime = 3600

Two things worth pointing out. First, default_pool_size is per user/database pair, so the one-role-per-service move from earlier now gives each service its own isolated server-side pool inside PgBouncer. Second, max_db_connections sits on top as a hard ceiling for the whole database, which is exactly the "one shared budget" idea expressed as config.

The app-side pools don't go away. Each pod still keeps a small pool of connections to PgBouncer, and those can be generous, since a client connection to PgBouncer is cheap. The expensive resource, a real Postgres backend, is now rationed in one place.

What transaction mode breaks

Transaction pooling isn't free, and the PgBouncer docs are blunt about it: clients must not rely on session-level state, because consecutive transactions can land on different server connections. Their compatibility table lists what never works in transaction mode:

  • SET / RESET (session settings leak or vanish; use ALTER ROLE ... SET or SET LOCAL inside a transaction instead)
  • LISTEN (notifications go to whichever backend you happened to be on)
  • WITH HOLD cursors
  • SQL-level PREPARE / DEALLOCATE
  • Temp tables with PRESERVE ROWS or DELETE ROWS (only ON COMMIT DROP is safe)
  • LOAD
  • Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock); the transaction-level pg_advisory_xact_lock variants are fine

The session-level advisory lock one deserves a warning, because it fails silently:

Warning
If a job runner uses pg_advisory_lock() for leader election behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, the lock is taken on one server connection and the "unlock" may run on another. The lock can outlive the job, or another instance can grab a different backend and believe it's the leader. Point those workloads at a session-mode pool or straight at Postgres.

A practical pattern is two PgBouncer databases pointing at the same Postgres: one in transaction mode for request/response traffic, one in session mode (per-database pool_mode is allowed in the [databases] section) for migrations, LISTEN-based consumers, and anything that needs session state.

Prepared statements used to be the deal-breaker

For years, the standard advice was "turn off prepared statements if you use PgBouncer in transaction mode," because a statement prepared on one backend doesn't exist on the next. PgBouncer 1.21 changed that: with max_prepared_statements set to a non-zero value, PgBouncer tracks protocol-level prepares and re-prepares them transparently on whichever server connection the client lands on. Through 1.23 that setting defaulted to 0 (off); since 1.24 it defaults to 200.

The catch: it only covers protocol-level prepared statements, the kind drivers send through the extended query protocol. A literal PREPARE foo AS ... in SQL is still invisible to PgBouncer and still breaks. And if you're on a managed pooler or an older PgBouncer, check the version before assuming it works.

PgBouncer has its own ceiling

PgBouncer is single-threaded. One process uses one CPU core, no matter how big the box is. For most setups that's plenty, but a very busy pooler can become the bottleneck itself. Since 1.12 you can run several processes on the same port with so_reuseport = 1 and let the kernel spread client connections across them, and newer versions add peer_id plus a [peers] section so cancellation requests reach the right process.

Here's the gotcha that brings us right back to the start of this article: each PgBouncer process has its own pools. Four processes with default_pool_size = 20 can open up to 80 server connections per user/database pair, not 20. Run PgBouncer as a sidecar in every app pod and you've rebuilt the original multiplication problem with extra steps. The pooler only centralizes the budget if it's actually central, or if you divide the per-process limits by the number of processes.

Watching the budget

Once the pooler is in place, you've got two queues to watch: the one inside each app (waitingCount in node-postgres, Stat() in pgxpool) and the one inside PgBouncer. Connect to the admin console and run:

SHOW POOLS;

The columns that matter are cl_active (clients linked to a server connection, or idle with nothing waiting), cl_waiting (clients waiting for one), sv_active / sv_idle (server connections in use or parked), and maxwait (how long the oldest waiting client has been waiting). A healthy transaction-mode pool under load looks like a lot of clients, a small number of active server connections, and cl_waiting that blips and drains. A maxwait that keeps climbing means the database-side budget really is too small for the work, or, more often, that some transaction is holding its server connection far too long.

On the Postgres side, the pg_stat_activity query from earlier is still your ground truth. The number you care about isn't count(*). It's count(*) WHERE state = 'active', compared against your core count.

Where this leaves you

If I had to compress all of this into one opinion, it's this: raising max_connections is almost never the fix. It's the database equivalent of widening the highway entrance while leaving the bridge the same width. Postgres 14 made idle connections cheap, so a bigger number won't crash you the way it used to, but it also won't give you more throughput, because throughput is bounded by cores and I/O, not slots.

The playbook, in order of how cheap it is:

  1. Count what you've actually got: sum pool_max * max_replicas * surge across every service and compare it to the real budget.
  2. Shorten W. Get network calls out of transactions, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, and fix nested checkouts. This often shrinks the needed pool by more than any tuning.
  3. Set explicit client pool limits and a connection-acquire timeout, and graph the waiting count.
  4. Give each service its own role with a CONNECTION LIMIT and per-role timeouts.
  5. When the sum still doesn't fit, put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front, with max_db_connections as the single shared ceiling, and route session-dependent workloads around it.

Queues are fine. You're always going to have one somewhere. The whole game is choosing where it lives, and the right answer is in your app or your pooler, where waiting is cheap, not inside Postgres, where every extra waiter makes everyone else slower.

Originally published at andriiboyko.com.

title: MedBOE: Optimization-Based Estimation of Complete Patient Body Models from Whole-Body Medical Imaging
description:
arXiv:2610.28985v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.

title: Self-hosted Plausible analytics, in one command
description:
For a while, railyard.run ran with zero analytics. Not out of principle — we just hadn’t gotten to it, which meant every “is anyone actually reading this” question was a guess. Fixing it became the first real test of whether “self-hosted, one click” actually holds up for something we’d use ourselves, not just something we built for other people’s apps.

What we launched#
Plausible Community Edition, as a Railyard stack template: three services — Plausible itself, Postgres for its own app data, and ClickHouse for the actual analytics events — provisioned together on one of our own servers.

railyard launch plausible --server Copy
That’s the whole provisioning step. No separate ClickHouse setup, no wiring connection strings by hand — the template declares all three services and how they talk to each other, and Railyard deploys the set as one unit.

What came after the launch command#
The rest was the normal first-run of any self-hosted app, not anything Railyard-specific:

Open the app’s URL, sign up as the instance owner — Plausible’s own first-run flow, nothing to pre-seed.

  • Add a website, enter the domain being tracked. Copy the tracking snippet it generates and drop it in the site’s . No custom domain was even necessary — the app’s default *.apps.railyard.run URL was enough to run the dashboard and serve the tracking script. We only use that path because it’s genuinely simpler, not because anything was missing.

Where it actually broke, briefly#
It didn’t — which is itself worth saying plainly, since the point of posting this at all is to be honest about what self-hosting something actually costs in practice. The template launched clean, the three services found each other over Railyard’s private networking without any manual env var wiring, and the tracking script started showing pageviews in Plausible’s Realtime view within seconds of being added to the site.

The one thing worth knowing going in: a fresh launch creates a new app every time you run it, so launching twice means two full stacks running side by side, not an update to the first one. Easy mistake, easy fix — apps:rm --confirm in the CLI removes the extra one cleanly.

Why self-hosted instead of Plausible Cloud#
Plausible Cloud is a fine product and the simpler choice for most teams. We picked self-hosted specifically because it’s the same category of claim we make about everything else on Railyard: you should be able to run the tools you depend on, on infrastructure you control, without a second vendor relationship for every piece of your stack. Cookie-free, no consent banner, and the data never leaves a server we provisioned ourselves.

If you’re weighing the same tradeoff for your own site, the Plausible template is one click away, and Logs, metrics and alerts covers the rest of what Railyard surfaces about traffic without a separate analytics stack at all.

for more : https://railyard.run/blog/self-hosted-analytics/

title: Building a Fast Estimate Calculator for Local Service Websites
description:
Hey, I am Kaleb. I build sites and run automations out of my setup here in Pompano Beach, Florida. When local trade businesses—like plumbers, electricians, or HVAC contractors—reach out or when I am refining my own lead-generation funnels at Dream Futures Tech, the conversation almost always lands on the same problem: potential customers hate waiting for a price.

Most contractor websites feature a generic contact form that goes straight into a crowded inbox. By the time the business owner calls back hours later while up to their elbows in a crawlspace, the homeowner has already moved on to the next competitor on Google Maps. To fix this drop-off, I started adding interactive, instant-estimate calculators directly onto service pages. Here is how I build a lightweight, dependency-free estimate calculator that turns passive browsers into qualified leads without slowing down the site.

Why Local Trade Sites Need Instant Estimates

Speed matters immensely for local service sites. Most traffic comes from mobile phones while a homeowner is standing in front of a leaking pipe or a broken air conditioner. They do not want to write a paragraph explaining their problem. They want a ballpark number immediately.

Building a custom calculator right in the browser gives users instant feedback. It keeps them engaged on the page longer and drastically increases the likelihood that they will submit their phone number for a formal dispatch. Because I prefer keeping local sites fast and maintainable, I build these using vanilla HTML, CSS, and a small block of JavaScript. No heavy frontend frameworks required.

Structuring the HTML Form for Speed

I start with a clean, semantic HTML form. Keeping the markup straightforward ensures it renders instantly on older smartphones connected to patchy cellular data. Here is a basic template I use for an HVAC or plumbing diagnostic estimator:

<form id="estimate-form">
  <h2>Get an Instant Estimate</h2>
  <label for="service-type">Select Service:</label>
  <select id="service-type" name="serviceType">
    <option value="standard">Standard Service Call</option>
    <option value="emergency">Emergency After-Hours</option>
    <option value="install">New Equipment Quote</option>
  </select>

  <label for="units">Number of Units / Fixtures:</label>
<input type="number" id="units" name="units" value="1" min="1" max="5">

  <div class="estimate-output">
    Estimated Range: <span id="price-display">$75 - $125</span>
  </div>

  <button type="submit">Book This Rate</button>
</form>

Keeping the inputs limited to a dropdown and a number selector reduces friction. The less typing a user has to do on a mobile keyboard, the higher your conversion rate will be.

Writing the Vanilla JavaScript Calculation Logic

Next, I attach a lightweight event listener to the form inputs. As the user changes options, the estimate updates in real-time. This creates an interactive experience that encourages them to play with the numbers.

const form = document.getElementById('estimate-form');
const serviceType = document.getElementById('service-type');
const unitsInput = document.getElementById('units');
const priceDisplay = document.getElementById('price-display');

const rates = {
  standard: { base: 75, multiplier: 25 },
  emergency: { base: 150, multiplier: 50 },
  install: { base: 500, multiplier: 200 }
};

function calculateEstimate() {
  const selected = serviceType.value;
  const count = parseInt(unitsInput.value) || 1;
  const rate = rates[selected] || rates.standard;

  const lowEnd = rate.base + (rate.multiplier * (count - 1));
  const highEnd = lowEnd + 50;

  priceDisplay.textContent = `$${lowEnd} - $${highEnd}`;
}

serviceType.addEventListener('change', calculateEstimate);
unitsInput.addEventListener('input', calculateEstimate);

This script runs entirely in the browser with zero external dependencies. It executes in microseconds and does not require loading bloated third-party plugin scripts that drag down page speed scores.

Hooking it Up to a Lightweight Backend Endpoint

Once the user likes the estimated range, they click the submit button to lock it in and send their contact details. Instead of relying on unreliable PHP mailer scripts, I route the form data through a minimal Node.js or serverless endpoint that forwards the lead details directly to an SMS gateway or a CRM webhook.

form.addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const formData = {
    service: serviceType.value,
    units: unitsInput.value,
    estimate: priceDisplay.textContent
  };

  try {
    const response = await fetch('/api/lead', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(formData)
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      alert('Estimate saved! We are dispatching a technician.');
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Submission failed:', error);
  }
});

Handling Mobile Viewports on Job Sites

One detail I always emphasize when styling these elements is touch target sizing. Contractors and homeowners visiting these pages on mobile need buttons that are easy to tap with a thumb. I ensure all inputs and buttons have a minimum height of 44 pixels and ample padding.

By replacing static contact forms with dynamic, transparent estimate tools, local service sites turn anonymous traffic into high-intent phone calls and booked jobs.

I build sites and automations for small businesses at dreamfuturestech.com.

title: Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation for Few-shot Image Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.28856v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-shot image classification (FSIC) frequently suffers from visual ambiguity, where background clutter and RGB appearance similarities hinder discriminative feature matching in data-scarce settings. To mitigate this, we propose DAFIC, a geometry-guided framework that incorporates monocular depth into representation learning, episodic adaptation, and dense support-query matching. DAFIC first learns geometry-aware token representations through RGB-D self-supervised pre-training. Subsequently, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module uses depth-derived geometry to refine patch representations with geometry-enriched class context while suppressing background interference. Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching (SBiM) then performs bidirectional dense matching on the refined features, reducing sensitivity to spurious correspondences and background clutter. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that DAFIC achieves strong performance against existing methods, with ablation and robustness analyses supporting the effectiveness of coupling geometry-conditioned episodic adaptation with bidirectional matching for few-shot visual recognition.

title: SlothPulse: I wrote the code. Gemma can draft the standup.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

💡 What I Built

After a day of writing code, “what did you do today?” shouldn’t require another Git archaeology session.

I built SlothPulse to turn recent commits and a terminal error into a standup draft using Gemma running locally through Ollama. One command produces three Markdown sections: completed work, blockers, and suggested next steps.

Every item has a receipt pointing back to its source, so you can check anything suspicious before sharing the draft. The note stays in a local file.

🎥 Demo

Open the recorded demo → — click a source badge to inspect its commit or error, or watch the 48-second video.


python3 slothpulse.py --since today --error-file error.txt

An excerpt from the actual saved draft:

### 🛠️ What I Did Today
- Fixed issue where export job IDs were lost during retries. [^C1]

### 🐛 Blockers & Bugs
- User-reported: KeyError: 'result' while downloading job results. [^E1]

### 🚀 Next Steps
- Suggested: Investigate the origin of the KeyError and potential data access issues in worker.py. [^E1]

The full captured run summarizes five commits and one traceback in 10.33 seconds inside the CLI. The fixture uses fictional authors and a deliberately fake key; the tiny worker really raises the captured error. The video replays timestamped output, including the measured wait.

💻 Code

TengByte / slothpulse

A 100% local, privacy-first CLI that turns Git commits and error traces into developer digests with Ollama and Gemma.

Setup and source · Exact input and output · Build log

🛠️ How I Built It

The first version produced a tidy recap—and attributed a pasted error to SlothPulse itself, although its source was unspecified. That unsupported connection mattered more than the formatting.

I moved the model’s response to JSON with required source keys. Every commit gets a C key. Each reported error gets an E object containing both its summary and investigation step. Python assigns their references and renders the Markdown.

That pairing came from another real failure: an error investigation cited an unrelated commit. Both IDs existed, so checking whether a source was known had missed the problem. Keeping the error and its follow-up together removes that particular mismatch.

The CLI validates coverage and reference types, retries an invalid plan once, and saves no digest if the second attempt fails. A valid reference still cannot prove that a sentence is correct; human review stays in the workflow.

The application uses Python’s standard library: subprocess for Git, urllib.request for Ollama, and json for the response contract. No external Python packages. The code is MIT licensed.

🔒 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Commit subjects and traces can contain private project details. Downloaded Gemma weights let the recap run on the same machine as that context, without a hosted inference account or API key. The model download needs internet access; generation stays local.

SlothPulse checks model metadata before sending context, rejects cloud-backed models, and bypasses HTTP proxies. The tested Ollama server runs with OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1. These checks trust the local server and its metadata.

Before generating, --preview shows the sanitized input without a model call or file write. Common credential patterns are masked, but masking is best effort: preview it, and treat saved notes as potentially confidential.

🦥 The Lazy Payoff

The chore becomes reviewing a draft instead of assembling one from scattered context. To check this beyond the demo fixture, I ran SlothPulse on this project’s six real commits, using local Gemma on an Apple M5 / 16 GB:

Invocation Whole process time
Model initially unloaded 13.619 s
Immediate repeat 8.720 s

Review caught one important correction among the six completed-work items: Gemma turned “submission handoff” into “submitted,” while this entry was still a draft. The receipt made that mismatch easy to locate. The raw output and the corrected version are both preserved in the repository trial.

This was an AI-assisted source check, not a human standup study. Manual preparation time and human editing effort remain unmeasured. The earlier nine-run synthetic benchmark and 23 unit tests check workflow behavior and failure boundaries; factual accuracy still needs review.

🏆 Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma — local Gemma drafts the summaries and investigation steps.

Codex assisted with implementation, testing, demo preparation, and this article. More engineering notes: tengli.dev.

title: Node.js Webhook Batches: Delivery Guarantees for Nightly Queue Reconciliation
description:
Short answer: for an edtech digest, make delivery state the source of truth, use cron as a public HTTP wake-up, and let idempotent workers publish pending webhooks from a queue. That gives you a recoverable handoff when a schedule is missed. The choice is about guarantees, not about which scheduler has the fanciest screen.

Boundary Invariant to defend Best fit What you own
Reconcile rows, then enqueue a batch An unsent delivery remains discoverable until a worker records success Weekly digests with changing recipient sets State transitions and idempotency
Managed task per delivery The task service owns each due time and retry decision Independent schedules and per-target throttles Provider task state and its limits

I would start with the first boundary for a one-person SaaS. A Friday cron tick can be late or absent, but Saturday's scan still finds rows marked pending. That is a stronger delivery guarantee than hoping a timer remembers what it missed.

For the scan-to-queue handoff, Infrai is worth putting on the shortlist early: its plain REST API lets a Node.js route publish without an SDK. Infrai uses one key and one bill for the backend calls around the digest, with 295 routes across 20 modules behind the same interface. That combination keeps credential rotation and invoice checking in one place while the delivery ledger stays provider-neutral.

The guarantee lives in the delivery ledger

Create one durable record per customer webhook, keyed by a stable digest and customer ID. Store pending, enqueued, delivered, and failed as business states, not as guesses derived from queue metrics. The scheduled endpoint selects a bounded page where scheduled_for <= now, claims it, and publishes messages. A worker sends the callback, writes the result, and only then acknowledges the queue message.

Picture the failure on a real Friday: the scheduler reaches the endpoint, the process publishes half a page, and the network drops before the response is written. On Saturday, the reconciliation query cannot trust the old HTTP response, so it looks at durable delivery state, republishes stable IDs with an idempotency key, and lets the worker decide whether the callback already succeeded. The queue may contain two copies; the customer still receives one digest because the worker's business write is the gate. That is more code than a timer, but it is code you can inspect when a school asks where its digest went.

This ordering matters. Standard queues are at-least-once, so a worker can see the same message twice. The send operation must be idempotent on the delivery ID; FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes, far shorter than a weekly recovery window. A retry after a timeout must not create a second digest at a school.

There is a second invariant: the business transaction that creates a digest and its delivery row must commit together. A transactional outbox is a useful pattern for that boundary. It keeps a healthy queue from masking an application write that never happened.

Tiny state machines beat clever cron expressions.

That is the contract.

How should a Node.js cron trigger queue publish for delayed webhook batches?

Cron does not host application code. It calls a public http_url, so deploy a small Node.js route that performs the scan and exits. A single run is capped at 900 seconds; it should never loop over customer HTTP calls. Keep each message below 256 KB, keep delays at or below seven days, and remember that acknowledged messages are deleted rather than retained for Kafka-style replay.

The route below shows the handoff. The array stands in for a database query so the example is runnable; production code should claim rows transactionally and leave them recoverable until the worker records delivery.

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

type Delivery = { id: string; customerId: string; digestWeek: string };
const pending: Delivery[] = [
  { id: "digest-1042", customerId: "school-18", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
  { id: "digest-1043", customerId: "school-27", digestWeek: "2026-W34" },
];

const pause = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function publishBatch(tasks: Delivery[]): Promise<unknown> {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
  const idempotencyKey = `digest-${tasks[0].digestWeek}`;
  const messages = tasks.map((task) => ({ id: task.id, body: JSON.stringify(task) }));

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ queue: "weekly-digest-webhooks", messages }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    const detail = await response.text();
    if (response.status !== 429) throw new Error(`publish failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    await pause(Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt);
  }
  throw new Error("publish remained rate-limited after five attempts");
}

createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/jobs/reconcile-digests") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }
  try {
    if (pending.length) await publishBatch(pending);
    response.writeHead(202, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ enqueued: pending.length }));
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error";
    response.writeHead(502, { "Content-Type": "application/json" });
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ error: message }));
  }
}).listen(port);

The scheduler should call the public HTTPS deployment of POST /jobs/reconcile-digests. The handler batches the handoff and returns; workers own slow destinations. A 429 honors Retry-After, while other status codes expose their response body. If cron was paused, the next scan reconciles every still-pending row instead of replaying a calendar event that never existed.

Two architectures, one uncomfortable question

The reconciliation queue is a ledger-driven architecture. Its recovery rule is simple: any row not durably marked delivered is eligible for a future scan. This is a good match for a weekly digest where recipients change and missed work must be found.

It also makes the support story legible.

The managed-task architecture creates one scheduled task per webhook. Google Cloud Tasks is a credible choice when each destination needs its own retry and schedule controls. BullMQ is practical when Redis is already part of the Node.js stack and keeping queue code in-process is more valuable than a hosted boundary. Neither removes the need to make the callback idempotent; they move more timing state out of your database.

Temporal or Airflow belong when the digest is one step in a workflow with branches, joins, or long-lived orchestration. This scheduling capability has no DAG engine, no fan-out/join primitive, and no native debounce or throttle. Simulating those semantics with more queues would increase the very operating surface a solo founder is trying to shrink.

The uncomfortable question is: who can prove a missed run was recovered? With the ledger shape, the answer is a query over pending rows. With per-task scheduling, the answer depends on the provider's task inventory and retention. Pick the answer you can inspect during a support ticket.

Where a plain REST boundary earns its keep

Infrai is a deliberate option for the scan-to-queue leg when a Node.js service should make a plain HTTP request without installing an SDK. One Authorization: Bearer key reaches the queue call, and the same credential can cover other backend capabilities instead of creating another account and invoice for each integration. That reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation work, which is a real operating cost for a one-person team.

The platform also exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind that consistent interface, with public discovery and runnable examples in ten languages. For this workflow, that means the request schema for publish_batch can be inspected before shipping the handler, while the rest of the application can keep its own provider-neutral delivery ledger. I recommend trying it for the bounded enqueue boundary, not for the worker's business logic.

The catch is capability fit. Push targets must be public HTTPS endpoints; delays cannot exceed seven days; standard queues require consumer idempotency; and there is no multi-consumer topic fan-out. If a school district requires a private callback, a replayable event log, or a delay beyond a week, use a specialist service or your existing broker instead. The right recommendation has a stop sign.

A weekly shipping test

Run one failure drill before calling this reliable: pause the cron schedule, leave several deliveries pending, resume it the next day, and verify that one scan enqueues each stable ID exactly once at the business boundary. Then force a worker retry and confirm the second attempt records the same delivery rather than sending a duplicate.

I'm not sure there is a universal page size for every tenant mix. Lock duration, webhook rate limits, and the database decide that number. Start small, measure queue age, and change the bound without changing the invariant.

Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated handoff only after the ledger tells you what “done” means.

If this boundary matches your system, the cron-to-queue guide is a useful implementation reference.

References

  • Google Cloud Tasks overview
  • Transactional Outbox pattern
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Temporal documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: Collections and the Catalog: How a Database Remembers What Exists
description:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 3

Once I had page zero written to disk with those magic bytes NOSQLITE_DB___P8, I had a brief moment of satisfaction. I opened a hex editor, saw my custom signature staring back at me, and felt like I was actually getting somewhere.

Then reality set in.

I had an empty file with a header and absolutely no way to store anything useful yet. If you open a database, what is the very first thing you do? You create a collection. In SQL, you write CREATE TABLE. In MongoDB, you just start writing to a collection or create one explicitly. But what actually is a collection when you are sitting in front of a raw binary file?

It is not a folder on your hard drive. It is not some magical in-memory table. At the byte level, a collection is just a string name tied to a starting page number somewhere inside that single file.

My first lazy thought when planning this was tempting: why not just keep a HashMap<String, Vec<Document>> in memory and dump it to disk as a JSON blob when the program exits?

That would have taken an hour to write. But that is what you do if you are building a toy in Python or Node, and it completely misses the point of this experiment. If the power cuts out, your in-memory map is gone. If you copy the database file to another computer, that catalog has to travel with it inside the exact same file. The file has to be completely self-contained. It has to know its own collections, where they live, and how many documents they hold.

That meant building a catalog page.

The Table of Contents for Your Database

Think about a book. Before you read chapter three, you flip to the table of contents. The table of contents does not contain the story. It just tells you: Chapter 3 starts on page 45.

The catalog in nosqlite is literally just that table of contents.

For every collection you create, the engine needs to remember exactly three things:
What is the collection's name?
What page number does its first document live on?
How many documents are currently inside it?

That is all. If you know those three things, you can find the data, display counts in the shell, and know where to start scanning.

Where does this table of contents live? It gets its own dedicated page in the file. Specifically, it lives on page 1, sitting right after the file header. If you remember from the previous article, the file header on page 0 stores a field called catalog_page that holds the value 1. When the database boots up, it reads page 0, checks catalog_page, and immediately loads page 1 into memory.

The Anatomy of the Catalog Page

Let us look at how page 1 is laid out in memory and on disk.

// Catalog page layout:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | Page Header                   |   16 bytes (generic header on every page)
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_count (u32)        |    4 bytes (how many collections exist)
// +-------------------------------+
// | entries...                    |   packed one after another
// +-------------------------------+
//
// Each entry looks like this:
//
// +-------------------------------+
// | collection_name (\0)          |   variable length, null-terminated
// +-------------------------------+
// | first_document_page (u64)     |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+
// | document_count (u64)          |    8 bytes
// +-------------------------------+

The first 16 bytes belong to the generic page header that every single page in nosqlite has. That header records the page number, the page type (in this case, PageType::CollectionCatalog), and a couple of reserved bytes.

Right after those 16 bytes, we store 4 bytes for collection_count. This is an unsigned 32-bit integer that tracks how many collections currently exist in the database.

Why do we need this count? Because without it, a loop reading through the file would have no idea when to stop. It would keep reading random bytes until it crashed or hit corrupted memory. With collection_count, the reader knows upfront: there are 3 collections here, so read exactly 3 entries and then stop.

The catalog header size is therefore 20 bytes:

pub const CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE: usize = PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4; // 16 + 4 = 20

Since a page is 4096 bytes total, that leaves 4076 bytes for collection entries. In an embedded database where you usually have five, ten, or maybe thirty collections, 4076 bytes is plenty of room.

Null Terminators and C Strings

Here is the struct that represents a collection entry in Rust:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct CatalogEntry {
    pub name: String,
    pub first_document_page: u64,
    pub document_count: u64,
}

In Rust, this looks clean and friendly. But when this struct gets serialized into raw bytes on disk, we have to make an important choice: how do we store the string name?

In modern high-level languages, a string always carries its length with it. But at the raw binary level, there are two classic approaches. You can either use a Pascal string, where you write a length byte first and then the characters, or you can use a null-terminated C string, where you write the characters and end with a literal zero byte (\0).

I chose the null-terminated C string approach.

When you create a collection named "users", the engine writes the ASCII bytes for u, s, e, r, s, followed by 0x00. In hex, that is 75 73 65 72 73 00. That zero byte acts as a red light for the reader. The reader walks forward byte by byte, and the instant it sees a zero, it knows the name is finished.

Right after that zero byte, we write 8 bytes for first_document_page and 8 bytes for document_count, both encoded as little-endian unsigned 64-bit integers.

This brings up a fascinating detail about variable-length binary layouts. Because collection names can have different lengths, the entries do not have a fixed size. A collection named "users" takes 6 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the two u64 numbers, totaling 22 bytes. A collection named "audit_logs_v2" takes 14 bytes for the name plus 16 bytes for the numbers, totaling 30 bytes.

Because of this, you cannot simply calculate an offset with math like index * entry_size. You cannot jump directly to the fifth collection. You have to start at byte 20 and walk forward with a cursor, reading each entry to know where the next one begins.

Why the Catalog Struct Is Completely Empty

When you look at the source code in crates/nosqlite-core/src/catalog/catalog.rs, you find something that might look bizarre at first:

pub struct Catalog;

The struct has no fields. It holds no data in memory. It is a zero-sized type.

Every single method on Catalog takes a reference to a Page or Pager and acts directly on the byte buffer:

impl Catalog {
    pub fn initialize(page: &mut Page) {
        page.set_page_type(PageType::CollectionCatalog);

        // collection_count = 0
        page.data[PAGE_HEADER_SIZE..PAGE_HEADER_SIZE + 4]
            .copy_from_slice(&0u32.to_le_bytes());
    }
}

Let us look closely at what 0u32.to_le_bytes() is doing here, because this is fundamental to how systems programming works.

The number 0 as an unsigned 32-bit integer occupies 4 bytes. The method to_le_bytes() converts that number into a 4-byte array in little-endian order, where the least significant byte comes first. For zero, that array is just [0, 0, 0, 0]. If the count were 1, it would be [1, 0, 0, 0].

The call to copy_from_slice takes those 4 bytes and copies them directly into page.data starting at offset 16. That is how the collection count is set to zero when the database is first formatted.

Why did I make Catalog stateless instead of storing a Vec<CatalogEntry> inside it?

Because holding an in-memory copy of the catalog creates two sources of truth. What happens if your in-memory list says there are three collections, but a disk write failed and the file only has two? Now your program is in an inconsistent state, and debugging that will make you question your career choices.

By making Catalog stateless, the page itself is always the single source of truth. Every time we need to create, delete, or list collections, we read the page, do the work, and flush the page. There is zero risk of in-memory cache drift.

Creating a Collection: The Journey of a Write

When you type create users in the shell, here is the exact journey that command takes through the engine.

First, the engine calls the pager to load the catalog page into memory. The pager gives back a 4096-byte mutable slice of memory representing page 1.

The engine reads the first 4 bytes after the page header to find out how many collections already exist. Let us say collection_count is 2.

Next, it has to make sure we are not creating a duplicate. It sets a cursor variable to offset 20 (the start of the entries). It loops twice, reading each existing collection name using a helper function called read_cstring. If any name matches "users", it stops immediately and returns an error. We do not allow duplicate collections.

If no duplicate is found, the cursor is now pointing to the exact byte where the previous entry ended. That is our insertion point.

The engine checks whether there is enough space left on page 1 for the new entry. The new entry needs 6 bytes for "users\0", 8 bytes for the page pointer, and 8 bytes for the document count, which is 22 bytes. If the page has enough room, it writes the string bytes, writes 8 bytes of zero for first_document_page (since a new collection has no documents yet), and writes 8 bytes of zero for document_count.

Then it goes back to offset 16, increments the collection_count from 2 to 3, and writes the new count back to the page buffer.

Finally, the pager marks the page as dirty and flushes it to disk.

Notice how simple and mechanical that is. There is no query planner, no schema validator, no background worker. It is just reading a small buffer, checking for duplicates, appending 22 bytes, incrementing a counter, and writing the page back.

Listing Collections with a Cursor

Reading the list of collections reverses that entire process:

pub fn list(pager: &mut Pager) -> Result<Vec<CatalogEntry>> {
    let page = pager.read_page(pager.header.catalog_page)?;
    let count = Self::collection_count(&page)?;
    let mut cursor = CATALOG_HEADER_SIZE;
    let mut entries = Vec::new();

    for _ in 0..count {
        let name = read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor)?;
        let first_document_page = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);
        let document_count = read_u64(&page.data, &mut cursor);

        entries.push(CatalogEntry {
            name,
            first_document_page,
            document_count,
        });
    }

    Ok(entries)
}

The cursor pattern is one of the most useful patterns in binary parsing. A cursor is simply a usize variable that keeps track of where we are currently reading in the byte slice.

When read_cstring(&page.data, &mut cursor) runs, it starts at cursor, reads characters until it hits 0x00, constructs a Rust String, and advances cursor past the zero byte.

Then read_u64 reads the next 8 bytes as a little-endian number and advances cursor by 8. Then it does it again for document_count.

After looping count times, the function returns a clean Vec<CatalogEntry> ready for the shell to print.

Now, someone who took a computer science algorithms class might look at this and say: wait, that is an O(n) linear scan. Why didn't you build a B-tree or a hash map for the catalog?

Because context matters. The entire catalog page is 4096 bytes. That is 4 kilobytes. A modern CPU can scan 4KB of contiguous memory in its L1 cache in a fraction of a microsecond. If you have 20 collections, an O(n) linear scan takes virtually zero time. Building a complex B-tree just to store 20 collection names would be textbook over-engineering. Never pay for complexity you do not actually need.

Deleting a Collection: The Shift-Left Trick

Deleting a collection is where the byte manipulation gets interesting.

When someone deletes a collection, you cannot simply write zeros over its entry and leave a hole in the middle of the page. If the reader encounters a gap of zeros, it will either think the collection name is an empty string or get confused about where the next entry begins. The entries must always remain packed tightly together.

To solve this, I used a shift-left strategy.

Imagine a row of physical books sitting on a shelf. If you remove the book in the middle, you get an empty gap. What do you do? You slide all the books to the right of that gap one position to the left. The gap disappears, and all the books are neatly packed again.

In Rust, the standard library provides a method called copy_within on slices that does exactly this:

page.data.copy_within(entry_end..used_end, entry_start);

copy_within takes a source range of bytes and copies them to a new destination offset inside the exact same slice. It safely handles overlapping memory regions, which is crucial because when you slide bytes to the left, the source and destination overlap.

After sliding the bytes left, we decrement collection_count by 1.

What happens to the leftover bytes at the far right of the entries region? Nothing! We do not even need to zero them out. Because collection_count is decremented, the reader will stop reading earlier and will never look at those leftover bytes. They will simply be overwritten the next time a new collection is created.

When a collection is deleted, we also free any document pages that belonged to it so they can be reused later. We will see how page reuse works when we talk about the free-page list.

Preventing Catastrophe with a Lock File

Above the Catalog and the Pager sits the Database struct. This is the main entry point that the shell and external applications interact with:

pub struct Database {
    pager: Pager,
    lock_path: PathBuf,
    _lock_file: File,
}

Notice that field named _lock_file with the leading underscore.

In Rust, if you declare a variable or a field and never call any methods on it, the compiler will yell at you about an unused variable. The underscore tells the compiler: I know this looks unused, but please leave it alone.

And leaving it alone is the whole point!

When Database::open is called, it creates a small file next to the database with a .lock extension. It opens that file and stores the open file handle inside _lock_file.

As long as the Database instance exists in your program, that file handle remains open. When your program finishes or the Database goes out of scope, Rust drops the struct. Rust's ownership system automatically closes the file handle, and the operating system releases the lock.

This is the classic RAII pattern, which stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. You acquire the resource on creation, and cleanup happens automatically on destruction. You do not have to remember to call a close() method.

But what happens if the power cord is pulled out of the wall while the database is running?

If the system crashes violently, the .lock file remains sitting on the hard drive even though the process is dead. If another program tries to open the database later, it sees the .lock file and thinks the database is still in use.

To solve this, nosqlite checks for stale locks on startup:

pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self> {
    let lock_path = path.with_extension("lock");

    if lock_path.exists() {
        let stale = match read_lock_file(&lock_path) {
            Ok(lock) => !process_exists(lock.pid),
            Err(_) => true,
        };

        if stale {
            eprintln!("Removing stale lock file");
            let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&lock_path);
        } else {
            return Err(Error::DatabaseLocked);
        }
    }
    // ... proceed with opening
}

When nosqlite creates a lock file, it writes the current process ID into it. On startup, if a lock file exists, the engine reads that PID and asks the operating system: is a process with this ID currently running?

If the answer is no, the previous process died without cleaning up. The lock is stale. nosqlite deletes the file and continues opening normally. If the process is still running, the database is genuinely in use by another instance, and the engine refuses to open to prevent data corruption.

It is a simple, pragmatic mechanism that prevents two processes from destroying the same database file while handling unexpected crashes gracefully.

Where We Stand

At this point in the project, nosqlite had a solid foundation.

It could format a file, stamp its magic bytes, maintain a catalog of collections, slide bytes around safely during deletions, and protect the file from concurrent access with process locking.

You could open the shell, run create users, run create orders, and run list. The database would print:

users: 0 documents
orders: 0 documents

Everything worked. But every single collection had first_document_page set to 0.

It was like having a filing cabinet with neatly labeled folders, but every single folder was completely empty. We had built the entire organizational structure of a database without storing a single byte of actual user data.

That changes in the next article.

In Part 4, we finally put real data into those folders. We take a JSON string typed into the terminal, break down why storing raw JSON is a terrible idea, convert it into binary BSON format, allocate document pages, link them together in a chain, and write our very first document to disk.

title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
description:
arXiv:2610.28441v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.

title: 🦥 Solace: Productivity That Adapts to Your Energy
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

As a college student juggling coursework, exams, lab submissions, personal projects, and daily habits, there are days when I wake up feeling completely overwhelmed. Facing a long list of 15 checkboxes on a low-energy day causes instant decision paralysis and guilt.

I built Solace Sanctuary—an adaptive, low-friction student sanctuary and life tracker designed specifically for low-battery days.
Instead of treating productivity like a rigid checklist, Solace works with your energy level:

  • 🔋 Vibe Check (Energy Scaling): Switch between High Energy, Normal, and Zombie Mode. Selecting Zombie Mode automatically downscales daily targets (e.g., changing 3 DSA problems to 1 quick snippet review, or 1 hour of workout to 10 minutes of stretching).
  • 🧘 One-Next-Step Focus Card: Shields you from feeling overwhelmed by showing ONLY ONE micro-task at a time. Pressing "I'm Too Tired / Break It Down" splits it into a tiny 2-minute step.
  • 📝 Smart Mind Dump & Auto-Tracker: Write or paste messy, unfiltered thoughts, daily notes, or voice transcripts. The system parses the input and auto-sorts it into a daily journal entry, checks off daily tasks (assignments, DSA, workout, anything!), and queues tomorrow's tasks.
  • 🎨 Custom Aesthetic Themes: Includes 3 switchable themes: Midnight Sanctuary (dark glassmorphism), Sage Matcha (earthy green), and Pastel Blossom (soft lavender/pink).

Anyone running on low battery gets to be a little lazier without the guilt—because doing 10% on a bad day is infinitely better than doing 0%.

sakshi-db / solace-sanctuary

The Low-Friction, Adaptive Student Sanctuary & Life Tracker
Built for Hacktoberfest 2026: Week 3 – Slow & Steady (International Sloth Day Theme)

🖤 The Problem: Student Overload & Decision Paralysis

As college students balancing coursework, exams, skill-building, personal habits, and daily life, there are days when we feel completely overwhelmed. Traditional productivity tools often make this worse—they treat every day like a 100% energy day and force you to manually track every single detail, turning task management into yet another chore.

When you're running on low energy, opening a complex planner creates instant burnout and guilt.

🌿 The Solution: What is Solace?

Solace is an anti-overwhelm, low-friction student workspace designed to work with your energy levels, not against them. Instead of pressuring you on low-battery days, Solace adapts to how you feel, automates manual logging, and keeps you moving forward without the friction.

✨ Key Features

  • 🔋…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Solace is built as a single-page React application powered by Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and modern glassmorphism styling. The core intelligence relies on lightweight open-weight text processing models (such as Gemma) to take unstructured "mind dumps" from tired students, parse out completed habits, extract journal notes, and structure tomorrow's action items without requiring manual input forms.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation and open-weight models make personalized, privacy-first tools accessible to everyone. As a student, having open models means I can run low-friction agents locally or on low-cost infrastructure without worrying about expensive API rate limits or handing private daily diary entries over to closed proprietary tech.

The Lazy Payoff

Solace completely removes the mental chore of "managing a productivity app". Instead of spending 15 minutes organizing lists, setting up priorities, and checking boxes, you dump your thoughts into one box or press one button. It saves at least 20–30 minutes of decision paralysis every morning.

  1. Best Use of Gemma (or open-weight models)
  2. General Challenge Category: Week 3 – Slow and Steady

Final Thoughts :)

Building Solace helped me reframe how I look at productivity during heavy college weeks. We don't have to be high-performance robots every single day. Taking things slow, keeping momentum steady, and letting smart tools handle the friction is how we build sustainable habits.
If you're a student running on low battery today, take a deep breath. You've got this! 🦥✨

title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
description:
arXiv:2610.28887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.
