title: LEAN: Loss-Engineered Modulation of the Model Weight-Sensitivity Distribution for Efficient, Error-Tolerant Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.28872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The weights of a trained network do not have uniform sensitivity to model accuracy: the 1% most sensitive weights carry about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. This distribution decides the bit-flip tolerance of a model, the fraction of weights a code must cover and the bits each weight needs; existing schemes work with the distribution training leaves. We show that we can systematically modulate or alter the weight sensitivity distribution of a trained model, thereby shifting weights from one sensitivity bin to another. The sensitivity of a stored weight is the product of its gradient and the step a flip takes in the storage format, and LEAN adds a composite regularizer on both factors, a range term that bounds the flip step and a tail term that lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, with one coefficient {\lambda} setting how far the distribution moves. Ten epochs with the term, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, shrink the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times on nine vision models (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) within 0.5 points of accuracy; real flips confirm that the reshaped weights do less damage, a plain gradient-norm penalty does not reproduce the effect, and a preliminary extension to three small language models shows the same tail shaping. With a BCH code over 1% of the weights the model then survives 300 progressive bit-search flips in every training seed and 500 in two of three, where three of four published defenses with the same code fail by 300 and WCAT falls to 75% at 500. The reshaped distribution also cuts the parity for a fixed guarantee 3.7 times and makes a sensitivity-ordered 8/6/4/3-bit format affordable, which stores ImageNet ResNet-50 at a 3.29-bit weight payload, 2.4 times smaller than INT8, above the accuracy of LSQ at 3 bits.

title: GBase Database Silent Installation: 6 Common Errors and How to Fix Them
description:
Silent installation helps automate GBase Database(GBase 8s) deployment, but a failed installation can interrupt an otherwise straightforward process. In most cases, the first places to check are the response file, installation permissions, component dependencies, and available disk space.

Here are six common issues to investigate when ids_install -i silent fails.

1. License Acceptance Is Missing

A silent installation needs the license acceptance parameter. Check that your response file contains the following setting:

LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE

Alternatively, pass the parameter directly to the installer:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the license acceptance parameter is missing or incorrectly configured, the installation may stop before completing.

2. The Response File Path Is Incorrect

The installer cannot read parameters from a response file that does not exist or is inaccessible.

Check the file first:

ls -l /opt/bundle.properties

Confirm that the path specified by -f matches the actual file location and that the user running the installation has read permission.

For example:

./ids_install -i silent -f /opt/bundle.properties -DLICENSE_ACCEPTED=TRUE

If the command references the wrong directory or filename, correct the path before investigating more complicated causes.

3. The Installation Directory Has Incorrect Permissions

Directory permissions can prevent the installer from creating or updating files.

Inspect the target directory:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

Check whether the installation process has the necessary permissions to write to the directory. If the directory already exists, also check its ownership and whether existing files could interfere with the installation.

Do not change ownership blindly. Choose permissions based on the installation procedure and the account intended to manage the database software.

4. Selected Components Have Missing Dependencies

A response file may specify multiple components through SELECTED_FEATURES. Some selected components may require additional dependencies or supporting packages.

If the installation fails during component setup:

  • Review the selected features in the response file.
  • Check the installation logs for dependency or package errors.
  • Install any required dependencies.
  • Remove unnecessary components from the selection if they are not needed for the current deployment.

Avoid removing components simply to make the installation pass. First identify the component responsible for the failure, then adjust the configuration accordingly.

5. There Is Not Enough Disk Space

A silent installation can fail if the target filesystem does not have enough free space for the installation files and temporary files.

Check available capacity:

df -h /opt

Also check the filesystem used for temporary files if the installer extracts packages under /tmp or another temporary directory.

If space is insufficient, clean up unnecessary files or select an appropriate filesystem with enough capacity. Remember that the installation package itself is not the only space requirement: extraction and installation can require additional temporary storage.

6. The Instance Initialization Runs as Root

Installing the GBase Database program and initializing a database instance are separate operations with different execution requirements.

Running ids_install as root is permitted. However, the instance initialization script must be run as the gbasedbt user.

If initialization is performed as root, files or directories may receive incorrect ownership, causing problems when the database instance is started or managed by gbasedbt.

Before starting the instance, verify that the relevant installation and instance files have the expected ownership. Follow the product's installation procedure to correct any ownership problems rather than repeatedly rerunning initialization commands.

A Practical Troubleshooting Order

When troubleshooting a failed GBase Database silent installation, check the following in order:

  1. Response file: Confirm that the file exists, is readable, and contains valid parameters.
  2. License acceptance: Verify LICENSE_ACCEPTED = TRUE or pass the command-line parameter.
  3. Permissions: Check the installation directory and the account running each step.
  4. Components: Review SELECTED_FEATURES and any dependency errors.
  5. Disk space: Check both the installation filesystem and temporary storage.
  6. Instance initialization: Make sure initialization is performed as gbasedbt, not root.

This order helps separate configuration problems from operating-system and instance-management issues.

Final Thoughts

Automating GBase Database deployment is not just about running ids_install -i silent. A reliable installation also depends on a valid response file, correct permissions, sufficient disk space, and proper separation between software installation and instance initialization.

When a silent installation fails, start with the response file and the installation logs before changing multiple settings at once. Identifying the first failing step is usually more effective than repeatedly rerunning the installer without knowing what went wrong.

title: Extreme Low-State Quantized Transformer for Electricity-Load Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.28784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aggressive low-state weight quantization can substantially reduce neural-network representational flexibility, making predictive performance difficult to preserve when only a few discrete weight states are available. We investigate this regime for Transformer-based electricity-load forecasting using 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization across feed-forward-only and attention-plus-feed-forward quantization. Two tasks predict either the next hour or the next 24 hours from the preceding 48 hours across two co-primary electricity-consumption datasets. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) increased mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to full precision by 6.25 and 7.04 percentage points in Datasets A and B, whereas quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAT-FT) recovered approximately 90.2% and 94.5% of these penalties. Quantization-aware training from random initialization (Scratch-QAT) also produced competitive low-state solutions, with particularly favorable behavior at three states. We further introduce accumulated-update thresholding, which accumulates optimizer-proposed weight changes before commitment. Relative to paired Scratch-QAT controls, this reduced committed shadow-weight updates by approximately 99.7% and discrete state transitions by approximately 77--80%, while mean NRMSE changed by only +0.042 and +0.197 percentage points. These results show that useful Transformer forecasting can be retained under highly discrete weight representations while strongly suppressing target-state activity, supporting a prospective route toward compact, low-activity edge forecasting using multilevel synaptic devices.

title: PGO for Faster Apps and Generational/Adaptive GC
description:
Your native compiler can optimize an app more effectively when it knows which code actually runs. Profile-guided optimization, or PGO, gives it that information. The build service runs an instrumented version of your application, records its execution and uses the profile to compile the binary your users receive.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

PGO is now a Pro and Enterprise cloud-build feature for iOS, native macOS and native Linux. You enable it with a build hint; the service handles the extra compilation and training. It is a way to improve native performance without rewriting application logic or managing a profiling pipeline yourself.

This release also adds adaptive generational garbage collection to ParparVM. We will start with PGO and how to use it, then look at the GC changes and the memory cost behind their CPU improvements. This continues our weekly release series and last week's object-layout work.

Let your app guide the compiler

An ordinary optimizing compiler has to estimate which branches are common and which functions are worth inlining. PGO replaces some of those estimates with counts from an actual run. Frequently executed code can be placed together and optimized for speed, while code outside those paths can stay compact.

The profile applies to translated Java, Codename One's runtime and your native sources. The instrumented binary stays on the build server. Your users receive the second build, without the training counters.

Turn on PGO for your target

Add the relevant hint to codenameone_settings.properties. This example enables it for iOS and sets a 90-second training period:

codename1.arg.ios.pgo=true
codename1.arg.pgo.trainingSeconds=90

Each target has its own switch:

Build hint Target Training environment
codename1.arg.ios.pgo=true iOS device app Temporary iOS simulator on the build server
codename1.arg.macos.pgo=true Native macOS app Build server
codename1.arg.linux.pgo=true Native Linux app Build server with a virtual display

The training period defaults to 60 seconds. Values below 10 or above 300 are brought into that range. Increasing it gives the application longer to exercise its startup work; it does not create user interactions.

If you already subscribe to Pro or Enterprise, enable the hint and submit a supported cloud build. PGO is included in those plans. You can compare plans here. These hints belong to the cloud build service; local builds do not consume them.

Give the training run useful work

The app starts from a clean state and runs unattended. Resource loading, initial layout and painting can contribute to the profile, as can animations, timers and network work that start automatically. Repeated work is particularly useful because the compiler can identify the paths that dominate execution.

Nobody signs in or taps a button during training. If the app stops at a login screen, the profile describes that screen. Code behind it remains correct, but the compiler has no evidence that it is an important execution path. Before enabling PGO, run the app from a clean installation and check what it does without input.

PGO adds build time because it requires two compilations and a training run. Start with a normal Release build and record the time for a representative task. Repeat that task with the profile-guided build on the same device. Check memory and the result of the task as well as elapsed time. The gain depends on how much of your workload the training run reached; we are not assigning a universal speedup percentage to it.

A requested profile-guided build either produces that binary or fails with a reason. An empty profile, a crash during training or an incompatible build mode does not silently produce an ordinary build. The performance guide lists the settings, training rules and incompatible configurations, including debug and simulator-only modes. PR #5945 introduced the build support.

Adaptive GC reduces the work left to run

PGO improves the generated native code. The collector changes reduce how much work that code needs to do. In our allocation workload, the concurrent collector spent time tracing fresh objects and sweeping their slots even when almost none survived.

ParparVM now has an adaptive generational phase. Holding more memory can reduce collection frequency, but it can also make the next full trace or transition much worse. The standard Codename One benchmarks use no PGO, so the following GC results measure the runtime changes separately.

Collect survivors instead of revisiting every allocation

A generational collector concentrates frequent work on young objects, based on the observation that many die quickly. References from older objects to young ones must still be tracked, and surviving objects cannot simply disappear when a young page is reset.

Our hybrid chooses between the existing concurrent path and stop-the-world generational cycles. On eligible multicore processes, it enters after repeated low-survival cycles with allocation demand and a concurrent collector busy for at least half the interval between cycles. Low available memory is an exit condition, not the trigger to enter.

An all-dead young page can be reset in constant time. The allocator's bump path is inline again, and accounting moves from each object to each page where possible. Those changes remove work rather than merely asking another CPU to do it.

A process that has created virtual threads stays concurrent. A registered native thread that the collector cannot hold also prevents these stop-the-world cycles. Pausing only some allocating threads is not a valid stop-the-world algorithm. The runtime implementation enforces those boundaries.

More memory can buy fewer collections

The young-generation budget responds to collection duty. Two successive minors consuming more than 5% of their intervals can grow it; below 1%, it can shrink. Growth is bounded, including by a fraction of host memory. Requiring two busy minors avoids treating one collection delayed by the OS scheduler as proof that the application needs a larger heap.

A larger young generation lets more short-lived objects die before the next collection. That can save CPU. It also leaves more memory resident, and increases the amount of work a later phase may inherit. You have to measure both sides.

Conceptual diagram, not benchmark data. Increasing a budget can reduce frequent collection work while increasing retained memory and the cost of a later scan. The actual curves depend on survival and reference patterns.

One failed transition made this concrete. Deferring the exit decision until the next cycle handed as much as 128 MB of young objects to a concurrent collection. Its fresh-object protection retained them, while application threads kept allocating behind it. The engineering record reports a roughly 500 ms cycle and a page-heap count rising from 3,446 to 10,538 in the affected stress test. The exit decision now runs at the end of the stopped cycle, before application threads resume.

Another attempted concurrent major promoted about 6.4 million dead objects into the old generation. The next minor then spent 260 to 305 ms examining the remembered set. Those are failure observations from the GC engineering record, not advertised pause bounds for the corrected collector.

Read time and memory together

The committed calibration change for PR #5940 gives a useful view of the trade. These are historical gate baselines for objectAllocation, with JDK 25 equal to 1. Lower is better in both columns.

Runner Time ratio, before → after Peak memory ratio, before → after
macOS ARM64, three-CPU runner 3.696 → 1.106 0.481 → 0.937
Linux x64, AMD EPYC 7763 5.011 → 1.649 0.370 → 0.370
Linux ARM64, Neoverse N2 3.043 → 3.043 0.239 → 0.378
Windows x64, AMD family 25/model 1 4.932 → 1.559 0.400 → 0.386

The macOS row is the clearest cost: much less allocation time, almost twice the previous memory ratio. Linux ARM64 records more memory with its time baseline unchanged. A value unchanged in the overlay can be a carried-forward baseline; it is not a fresh measurement of zero change. The ratios still show ParparVM slower than JDK 25 on this allocation workload after the improvement.

These are calibration records, not a new controlled before/after experiment. Most selected rows record one calibration run; the Windows row records three. They have no confidence intervals, and later master baselines include further recalibrations. The data CSV and original overlay retain that context. Compare within a runner row; do not rank different machines from these ratios.

The allocation workload is deliberately narrow. It tells us about allocation and collection behavior for that survival pattern, not frame latency, network throughput or every application. A backend using virtual threads also follows the concurrent path, so an allocation microbenchmark's hybrid gain cannot be assigned to that backend.

Make a speed gain part of the next baseline

The performance gate runs paired ParparVM and JDK 25 workloads on Linux x64 and ARM64, Windows x64 and ARM64, and macOS ARM64. It alternates which runtime goes first, verifies output and records median ratios. CPU-specific baselines keep one runner model from silently standing in for another.

For workload timings, the gate uses the fastest measured repetition inside each process; JVM startup is not charged to the workload. Memory is a process peak: footprint on macOS, RSS on Linux and working set on Windows. Those are related measurements, not identical operating-system counters.

A change outside the permitted tolerance fails in either direction. A large improvement needs a reviewed baseline update too, otherwise a later regression could give it back while remaining below the old limit. Each PR owns an overlay, records a reason for an intentional change and names the value it replaces. Merged overlays are folded without changing the resolved baseline.

# Run locally on the appropriate platform and inspect both metrics.
vm/selfhost/ci-perf-gate.sh run macos-arm64 /tmp/cn1-perf
vm/selfhost/ci-perf-gate.sh verdict /tmp/cn1-perf

This comparative gate covers the five host OS/architecture combinations above. It is not a JDK comparison running on an iPhone, Android device or browser. Those ports have their own behavior and screenshot coverage. The port status page exposes the distinction, and PR #5930 explains the baseline workflow.

Keep the gain you measured

PGO and adaptive collection improve different parts of execution. Compare a profile-guided build with a regular build using the same application workflow, and keep the time and memory results together. For compiler and runtime changes, the performance gate gives the next release a baseline to preserve.

Discussion

Which part of your app would benefit most from a profile-guided build: startup, rendering, or repeated background work?

title: Stop Hardcoding Sunday as Day One. Intl.Locale Has getWeekInfo()
description:
TL;DR: new Intl.Locale("en-GB").getWeekInfo() tells you the week starts on Monday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday. With Firefox 153, the whole Intl.Locale info family is Baseline Newly available, so you can delete that hand-rolled "first day of week" table.

The line nobody wants to touch

Every date picker has it somewhere.

const FIRST_DAY = 0; // Sunday. Probably. Ask product.

Then a user in London opens the calendar and the week starts on the wrong day. Someone adds if (locale === "en-GB") ..., then a lookup table, then a ticket about Israel, where the weekend is Friday and Saturday. The table grows. Nobody is sure where the data came from.

The browser already ships that data. It has been sitting in the Unicode CLDR tables that power Intl.DateTimeFormat all along. Now there is a standard way to ask for it.

What it is

Intl.Locale has seven get methods that answer "how does this locale do things?":

Method What you get back
getWeekInfo() { firstDay, weekend }
getHourCycles() Hour cycles such as ["h12"] or ["h23"]
getTextInfo() { direction: "ltr" } or { direction: "rtl" }
getTimeZones() IANA time zones for the locale's region
getCalendars() Calendars in use, most preferred first
getCollations() Sort orders in use
getNumberingSystems() Digit systems in use

They came from the TC39 Intl Locale Info proposal, which is now Stage 4 and part of ECMA-402.

A minimal example 

for (const tag of ["en-US", "en-GB", "he-IL", "ar-AF", "fa-IR"]) {
  console.log(tag, new Intl.Locale(tag).getWeekInfo());
}

Run in Node 24.11:

en-US { firstDay: 7, weekend: [ 6, 7 ] }
en-GB { firstDay: 1, weekend: [ 6, 7 ] }
he-IL { firstDay: 7, weekend: [ 5, 6 ] }
ar-AF { firstDay: 6, weekend: [ 4, 5 ] }
fa-IR { firstDay: 6, weekend: [ 5 ] }

Days are numbered 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday. Notice fa-IR: a one-day weekend. Your two-element array assumption just left the chat.

The siblings work the same way:

new Intl.Locale("en-US").getHourCycles(); // ["h12"]
new Intl.Locale("en-GB").getHourCycles(); // ["h23"]
new Intl.Locale("ar").getTextInfo();      // { direction: "rtl" }
new Intl.Locale("th-TH").getCalendars();  // ["buddhist", "gregory"]

A realistic example: a calendar header

Here is a week header that starts on the right day and marks the weekend, with no lookup table. The day labels are in English so the output stays readable here; drop the second argument to get them in the user's language.

// firstDay and weekend use 1 = Monday ... 7 = Sunday.
// Date#getDay() uses 0 = Sunday ... 6 = Saturday.
const isoDay = (date) => date.getDay() || 7;

function weekHeader(tag, labels = tag) {
  const locale = new Intl.Locale(tag);
  const { firstDay, weekend } = locale.getWeekInfo();
  const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(labels, { weekday: "short", timeZone: "UTC" });

  // 2024-01-01 was a Monday, so day n (1-7) is January n.
  return Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => {
    const day = ((firstDay - 1 + i) % 7) + 1;
    const label = fmt.format(new Date(Date.UTC(2024, 0, day)));
    return weekend.includes(day) ? `[${label}]` : label;
  }).join(" ");
}

function isWeekend(date, tag) {
  return new Intl.Locale(tag).getWeekInfo().weekend.includes(isoDay(date));
}

for (const tag of ["en-US", "en-GB", "he-IL", "fa-IR"]) {
  console.log(tag.padEnd(6), weekHeader(tag, "en"));
}

const friday = new Date(2026, 9, 23); // October 23, 2026
console.log(friday.toDateString(), "en-US:", isWeekend(friday, "en-US"), "he-IL:", isWeekend(friday, "he-IL"));

Output from Node 24.11:

en-US  [Sun] Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri [Sat]
en-GB  Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri [Sat] [Sun]
he-IL  Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu [Fri] [Sat]
fa-IR  Sat Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu [Fri]
Fri Oct 23 2026 en-US: false he-IL: true

Same Friday, two answers. Both correct.

The same idea fixes time pickers: getHourCycles()[0] tells you whether to show an AM/PM toggle (h12) or a 0 to 23 clock (h23), and getTextInfo().direction tells you which way to lay out the arrows.

Can I use it?

Yes. The feature is Baseline Newly available since July 21, 2026, when Firefox 153 shipped all seven methods. Chrome and Edge have had the method form since 130, and Safari since 17. Node has it from 24.0.

Older Chrome (99 to 129) and Safari 15.4 to 16 exposed the same data as getters named weekInfo, hourCycles and so on. If you need those users, feature-detect:

const weekInfo = (locale) => locale.getWeekInfo?.() ?? locale.weekInfo;

Gotchas

  1. Days are ISO, not getDay(). firstDay uses 1 for Monday and 7 for Sunday, while Date#getDay() uses 0 for Sunday. Convert with date.getDay() || 7, or enjoy a calendar that is off by one only on Sundays.

  2. minimalDays is gone. MDN's getWeekInfo() page still shows a minimalDays property, but it was dropped from the proposal. MDN's own compat data says Chrome removed it in 136, and Node 24.11 does not return it. Do not build week numbering on it.

  3. The weekend is not always two days, or a Saturday. fa-IR returns [5], and ar-AF returns [4, 5]. Use weekend.includes(day), never day >= 6.

  4. getTimeZones() needs a region. new Intl.Locale("en-AU").getTimeZones() returned 12 zones in Node, but new Intl.Locale("en").getTimeZones() returned undefined. Handle the missing case.

  5. Unicode extensions win. In Node, new Intl.Locale("en-US-u-fw-mon").getWeekInfo().firstDay is 1, and en-US-u-hc-h23 gives ["h23"]. That is handy for a "week starts on" user setting, but it means the result is not always the region default.

  6. Each call returns a new object. locale.getWeekInfo() === locale.getWeekInfo() is false. That is exactly why the spec moved from getters to methods, so cache the result if you call it in a render loop.

Wrap-up

The week-start table in your codebase was always a guess about data the browser already had. Find your FIRST_DAY constant, swap it for getWeekInfo(), and let CLDR take the tickets.

Sources

  • MDN: Intl.Locale.prototype.getWeekInfo()
  • MDN: Intl.Locale.prototype.getHourCycles()
  • MDN: Firefox 153 release notes for developers
  • web.dev: July 2026 Baseline monthly digest
  • web-features: intl-locale-info status
  • MDN browser-compat-data: Intl.Locale
  • TC39: Intl Locale Info proposal

title: GPT-Live 1 now available on AI Gateway

GPT-Live 1 from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-Live 1 is a full-duplex voice model and can listen and speak at the same time. Many voice models use turn detection to respond. Full duplex removes that boundary, so a user can pause, interrupt, or add detail while GPT-Live is speaking.

title: TIL: GBase Database Connection Failed? Check sqlhosts First
description:
Today, I ran into a familiar problem: dbaccess couldn't connect to GBase Database(GBase 8s). The culprit wasn't a password or an obvious network failure. The hostname configured in sqlhosts didn't match the hostname resolution settings in /etc/hosts.

Here's how I tracked it down.

3 Quick Checks for GBase Database Connection Issues

1. Check the hostname in sqlhosts

cat "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210"

Look at the hostname field in the connection entry. Make sure it matches the intended server address and instance configuration.

2. Check the system hostname

hostname

Compare the output with the hostname used in sqlhosts. A mismatch is worth investigating, especially after installation or hostname changes.

3. Check hostname resolution

cat /etc/hosts

Confirm that the hostname can resolve to the correct IP address. You can also test resolution directly:

getent hosts your-hostname

Replace your-hostname with the hostname configured in sqlhosts.

The key isn't that all three files or commands must display exactly the same text in every setup. It's that the hostname used by the connection configuration must resolve correctly to the intended server.

Why This Matters

When troubleshooting a GBase Database connection failure, it's tempting to start changing passwords, firewall rules, or network settings.

But if sqlhosts points to a hostname that resolves incorrectly—or doesn't resolve at all—the connection can fail before those other factors become relevant.

Start with the connection entry and hostname resolution. They're quick to verify and can save you from unnecessary troubleshooting.

TIL takeaway: When dbaccess reports a connection error, check sqlhosts and hostname resolution first. If they look correct, move on to instance status, port configuration, network reachability, and credentials.

One small configuration mismatch can look like a much bigger database problem.

Regular expression matchers in host and route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA).

You can now use regular expressions (regex) matchers to configure more flexible and precise traffic routing rules within URL maps for Application Load Balancers. This feature allows you to leverage the power of RE2 syntax for matching on:

CodeMender updates (v0.14.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Better pull request scans: cm find --diff now catches removed security controls and gives large files more time (configurable with --diff-job-timeout).
  • Unified sessions: --deep and --diff scans now appear as a single session in cm session list, cm report, and cm stats.
  • Moved code in cm verify: cm verify now finds code that moved since cm find and updates the finding's location.
  • Guided activation: cm now opens the activation page and waits for activation instead of exiting.
  • New cm find flags: --deep-max-turns limits exploratory steps per file in --deep scans, and --enable-bash allows shell commands during scans.
  • Improved detection: More distinct findings per file and more precise CWE classification for weak hashing and randomness.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed scans of repositories reached through nested symbolic links.
    • Fixed findings for nonexistent files and over-merged findings.
    • Shell scripts created by cm verify are now executable.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.35.600-gke.140 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.35.600-gke.140 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

You don't need to take any action for curated rules. Updated rules continue to match only on reviewed, stable indicators. If you have custom rules that still reference the legacy feeds, update them to use the GTI_IOC feed. For more information, see Migrate to GTI_IOC.

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
description:
arXiv:2610.28915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

title: Recovering Delayed Webhook Jobs Under At-Least-Once Queue Delivery
description:
Short answer: use a queue for delayed webhook retries, but make the worker idempotent because standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so the same webhook event can be processed more than once.

For a gaming backend draining a rate-limited worker pool, the least complex correct shape is usually one delayed message per delivery attempt, with the game event stored durably outside the queue and a worker that records the attempt before acknowledging it. Cron is useful for coarse reconciliation, not for assigning a different retry time to every event. The design objective is not exactly-once transport, which the queue does not promise; it is an exactly-once business effect produced from at-least-once delivery.

Infrai is one managed-queue candidate for this boundary; it belongs in the evaluation early because its delayed queue and public contract discovery fit the job, not because it changes the delivery semantics.

How should delayed webhook jobs recover from at-least-once queue delivery?

A standard queue may redeliver a message. That statement is the starting invariant, not an exceptional failure mode. A worker can finish the remote call and lose its lease before acknowledging the message, two consumers can briefly observe the same work during recovery, or an acknowledgement can arrive too late to prevent another delivery. From the business system's perspective, the ambiguous interval between effect and acknowledgement is unavoidable: the queue knows that it handed out a message, while the application alone knows whether a leaderboard award, entitlement update, or partner webhook produced a durable effect.

The consequence is sharp. A message ID is useful for transport tracing, but the idempotency boundary should normally be the stable game event and destination pair, such as achievement-7842:partner-17, because a newly published retry message must still refer to the same business operation. Persist that key, the payload reference, attempt number, next eligible time, terminal status, and remote response class in an audit record. Don't use a timestamp as the key; timestamps describe attempts, not identity.

Ambiguity is normal.

Consider event match-92817-settled. Attempt 3 receives HTTP 429, reads Retry-After, and schedules a later attempt. Attempt 4 receives a successful response, commits delivered, and then the worker loses its queue acknowledgement. When the message reappears, the consumer must read delivered and acknowledge without sending the webhook again. No drama. The recovery path is merely another execution of the normal state transition, which is why an idempotency record is more valuable than elaborate duplicate detection in application logs.

There is a second idempotency boundary at the receiving service. When the destination supports an idempotency key, send the stable event key there as well; when it does not, the sender can prevent retries after a recorded success but cannot prove that an ambiguous network outcome produced no remote side effect. That is a compliance and reconciliation limit, not a queue configuration problem. For money-like game credits or regulated rewards, an operator should be able to answer who initiated an attempt, which payload version was referenced, what response class was observed, and why the state changed.

Start with the audit record, then choose the transport

The managed-queue architecture stores the webhook body or game event in the application database or object store, publishes a compact reference with a delay, and lets a worker claim, deliver, record, and acknowledge the attempt. In the evaluated service, delayed messages are capped at 7 days and payloads at 256KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. Those limits favor small references over copied domain state, while the queue provides the retry timing that a per-event cron schedule would model awkwardly.

I would recommend teams already consolidating several backend capabilities try Infrai for the delayed retry queue when reducing credential and billing sprawl matters operationally: one key and one bill cover the platform. Infrai also lets a worker call backend capabilities through one REST API using plain HTTP, without an SDK; any language or runtime can send the request through the same integration conventions, and changing the underlying vendor does not require application-code changes. The documented breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules rather than a queue-only wrapper. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it exposes request schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages, so an integration can verify the current contract before a recovery rather than depend on an assumed path or stale client package. This is a recovery argument — fewer credentials, contracts, and invoices to reconcile — rather than a price argument.

The invariants for that architecture are these:

  1. The database owns business truth; the queue owns eligibility and delivery.
  2. Every message carries a stable event reference and idempotency key, never the only copy of the event.
  3. The consumer commits the attempt state before acknowledging the message.
  4. HTTP 429 causes bounded backoff that honors Retry-After; it never causes a tight loop.
  5. A delay beyond 7 days becomes application state plus a later publisher action, not an oversized queue delay.

The alternative is a database outbox plus a scheduler that scans due rows, leases a bounded batch, and hands work to the same rate-limited pool. Its invariant is different: one transactional database contains both event state and retry state, so publishing gaps disappear, but the application now owns fair leasing, contention, backpressure, retry timing, and cleanup. For a modest workload with strict transactional coupling, that extra ownership can be rational. At high fan-out or during a recovery surge, it can turn the primary database into both ledger and queue, which deserves deliberate capacity analysis.

Either architecture needs reconciliation. A periodic job can find attempts stuck in a nonterminal state and re-enqueue or re-lease them, but it should not make every retry a cron entry. Cron executions here are limited to 900 seconds, paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and timing can have second-level jitter; a long reconciliation task should therefore use cron only to trigger queue publication, then let workers consume the resulting work.

A recovery matrix for the two system shapes

Option Best fit in this design Operational catch
Infrai queue Managed delayed retries where one REST contract, one key, and one bill reduce recovery overhead No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; standard delivery remains at-least-once; no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups
BullMQ A team prepared to evaluate and operate its own queue stack alongside the application The team owns the surrounding datastore operations and recovery practice; validate the current behavior against its documentation
Temporal or Airflow Work that truly requires workflow orchestration rather than one delayed delivery attempt More machinery than a simple webhook retry queue; this queue service does not replace the DAG/workflow category
Kafka Retained event history, replay, or several independent consumer groups A different system shape from an acknowledgement-deletes retry queue
Database outbox and due-row scanner Tight transaction coupling and a bounded workload Leasing, fairness, backpressure, and cleanup become application responsibilities

Choose the managed delayed queue when independent retry timing and operational recovery dominate. Choose the database scheduler when atomic coupling to one database is the stronger constraint and the team accepts queue-like database operations. Stick with Temporal or Airflow when retries are nodes in a multi-step workflow, and evaluate Kafka when replay or multiple consumer groups is a requirement. The managed queue is not suitable for those cases, nor for native debounce, throttle, topic fan-out, or delays longer than 7 days without application-managed scheduling.

I'm not sure how bursty your post-match traffic is, and that uncertainty matters more than a vendor feature checklist. Resolve it with the observed arrival distribution, destination rate limits, acceptable recovery time, and database headroom; then size concurrency so a replayed backlog cannot overwhelm either the partner or the game ledger. Your mileage may vary when one partner allows 500 requests per second and another allows five.

There is also a security boundary. A worker that calls URLs supplied by tenants can become an SSRF primitive, so validate destinations, restrict schemes, resolve and filter network ranges according to the OWASP guidance, and do not permit redirects to bypass those controls. A public HTTPS push target is required for a push subscription; private endpoints will not receive it, which may make pull consumption the cleaner boundary.

Inspect the live queue contract, then encode idempotency

Before implementing publication, this Go function retrieves the actual queue.publish contract through the verified public discovery route. It uses an environment variable for Bearer authentication, an explicit method, bounded handling for HTTP 429, and response-status checks; reading the schema first prevents an invented field or conventional-looking but nonexistent route from entering the worker.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func LoadPublishContract(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery retry limit reached")
}

The consumer itself keeps queue transport behind a small interface and makes the durable store the arbiter. Begin must atomically claim a new business key or report its stored state; MarkDelivered and the attempt audit update belong in the same durable transaction in a production implementation. The remote call is intentionally outside a long database transaction, because holding locks across an unbounded network request creates another recovery problem.

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Message struct {
    Receipt    string
    EventKey  string
    TargetURL string
    Attempt   int
}

type Queue interface {
    Ack(ctx context.Context, receipt string) error
    Retry(ctx context.Context, msg Message, delay time.Duration) error
}

type Store interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, attempt int) (alreadyDelivered bool, err error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int) error
    MarkAttempt(ctx context.Context, eventKey string, status int, next time.Time) error
}

type Worker struct {
    Client *http.Client
    Queue  Queue
    Store  Store
}

func (w Worker) Handle(ctx context.Context, msg Message) error {
    done, err := w.Store.Begin(ctx, msg.EventKey, msg.Attempt)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if done {
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, msg.TargetURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", msg.EventKey)

    res, err := w.Client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()

    if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
        if err := w.Store.MarkDelivered(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Ack(ctx, msg.Receipt)
    }

    if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        delay := retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), msg.Attempt)
        if err := w.Store.MarkAttempt(ctx, msg.EventKey, res.StatusCode, time.Now().Add(delay)); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return w.Queue.Retry(ctx, msg, delay)
    }

    return errors.New("webhook returned a non-success status")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if attempt > 8 {
        attempt = 8
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

This skeleton does not pretend that a local mutex is durability. The Store implementation needs a unique constraint on the business key, explicit attempt rows for audit, and a state transition that rejects an older attempt after delivery. The Queue.Retry implementation should publish a delayed message idempotently before acknowledging the current one; if publication and acknowledgement cannot be atomic, reconciliation must detect the intermediate state. Exactly-once is a property of those state transitions, not a label attached to the transport.

Migrate by proving the ambiguous interval

Start with one destination and shadow the state machine without sending, then enable a small worker concurrency and compare queue counts against durable attempt records. Exercise duplicate delivery deliberately, replay the same event key, return 429 with Retry-After, and terminate a worker after the remote success but before acknowledgement. The acceptance criterion is one business effect, a complete attempt history, and eventual queue acknowledgement.

Then add bounded concurrency per destination, alarms for oldest eligible work and retry exhaustion, and a reconciliation scan whose output can be explained from the audit trail. Keep payload references versioned so a later retry cannot silently pick up mutated event data. Short test.

Prove it twice.

Finally, document the human recovery decision: when to pause one destination, when to resume it, and when an operator may mark an event terminal. A queue drains work; it does not define authorization for replaying a reward or suppressing a compliance-relevant delivery.

title: SAIL: A Learnable Generalisation of Spatial Autocorrelation over Graph-Structured Data
description:
arXiv:2610.28806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In vision and scientific domains involving spatial data, a key question is whether node feature values vary independently across space or form coherent spatial structures. Classical spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ and Geary's $C$ quantify this phenomenon but operate on a single scalar variable with fixed neighbourhood weights, limiting their use for high-dimensional graph-like data. We introduce SAIL (Spatial Autocorrelation Index Learner), a differentiable framework that generalises spatial autocorrelation into a learnable operator by jointly learning feature projections defining candidate scalar fields and inter-node neighbourhood affinities. SAIL produces interpretable local and global spatial coherence descriptors, enabling supervised prediction and unsupervised discovery of spatial autocorrelation modes and hotspots. We show that SAIL exactly recovers classical spatial statistics under appropriate parametrisations and, for tasks driven by latent spatial autocorrelation, can approximate the Bayes-optimal predictor with an inductive bias matched to such tasks. Experiments on synthetic data and large-scale biomedical graphs demonstrate statistical correctness and discovery of spatial coherence with applications across vision, geospatial analysis, and biomedicine. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/pkeller00/SAIL.

title: ECHO: Emergent Common-Mode Hidden Offsets Drive Vocabulary Collapse in Preference Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.29410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Preference optimization can improve every ranking metric while building a hidden, shared representation shift that the relative loss barely sees, one that can eventually destroy generation. We trace this failure to the common-mode offset, a shared directional shift in the model's hidden states that appears across token positions, prompts, and both chosen and rejected responses. Because it moves chosen and rejected representations together, the relative ranking loss barely reacts to its accumulation. As this offset grows, it projects onto the output layer to form a vocabulary well, elevating a single token's probability until it dominates decoding and causes generation collapse. The isolated offset alone reconstructs the vocabulary well, injecting the learned offset into an untreated base model recreates the collapse where norm-matched random directions do not, and masking this common component from the loss prevents the well in our flagship setting. Under the per-token ranking loss we study, the same collapse appears in 14 of 17 base-model lineages and under full-parameter fine-tuning. Moreover, the offset is not merely an artifact of collapse, since it is already present in textbook DPO and SimPO runs that form no well. Textbook DPO keeps it weakly aligned with any single vocabulary direction even with three times our base budget. Trained from base models for that budget, however, full-parameter SimPO drives it into collapse on both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, and the same kind of offset grows, without a well, from a public SFT checkpoint under the official SimPO recipe. Across 17 UltraFeedback runs, the better a run ranks held-out responses, the less often two public reward models prefer its samples to the base model's. These findings expose a blind spot in standard ranking metrics and introduce a representation-level signal that can warn of generation collapse before it occurs.

title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
description:
arXiv:2610.29162v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.29249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.

title: Polyscene: Scenario Planning as Diversity Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.28102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scenario planning is a foresight practice in which analysts construct a small set of plausible futures and prepare an organisation for each. Each scenario is a narrative that must be plausible, internally consistent, relevant and challenging, and the set as a whole must be differentiated. The practice remains manual: a workshop (i.e., a facilitated meeting in which a small group of experts writes the narratives) considers only the factors it has time for, carries the biases of the experts who run it, and cannot be redone whenever conditions change. In this paper, we automate scenario planning by casting it as a diversity planning problem, in which two scenarios differ when they end in different narratives on the analyst's drivers. The result is a set of scenarios, one for each narrative that the topic can reach within a budget. Our implementation, Polyscene, is a generic engine that generates scenarios from a topic. We use geopolitical conflicts and shipping-route disruptions as case studies. For the first, we build the planning problem's initial state from the GDELT Project so it reflects current relationships among the countries involved. Polyscene then generates scenarios showing how relationships among those countries change. With a board of six countries as of 1 January 2021 and a budget of five events, the conflict set puts five of the 15 country pairs at war, and each of the three wars that break out among these countries by 1 January 2026 ends a scenario. For the second, we build the initial state from ship traffic, a supply-pressure index, and the news, and Polyscene generates scenarios showing what a closed or diverted route could do to a manufacturer's parts stock. With four routes per board and the same date and budget, each set includes three outcomes, and the Suez Canal set includes the March 2021 blockage and the December 2023 Red Sea container diversion.

title: Hibernate Under the Hood. Part 5: Caching
description:
Caching in Hibernate is a multi-level system, and understanding its architecture is critical for application performance. The golden rule: caching is disabled by default (except for the first-level cache), and it must be enabled consciously for specific data. The system consists of three independent layers, each with its own area of responsibility.

First-Level Cache

This is the foundation that cannot be disabled. It is always active and bound to a specific session (Session/EntityManager).

  • What it is: Essentially, this is the Persistence Context. All entities loaded within a single session are placed into this cache.
  • Scope: Only within a single session (usually a single transaction). Once the session is closed, the cache is destroyed.
  • Guarantees: It ensures the identity map (a repeated get for the same ID returns the exact same Java object instance) and dirty checking (Hibernate compares the current state with the snapshot upon flush).
  • Management: You cannot disable it, but you can manage its contents: session.evict(entity) removes a specific object, and session.clear() completely empties the cache. This is highly useful during batch processing of large data volumes to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.

Second-Level Cache

This is a shared cache that lives at the SessionFactory level and is shared across all sessions. It is designed for data that is rarely updated and frequently read.

  • Scope: Process level (or cluster level, if a distributed provider is used). Data survives session closure.
  • What is cached: Entity state (by their ID). It does not cache query results.
  • Disabled by default. To enable it, three conditions must be met:
    • Activate the cache in the settings (hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true).
    • Provide a cache provider (Ehcache, Caffeine, Infinispan, Redis, etc.).
    • Explicitly mark each entity with the @Cache annotation. Global activation does not cache everything indiscriminately — entities must "opt-in" to caching.

Concurrency Strategies (CacheConcurrencyStrategy):
When configuring @Cache, you must specify a strategy that defines how the cache behaves during concurrent updates.

Strategy When to use Characteristics
READ_ONLY Immutable reference data Fastest and safest. Throws an exception on update attempts.
NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE Updates are rare and unlikely No locks. Slight risk of reading stale data during an update.
READ_WRITE Updates are possible Uses "soft" locks to prevent reading stale data during a transaction.
TRANSACTIONAL Strict consistency required Full transactional locks. Requires explicit support from the cache provider.

Management: sessionFactory.evict(Entity.class, id) allows targeted removal of an entity from the second-level cache.

Query Cache

  • This is a specialized cache for query results. It works as an extension to the second-level cache and does not replace it. What is cached: The result of a query (JPQL/Criteria) with a specific set of parameters. Only the identifiers of the found entities and scalar values are cached, not the state of the entities themselves.
  • Dependency: Since the query cache stores only IDs, Hibernate will reach out to the second-level cache to fetch the actual entity data. If the entity is not there, a database query will be executed. Therefore, the query cache is always used in tandem with the second-level cache.
  • How to enable:
    • Activate globally: hibernate.cache.use_query_cache=true.
    • For each specific query, call .setCacheable(true).
  • Invalidation: The query cache is highly sensitive to changes. Any update to a table involved in the query invalidates the corresponding cached results. Hibernate tracks this via the UpdateTimestampsCache region.

Pitfalls and Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting the second-level cache to work "out of the box". This is the most common mistake. Enabling the global setting is completely useless if the entities lack the @Cache annotation.
  2. Caching "volatile" data. If an entity is frequently updated, the cache will constantly invalidate, creating overhead without providing any performance benefit. Cache only "reference" or rarely changing data.
  3. Cluster consistency issues. When using multiple application instances, a standard second-level cache (e.g., based on local memory) does not synchronize between them. One instance might update data, while another continues to serve stale data from its local cache. The solution is a distributed cache (Redis, Infinispan, Hazelcast) that synchronizes invalidation across nodes.
  4. Using READ_WRITE without lock support. The READ_WRITE strategy requires the cache provider to support locking. Not all providers can do this, and the provider's documentation usually contains explicit warnings about it.
  5. Query cache overhead. The query cache only makes sense for frequently repeated queries with the exact same parameters. For ad-hoc or unique queries, it creates unnecessary invalidation overhead.

Summary

  1. First-level cache is always on, lives within a session, and ensures identity and dirty checking. Manage it via evict/clear during batch processing.
  2. Second-level cache is shared across sessions but off by default. It requires a provider and an explicit @Cache annotation on each entity. Choose the strategy (READ_ONLY, READ_WRITE, etc.) based on the data's update frequency.
  3. Query cache caches only the IDs of results for repetitive queries. It always works in tandem with the second-level cache; otherwise, it is pointless.
  4. Caching is a trade-off between read speed and the risk of serving stale data. Do not cache everything indiscriminately; start with READ_ONLY for reference tables.
  5. In a cluster, always use a distributed cache (Redis/Infinispan), otherwise data consistency will be compromised.

title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28772v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment measures how faithfully a therapist adheres to a treatment protocol, a critical determinant of positive patient outcomes. However, fidelity assessment is bottlenecked by manual expert review, rendering the process labor-intensive and unscalable. To scale therapy supervision and support clinician self-learning, we present an integrated application of large language models (LLMs) that automates psychotherapy fidelity workflows and generates actionable supervisory feedback from authentic, long-form clinical transcripts. We evaluate three open-weight models across multiple task decomposition configurations and reasoning strategies, demonstrating that evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation. Furthermore, we establish the framework's external construct validity on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT), where it reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills. Through a user study that evaluates the generated feedback, mental health experts indicate that the pipeline synthesizes actionable clinical feedback. Ultimately, our work offers a practical, scalable solution toward bridging the community mental health supervision gap.

title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
description:
arXiv:2610.29196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.

title: How to Run a Brainstorming Session That Actually Works
description:
In 1953, advertising executive Alex Osborn promised that a group brainstorming together could think up twice as many ideas as the same people working alone. Five years later, Yale ran the first controlled test of that claim and found the opposite: people working on their own produced roughly twice as many good ideas as people brainstorming together. Here is how to run a brainstorming session that respects that result — because the meeting is still worth having, just not the way most teams run it.

The experiment that ruined brainstorming

In 1958, Taylor, Berry and Block at Yale ran 12 real groups of four through three problems using Osborn's official rules: no criticism, freewheeling, quantity first, build on each other's ideas. They also had 48 other people work alone, then randomly recombined those individuals into "nominal" groups of four and scored them as if they had worked together. The nominal group is exactly what the real group would have produced if talking to each other were neutral.

It wasn't neutral. The real groups were, in the authors' words, "markedly inferior" on total ideas, unique ideas, and three quality-weighted measures. The people who never spoke to each other produced roughly twice as many ideas.

The part that stings is the precision of the reversal. Osborn had written that "the average person can think up twice as many ideas when working with a group than when working alone." The first proper test found the effect going the other direction by about the same factor. One honest caveat: both conditions used Osborn's rules, so the study tested group versus individual under brainstorming rules — not brainstorming versus no method at all. The enemy was the group, not the rules.

Why talking first loses: production blocking

Three candidates were tested: social loafing (people coasting), evaluation apprehension (fear of sounding stupid), and production blocking — only one person can talk at a time, so everyone else waits, and while they wait their ideas decay. You forget the idea, or you spend your mental energy tracking the speaker instead of thinking.

Diehl and Stroebe (1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) manipulated all three mechanisms directly and found that blocking accounted for "most of the productivity loss" of real brainstorming groups. A 1991 follow-up with 400 students confirmed it, and pinned down something sharper: the damage comes from cognitive interference during the delay between generating an idea and getting to say it, not from limited speaking time itself. The waiting is the poison.

Then the meta-analysis made it undeniable. Mullen, Johnson and Salas (1991) pooled 20 studies from 1958 to 1990: nominal groups produce substantially more nonredundant ideas and substantially more high-quality ideas than interactive groups — a large effect (r around .56–.57 on both counts). And the deficit grows with group size. Your eight-person war room is worse than two four-person ones.

Why it feels like it works anyway

This is the objection every manager raises, and it deserves an honest answer: if brainstorming is so bad, why does every company still do it?

Part of the answer is a documented self-deception. Stroebe, Diehl and Abakoumkin (1992) showed that group members rate their own brainstorming as more effective than it was — the "illusion of group effectivity." Group brainstorms are enjoyable, social, and loud. They feel creative. So we conclude they were.

The deeper answer comes from Sutton and Hargadon (1996), who spent a field study inside IDEO, then the largest product-design firm in the US. Judged purely on ideas per person, IDEO's brainstorms were no better than the lab said. But they served at least six functions the labs never measured: organizational memory, designer skill-building, an "attitude of wisdom" (acting with knowledge while doubting it), status competition, impressing clients who watched and joined — and, as they put it, fun. "Nearly everyone at IDEO likes them, and they feel their jobs are more interesting because of them."

So the ritual does real social work. The correct response is not to cancel the meeting. It is to keep the meeting and fix the mechanics.

What the evidence says actually works

The fix has a name: the hybrid approach. Write alone first, talk second. Girotra, Terwiesch and Ulrich (2010, Management Science) ran 4-person groups in both orders: the hybrid process generated about three times as many ideas, with average quality roughly 30 percentile points higher — "the difference between the 1st and the 30th idea in a pool of 100." And then the knife twist: Osborn's beloved "build on each other's ideas" rule was measured as counterproductive. Teams that did more building produced neither more ideas nor better ones.

The oldest working version of this is brainwriting 6-3-5, published by Bernd Rohrbach in 1968. Six people, each writes 3 ideas every 5 minutes, worksheets rotate through 6 rounds: 108 ideas in 30 minutes. Silent simultaneous writing kills production blocking and verbal dominance in one move — and everyone sees everyone else's written ideas without paying the turn-taking tax.

One more data point: when groups contribute simultaneously by typing instead of speaking, the verdict flips. Electronic brainstorming groups have been measured beating nominal groups — simultaneous typing removes blocking entirely and the synergy researchers kept hoping for finally shows up. (A caveat from the video era: camera-on video groups underperform face-to-face ones on fluency, which is why "write before you talk" is the design principle.)

And it is the best idea that counts, not the pile. Kornish and Ulrich (2014, Journal of Marketing Research), using real sales data from crowd-designed products, found that raw ideas one standard deviation better translated to roughly 50% higher sales. Organizations don't need more ideas. They need the ceiling raised.

The 60-minute agenda that actually works

Here is the session, end to end, with the research baked in. No special tools required.

0:00 — State the question as one sentence. "How might we improve onboarding?" is too broad. "How might we cut the time from signup to first value from five days to one?" is a brainstormable question. Write it where everyone can see it, and don't start until it's sharp.

0:05 — Silent writing, 15 minutes. Everyone writes alone. One idea per sticky note or card, no talking, no laptops, no peeking. This is the entire game — the science says this phase is where the ideas come from. Push for quantity; ten per person is a good floor.

0:20 — Round-robin read-out, 15 minutes. Each person reads their ideas out, one at a time, with no commentary or defense. A scribe clusters them into themes as they emerge. The rule is simple: evaluate nothing, capture everything.

0:35 — Silent dot-vote, 15 minutes. Everyone gets three votes (anonymous if the room has hierarchy) across two criteria: impact and feasibility. Voting creates a shortlist, not a verdict — but five survivors is about right.

0:50 — Convergence, 10 minutes. For each surviving idea, name an owner, one deliverable, and one deadline. An idea with no owner is entertainment, not work. And once the meeting ends, the notes still matter — write them for the person who wasn't there, or the decisions you just made won't survive the week.

Three rules that hold the whole thing together: no devices during the session, the same single question for everyone, and the meeting ends with owners or it failed.

Next week, change one thing about your next brainstorm: fifteen silent minutes before anyone speaks. The research has been sitting there since 1958. The only teams that benefit from it are the ones that rearrange the chairs.

References

  • Taylor, D. W., Berry, P. C., & Block, C. H. (1958). Does group participation when using brainstorming facilitate or inhibit creative thinking? Administrative Science Quarterly, 3(1), 23–47.
  • Diehl, M., & Stroebe, W. (1987). Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(3), 497–509.
  • Diehl, M., & Stroebe, W. (1991). Productivity loss in idea-generating groups: Tracking down the blocking effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 61(3), 392–403.
  • Mullen, B., Johnson, C., & Salas, E. (1991). Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: A meta-analytic integration. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 12(1), 3–24.
  • Girotra, K., Terwiesch, C., & Ulrich, K. T. (2010). Idea generation and the quality of the best idea. Management Science, 56(4), 591–605.
  • Sutton, R. I., & Hargadon, A. (1996). Brainstorming groups in context: Effectiveness in a product design firm. Administrative Science Quarterly, 41(4), 685–718.
  • Rohrbach, B. (1968). Kreativ nach Regeln — Methode 635, eine neue Technik zum Lösen von Problemen. Absatzwirtschaft, 12, 73–75.
  • Kornish, L. J., & Ulrich, K. T. (2014). The importance of the raw idea in innovation: Testing the sow's ear hypothesis. Journal of Marketing Research, 51(1).
