title: Your AI agent runs with all your permissions. I built a cage for each tool call, in Rust
description:
A subagent got a simple task: read a project's docs and say how to run it. It read docs/readme.txt, found "make run", and then asked for one more file: ~/.ssh/id_rsa.

Why it asked doesn't matter. A hidden instruction in something it read, a buggy third-party tool, a model that "thought" the key would help. What matters is what happens next, and in most setups today the file is read. Not because anyone granted the subagent access to the key, but because nobody granted anything to anyone: the tool runs as your user, and your user can read your key.

There's an old name for this: ambient authority. The kernel doesn't know about agents. It sees user ana and processes of ana. It can't ask "was this Ana, Ana's agent, or the tool her agent's subagent downloaded yesterday?".

Where the usual defenses stop

  • Gateways and proxies check permissions at the door, then let the tool run natively with full access.
  • Agent sandboxes (NVIDIA OpenShell, AWS Strands Box, Anthropic's sandbox-runtime) contain the whole agent process with one policy. Useful, but every subagent and tool inside shares it.
  • Logs ask you to trust whoever wrote them.

I wanted something one level down: per tool call, decided by a permission that can only shrink as it is handed on, and proved afterwards.

Five pieces

CleiMesh is a Rust node (MIT or Apache-2.0) that puts five pieces together:

  1. Delegable, signed permissions. A token, following the IETF Attenuating Agent Tokens JWT profile. An agent can hand a narrower part to a subagent, offline, never more than it got.
  2. The permission becomes the sandbox. Tools run in WebAssembly (wasmtime + WASI) where nothing is allowed by default. The token decides the preopened directories, network or not, instruction and memory limits. A subagent granted ./project/docs can't physically open ./project.
  3. A signed receipt for every call, allowed or denied: Ed25519, hash-chained JSONL with a signed head, in the draft-sahu-agent-action-receipts format. Digests and pseudonyms, never the data. No receipt, no run.
  4. Don't trust the receipt, replay it. Calls run with a frozen clock and seeded RNG recorded in the receipt, so an auditor re-runs the call and compares the output byte for byte. A node that signs a false result is caught.
  5. Taint that follows the delegation chain. Once a tool marked --taints (mail, web) returns content to an agent, tools marked --clean-only (write, send) are refused for that agent's whole chain until a human clears it. Handing the work to a fresh subagent doesn't launder it. 
# Reading the inbox brings in outside content; writing to the outbox acts on the world
cleimesh token issue <agent> --tool file_read --read ~/inbox --taints -o read.json
cleimesh token issue <agent> --tool file_write --write ~/outbox --clean-only -o write.json

A real model, a poisoned mail

I ran OpenClaw with a local Qwen3 4B on Ollama and a mail carrying a hidden instruction to write a secret to a file.

  • With OpenClaw's own file tools on, the model obeyed and wrote the file, without ever calling CleiMesh.
  • With only CleiMesh's tools, the read tainted the chain, the write was refused by the node, and the refusal is on a signed receipt.

That first act is the honest limit: CleiMesh only contains what goes through it. cleimesh doctor reads Claude Code's and OpenClaw's config and warns when the agent still has its own file or shell tools. And it doesn't "solve" prompt injection: the model can still be fooled, and an allowed action can still be the wrong one. What the node adds is a rule outside the model that the model can't argue with.

Numbers, measured

  • One static musl binary, 37 MB (13.7 MB gzipped), starts in ~2.5 ms.
  • A cached WASM instance per call is ~0.5 ms; a full call with two fsynced receipts is ~3 ms on a laptop.
  • A load test with 5,000 simulated agents, part of them hostile: zero escapes, a verified log, ~400 calls/s, bounded by fsync. Group commit is next.

Try it 

curl -fsSL https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
# or from source:
cargo build -p cleimesh-cli
CLEIMESH=target/debug/cleimesh examples/demo/demo.sh

The demo runs in a fresh /tmp directory with a fake project, a fake ~/.ssh and throwaway keys. It's alpha: the threat model in the repo lists what it protects, what it doesn't, and the gaps before 1.0.

Repo: https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh

I'd like opinions on two things: grouping receipt fsyncs without weakening "no receipt, no run", and the guest ABI (core module now, Component Model before 1.0).

I also wrote up the design, the attacks and the mistakes in a book, AI Agents in a Cage.

title: Intergroup Bias Predicts Expressions of Social Judgment and Empathy in the r/AmITheAsshole Reddit Community
description:
arXiv:2610.29254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People share and understand others' experiences differently based on their social identities; often, people empathize more when the other person belongs to their ingroup compared to an outgroup. While this intergroup empathy gap is well-studied in social psychology, it remains unclear how it manifests in naturally occurring online social interactions. To this end, we measure how commenters express social judgments, as an indirect outcome of their understanding towards the posters, and empathy in text, based on whether commenters share the poster's gender or are of similar ages. We focus on posts where the poster self-reports these demographics, and analyze 126,716 comments associated with 36,163 posts from 18,111 commenters in r/AmItheAsshole, while controlling for commenter and poster group identities, post features (topic, length, and score), and both commenter- and post-level variance. Our results show that when commenters and posters are ingroup, in either gender or age, commenters are more likely to provide a Not the Asshole verdict and show greater text-based understanding as measured by LLMs. We also observe that older commenters behave differently from younger ones. Furthermore, in a subset of posts where the gender and age of the other party in the conflict are explicitly mentioned, we find that commenter-poster ingroup effects are moderated by the group relationships between the poster and the other party when commenters make social judgments. Our work highlights the importance of intergroup context and social group nuances in understanding online discourse.

title: How Delphi ships 100 times a day with its Python backend on Vercel
description:
Delphi on Vercel

  • 10 engineers with no dedicated infrastructure role

  • Everyone ships code, including product and design

  • 100+ production deploys a day behind feature flags

Delphi builds digital minds. They capture what someone has written, recorded, and taught, so anyone can tap that expertise on demand. Delphi is “a destination where you can find and interact with interesting minds,” says founding engineer Spencer Schoeben.

Nobody has built a digital mind network before, so Delphi figures out what to build by shipping features and watching how people use them. That only works if the product is fast to change. "If we are going to win, we need to have an excellent developer and agentic experience," Spencer says. "Otherwise, we could not adapt to how fast our user’s demands change."

Delphi's frontend had run on Vercel since day one. "The frontend has always been easy," Spencer says, "but the backend was a nightmare." Six months ago, the team rebuilt its Python backend on Vercel as well. Today the whole team ships to production 100+ times a day.

Building a Python backend that's easy to work on

The backend slowed every change

Delphi's backend previously ran on AWS, with ECS, Docker Desktop, and local databases. In the earliest days, the setup worked because the team was small and much of the context lived in people’s heads. As Delphi grew, that made onboarding slower than the team wanted: getting a new engineer to their first deploy took a full day of environment setup. 

Delphi could have fixed that without leaving AWS. But fixing it properly would have meant designing and owning the infrastructure themselves, and the team didn't want to own infrastructure at all. "That is not our current goal as a company," Spencer says. After moving the backend to Vercel, new engineers could get to production much faster, with the same deploy workflow the rest of the team used every day.

Workflows and Queues made the move possible

When Delphi was founded, Vercel Workflows and Vercel Queues didn't exist. Without them, Spencer says, the move would have been much harder, if possible at all.

Delphi's backend depends on long-running work and queued background jobs. Digital minds need durable agents that generate content ahead of time, plus ingestion that turns a person's books and talks into a knowledge graph.

Workflows handles the long-running work and Queues handle the background jobs. Neither requires setup. A developer writes the workflow or the queue handler as a function in the codebase, and Vercel provisions what's needed to run it on deploy.

100+ deploys a day, straight to production

Moving the backend to Vercel let Delphi stop treating backend changes as heavyweight releases and ship them as everyday product work. The team used to deploy to staging, then production. Now it skips the middle step, shipping 100+ times a day behind feature flags and running A/B tests instead of batching changes into a release.

Vercel Agent's anomaly detection watches production at that pace, flagging when something is misbehaving and why. Before, Spencer says, they often would not have known.

Moving fast has helped clear a backlog of small experiments that never used to make the priority list. Many of those experiments test how to turn a visitor into an owner, someone who arrives to talk to a mind and leaves having started their own.

Shipping isn't limited to engineers, either. Delphi's CPO and its growth teams build and deploy dashboards, prototypes, and experiments themselves, which Spencer says wouldn't have happened on the old setup.

Infrastructure built for agents and engineers

Preview deployments are how agents check their work

Delphi's engineers hand problems to cloud agents, with very little development happening locally. The preview deployment is where they first see what the agent built. Vercel preview deployments give every push its own live URL, so anyone can check the result from a phone or a Slack thread without pulling the branch.

When an agent fails, it's usually because it couldn't get at the information it needed. Vercel exposes the data and controls agents need through the SDK, MCP, and CLI, so an agent can read logs, inspect a deployment, or change an environment variable through whichever it's using. For Delphi, agents are now the main users of those tools, so the platform has to be as easy for them as it is for people.

An internal agent on Sandbox for customer success

Delphi's own agents run on Vercel as well. One of them, an internal agent on Vercel Sandbox, simplifies working with the company's codebase. The customer success team uses Slack to ask it about reported issues, find the problem, and hand an engineer a root cause and a proposed fix.

Edge cases used to fall through the cracks. "Before, we either couldn't get to everything, or we had to spend way more time than we had available," Spencer says. "Now we have an agent they can just ask in Slack."

Vercel Sandbox gives the agent an isolated environment with a file system, where it can check out the codebase, run it, and pull in whatever data a question needs. The agent itself is built with eve, Vercel's agent framework. Delphi's first version ran on a hosted agent platform and could only use the integrations that platform offered. In eve, tools are code Delphi writes, so when a question needs one that doesn't exist, the team adds it.

AI Gateway picks the model for each mind

Delphi's chat traffic runs through AI Gateway. Every digital mind is different, and some come out better on one model than another, so Delphi picks the model for each customer and adjusts as its own evals change. When a new model ships, open-source or otherwise, Delphi can route to it the same day.

Gateway also handles failover. Before, Delphi worked directly with a model provider to line up fallback capacity on other clouds, and it was hard. "With AI Gateway, we always know that we're going to get the fallbacks if they exist," Spencer says.

What's next

Delphi's first chapter was training digital minds and letting people chat with them. Now it is building the interface beyond chat. Spencer describes a search page where you bring a question, get perspectives from several minds at once, and have the page adapt to who you are.

That work runs as long-running agents on Workflows, with AI Gateway supplying whichever model each experiment calls for.

About Delphi: Delphi is a platform that turns a person's knowledge, thinking, and voice into a digital mind others can talk to. Anyone can create their own Delphi to make their expertise discoverable and accessible, part of a network of minds people can seek out, learn from, and converse with.

title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics
description:
arXiv:2610.28611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability, an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, it bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building on this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We show conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. We also specify an open-source validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper on exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking.

title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28779v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.

title: SlothSort: The Zero-Effort Clutter Tidier for International Sloth Day
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3

🦥 What I Built: SlothSort

Tomorrow is International Sloth Day, and sloths have life figured out: move at your own pace, conserve energy, and let automation do the tedious heavy lifting so you don't have to.

Every developer and knowledge worker knows the dread of opening their ~/Downloads or Desktop folder: a terrifying graveyard of chaotic filenames:

  • Screen Shot 2026-10-21 at 11.45.12 PM.png
  • final_pitch_deck_v3_revised_FINAL2.pptx
  • Receipt_Uber_Eats_Oct14.pdf
  • IMG_20261019_142311.jpg
  • contract_nda_mutual_signable_oct.pdf

Cleaning this manually takes endless clicking, dragging, and cognitive fatigue.

SlothSort is a zero-effort desktop and download tidier that channels your inner sloth:

  1. Drop or Paste Clutter: Toss in messy filenames, downloads, or unorganized project files.
  2. Local Gemma 2 Semantic Intelligence: Google's open-weight Gemma 2 (running 100% locally via Ollama) inspects context, categorizes files, and renames them to clean, consistent, ISO/semantic standards (e.g., 2026-10_Invoice_AcmeCorp.pdf).
  3. Lazy Voice Debrief with ElevenLabs: Listen to a soothing, witty sloth audio debrief celebrating how much effort you saved today.
  4. 1-Click Execution Script: Provides an auto-generated bash script (organize.sh) so you can execute the sorting on your machine in one terminal command.

🎥 Video Demo & Walkthrough

▶️ Watch the full walkthrough on YouTube: https://youtu.be/TANmvRYIfnw

📸 Screenshots

SlothSort running 100% on-device with Gemma 2 sorting queue, ElevenLabs voice debrief player, and 1-click terminal execution script.

🔒 Why Open Innovation Matters

The Hacktoberfest prompt asks: Why does open innovation matter for what you built?

For personal file management, open-weight, on-device AI is not just a nice-to-have; it's a non-negotiable requirement:

  1. Absolute Privacy on Sensitive Files: Desktop clutter is full of private data — bank statements, unreleased source code, medical invoices, passwords, and client NDAs. Sending this metadata to commercial cloud LLMs creates catastrophic privacy risks. With Gemma 2 running locally via Ollama, zero bytes ever leave your laptop.
  2. $0 API Costs Forever: Commercial cloud LLM tokens add up quickly when organizing hundreds of files. With open-weight models, you set it up once and clean your folders an unlimited number of times for free.
  3. Offline Resilience: Whether you're on a long flight without Wi-Fi or working in a remote cabin, your sloth organizer works completely offline.

🛠️ How I Built It

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (Turbopack, App Router) with Tailwind CSS and TypeScript.
  • Open-Source AI Core: Google Gemma 2 (gemma2:9.2B) served locally through Ollama (http://localhost:11434), producing structured JSON categorization plans.
  • Voice AI: ElevenLabs Multilingual v2 generating soothing, sloth-themed audio debriefs.
  • Automation Pipeline: Client-side interactive dashboard + auto-generated Bash script builder.

title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?
description:
arXiv:2610.28595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.

title: DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Decision Models in LLM Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.28522v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models support routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems. However, item accuracy alone cannot establish whether models make correct decisions across controlled variations or assign reliable confidence to their predictions. We introduce DecisionPivot, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. Its core track contains 7,800 items from 13 generated task families, organized into contrast groups with computed answers verified by independently implemented solvers. The complementary reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving their original evaluation metrics. We evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models using documented, model-specific protocols, assessing item and contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and empirical selective coverage. Our results reveal substantial differences obscured by aggregate scores: two 27B models separated by only 2.6 points on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. Across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative member in 92.3% of pairs but answers both members correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness. Models with similar item accuracy also differ in the reliability of their high-confidence predictions. On a separate 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5\% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting, compared with 81.5% at its lowest effort. By linking errors to pivotal details and difficulty levels, DecisionPivot provides fine-grained diagnostics of decision failures that aggregate evaluation alone cannot reveal.

title: Novo CNPJ Alfanumérico da Receita Federal: Como preparar seus testes e sistemas
description:
A transição para o CNPJ Alfanumérico regulamentada pela Receita Federal é uma das mudanças estruturais mais relevantes para ecossistemas de software no Brasil. Com a iminência do esgotamento das combinações estritamente numéricas, a introdução de caracteres alfanuméricos exige atenção imediata de desenvolvedores, arquitetos e equipes de QA.

Se a sua aplicação lida com cadastro de pessoas jurídicas, emissão de notas fiscais, integrações com ERPs ou checkout B2B, diversos pontos da sua stack precisarão de revisão.

O que muda e quais os impactos práticos no software?

  1. Máscaras de Input no Front-end:
    Muitos formulários utilizam bibliotecas de máscara que aceitam apenas dígitos ([0-9]). Com a mudança, esses componentes precisam aceitar letras nas posições previstas pela nova especificação, sem quebrar a experiência do usuário.

  2. Tipagem e Modelagem de Banco de Dados:
    Campos legados que utilizavam BIGINT ou colunas numéricas precisarão ser migrados para campos de texto (VARCHAR / CHAR), garantindo armazenamento e indexação consistentes.

  3. Expressões Regulares e Validações de API:
    Rotas de backend que aplicam regex restritas a dígitos ou validações de schema (como Zod, Yup ou Joi) precisarão de ajustes para reconhecer a nova estrutura.

  4. Ambientes de Teste e Homologação (QA):
    Garantir que as pipelines de CI/CD e suítes de teste automatizado possuam massas de dados atualizadas, cobrindo tanto o padrão tradicional numérico quanto o novo formato alfanumérico.

title: A Parallel Multi-Dialect Arabic Dependency Treebank
description:
arXiv:2610.28823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dependency parsing resource development for Arabic has largely focused on Modern Standard Arabic, leaving dialectal Arabic comparatively under-resourced. We introduce MADARTB, the first large-scale parallel dependency treebank spanning five city dialects: Beirut, Cairo, Doha, Rabat and Tunis, and extending an existing parallel MSA version. In total MADARTB consists of 5,000 sentences annotated using the CATiB dependency scheme. We analyze syntactic similarity across all city dialects and MSA. Although global construction profiles exhibit high similarity across varieties, local syntactic structures frequently diverge, revealing substantial structural variation across dialects. We further establish a cross-dialect dependency parsing comparison using a supervised parser and four LLMs. The supervised parser achieves 87.5% LAS, while the best LLM setup trails at 85.7% LAS across all six varieties on the test set. We release our annotations and models publicly.

title: Seeing the Forest for the Trees: Emergent Agreement from Individual Conversations
description:
arXiv:2610.29328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLM agents interact in the wild and shape each other's decisions, understanding how they converge toward agreement becomes important. We study this in multi-turn conversations where two LLMs discuss subjective matters, can agree or disagree, and may change their stances. Using a linear classifier on individual conversation activations, we identify an internal representation of agreement. We find that it varies substantially across turns and conversations and does not reliably track external agreement at the individual conversation level. We therefore move beyond the representation of agreement in individual conversations, by aggregating the agreement representation across conversations. Externally, this aggregate view reveals a simple structure: when pooled across conversations, agreement can be predicted well with a Markov process, with agreement at each turn being a direct function of agreement at the previous turn. Similarly, when internal agreement is aggregated, it couples with the external Markov agreement through a power-law mapping, exposing Markovian dynamics in internal representations. Additionally, we find that after a change of stance, models express agreement externally before their internal representations reflect the same shift. These results reveal a joint structure between internal and external agreement that emerges only when internal features are aggregated across conversations. Code available at https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/SeeingTheForestForTheTrees.

title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.28838v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

title: DriftNeRF: Cross-Ray Density Drifting for Sparse-View Neural Radiance Fields
description:
arXiv:2610.29106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We attribute a specific, measurable defect to the objective itself: the rendering loss is a sum over independent rays and contains no term comparing densities that different rays assign to the same region of space, so nearby 3D points can settle on contradictory densities while every training pixel is reproduced correctly. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. We then close the gap with DriftNeRF, a drop-in regularizer that instantiates the drifting-field template on density samples: a masked exponential kernel aggregates densities from nearby points on other rays into a stop-gradient consensus target, and the resulting drifting field penalizes unsupported disagreement while leaving agreed-upon boundaries intact. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. On NeRF-Synthetic it reduces residual disagreement by an order of magnitude, and across NeRF-Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF it improves 3-view PSNR over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline by 0.42-0.65 dB and remains competitive with sparse-view Gaussian pipelines under a matched protocol without their depth, flow, or covisibility preprocessing.

title: A Practical CI/CD Pipeline: Build Once, Tag by Commit, Deploy Anywhere
description:
A good CI/CD pipeline is boring. Every change goes through the same steps, deploys look the same every time, and rolling back takes seconds.

This post builds a minimal pipeline for a containerised app using GitHub Actions. The principles also apply to other CI systems and cloud providers.

Principles first

  1. Build once. Create a single artefact (a container image) and promote that same artefact through staging and production. Don't rebuild per environment, or you're not testing what you ship.
  2. Make artefacts immutable. Tag images with the commit SHA. Avoid deploying latest, because you can't tell what it is or roll back to it reliably.
  3. Keep config out of the image. Environment variables and secrets come from the environment at runtime.
  4. Automate the check after deploy. A deploy isn't done until a health check passes.

Step 1: Test and build on every push 

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint --if-present
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Pull requests run tests only. Merges to main also build and push an image tagged with the exact commit.

Step 2: A small, secure Dockerfile 

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

Multi-stage builds keep the final image small, and USER node avoids running as root.

Step 3: Deploy the exact image

How you deploy depends on your platform (ECS, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, a VM with Docker, and so on). The pattern is the same: tell the platform to run the image tagged with this commit SHA.

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - name: Deploy image
        run: |
          echo "Deploying ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} to staging"
          # replace with your platform's command, for example:
          # kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Wait for health check
        run: |
          for i in {1..20}; do
            if curl -fsS https://staging.example.com/healthz; then exit 0; fi
            sleep 5
          done
          echo "Health check failed" && exit 1

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # add required reviewers in repo settings
    steps:
      - name: Deploy the same image
        run: echo "Deploying the same SHA to production"

Using GitHub Environments lets you add required approvals for production and keep secrets separate per environment.

Step 4: Add a real health endpoint 

app.get("/healthz", async (req, res) => {
  try {
    await db.query("SELECT 1");     // check critical dependencies
    res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
  } catch {
    res.status(503).json({ status: "unhealthy" });
  }
});

Keep it fast and cheap. Platforms use it to decide whether to send traffic to a new version, and your pipeline uses it to decide whether a deploy succeeded.

Step 5: Rollback is just another deploy

Because every image is tagged with a commit SHA, rolling back means deploying the previous known-good SHA. No rebuild required.

# example: redeploy the previous version
kubectl set image deployment/app app=ghcr.io/org/app:<previous-sha>

Practice this before you need it. A rollback you've never tried isn't a plan.

Beyond the basics

  • Secrets: prefer short-lived credentials via OIDC (for example, GitHub Actions to AWS, Azure or GCP) over long-lived keys stored in secrets.
  • Infrastructure as code: manage cloud resources with Terraform or similar, reviewed through pull requests.
  • Progressive delivery: canary or blue/green releases reduce the impact of a bad deploy.
  • Observability: logs, metrics and alerts tied to each release, so you can see when a deploy changed behaviour.
  • Database migrations: make them backward-compatible so old and new versions can run side by side during a rollout.

Checklist

  • [ ] One build, promoted across environments
  • [ ] Images tagged by commit SHA, never latest
  • [ ] Config and secrets injected at runtime
  • [ ] Health check gates every deploy
  • [ ] Manual approval for production
  • [ ] Rollback tested

What does your deployment pipeline look like, and what's the one thing you'd change?

Further reading: Cloud DevOps Solutions

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

  • Deploy the Vercel Drives eve agent starter template in one click

title: v0 now reads npm credentials from shared environment variables
description:
v0 now installs private packages from npm and custom registries using credentials stored as shared environment variables on Vercel.

This makes it easier for teams to build with their existing design systems, component libraries, and internal packages directly in v0.

To get started, add one of the following as a shared environment variable on Vercel, scoped to Development and/or Preview:

  • Use NPM_TOKEN for private packages hosted on registry.npmjs.org.

  • Use NPM_RC to configure custom or multiple registries.

NPM_RC supports scoped registries and references to other environment variables. For example, configure an organization scope such as @acme for GitHub Packages, or direct package requests through a private JFrog Artifactory registry.

Credentials can be marked sensitive, and v0 never exposes them to the model or writes them to the sandbox filesystem.

title: The Commit Gap: Browser Original Image Upload to a Backend Thumbnail Worker Queue
description:
Short answer: let the browser upload the original image under a server-issued key, but do not generate thumbnails until the backend has verified that exact object version and committed a durable queue job; treat an object-storage webhook notification as evidence to reconcile, not as the transaction boundary.

That rule closes the awkward gap between “the bytes arrived” and “the application accepted these bytes.” It also gives a Node.js application a status it can defend after a client disconnect, a duplicate event, or a worker restart. The resize library is rarely the difficult part. Ownership is.

What should commit a browser upload before a Node.js worker generates image thumbnails?

The backend should commit it. Before any transfer, the backend authenticates the user, allocates an opaque upload ID and object key, records the permitted content type and size, and issues narrowly scoped, short-lived upload authorization. The browser sends the original directly to object storage. If upload progress matters, XMLHttpRequest.upload exposes progress events; those events describe client-side transfer progress, not acceptance by the application.

After transfer, the browser calls a finalize endpoint with the upload ID. The backend reads authoritative object metadata, verifies that the key belongs to that upload, captures an immutable version identifier or checksum, and changes the application record from authorized to committed. In the same application transaction, it writes an outbox row for each requested rendition. An outbox publisher then moves those jobs to the queue. This avoids the classic dual-write hole where the database says “uploaded” but the process stops before publishing work.

Return 202 Accepted with a status URL. RFC 9110 defines 202 as accepted for processing but not completed, which is exactly the contract here. A browser progress bar at 100% is not a thumbnail-completion signal, and a successful finalize response must not pretend otherwise.

There is still a gap if the client uploads all bytes and disappears before finalizing. Keep that state visible: a scheduled reconciler finds authorized uploads whose objects exist, verifies them under the same rules, and either commits them according to application policy or expires them. I am not sure one universal expiry window exists; object size, mobile-client behavior, and retention requirements should determine it. Your mileage may vary.

Model notification delivery as hostile timing

Object-created notifications can arrive twice, arrive late, or race the finalize request. None of those conditions should produce a second logical resize. The notification handler authenticates the sender, validates the bucket namespace and key shape, looks up an existing upload record, and requests the same deterministic job identity as every other trigger. Unknown objects go to an audit path. They do not go straight to an image decoder.

This is the failure-mode table I want during design review:

Failure mode Durable evidence Recovery action
Browser vanishes after transfer authorized row plus stored object Reconciler verifies, commits, or expires it
Finalize commits before publish Committed outbox row Publisher retries the same job identity
Notification is duplicated Unique job key already exists Acknowledge after the durable lookup
Old work finishes after replacement Source version differs from current version Preserve output, but reject it as current
Worker loses its lease Attempt has no completion record Redeliver and converge on the same output key
Decoder rejects the source Terminal reason is recorded Quarantine input and expose a safe user status

Do not collapse these into a single failed state. A corrupt image is terminal for that source version; a lease expiry is retryable; an unknown notification may be irrelevant or evidence of an authorization bypass. Those are different operational facts, and one red counter cannot tell an operator what to do.

No magic here.

The job key can be a hash of (upload_id, source_version, variant, transform_revision). Include the transform revision because changing crop behavior or encoder settings creates a new derived artifact even when the original is unchanged. The output key should carry the same identity. A read-before-write existence check is insufficient because two workers can pass it together; use the storage system's conditional-create operation, or write immutable versioned outputs and resolve the current pointer with a compare-and-set in application state.

Make the queue consumer converge

A worker crosses the queue, source storage, image decoder, destination storage, and application database. There is no useful atomic transaction across all of them, so correctness comes from repeatable transitions and conditional commits. The message carries identifiers, never authorization claims copied from the browser.

The following Python sketches the contract that a Node.js service can publish. state, objects, and decoder are application-owned interfaces; their names deliberately avoid implying a vendor SDK.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ThumbnailJob:
    upload_id: str
    source_key: str
    source_version: str
    variant: str
    transform_revision: str

    @property
    def identity(self) -> str:
        fields = (
            self.upload_id,
            self.source_version,
            self.variant,
            self.transform_revision,
        )
        return sha256(":".join(fields).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    @property
    def output_key(self) -> str:
        return f"derived/{self.upload_id}/{self.identity}.webp"


def consume(message, state, objects, decoder) -> None:
    job = ThumbnailJob(**message.body)

    if state.is_complete(job.identity):
        message.ack()
        return

    source = state.committed_source(job.upload_id)
    if (source.key, source.version) != (job.source_key, job.source_version):
        state.mark_superseded(job.identity)
        message.ack()
        return

    original = objects.read(job.source_key, version=job.source_version)
    thumbnail = decoder.resize_with_limits(original, variant=job.variant)
    digest = sha256(thumbnail).hexdigest()

    objects.create_if_absent(
        job.output_key,
        thumbnail,
        content_type="image/webp",
        metadata={"source-version": job.source_version, "sha256": digest},
    )
    state.complete_if_current(
        job.identity,
        source_version=job.source_version,
        output_key=job.output_key,
        digest=digest,
    )
    message.ack()

The acknowledgement is last. If the process stops after the conditional object create, redelivery recomputes or discovers the same immutable output and completes the state transition. If it stops after the database commit but before acknowledgement, is_complete makes the next delivery cheap. Keep attempt counts separate from logical job counts — otherwise retry amplification disappears inside an apparently healthy throughput graph.

Image decoding also needs explicit limits on input bytes, decoded pixels, dimensions, frames, memory, and execution time. File extensions and browser-supplied media types are hints. Decode the content, strip metadata that the product does not need, and decide deliberately whether orientation and color profiles affect the transform revision. A 12 MB compressed file can demand far more working memory after decoding; queue concurrency must be bounded by worst-case resident memory, not by average file size.

Compare triggers only after defining the invariant

Once a thumbnail job has one identity and one conditional completion rule, triggers become delivery choices rather than competing sources of truth.

Trigger What it proves What it cannot prove Suitable role
Browser finalize request An authenticated client claims transfer completion The stored bytes satisfy policy Ask the backend to verify and commit
Storage webhook notification An object operation occurred in a namespace The application intended or accepted that object Accelerate lookup and reconciliation
Transactional outbox Application state and job intent committed together A queue consumer has finished Primary handoff to the queue
Scheduled scan A durable state remains unfinished Immediate user intent Repair missed or stalled transitions

The catch is that direct browser upload is not suitable when every byte must pass synchronously through malware inspection, data-loss controls, or a regulated ingest boundary before storage. Proxy the stream through a controlled ingest service in that case, accepting its bandwidth, timeout, and scaling costs. A queue is also needless complexity for a genuinely small internal tool whose bounded resize completes within the request deadline and can be retried without ambiguity; stick with synchronous processing until workload measurements justify another durable component.

Webhook-only designs are attractive because they remove a visible application step, but they blur intent. A bucket may contain test objects, abandoned uploads, lifecycle copies, or writes from another trusted service. Finalize-only designs have the opposite blind spot when a client disappears. The outbox plus reconciliation model costs a state table and an operator-owned scan, yet it preserves both intent and repairability. That's the trade.

Observe queue age rather than only queue depth, unique jobs alongside delivery attempts, and terminal decode outcomes separately from transient attempts. Track originals waiting for each variant, superseded completions, reconciler lag, and conditional-write conflicts. Storage bytes, requests, egress, decoding CPU, and retained duplicate versions are the cost units worth measuring. A generic “jobs processed” dashboard won't explain a missing thumbnail.

Roll out around the commit boundary

Start with one upload class, one rendition, a dedicated object prefix, and worker concurrency below the decoder's measured memory ceiling. Test duplicate messages, a notification that precedes finalize, a client that never finalizes, lease expiry after output creation, and replacement of an original while an older job is active. The assertions matter more than the injected timing: one committed source version maps to one logical job per variant and transform revision, stale work cannot become current, and every nonterminal state has a retry or reconciliation owner.

Canary by upload ID so every event for one image follows the same state machine. Rollback should stop new commits first, leave immutable originals intact, and drain or park already committed jobs. Only after status records reconcile should a lifecycle policy remove abandoned originals or obsolete renditions.

The final acceptance test is blunt: given an upload ID, can an operator determine from durable state whether the original was merely transferred, accepted by policy, queued, rendered, superseded, or rejected? If the answer requires logs from a particular process, the architecture still has a commit gap.

References

  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • MDN, Using XMLHttpRequest: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.28361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon deep search requires LLM agents to iteratively decompose complex information needs, gather evidence from external sources, and maintain a reliable research state under multiple constraints. A central challenge is that early mistakes can be amplified over the search trajectory: agents may anchor on an incorrect candidate, collect partially supporting evidence, overlook contradictions, and accumulate errors that misguide subsequent reasoning. We propose FALCA, a falsification-aware framework that formulates deep search as a propose-falsify process. FALCA adopts a collaborative Searcher-Falsifier architecture, where the Searcher proposes candidate answers or sub-answers, while independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence, check unmet constraints, identify conflicts, and produce concise falsification reports for research-state revision. To strengthen this loop, we introduce falsification-aware training, combining SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Experiments on five search benchmarks show that FALCA improves long-horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations, while reducing confirmation bias and error accumulation through more effective falsification and research-state revision.

title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
description:
arXiv:2610.29098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

title: Conditional Imaging for Privacy-Preserving Visual Sensing
description:
arXiv:2610.28835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional visual sensing faces a fundamental dilemma: information that should remain private today may need to be recovered tomorrow. This challenge is becoming increasingly important as cameras become pervasive in our daily surroundings. Existing safeguards either protect visual content only after an image is formed or suppress information during capture in ways that prevent its later recovery. Here, we show through an information-theoretic analysis that privacy and recoverability cannot be achieved simultaneously in static optical systems. Information preserved in a measurement for later reconstruction also remains available to an observer of that measurement, limiting the privacy such systems can provide. To overcome this limitation, we introduce conditional imaging, an imaging approach that changes the optical state for every captured frame. The measurement alone conceals the scene, while knowledge of the corresponding physical system state enables its reconstruction. We analyze how the optical parameters determine the information that can be recovered and use this analysis to guide the design of a camera prototype. We evaluate the system on a captured dataset of human faces using increasingly powerful attempts to recover the scene, from direct visualization and computational inversion to learned reconstruction and identity recognition. Our experiments show that conditional imaging preserves identity in authorized reconstructions while withholding visual information from observers without access to the system state. By making the physical state of the camera part of the information needed for reconstruction, conditional imaging enables visual information to be protected at the point of capture while remaining recoverable for future authorized use.

title: Big Claims, Small Margins: Do Reported GraphLLM Gains Survive Simple Baselines?
description:
arXiv:2610.28714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based methods for node classification on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) routinely report state-of-the-art accuracy. We ask how these results compare with inexpensive baselines run on the same splits. On the splits of three recent studies, we tune four baseline representatives with validation-only selection and compare them with the highest mean that each paper reports for an LLM-based method in the matched setting. Correct & Smooth on TF-IDF features trails this reference by a median of 2.3 percentage points, and an MLP on frozen e5-large-v2 embeddings by 2.8 points. Correct & Smooth is within 3 points of the reference or better on 15 of 24 tasks, but the reference is significantly higher on 12 of 22 testable tasks, so several reported gains remain substantial. Reading released code next to the papers, we also document evaluation risks: selection of hyperparameters or checkpoints on the test set, labels of test-pool nodes used in training, baseline numbers reused without disclosure, and a text-label misalignment in a released Cora loader. Reports of the same method on the same split also differ by up to 12.5 points across papers whose configurations are not documented to match.

title: DynaWeave: Learning to Adapt through Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.29443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools to complete tasks in stateful environments. However, many training environments remain largely static apart from changes caused by the agent's own actions, whereas external events introduced by other users, services, or sudden contingencies in real environments can invalidate ongoing plans. To address this gap, we introduce DynaWeave, an automated synthesis framework that transforms existing static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios. The framework generates exogenous events relevant to each task, covering changes in task requirements, environment state, and external information. It uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to represent dependencies between events and an execution engine to activate them during agent interaction. A dynamic verifier revises only the evaluation checks affected by events that actually occur and retains all other checks. Using DynaWeave, we collect 2,095 verified interaction trajectories across 36 environments and use them for supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5 models. Experiments on Gaia2, CostBench, and ToolMaze show that DynaWeave achieves consistent improvements in overall performance across all three evaluated model sizes, increasing the task completion rate on CostBench by 67.34 percentage points and even exceeding the performance of Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview on ToolMaze. These results support dynamic scenario synthesis as a practical approach to training agents to adapt to changing environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/DynaWeave.
