title: How to Build a Finance AI Agent With Audit Trails, Controls, and Human Oversight
description:
Here’s a truth about building AI agents for finance that nobody puts in the tutorial: the agent intelligence is maybe 30 percent of the work. The audit trail, the access controls, the human oversight checkpoints, the compliance documentation, that’s the other 70 percent. And that 70 percent is what determines whether your agent runs in production or gets killed in the compliance review before it processes a single transaction.

We learned this the expensive way on our first finance AI agent deployment. Built a beautiful underwriting agent. Elegant reasoning. Clean tool use. Impressive accuracy on test data. The compliance team looked at it for two hours and rejected it because they couldn’t answer one question: “If a regulator asks why the agent recommended denying this loan application, can you show them the exact data and reasoning that produced that recommendation?”

We couldn’t. The agent worked. It just didn’t prove it worked. And in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

This article is the guide we wish existed when we started. It covers the audit trail architecture, the access control design, the human oversight implementation, and the code patterns that make a finance AI agent not just functional but auditable, controllable, and compliant.

If you’re building agents that touch money, customer data, or regulatory workflows, this is the engineering that separates a demo from a deployment.

The audit trail isn’t logging. It’s the primary deliverable

Most developers think of audit trails as application logging. Write some events to a log file. Query them when something goes wrong. That’s not what finance compliance requires.

A finance audit trail must capture what data the agent received, what reasoning it applied, what tools it called, what each tool returned, what decision it reached, how confident it was, and what action it took, for every single transaction. And it must store this immutably for seven to ten years in a format that a non-technical regulator can review.

Here’s the data model:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional
import hashlib
import json


class EvaluationType(Enum):
    DETERMINISTIC = "deterministic"
    AI_ASSISTED = "ai_assisted"
    HUMAN_REVIEWED = "human_reviewed"


class ActionType(Enum):
    AUTO_APPROVED = "auto_approved"
    AUTO_DENIED = "auto_denied"
    ESCALATED = "escalated"
    PENDING_REVIEW = "pending_review"


@dataclass
class AuditRecord:
    """Immutable record of every agent decision."""
    record_id: str
    timestamp: datetime
    agent_id: str
    agent_version: str

    # What was evaluated
    transaction_id: str
    transaction_type: str
    input_data_hash: str          # SHA-256 of exact input
    input_data_snapshot: dict      # Frozen copy of input state

    # How it was evaluated
    evaluation_type: EvaluationType
    rules_applied: list[str]       # Rule IDs for deterministic checks
    model_version: Optional[str]   # For AI-assisted evaluations
    prompt_hash: Optional[str]     # For reproducibility

    # What was concluded
    decision: ActionType
    confidence: Optional[float]
    reasoning_chain: list[dict]    # Step-by-step reasoning

    # What happened next
    escalated_to: Optional[str]
    human_reviewer: Optional[str]
    human_decision: Optional[str]
    human_override_reason: Optional[str]
    human_decision_timestamp: Optional[datetime]

    # Integrity
    previous_record_hash: Optional[str]  # Chain integrity
    record_hash: str = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        """Compute hash for tamper detection."""
        content = json.dumps({
            'record_id': self.record_id,
            'transaction_id': self.transaction_id,
            'input_data_hash': self.input_data_hash,
            'decision': self.decision.value,
            'timestamp': self.timestamp.isoformat(),
            'previous_hash': self.previous_record_hash
        }, sort_keys=True)
        self.record_hash = hashlib.sha256(content.encode()).hexdigest()

Two fields in this model deserve specific attention.

input_data_hash and input_data_snapshot serve different purposes. The hash proves that the data hasn’t been modified since the decision was made. The snapshot preserves the exact data state at decision time, because the source data in the ERP may change after the agent evaluated it, and the regulator needs to see what the agent saw, not what the database currently contains.

previous_record_hash creates a chain where tampering with any historical record breaks the hash chain on every subsequent record. This isn’t blockchain, it’s a simple integrity mechanism that makes after-the-fact modification detectable.

The storage architecture matters:

class AuditStore:
    """Append-only audit storage with hot and cold tiers."""

    def __init__(self, hot_store, cold_store, retention_years=7):
        self.hot = hot_store      # PostgreSQL - last 90 days, fast queries
        self.cold = cold_store    # S3 + Parquet - long-term, cost-efficient
        self.retention = retention_years

    async def append(self, record: AuditRecord) -> str:
        """Write to hot store. Never update. Never delete."""
        # Verify chain integrity
        last_record = await self.hot.get_latest(record.agent_id)
        if last_record and record.previous_record_hash != last_record.record_hash:
            raise IntegrityError("Chain broken - previous hash mismatch")

        await self.hot.insert(record)
        return record.record_hash

    async def archive(self, older_than_days=90):
        """Move aged records to cold storage. Hot store stays fast."""
        records = await self.hot.get_older_than(older_than_days)
        await self.cold.write_parquet(records)
        # Mark as archived in hot store - never delete
        await self.hot.mark_archived(records)

The append-only constraint is non-negotiable. No updates. No deletes. No “soft deletes.” If a record needs correction, you append a correction record that references the original. The original stays forever.

The access control layer: least privilege isn’t optional

The agent’s service account should have exactly the permissions it needs and nothing more. This sounds obvious. In practice, it’s the control that most teams get wrong because scoping permissions precisely requires understanding every data access and system interaction the agent performs.

class AgentPermissions:
    """Define and enforce what the agent can access and do."""

    def __init__(self, agent_role: str):
        self.role = agent_role
        self.permissions = self._load_permissions(agent_role)

    def _load_permissions(self, role: str) -> dict:
        """Each agent role has explicit read/write scopes."""
        roles = {
            "ap_processor": {
                "read": [
                    "invoices",
                    "purchase_orders", 
                    "goods_receipts",
                    "vendor_master",        # Read vendor info
                    "approval_matrix",      # Read routing rules
                ],
                "write": [
                    "invoices.status",       # Update processing status
                    "invoices.match_result", # Record match outcome
                    "approval_queue",        # Route for approval
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "payments.execute",     # Cannot trigger payments
                    "vendor_master.modify", # Cannot change vendor data
                    "general_ledger",       # No GL access
                    "payroll",              # No payroll access
                    "treasury",             # No treasury access
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": 100_000,  # Escalate above this
            },
            "underwriting_analyst": {
                "read": [
                    "loan_applications",
                    "credit_bureau_data",
                    "financial_documents",
                    "compliance_rules",
                ],
                "write": [
                    "applications.risk_assessment",
                    "applications.recommendation",
                    "escalation_queue",
                ],
                "blocked": [
                    "applications.approve",  # Cannot approve loans
                    "applications.deny",     # Cannot deny loans
                    "disbursement",          # No access to funds
                ],
                "amount_ceiling": None,  # All amounts escalate
            }
        }
        return roles.get(role, {"read": [], "write": [], "blocked": []})

    def check_access(self, operation: str, resource: str) -> bool:
        """Enforce permission before every system interaction."""
        if resource in self.permissions.get("blocked", []):
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' is blocked from '{resource}'"
            )

        allowed_resources = self.permissions.get(operation, [])
        if resource not in allowed_resources:
            raise PermissionDenied(
                f"Agent role '{self.role}' lacks '{operation}' on '{resource}'"
            )
        return True

The blocked list is as important as the read and write lists. Explicitly defining what the agent cannot access, even when those resources exist in the same system, creates a documented boundary that compliance teams can review. An AP processing agent that has no path to the payroll system, the treasury system, or the general ledger is an agent whose blast radius is bounded by design.

The amount_ceiling field is the operational authority limit. Transactions above this threshold escalate to a human regardless of how confident the agent is. The ceiling is a business decision, not a technical one, set by the finance leadership based on the organisation’s risk tolerance.

Human oversight: the checkpoint architecture

Human-in-the-loop for finance agents isn’t “a human can review if they want.” It’s a set of defined checkpoints where the agent must stop, present its work, and receive human authorisation before proceeding.

class OversightCheckpoint:
    """Defines when and how the agent pauses for human review."""

    def __init__(self, rules: list[dict]):
        self.rules = rules

    async def evaluate(
        self, 
        transaction: dict,
        agent_assessment: dict,
        audit_trail: list[AuditRecord]
    ) -> CheckpointDecision:
        """Determine if human review is required."""

        for rule in self.rules:
            if self._matches(rule, transaction, agent_assessment):
                return CheckpointDecision(
                    requires_human=True,
                    reason=rule["reason"],
                    reviewer_role=rule["reviewer_role"],
                    context=self._assemble_context(
                        transaction, agent_assessment, audit_trail
                    ),
                    sla_hours=rule.get("sla_hours", 24)
                )

        return CheckpointDecision(requires_human=False)

    def _matches(self, rule, transaction, assessment) -> bool:
        """Check if this transaction triggers a checkpoint."""
        checks = {
            "amount_exceeds": lambda: (
                transaction.get("amount", 0) > rule.get("threshold", 0)
            ),
            "confidence_below": lambda: (
                assessment.get("confidence", 1.0) < rule.get("threshold", 0.85)
            ),
            "new_counterparty": lambda: (
                transaction.get("counterparty_history_days", 999) < 
                rule.get("minimum_days", 90)
            ),
            "exception_type": lambda: (
                assessment.get("exception_type") in 
                rule.get("escalation_types", [])
            ),
            "regulatory_flag": lambda: (
                assessment.get("regulatory_flags", []) != []
            ),
        }

        check_fn = checks.get(rule["condition"])
        return check_fn() if check_fn else False

    def _assemble_context(self, transaction, assessment, trail) -> dict:
        """Give the human everything they need to make a decision."""
        return {
            "transaction_summary": transaction,
            "agent_recommendation": assessment.get("recommendation"),
            "agent_confidence": assessment.get("confidence"),
            "agent_reasoning": assessment.get("reasoning_chain"),
            "relevant_history": self._get_relevant_history(transaction),
            "applicable_rules": assessment.get("rules_checked"),
            "escalation_reason": assessment.get("escalation_reason"),
            "suggested_action": assessment.get("suggested_action"),
            "audit_trail": [r.record_id for r in trail[-5:]],  # Last 5 steps
        }


# Checkpoint rules configuration
CHECKPOINT_RULES = [
    {
        "condition": "amount_exceeds",
        "threshold": 100_000,
        "reason": "Transaction exceeds autonomous authority limit",
        "reviewer_role": "senior_finance",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
    {
        "condition": "confidence_below",
        "threshold": 0.85,
        "reason": "Agent confidence below threshold",
        "reviewer_role": "domain_specialist",
        "sla_hours": 8
    },
    {
        "condition": "new_counterparty",
        "minimum_days": 90,
        "reason": "Counterparty has less than 90 days of history",
        "reviewer_role": "risk_analyst",
        "sla_hours": 24
    },
    {
        "condition": "regulatory_flag",
        "reason": "Transaction flagged for regulatory review",
        "reviewer_role": "compliance_officer",
        "sla_hours": 4
    },
]

The _assemble_context method is where the oversight becomes genuinely useful rather than merely procedural. A human reviewer who receives “please review this transaction” makes a worse decision than one who receives the transaction data, the agent’s recommendation, the reasoning chain, the applicable rules, and the suggested action. The context assembly is what makes human oversight efficient, the human starts with understanding, not investigation.

The sla_hours field is the detail that operational teams care about. A checkpoint without a response deadline creates a queue that grows without bound. The SLA ensures that escalated transactions are reviewed within a defined window, and transactions that aren’t reviewed within the SLA trigger secondary escalation.

Putting it together: the compliant agent loop

Here’s how the components compose into a complete agent execution loop:

class FinanceAgent:
    """A finance agent that's auditable, controlled, and supervised."""

    def __init__(self, tools, permissions, checkpoints, audit_store, llm):
        self.tools = tools
        self.permissions = permissions
        self.checkpoints = checkpoints
        self.audit = audit_store
        self.llm = llm

    async def process(self, transaction: dict) -> ProcessingResult:
        trail = []

        # Step 1: Deterministic compliance checks first
        compliance_result = await self._run_compliance_checks(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "compliance_check", 
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, compliance_result
        ))

        if not compliance_result.passed:
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="compliance_failed",
                details=compliance_result.failures,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 2: AI-assisted assessment where judgment is needed
        assessment = await self._run_ai_assessment(transaction)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "ai_assessment",
            EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, assessment
        ))

        # Step 3: Check if human oversight is required
        checkpoint = await self.checkpoints.evaluate(
            transaction, assessment, trail
        )

        if checkpoint.requires_human:
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "escalated",
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED, 
                {"reason": checkpoint.reason}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="pending_human_review",
                context=checkpoint.context,
                reviewer=checkpoint.reviewer_role,
                sla=checkpoint.sla_hours,
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 4: Execute within authority
        self.permissions.check_access("write", f"{transaction['type']}.status")

        if transaction.get("amount", 0) > self.permissions.permissions.get(
            "amount_ceiling", float("inf")
        ):
            trail.append(await self._audit(
                transaction, "amount_escalation",
                EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC,
                {"ceiling": self.permissions.permissions["amount_ceiling"]}
            ))
            return ProcessingResult(
                status="escalated_amount_ceiling",
                audit_trail=trail
            )

        # Step 5: Execute and document
        action_result = await self._execute_action(transaction, assessment)
        trail.append(await self._audit(
            transaction, "action_executed",
            EvaluationType.DETERMINISTIC, action_result
        ))

        return ProcessingResult(
            status="completed",
            action=action_result,
            audit_trail=trail
        )

    async def _audit(self, transaction, step, eval_type, data) -> AuditRecord:
        """Every step gets an immutable audit record."""
        record = AuditRecord(
            record_id=generate_uuid(),
            timestamp=datetime.utcnow(),
            agent_id=self.agent_id,
            agent_version=self.version,
            transaction_id=transaction["id"],
            transaction_type=transaction["type"],
            input_data_hash=hash_data(transaction),
            input_data_snapshot=freeze(transaction),
            evaluation_type=eval_type,
            rules_applied=data.get("rules", []),
            model_version=self.llm.model_version if eval_type == 
                EvaluationType.AI_ASSISTED else None,
            prompt_hash=data.get("prompt_hash"),
            decision=data.get("decision", ActionType.PENDING_REVIEW),
            confidence=data.get("confidence"),
            reasoning_chain=data.get("reasoning", []),
            escalated_to=data.get("escalated_to"),
            human_reviewer=None,
            human_decision=None,
            human_override_reason=None,
            human_decision_timestamp=None,
            previous_record_hash=await self.audit.get_latest_hash(
                transaction["id"]
            )
        )
        await self.audit.append(record)
        return record

The execution order matters. Compliance checks run first, deterministic, binary, fast. If the transaction fails a regulatory requirement, there’s no point running the AI assessment. The AI assessment runs second, only for transactions that need interpretive evaluation. The checkpoint evaluation runs third, comparing the transaction characteristics and agent confidence against the oversight rules. The action execution runs last, only for transactions that passed compliance, received a confident assessment, and didn’t trigger a checkpoint.

Every step produces an audit record. The complete chain for a single transaction typically contains four to six records, each linked to the previous by hash. A regulator reviewing a decision can trace the complete chain: what data came in, what compliance checks passed, what the AI assessed and why, whether a human reviewed it, and what action was taken.

The testing that makes compliance teams comfortable

The code above gets you an architecture. The testing below gets you the approval to deploy it.

# Golden test set: known-outcome transactions for regression testing
class ComplianceRegressionSuite:
    """Run against every agent update, every prompt change, every model version."""

    def __init__(self, golden_set_path: str, drift_threshold: float = 0.02):
        self.golden_set = load_golden_set(golden_set_path)
        self.threshold = drift_threshold  # Max 2% decision drift

    async def run(self, agent: FinanceAgent) -> RegressionResult:
        results = []
        for case in self.golden_set:
            actual = await agent.process(case.transaction)
            results.append({
                "case_id": case.id,
                "expected_decision": case.expected_decision,
                "actual_decision": actual.status,
                "match": actual.status == case.expected_decision,
                "confidence": actual.audit_trail[-1].confidence
            })

        match_rate = sum(r["match"] for r in results) / len(results)
        drift = 1.0 - match_rate

        return RegressionResult(
            passed=drift <= self.threshold,
            match_rate=match_rate,
            drift=drift,
            failures=[r for r in results if not r["match"]],
            recommendation="BLOCK" if drift > self.threshold else "APPROVE"
        )

The golden test set contains 300 to 500 transactions with known correct outcomes, labelled by experienced finance professionals, not by the development team. Every agent update, every prompt change, and every model version upgrade runs against this set. If the decision outcomes drift by more than 2 percent from the baseline, the update is blocked.

This regression suite is what we point to when compliance asks “how do you know the agent still works correctly after a change?” The answer is: we run it against 500 transactions where we know the right answer, and we block any change that moves the outcomes by more than 2 percent.

For a deeper dive into the full development lifecycle, from workflow assessment through architecture selection, integration patterns, and deployment, our guide on how to build finance AI agents covers the engineering decisions we make before writing any agent code.

What most teams get wrong

Three patterns consistently cause compliance rejections or production failures.

Building the audit trail as an afterthought. If the audit architecture isn’t designed before the agent logic, the audit records won’t capture the right data at the right granularity. Retrofitting audit trails onto a working agent means re-engineering the decision flow to emit records at each step, which is more expensive than building it in from the start.

Testing with synthetic data only. Compliance teams want to see the agent’s performance on real transactions, transactions that humans have already processed with known correct outcomes. Synthetic test data proves the code works. Real test data proves the agent works on your actual business workflows.

Treating the human oversight as a failure mode rather than a design feature. The checkpoint architecture isn’t the system failing and asking for help. It’s the system correctly identifying which transactions need human judgment and routing them efficiently. The 20 to 30 percent of transactions that escalate aren’t a limitation, they’re the system working as designed.

The bottom line for finance developers

A finance AI agent that works but can’t prove it works is a demo, not a deployment. The audit trail, the access controls, and the human oversight checkpoints are what transform working code into a production system that compliance teams approve, regulators can examine, and operations teams trust.

Build the audit architecture first. Design the permissions before the agent logic. Define the oversight checkpoints with the compliance team, not for them. Test against real transactions with known outcomes. And treat every deployment as the beginning of a continuous proving process, not the end of a build project.

For teams ready to build finance agents that survive audit, the bespoke AI agent development practice at Dextra Labs designs and deploys agents with the compliance architecture described in this article as a foundational requirement, not an add-on. The audit trail, the access controls, and the oversight checkpoints are built into the agent from day one, because in finance, working without proving it is the same as not working.

title: Cold Chain, Cold Comfort: What the Danfoss Case Says About Buying Exposed Equipment
description:
Cold Chain, Cold Comfort: What the Danfoss Case Says About Buying Exposed Equipment

The French supermarket attack of 11 October 2026 is usually filed under incident response. It belongs equally in procurement. Every controller in the affected class was bought, installed and configured by somebody, and the configuration that put a control panel on a public address was a purchasing and commissioning decision before it was a security one.
The exposure data makes that case more sharply than any policy document.

What was purchased

Danfoss confirmed its equipment was targeted in the attack on cooling systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Its statement separated the fleet into two groups: AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 controllers that no longer receive security updates, and AK-SM800A controllers running outdated firmware. The StoreView panel is the interface in front of those controllers.
Both groups share a property that no datasheet advertises. They can be reached on the public internet, and a portion of them were. Censys counted 2,991 exposed StoreView panels on 11 October, 1,825 of them in France, and by 14 October the French figure had fallen 71% to 537.
The version distribution describes a purchasing pattern as much as a patching pattern. On 11 October, 74% of French exposed instances ran below 4.3.1, the release covering CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Poland sat at 81%, Romania at 80% and Belgium at 76%. The current release is 5.3.2.
A fleet with three quarters of its exposed units behind a fix that shipped over a year earlier is not a fleet with a patching backlog. It is a fleet whose owners did not know they held a patching obligation, which is a contract problem.

The measurement that belongs in a tender

An independent engine cannot read a firmware version, but it can establish whether a class of equipment tends to face the internet. That is a question a buyer can ask before signing.
The ZoomEye header query run on 22 October 2026 is one way to obtain the evidence:
| Query | Result |
| --- | --- |
| http.header="Danfoss" | 260 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && port="80" | 120 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && port="443" | 132 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="NL" | 54 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="US" | 28 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="DE" | 25 |
| http.header="Danfoss" && country="FR" | 1 |
What a buyer should not do is read 260 as a quality verdict on the vendor. It is a count of assets emitting a particular header. What a buyer can do is use the technique on the class of equipment actually being considered, record the result, and ask the supplier why a device with a web management interface appears on the public internet at all.
The Netherlands figure of 54 against a French figure of 1 four days after a French incident is a useful thought experiment in that conversation. The header string does not concentrate where the incident happened; it concentrates wherever those devices were installed and configured with public reachability.

The three questions a specification should force

The incident supplies the questions, and they are not the usual security questionnaire items.

  1. Does the device need a public address to function? A refrigeration control panel that supports remote maintenance is not the same product as one that requires a public interface. If the vendor's answer is that internet connectivity is optional, the commissioning decision becomes the operator's to defend.
  2. What is the supported-version lifetime, in writing? Danfoss divided its fleet into models still receiving updates and models that no longer do. A buyer who does not know which side of that line a purchased controller sits on has bought an indefinite obligation with a finite vendor commitment.
  3. Who patches it, and with what outage? The Claroty demonstration of CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451 chained to remote code execution and falsified temperature readings describes a device whose compromise is measured in stock loss. The patch for it competes with a refrigeration loop that cannot be safely restarted at will. That trade-off belongs in the contract, not in the incident review.

Why disconnection is a purchasing signal

Censys concluded that operators disconnected panels rather than patched them, because all three version categories shrank by roughly 70%, including the ones already on patched releases. That is a rational choice for a single site under pressure. Across a market it is a signal that the equipment's maintenance model does not accommodate firmware updates.
A buyer reading that signal has three options, and only one of them is comfortable. Accept the model and budget for disconnection as a routine control. Accept the model and negotiate an update window into the maintenance contract. Or buy equipment whose update path does not require a cold-chain risk assessment.
None of this requires naming a vendor as negligent. The three CVEs were patched, the versions were published, and the vendor stated which models remain supported. The gap sits in the space between a shipped fix and a fleet that could apply it.

A practical procurement checklist

For the next refrigeration, HVAC or building-management procurement round:

  • Search the public internet for the equipment class before signing, using a fixed query and recording the date.
  • Ask for the supported-version end date of every controller model in the bid, not the product family.
  • Ask what the vendor's remote-access architecture requires, and whether the panel can sit behind a broker rather than on a public address.
  • Write a firmware update window into the maintenance contract, with an agreed outage tolerance for the refrigeration loop.
  • Re-run the external query after commissioning and compare it with the pre-purchase baseline. The last item is where a tool like ZoomEye earns its place in a procurement file: not as a compliance tick, but as evidence that the configuration is what the specification said it would be.

The uncomfortable takeaway

The French operators who disconnected their panels in 72 hours acted faster than their contracts had prepared them to act. The equipment worked, the fixes existed, and the mechanism to apply them did not.
That is the part of this incident worth carrying into a supplier negotiation. Exposure counts are volatile and engine-dependent. A maintenance model that expects a controller to be patched on a live refrigeration loop is a durable thing to fix.

References

  • Infosecurity Magazine, "France: Internet-Exposed Danfoss Controllers Drop 71% After Cyber-Attack", https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/france-expose-danfoss-controllers/
  • Censys, "Frostbitten in France: A Danfoss StoreView internet exposure report", https://censys.com/blog/frostbitten-in-france-a-danfoss-storeview-internet-exposure-report/
  • ZoomEye search syntax baseline, https://zoomeye.ai/agent.md

title: HumanCentric-Scenes-AI: A Human-Curated Multimodal Dataset of AI-Generated Human-Centric Scenes Across Surveillance, Occupational Portraits, AI-Edited Images, and Short-Form Video
description:
arXiv:2610.29045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56 AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and per-stimulus metadata. We report depicted-gender distributions from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset and subject-category coverage for the Video subset. HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research, and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of generative models.

title: Go RAG Citations Point to Wrong Page: Debug Chunk Offset Metadata
description:
A citation span is valid only when its text, byte offsets, page label, and document version come from the same parse. For an edtech policy lookup system that aggregates catalogs and compliance documents from several sources, reject an ingestion run that cannot preserve that lineage; do not patch page numbers after retrieval.

TL;DR: re-parse each source version once, derive chunks and citation metadata from that parse, and atomically replace the indexed version. Keep the prior version available for rollback. After any parser or chunker change, spot-check ten citations against the rendered source because this failure is silent: retrieval can return exactly the right policy sentence while the UI opens the wrong page.

This is a data-provenance problem before it is a ranking problem. Tuning embeddings, adding a reranker, or changing the prompt may move which chunk wins, but none can repair coordinates computed over different text.

It fails quietly.

Why can the answer be right while its citation opens the wrong page?

A common ingestion path has two representations of one PDF. The chunker reads normalized text: ligatures are expanded, repeated headers disappear, and whitespace collapses. A separate utility later scans raw extracted text to calculate offsets or pages. Once either representation removes one character, every later absolute offset can drift; once it removes a header, the page boundary can drift too. The retrieved chunk still contains the right policy language, so answer-quality tests pass. The citation target is already corrupt.

Freshness makes the defect harder to see. Suppose a course provider revises its accessibility policy while an index update is in flight. Search may retrieve a chunk from the new text and attach coordinates from the old document unless every record carries an immutable source version. A citation request must compare that stored version with the version being rendered. A mismatch should produce a controlled stale-citation result, not a confident jump into whichever file happens to be current.

Short version: coordinates are derived data.

For capacity planning, count the expensive unit correctly. A change to the chunker is a full corpus transformation, even when the embedding model remains unchanged, because every boundary and therefore every citation span may move. The operational budget includes parsing, validation, vector writes, retained old-version storage, and enough overlap to avoid serving a half-rebuilt collection. Treating this as a tiny metadata update creates an attractive but false rollout estimate.

Rebuild citation metadata from one parse

The safe ingestion contract has one owner for text coordinates. Parse a specific document version, retain its page boundaries, and pass that exact byte slice into the chunker. Each chunk stores document_id, document_version, start_byte, end_byte, start_page, end_page, and a digest of its text. Do not calculate any of those fields by searching for the chunk in a second extraction: repeated boilerplate can make the search ambiguous even when normalization happens to match.

Byte offsets need an explicit convention. The example below uses half-open UTF-8 byte intervals, [start, end), because Go slices use that representation. A browser client using UTF-16 code units cannot consume these numbers directly; either send byte-addressed spans to a service that owns rendering or convert against the same versioned text. Naming the unit in the schema is less glamorous than tuning retrieval, and far more useful during an incident.

Before coupling ingestion code to a request body, inspect the live capability record and take its method and path from discovery. This runnable Go program fetches the manifest, locates the verified vector-upsert path, retries rate limits with Retry-After when available, and fails with the real response body on other non-2xx statuses. Discovery itself is public, but the sample reads the shared key from the environment because the subsequent capability call will require the same Bearer convention.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string `json:"id"`
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    Path      string `json:"path"`
    Available bool   `json:"available"`
}

type manifest struct {
    Version      string       `json:"version"`
    GeneratedAt  string       `json:"generated_at"`
    Capabilities []capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if key == "" || baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL are required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    var body []byte
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, err = io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, body))
        }

        var result manifest
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        for _, item := range result.Capabilities {
            if item.Method == http.MethodPost && item.Path == "/v1/vector/upsert" {
                fmt.Printf("version=%s generated_at=%s id=%s method=%s path=%s available=%t\n",
                    result.Version, result.GeneratedAt, item.ID, item.Method, item.Path, item.Available)
                return
            }
        }
        panic("vector upsert capability is absent from discovery")
    }
    panic("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

The discovery result is the contract input, not a substitute for source lineage. Generate the integration from its declared schema, then attach the versioned chunk fields below to each record; if a future manifest changes, the ingestion build should detect that change before the corpus write begins. For a multi-source edtech catalog, this ordering matters because a provider PDF, a regulator bulletin, and an internal policy may each have different page extraction behavior, yet all three must arrive at the index with the same citation invariants. Keeping contract discovery and document parsing as separate gates makes the failure domain legible: a request-schema change stops the writer, while an offset mismatch rejects the document batch.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

type Page struct {
    Number int
    Text   string
}

type Chunk struct {
    DocumentID      string
    DocumentVersion string
    StartByte       int
    EndByte         int
    StartPage       int
    EndPage         int
    TextSHA256      string
    Text            string
}

type parsedPage struct {
    number int
    start  int
    end    int
}

func ingest(documentID, version string, pages []Page, maxBytes int) ([]Chunk, error) {
    if documentID == "" || version == "" || maxBytes < 1 || len(pages) == 0 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid ingestion input")
    }

    var source strings.Builder
    bounds := make([]parsedPage, 0, len(pages))
    for i, page := range pages {
        if i > 0 {
            source.WriteByte('\n')
        }
        start := source.Len()
        source.WriteString(page.Text)
        bounds = append(bounds, parsedPage{page.Number, start, source.Len()})
    }

    data := []byte(source.String())
    chunks := make([]Chunk, 0, (len(data)+maxBytes-1)/maxBytes)
    for start := 0; start < len(data); {
        end := start + maxBytes
        if end > len(data) {
            end = len(data)
        }
        for end < len(data) && end > start && (data[end]&0xc0) == 0x80 {
            end--
        }
        if end == start {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("maxBytes %d cannot hold next UTF-8 rune", maxBytes)
        }

        sum := sha256.Sum256(data[start:end])
        first, last, err := coveringPages(bounds, start, end)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        chunks = append(chunks, Chunk{
            DocumentID: documentID, DocumentVersion: version,
            StartByte: start, EndByte: end, StartPage: first, EndPage: last,
            TextSHA256: hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]), Text: string(data[start:end]),
        })
        start = end
    }
    return chunks, nil
}

func coveringPages(pages []parsedPage, start, end int) (int, int, error) {
    first, last := 0, 0
    for _, page := range pages {
        if start < page.end && end > page.start {
            if first == 0 {
                first = page.number
            }
            last = page.number
        }
    }
    if first == 0 {
        return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf("span [%d,%d) has no source page", start, end)
    }
    return first, last, nil
}

func main() {
    pages := []Page{
        {Number: 1, Text: "Enrollment policy: verify the learner's region."},
        {Number: 2, Text: "Accessibility policy: retain the accommodation record."},
    }
    chunks, err := ingest("policy-handbook", "sha256:7f83b165", pages, 64)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, chunk := range chunks {
        fmt.Printf("%d:%d pages=%d-%d hash=%s text=%q\n",
            chunk.StartByte, chunk.EndByte, chunk.StartPage, chunk.EndPage,
            chunk.TextSHA256[:12], chunk.Text)
    }
}

Production chunking will usually honor headings, paragraphs, token limits, and overlap rather than fixed bytes. That does not change the invariant. Semantic boundaries choose the chunk; the same parse supplies the span. If overlap is used, two records may legitimately cover some of the same bytes, and their digests still make each record independently verifiable.

Publish the new vectors only after validation succeeds. With an index that supports namespaces or aliases, write under the immutable document version and switch the read pointer after the batch is complete. With an index that lacks an atomic alias operation, put the active version in application-owned metadata and make queries filter on it. In either design, deletion of the old version is delayed until the rollback window closes.

Choosing the retrieval layer without confusing it with the fix

Vector products differ in operational ownership and filtering surfaces, but none can reconstruct lost provenance. The decision below is about who carries the on-call burden and where version filtering lives; it is not a claim that one engine produces more truthful citations.

Option Operating model Useful fit for this runbook Boundary to plan for
Elasticsearch Self-managed or Elastic-managed search platform Teams already combining lexical search, vector search, and document filters Cluster sizing, upgrades, and index lifecycle remain substantial concerns when self-hosted
Pinecone Managed vector database Teams that want namespaces and metadata filtering without operating the database The application still owns parsing, source versions, and span validation
Weaviate Open-source database with cloud and self-managed choices Teams that value deployment choice and collection-level vector search More deployment freedom also means an explicit buy-versus-build decision for operations
Qdrant Open-source vector database with managed cloud Teams that want payload filtering and the option to self-host Payload fields preserve only the metadata the ingestion pipeline supplies correctly
Infrai Managed REST aggregation surface Teams adding retrieval beside other backend capabilities can inspect a public, self-describing discovery response with schemas and runnable examples before wiring a capability It does not remove the need to define and test the document-version and offset contract

The final row's discovery surface is unusual in a useful way: one unauthenticated discovery request describes the request schema, response schema, billing, and runnable examples, so evaluating an integration starts from machine-readable behavior rather than SDK archaeology. Its shared API surface can reduce credential and integration sprawl for a platform team, but that advantage is separate from citation correctness.

For Infrai, one API key covers all 295 routes in 20 modules, with usage consolidated into one bill. In this workflow, that means a platform team can govern one credential convention while adding adjacent parsing or storage capabilities, instead of distributing another set of service keys and reconciling another vendor invoice; it does not justify using a capability whose declared metadata or residency does not meet the policy-search requirements.

My default choice for a small platform team is managed infrastructure when its metadata filtering and version-isolation model meet the rollback requirement; fewer database pages at 02:00 is real engineering value. I would self-host when data residency, extension requirements, or sustained scale justify owning upgrades and capacity. The burden of proof belongs on the self-hosted option because its tail work lands on the same people carrying the ingestion SLO.

Decision Managed service Self-hosted engine
On-call load Vendor owns more of the storage control plane Team owns upgrades, saturation, backups, and recovery tests
Control Constrained by exposed APIs and service regions Greater control over topology and extensions
Lock-in Reduce it with portable records and export tests Reduce it with reproducible builds and documented restore drills
Capacity Validate quotas and batch-write behavior Model peak rebuild load, not only steady query traffic

No price row. A stale price table will not tell you who can complete a corpus rebuild inside the freshness objective, and that is the capacity question that matters here.

Correctness wins.

Verify before the pointer moves

Set two distinct objectives. The freshness SLO measures how long a newly approved policy version takes to become searchable. A citation-integrity SLO measures whether a returned span resolves to the stored chunk text in the same document version. Combining them conceals the exact trade-off during a rebuild: serving the prior verified version for a few more minutes may be preferable to serving fresh text with unverified coordinates.

Before activation, verify every chunk mechanically. Check 0 <= start_byte < end_byte <= len(parsed_text), slice the source, recompute the digest, and require equality with the stored chunk digest. Confirm that page coverage contains the span and that every record has the intended document version. Also reject mixed parser or chunker configuration IDs within one versioned batch if those IDs are part of your ingestion contract.

Then inspect the rendered result. Spot-check ten citations after every chunker change: include the first and last chunk, at least one span crossing a page boundary, non-ASCII text, repeated header text, and documents from more than one upstream source. Ten is a release check from the problem constraints, not statistical proof. If the corpus has materially different formats, sample each format and automate a larger validation set.

Retrieval evaluation comes after lineage validation. Ask policy questions whose answers are known to occur on specific pages, query the candidate index, and assert both answer relevance and citation resolution. A passing retrieval score with a failing span digest blocks activation. So does a correct span attached to the wrong document version.

Watch four rollout signals: ingestion rejection count, citation version-mismatch count, span-digest mismatch count, and time from source approval to active version. Alerting on answer-generation errors alone misses this class of defect completely.

Roll back the index, not the evidence

Keep the previous verified index version immutable until the new version has passed validation and remained healthy through the chosen observation window. Rollback is a pointer change: stop activating the candidate version, restore reads to the prior version, and preserve the failed batch for diagnosis. Do not mutate its offsets in place, because that destroys the evidence needed to identify which parser or chunker introduced drift.

The rollback trigger should be crisp. Any digest mismatch is correctness failure, not a warning; a version mismatch means the renderer must refuse the jump; freshness-budget exhaustion may justify continuing to serve the older verified version while ingestion is investigated. Recovery ends only after the source is parsed again and all derived records are replaced as one version.

This design has an unappealing cost: for a while, two versions consume storage, and a full rebuild can double write pressure. Plan for it. Capacity headroom and a reversible cutover are cheaper than asking compliance users to guess which page supports an answer.

title: ART-MPG: Autoregressive R/T Manifold Path Guiding
description:
arXiv:2610.29049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Specular chains concentrate important transport in small regions of path space and the structure depends on chain topology. We introduce ART-MPG, a compact neural model that samples chain length, an autoregressive reflection/transmission (R/T) string, and a direction from a topology-conditioned four-component von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture. We extend the repeated trial weighting in Manifold Path Guiding (MPG) by conditioning retry sampling on both chain length and the sampled R/T string, accounting for its known mass outside the stochastic re-hit trials. For a fixed proposal and target chain, this preserves the ideal expectation while reducing the expected retry count and reciprocal-estimator variance compared with retries conditioned on chain length alone. We distinguish the formal unbiasedness result from the capped and clamped renderer used in experiments. We evaluate fourteen scenes across a range of samples per pixel (SPP) against existing online and offline rendering algorithms. Our method consistently produces lower mean squared error at equal SPP than the online and offline baselines, with lower standard deviation across runs.

title: Disentangling Depression from Cognitive Decline in Elderly Speech Using Concurrent Clinical Assessments
description:
arXiv:2610.26890v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Detecting depression from speech in elderly patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is complicated by overlapping acoustic effects of cognitive decline. Without disentangling these, classifiers risk learning cognitive rather than depression-specific patterns. We present a Korean elderly speech corpus of 89 MCI speakers collected over three years with concurrent depression (SGDS) and cognitive (MMSE) assessments. Both linear mixed-effects models and partial correlations identify the same pattern: of seven feature groups, only formant features are associated with depression after controlling for cognitive function, while widely used F0 features carry no signal. The F1+F2 subset achieves UAR 0.760 with just 12 features, outperforming both the full eGeMAPS baseline and self-supervised representations. These findings show that concurrent clinical assessments can identify interpretable, depression-specific acoustic markers in populations where cognitive and affective symptoms co-occur.

title: DGCM-SSFA: Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulation and Sparse Strip Frequency Attention for Efficient 3T-to-7T MRI Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.29141v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesizing high-fidelity 7T MRI from routinely acquired 3T scans offers a practical pathway to enhanced neuroimaging without the prohibitive cost of ultra-high-field scanners. While existing deep learning approaches have achieved promising results, state-of-the-art methods typically rely on either large-scale architectures exceeding 45 million parameters or computationally intensive ensemble strategies, limiting their practicality in resource-constrained clinical environments. In this work, we propose a compact multi-domain attention framework, termed DGCM-SSFA, that achieves competitive synthesis quality with only 11M parameters. The proposed architecture integrates two complementary modules into a U-Net Transformer backbone. First, a Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulated Feature Modulator (DGCM) is embedded at multiple hierarchical levels to enhance local edge and texture details through Sobel-guided spatial attention and depthwise frequency-aware channel attention with cross-branch gating. Second, a Sparse Strip Frequency Attention (SSFA) module at the bottleneck captures global spatial context via strip-pooled attention with near-linear complexity, while simultaneously performing FFT-based spectral modulation in the frequency domain. These two modules operate synergistically with the backbone's native channel attention, forming a triple-granularity feature refinement pipeline. Extensive experiments on the UNC and BNU 3T-to-7T MRI datasets across T1w and T2w modalities demonstrate that DGCM-SSFA achieves strong structural fidelity, attaining an SSIM of 0.8431 on BNU T2w---approaching the best benchmark value of 0.8624---and 0.8100 on BNU T1w, while using substantially fewer parameters than Transformer-based alternatives such as ResViT (123.4M) and FS-RWKV (45.4M).

title: NeuralSRender: G-Buffer Guided Video Diffusion for Sim-to-Real Rendering
description:
arXiv:2610.29200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The scarcity of high-quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous-driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim-to-real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G-buffers, and LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G-buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers, then adapts to real-world appearance using real videos with estimated G-buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first-stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45\% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer-grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large-scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real-world videos with corresponding G-buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/NeuralSRender.

title: IECG: Weakly-Supervised Interpretability-Enhancing Foundation Model for Electrocardiogram
description:
arXiv:2610.28083v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac diagnosis, yet most machine learning methods for ECG analysis lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. We present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without requiring manual abnormal region annotations, overcoming a long-standing bottleneck in interpretable ECG learning. Central to IECG is a weakly-supervised attention strategy that explicitly incorporates clinical priors by deriving abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established ECG clinical knowledge. These pseudo-labels guide the model's CLS-token attention through a KL-divergence loss, encouraging it to focus on diagnostically relevant waveform regions. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, enabling it to learn rich multimodal representations while producing localized waveform evidence. By explicitly aggregating features from clinically guided attention regions, IECG grounds its diagnostic predictions in interpretable waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IECG achieves state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance, advancing trustworthy foundation models for ECG analysis.

title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2610.28849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline.
  We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

title: Toolflation: Seller Agents Distort Tool Markets Through Spontaneous Generative Engine Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.28454v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents are starting to sell to other agents. Seller agents write the listings of tools, services and products, and buyer agents read these listings when they choose what to use. We show that seller agents told only to be selected more often practice generative engine optimization on their own, and that this distorts the market for sellers and for buyers. We build tool markets from real data tools on Amazon and Instagram and run every tool on every question, so we know which tools can answer each question. Under all five production models we test, sellers rewrite their descriptions to claim more and more fields, including fields that their tools return for fewer than half of the targets. We call this process toolflation. Nothing in the market limits it, and how far it goes depends on the model, as the number of claims that contradict the sellers' own evidence differs by an order of magnitude between models. Toolflation shifts the buyers' choices between sellers, and the most capable tool loses share in seven of the ten combinations of seller model and platform. Under four models, the choices stay with capable tools and buyer agents keep their task success. Under the fifth, sellers copy one another until the descriptions no longer tell the tools apart. Buyer agents then pick tools by their position in the list, tools that answer almost nothing win a quarter to two fifths of the choices, and task success falls from 89% to about 30% on Amazon, close to random choice, and from 77% to 40% on Instagram. The sellers did only what their vendors asked, and the cost fell on buyers they never dealt with. We therefore argue that honesty toward third parties under competition is part of safety alignment, and that models should be tested as sellers before they are deployed as sellers.

title: MaD-RSI: Model-as-Data for Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.28201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of agent harnesses has emerged as an effective approach to enhancing the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents. By searching the harness space for a specific LLM on a given dataset, RSI can discover a harness tailored to the capabilities and behavioral characteristics of that model. However, such optimization often creates a strong coupling between the learned harness and its target LLM, limiting generalization across models and requiring substantial computational resources to adapt to new LLMs. Moreover, existing RSI methods typically optimize a harness using feedback from a single model and evaluate its generalization to other models only after training. This paradigm treats model differences primarily as a criterion for evaluating generalization rather than as valuable evidence for optimization. In this paper, we introduce a new perspective that treats models as data and places the harness at the center of optimization. Building on this perspective, we propose \textsc{MaD-RSI}, a framework that directly optimizes a shared harness across multiple heterogeneous LLMs by incorporating their diverse failure trajectories into the training process. Rather than assessing model differences only after optimization, \textsc{MaD-RSI} leverages these differences as training evidence to guide the self-improvement of a shared harness. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation framework with two complementary metrics designed to assess the effectiveness of harness optimization across models. Experiments across multiple datasets and LLMs demonstrate that \textsc{MaD-RSI} improves generalization over existing approaches while reducing training costs.

title: CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2610.28797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). Unlike traditional and even recent LLM-augmented approaches that ultimately rely on clustering vector embeddings, our framework leverages LLM capabilities directly for the entire pipeline. Experiments demonstrate that this approach provides better utility over existing (embedding-based) methods in the DP setting, especially in the high privacy regime. We evaluate the quality of CALLIOPE outputs using a variety of traditionally studied clustering metrics, as well as some novel utility metrics that we introduce.

title: 39 screenshots and not one useful name, so a local Gemma names them for me
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

slothshot renames screenshots after what's in them. Screenshot 2026-10-03 at 08.15.44.png becomes 2026-10-03 railbook-e-ticket-pnr-4421907736.png.

My screenshots folder had 39 files in three naming schemes, because they came over from a Linux laptop: Screenshot from 2026-02-17 19-14-51.png, 2026-04-09_01-26-24.png and the macOS Screenshot 2026-10-17 at 13.34.06.png. None of them said what was in the picture. When I needed one, I opened thumbnails until I found it.

Renaming them by hand would fix that, and I was never going to do it. So now a vision model on my laptop looks at each screenshot and picks a name: the app or site, and the specific thing on screen. The date stays at the front so the folder still sorts by time. It's for me, and for anyone whose Desktop looks like my Screenshots folder.

Demo

Eight made-up screenshots (a failing Go test, a flat group chat about the electricity bill, a UPI payment, a code review, a train ticket, a Grafana-style alert, a poha recipe and a macOS dialog):

The default is a dry run. -apply renames, -undo puts every old name back from a log file in the folder, and -watch 1m keeps it running so each new screenshot gets a name within a minute of me taking it.

It isn't perfect. It spelled SanDisk "sandsik". On the Go test it wrote "test-monthly-rollup-fail" and left out the actual panic, which is what I'd search for. On my own folder it named a black screenshot the-image-provided-is-completely-black, which is accurate. A name that's mostly right is still easier to search than Screenshot 2026-10-16 at 16.30.00.png.

Code

omlahore / slothshot

Renames your screenshots after what's in them, using a local vision model (Gemma 4 on llama.cpp)

slothshot

Renames your screenshots after what's in them. Screenshot 2026-10-03 at 08.15.44.png becomes 2026-10-03 railbook-e-ticket-pnr-4421907736.png, so Finder and Spotlight can find it when you type "pnr" three weeks later.

A local open-weight vision model (Gemma 4 E4B through llama.cpp) looks at each picture. Nothing leaves your machine, which matters because screenshot folders are full of chats, bank pages and login screens.

Run it

You need llama.cpp and Go.

brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-E4B-it-GGUF:Q4_0 --port 8092 -c 8192
go install github.com/omlahore/slothshot@latest

slothshot ~/Pictures/Screenshots            # dry run, prints the new names
slothshot -apply ~/Pictures/Screenshots     # renames them
slothshot -undo ~/Pictures/Screenshots      # puts the old names back
slothshot -watch 1m ~/Pictures/Screenshots  # leave it running, new screenshots get named as they land

It only touches files with a default screenshot name: macOS (Screenshot ... at ...), GNOME (Screenshot from ...), Flameshot (2026-04-09_01-26-24.png), Android and CleanShot…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

The model is Gemma 4 E4B, Google's open-weight model that takes images, quantized to 4 bits (the Q4_0 GGUF from ggml-org) and served by llama.cpp's llama-server on localhost. The CLI is about 230 lines of Go with one dependency, golang.org/x/image, for resizing.

For each file:

  1. A regex decides whether the name is a default screenshot name (macOS, GNOME, Flameshot, Android, CleanShot). Files it has already renamed have words after the date, so they never match. Running it twice does nothing the second time.
  2. The image is scaled so its long side is 1536 px and sent to llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a short prompt: 3 to 6 words, name the app only if its name is on screen, include the specific thing (the error, the merchant and amount, the page title).
  3. Go turns the answer into a slug: lowercase, hyphens, at most six words. If the name is taken, it adds -2. Every rename is appended to .slothshot.tsv.

Two things went wrong first.

Every answer came back empty. Gemma 4 thinks before it answers by default, and with max_tokens at 40 it spent all of them on "Thinking Process: 1. Analyze the Request". Passing chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false} turned that off, and answers came back in about a second.

At 1024 px the model read the PNR 4421907736 as 44197736, two digits gone. A wrong PNR in a filename is worse than none, because you search for the right one and it isn't there. At 1536 px it read all ten digits. Each image now takes roughly 2.5 seconds instead of 1.3. A file gets renamed once, so I took the slower, correct version.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I didn't think of my screenshots folder as private until I read the names slothshot proposed for it. There were chats with friends, video calls with other people's faces in them, and a few login pages. Naming those with a hosted API means uploading every one of them, and with -watch on, every new one as well.

With Gemma on llama.cpp none of it leaves the laptop. It works with Wi-Fi off, and there's no per-image bill, so leaving it on to watch the folder costs nothing. The model is a 5 GB file on my disk. When a better open model comes out I change one flag, and if a provider retires this one next year, my copy keeps working.

The Lazy Payoff

I ran it on my real folder in dry-run mode:

  • It proposed names for 39 screenshots in 1 minute 47 seconds, between 0.6 and 3.8 seconds each, on a 16 GB MacBook Air. I didn't have to watch it.
  • Doing it by hand means opening each one, working out what it is and typing a name. Call it 30 seconds each, so about 20 minutes. I'd been putting that off since the oldest file, which is from December 2025.
  • I took 13 screenshots between October 6 and October 17, about one a day. With -watch running from a LaunchAgent (the plist is in the README), each one has a name by the time I go looking for it, and I don't lift a finger.
  • Finding one meant scrolling thumbnails. After -apply, it's typing "mailbox" or "pnr" into Finder.

Nine of the 39 were screens from the same dashboard, and four of those came out with exactly the same name. -apply numbers them -2, -3 and -4 instead of overwriting anything.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: slothshot runs Gemma 4 E4B (open weights, GGUF on llama.cpp) for every name it gives.

title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing
description:
arXiv:2610.28949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
