title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits
description:
arXiv:2610.29029v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.

title: Toán Tử (Operators) Trong Java
description:
Toán tử là những ký hiệu được sử dụng để thực hiện các phép toán và so sánh trong lập trình. Java cung cấp nhiều loại toán tử khác nhau, bao gồm: 

I. Toán tử số học (Arithmetic Operators)
II. Toán tử bit (Bitwise Operators)
III. Toán tử so sánh (Comparison Operators)
IV. Toán tử logic (Logical Operators)
V. Toán tử điều kiện (Conditional Operators)
VI. Toán tử gán (Assignment Operators)
Ảnh mô tả các loại toán tử trong java.<!--more-->

Ⅰ. Toán tử số học

Sử dụng cho các phép toán cộng, trừ, nhân, chia, modulo (lấy dư).

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

+

Phép cộng

a + b

-

Phép trừ

a - b

*

Phép nhân

a * b

/

Phép chia

a / b

%

Phép chia lấy dư

a % b

++

Tăng thêm 1

a + 1

--

Giảm đi 1

a - 1

Ⅱ. Toán tử bit

Các toán tử bit thực hiện các phép toán trên các bit của số nguyên.

Toán tử

Mô tả

~

Phủ định NOT: Trả về giá trị phủ định của một bít. Chuyển đổi các bit 1 thành 0 và ngược lại.

&

Toán tử AND: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi cả hai bit đều là 1, 0 trong các trường hợp khác.

|

Toán tử OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 nếu một trong hai bit là 1, 0 trong trường hợp cả hai bit đều là 0.

^

Toán tử Exclusive OR: So sánh từng bit của hai số. Kết quả là 1 chỉ khi hai bit khác nhau, 0 trong trường hợp hai bit giống nhau.

>>

Dịch phải: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang phải một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit dấu (0 cho số dương và 1 cho số âm).

<<

Dịch trái: Dịch các bit của số nguyên sang trái một số vị trí nhất định. Các bit trống được lấp bằng bit 0.

Ⅲ. Toán tử so sánh

Các toán tử so sánh dùng để so sánh các giá trị và trả về kết quả dạng boolean.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

==

Bằng nhau

a == b

!=

Khác nhau

a != b

>

Lớn hơn

a > b

<

Nhỏ hơn

a < b

>=

Lớn hơn hoặc bằng

a >= b

<=

Nhỏ hơn hoặc bằng

a <= b

Ⅳ. Toán tử logic

Các toán tử logic làm việc với các toán hạng Boolean. Các toán tử quan hệ được sử dụng trong các cấu trúc điều khiển.

Toán tử

Mô tả

&&

Toán tử (AND) đọc là “Và”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True.

False: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là False.

||

Toán tử (OR) đọc là “Hoặc”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu ít nhất một toán hạng là True.

False: chỉ khi cả hai toán hạng đều là False.

^

Toán tử XOR đọc là “Hoặc ngoại trừ”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu chỉ một trong hai toán hạng là True.

False: nếu cả hai toán hạng đều là True hoặc cả hai đều là False.

!

Toán tử (NOT) đọc là “Không”. Trả về giá trị:

True: nếu toán hạng là False.

False: nếu toán hạng là True.

Ⅴ. Toán tử điều kiện

Toán tử điều kiện, còn được gọi là toán tử ba ngôi, là một loại toán tử đặc biệt trong Java được sử dụng để xác định điều kiện và trả về giá trị tương ứng dựa trên điều kiện đó. Nó là một cú pháp ngắn gọn để thay thế cho các câu lệnh if-else truyền thống. Bạn sử dụng cú pháp sau:

Cú Pháp 
<điều_kiện> ? <giátrị_khiđúng> : <giá_trị_khi_sai>

Giải thích các thành phần:

↳ <điều_kiện>: Biểu thức logic trả về giá trị true hoặc false.

↳ <giátrị_khiđúng>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là true.

↳ <giá_trị_khi_sai>: Giá trị được trả về nếu <điều_kiện> là false.

↳ Nếu điều kiện đúng: Trả về giá trị sau dấu ?.

↳ Nếu điều kiện sai: Trả về giá trị sau dấu :.

Main.java 
public class Main {

   public static void main(String[] args) {

      int age = 20;

      String message = (age >= 18) ? "Bạn đã đủ tuổi" : "Bạn chưa đủ tuổi";

            System.out.println(message); // In ra "Bạn đã đủ tuổi"

    }

}

Kết quả của chương trình là: 

Bạn đã đủ tuổi

Ⅵ. Toán tử gán

Toán tử gán mở rộng trong Java là những toán tử kết hợp phép toán và phép gán trong cùng một biểu thức. Giúp cho việc viết code ngắn gọn và dễ đọc hơn.

Toán tử

Mô tả

Ví dụ

=

Gán giá trị của toán hạng phải cho toán hạng trái.

c = 10

+=

Cộng và gán Thực hiện phép toán cộng giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c += a tương đương với c = c + a

-=

Trừ và gán Thực hiện phép toán trừ giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c -= a tương đương với c = c - a

*=

Nhân và gán Thực hiện phép toán nhân giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c *= a tương đương với c = c * a

/=

Chia và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c /= a tương đương với c = c / a

%=

Lấy số dư và gán Thực hiện phép toán chia lấy phần dư giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c %= a tương đương với c = c % a

&=

AND và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise AND giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c.

c &= a tương đương với c = c & a

^=

XOR và gán Thực hiện phép toán bitwise XOR giữa c và a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c ^= a tương đương với c = c ^ a

<<=

Dịch trái và gán Dịch trái c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c <<= a tương đương với c = c << a

>>=

Dịch phải và gán Dịch phải c với số bit bằng giá trị của a, sau đó gán kết quả cho c

c >>= a tương đương với c = c >> a

title: Legal Knowledge Bases on Premise: Compression, Tokens, and RAG Without Leaking Data
description:
If you are an engineer asked to build "a searchable legal knowledge base" for a law firm or an in-house legal team, the easy part is the search UI. The hard part is everything underneath: hundreds of gigabytes of scanned contracts, stamped pages, exhibit photos, and counterparty PDFs that nobody can open quickly, that blow past any context window if you try to feed them to a model, and that absolutely cannot leave the building. This piece is the hands-on, engineering-minded version of that problem — the one that talks about compression math, token budgets, and pipeline topology rather than vendor brochures.

The thesis is simple to state and annoying to implement: shrink the documents before you try to retrieve over them, keep the whole chain on hardware you control, and treat token cost as a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought. Below we walk through why document size is really a token problem, what compression does at a conceptual level, how RAG over private legal data actually works, the token-cost math you should run before writing any code, and how to assemble an on-prem pipeline. We close with a selection framework so you can evaluate tools without trusting marketing.

Why document size is really a token problem

Most engineers first meet this problem as a storage problem. "Our case files are big." That framing is a trap, because storage is cheap and getting cheaper. The real cost shows up later, when you try to make the data useful to a language model. Three distinct cost centers all scale with the size and shape of the source documents:

  1. Ingestion compute. Every page you want to search must be parsed, extracted, and embedded. Uncompressed, low-quality scans force repeated OCR passes and waste embedding calls.
  2. Retrieval payload. Whatever chunks you retrieve get stuffed into the model's context at query time. Big, poorly chunked documents mean more tokens per query, every single query.
  3. Transfer and storage tier. Legal material is retained for years. A storage-industry analysis by Komprise found that 60–70% of files on corporate network storage had not been opened in over 90 days, yet they still occupy the most expensive storage tier. For legal teams this is not a one-time annoyance — it is a permanent tax, because you cannot delete and you cannot keep paying premium rates for files nobody opens.

So "make it smaller" is not about disk savings. It is about making the document ingestible, retrievable, and transferable without a budget explosion. That is the through-line of this whole article.

How images become tokens (or why a "PDF" lies to you)

Here is the part junior pipeline code gets wrong. A 300-page "contract PDF" that a paralegal hands you is usually not text. It is 300 raster images of paper, possibly with a thin text layer that does not line up with the stamps. When you load it, you are not loading 300 pages of words; you are loading 300 photographs of words.

There are two ways a model ends up paying for those pages:

Path A — vision tokens. If you feed the page images directly to a multimodal model, each image is tiled and encoded into a grid of vision tokens. A single A4 scan at reasonable resolution can easily consume a few thousand vision tokens. Multiply by 300 pages and a few hundred exhibit photos and you are in the high hundreds of thousands of tokens just to read the bundle once. And you re-read it every time you reprocess, re-embed, or re-index. This is the silent killer of naive "just point the model at the folder" approaches.

Path B — OCR to text. The sane path is to run OCR, get real text, chunk the text, embed the chunks. Now a page is a few hundred to a thousand tokens of text instead of a few thousand vision tokens. The catch: OCR quality depends entirely on the clarity of the source image. If your "compression" blurred the stamp or the signature, OCR fails, entities get dropped, and your retrieval silently returns wrong answers. For legal data, a wrong answer is worse than no answer.

This is the crux of why compression for legal material is not the same as compression for a photo gallery. You are optimizing for perceptual fidelity of structured marks — stamps, signatures, seals, exhibit numbers — not for aesthetic smoothness. A generic image compressor that shaves bytes by softening edges will happily destroy the one pixel pattern that proves a document was executed. The engineering requirement is: compress hard enough to win the storage and transfer battle, but preserve the marks that carry legal meaning.

Compression principles at a conceptual level

You do not need to be a codec engineer to design this pipeline, but you should understand the levers.

Lossless vs. lossy. Lossless compression (think of it as a perfect repacking) shrinks without throwing anything away. For already-digital text PDFs and Office files it is the right default — there is no reason to lose a comma. But scanned pages and exhibit photos are inherently continuous-tone raster data; lossless only gets you so far because paper scans carry noise, dust, and background texture that do not compress well. There, a carefully tuned lossy step is where the real byte savings come from.

Perceptual vs. flat bitrate. A good compressor for documents spends its bit budget where human-meaningful structure lives — sharp edges, high-contrast marks, fine text strokes — and spends less on smooth backgrounds. The failure mode is the opposite: spreading the bit budget evenly so that backgrounds look fine but the seal in the corner turns to mush. For legal work you want the perceptual model biased toward marks, not toward "pleasing photo."

Consistency across formats. This is the part that quietly breaks pipelines. The same contract arrives as a PDF from one counterparty, a Word file from another, and a phone photo of a signed page from a third. If your compression behaves differently per format — clean on PDF, blurry on the photo — your downstream OCR and retrieval quality becomes a lottery determined by whoever sent the file. A recent product update from one vendor consolidated the image-compression core so that scanned pages, stamps, and exhibits compress under one consistent standard whether the source is PDF, Word, or a raw scan. The engineering payoff is not "smaller files" in the abstract; it is predictable output, so the rest of the pipeline can assume a stable input quality instead of branching on format. Search the name and you'll find it if you want to look at that approach.

The headline number that matters operationally: volumes can drop 60–80% on these bundles. That is not a compression-ratio bragging point. It is what makes an email attachment that would not send actually send, a multi-hundred-megabyte case folder sync cleanly to a branch office, and the preprocessing before indexing cheap enough to re-run whenever your chunking strategy improves.

How RAG over private legal data works

Retrieval-augmented generation, stripped of hype, is a six-stage pipeline. Each stage has an engineering decision that interacts with document size.

1. Ingest and normalize. Pull the source files, normalize formats, and run the compression step described above. This is where 60–80% of the byte weight dies. Critically, do this before anything leaves the machine.

2. Extract. For digital files, pull the text layer. For scans, run OCR. For exhibits, decide whether the image itself carries information (a photograph of a defect) or just needs to be attached as evidence (a signed page). This decision drives your token budget later.

3. Chunk. Split the extracted text into overlapping windows — say 400–800 tokens with a small overlap. For contracts, chunking by section (recital, definitions, representations, covenants, signature block) beats blind fixed windows, because a clause is a semantic unit. A naive fixed window will split "the liability cap is $X, except in cases of fraud" right down the middle.

4. Embed. Each chunk becomes a vector via an embedding model. Embedding cost scales with total tokens ingested, which is why the compression-upfront discipline pays off: you embed less, and you embed cleaner text.

5. Index. Store vectors in a vector store and, in parallel, keep a full-text (lexical) index — BM25-style — over the same chunks. Legal retrieval leans heavily on exact phrases ("Section 7.2", "Force Majeure", "indemnification"), which lexical search nails and pure semantic search often misses.

6. Retrieve and generate. At query time, run hybrid retrieval: combine the semantic nearest-neighbor hits with the lexical hits, rerank, take the top-k chunks, and inject them into the prompt with citations. The model never sees the whole document; it sees a few thousand tokens of the most relevant slices.

The privacy property falls out of topology, not features: if every one of those six stages runs on hardware inside your network, with no stage calling an external API, then the data simply has no path to leave. That is the entire argument for on-prem RAG in legal. It is not "we added encryption"; it is "there is no outbound call to intercept."

A note on the embedding model itself, because engineers often agonize over which one to pick and then ignore the part that actually matters. Embeddings convert a chunk of text into a fixed-length vector — commonly 384 to 3072 dimensions depending on the model. Two properties drive your design: the vector's dimensionality sets how much memory the index consumes (dimensions × chunks × bytes), and the model's notion of "similar" determines whether "indemnification" retrieves "hold harmless" or retrieves a unrelated mention of "insurance." For legal text, domain mismatch hurts: a general-purpose embedding trained on web text may treat "consideration" as a thoughtful opinion rather than a contract's exchanged value. If retrieval feels random, the embedding model is a more likely culprit than your chunk size. You do not need the largest model; you need one whose similarity space matches contract language, and you need to verify that with measurement rather than intuition.

The token-cost math you should run before coding

Do not estimate. Compute. Here is the spreadsheet logic, using a representative matter bundle:

  • Bundle: a 300-page scanned contract PDF + 200 exhibit photos.
  • Uncompressed footprint: ~650 MB (scanned raster + photos).
  • Vision-only ingestion (Path A): ~2,500–3,000 vision tokens per page/image. Call it 2,800. Bundle = 500 items × 2,800 = 1.4 million tokens to read once. Re-embed on every pipeline tweak and the cost multiplies.
  • OCR-to-text ingestion (Path B): 300 pages × ~700 words ≈ 210,000 words ≈ 280,000 tokens of source text. Plus exhibits that carry text. So you dropped ingestion from ~1.4M to ~0.3M tokens — roughly a 5× reduction — by refusing to feed vision tokens.
  • Chunking: at 600 tokens/chunk with overlap, ~600 chunks. Embedding calls scale with chunks, not pages, so this is stable and cheap.
  • Query payload: top-8 chunks × ~500 tokens = 4,000 tokens per query into the model. This is the recurring cost, and compression does not change it much — chunk design does. That is the key insight: compression wins the ingestion and storage battle; chunk design wins the query battle. Confusing the two is why teams over-spend.

Now fold in storage. That 650 MB, uncompressed, sitting on the premium tier for years (recall the 60–70% untouched-files finding) is a recurring bill. At 60–80% reduction you are paying for a fraction of it, and the bundle becomes small enough to replicate to a branch office over a normal link instead of shipping disks.

Cost formula to put in your design doc:

ingestion_cost ≈ total_source_tokens × embedding_rate
query_cost      ≈ avg_retrieved_tokens × generation_rate × queries_per_month
storage_cost    ≈ compressed_bytes × premium_tier_rate × retention_years

The lever you control most is total_source_tokens (via compression + OCR discipline) and avg_retrieved_tokens (via chunk design). Everything else is someone else's price list.

Building an on-prem knowledge base pipeline

You do not need a single monolith. You need five loosely coupled components, each of which can be a self-hosted service:

A. Compressor/normalizer. Sits first in the line. Takes any format, applies consistent image compression, preserves marks. Output is normalized files plus extracted text where available. This is the component most teams underestimate; it is also the component whose quality determines whether stage B (OCR) succeeds on the first pass.

B. Parser/OCR. Turns normalized inputs into clean text. Keep it on-prem; cloud OCR means the document left. For exhibits that are pure images, decide per-file whether to OCR or to store the image as attached evidence with a caption.

C. Chunker + embedder. Applies your legal-aware chunking policy and produces vectors. The embedder is a model you host; pick one sized for your latency and privacy needs. Run embeddings in batches to keep GPU/CPU busy.

D. Hybrid store. A vector index for semantics plus a lexical index for exact phrases, with a reranker on top. Keep both behind the same internal network boundary.

E. Retrieval gateway. The only component users touch. It builds the prompt from retrieved chunks, attaches citations, and calls your self-hosted generation model. It should also enforce authorization — a junior associate should not retrieve a partner-only matter just because they can type.

Notice what is not in the pipeline: any outbound network call. If your design doc has a line that says "send to for processing," you have defeated the purpose. The whole point is that the six RAG stages and the compressor all run where the disk lives.

One more engineering note: redaction belongs in the pipeline, not in the prompt. Names, ID numbers, bank accounts, and privileged notes should be detected and masked before indexing, so they never become retrievable chunks and never reach the generation model. Doing it in the prompt ("please ignore sensitive data") is theater; the data is still in the index.

Measuring retrieval quality before you trust it

A RAG pipeline that returns confident, well-cited answers can still be wrong, and in legal work a wrong citation is a liability. You should treat retrieval as a measurable subsystem with its own eval, independent of whether the final text "looks right." The cheap version of this is a gold set: take fifty real questions a lawyer would ask — "what is the cap on liability in the 2024 Acme agreement," "which matters reference arbitration in London" — and hand-label the chunks that should have been retrieved. Then measure precision@k and recall@k on your top-k window. If precision is low, your reranker or chunking is surfacing noise; if recall is low, your embedding or lexical index is missing the answer entirely.

The subtler metric is citation faithfulness: does the generated answer actually point at the chunk that supports the claim? A system can retrieve the right chunk and then ignore it. Log the retrieved chunks alongside the output during a pilot and sample them. None of this requires a fancy framework — a spreadsheet of question, expected chunk, retrieved chunk, and a pass/fail column will tell you more in an afternoon than a quarter of vibes. The point is to instrument the retrieval layer explicitly, because once the pipeline is in production nobody revisits it until something blows up.

Operational failure modes worth designing against

A few problems show up only after real volume accumulates, and they are cheaper to prevent than to clean up.

Duplicate and near-duplicate matter files. The same contract gets re-uploaded with a different filename, or a counterparty sends the same exhibit twice. Without deduplication, your index grows and retrieval returns two near-identical chunks, diluting the top-k. A content-hash or near-duplicate detection step before indexing is a small addition that pays for itself.

Version drift. A contract is amended; the old version stays indexed. Now a query returns contradictory clauses from two versions. You need a versioning policy — index by matter-plus-version, and prefer the latest unless the query explicitly asks for history.

OCR drift on low-quality scans. Even good compressors cannot save a source that was unreadable to begin with. Build a quality gate: if OCR confidence on a page falls below a threshold, flag it for human review instead of silently embedding garbage. Silent garbage is worse than a visible gap, because the gap at least gets noticed.

Authorization leakage. The retrieval gateway must enforce matter-level access. If chunks from a partner-only matter are reachable by a junior associate through a clever query, your "private" system has a privilege bug, not a privacy feature. Treat the gateway's authz layer as part of the security boundary, because it is.

None of these are exotic. They are the difference between a demo that impresses and a system a firm will actually stake client confidences on.

The governance risk that makes on-prem non-optional

This is not paranoia; it is the reported failure mode. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach study found that about one in five organizations had a breach caused by employees using AI tools on their own — so-called shadow AI — and those breaches cost on average $670,000 more than peers'. Among organizations that were breached, 63% had no AI governance policy at all.

Read that against a legal team. The moment a paralegal pastes a confidential contract into a public chat window "to summarize it," the data has left, silently, with no policy catching it. The engineering answer is not a training video; it is to remove the outbound path entirely. If the only way to use AI on the matter is through the on-prem gateway (component E above), then shadow AI cannot exfiltrate, because there is nowhere to paste. That is governance by architecture, which is the only kind that survives a busy Tuesday.

There is also a quieter productivity argument, and it is worth putting in the same deck. A 2025 knowledge-worker report compared teams with and without knowledge management: those without spent 8.5 hours a week searching for things; those with a system dropped to 4.6 hours. Scaled to 1,000 employees, that swing frees the equivalent of 98 full-time roles. Legal time is expensive and billable; the reclaimed hours convert directly into client work, not into folder archaeology.

What to check when choosing

Whether you build the pipeline yourself or evaluate a tool, run every candidate through the same lens. This is a selection framework, not a vendor scorecard — fill it in per option and let the gaps speak.

Dimension Why it matters What good looks like
Data boundary Legal material cannot leave the network; an outbound call is a compliance event Entire pipeline, including OCR and embedding, runs on-prem with no external API
Compression consistency Mixed PDF/Word/scan inputs must produce stable, predictable output quality One compression standard across formats; marks and stamps preserved, not blurred
Retrieval type Lawyers search by clause, exhibit number, and exact phrase, not vague meaning Hybrid semantic + full-text, with reranking and cited source snippets
Sensitive-data handling PII and privilege must not become retrievable or model-visible Auto-detection and redaction before indexing; return only under authorization
Chunking policy Bad chunking splits clauses and returns half-answers Section-aware chunking for contracts, not fixed windows
Cost model Token and storage bills compound over years of retention Predictable ingestion/query math; compression reduces both storage tier and re-embed cost
Scale path Matter volume grows; the design must not require a rewrite Batch embedding, replicable index, clean separation of compressor from retriever

Any option that cannot check the first row should be disqualified before the demo starts. The rest of the table separates "looks impressive in a slide" from "survives a real matter."

Closing thoughts for the engineer

The mistake is to treat this as a search problem with a legal skin. It is really a data-shape problem: legal documents are big, image-heavy, format-fragmented, and toxic if they escape. Solve the shape first — compress consistently, OCR cleanly, chunk by meaning — and the retrieval almost designs itself. Solve it on hardware you control, and the compliance conversation becomes a one-liner instead of a fire drill.

Run the token math before you write a line of code. Know your total_source_tokens and your avg_retrieved_tokens, and you will know your bill. Everything else in this space is variation on those two numbers and the single rule that the data never crosses the boundary.

title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
description:
arXiv:2610.28479v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

title: Register Anything Model for Generalizable and Robust Point Cloud Registration
description:
arXiv:2610.28821v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Register Anything Model (RAM), a unified model for generalizable 3D point cloud registration that robustly estimates 6-DoF transformations across diverse domains spanning sensors and environments. Existing registration methods are typically tailored to a single domain, with carefully tuned architectures and hyperparameters, and thus degrade markedly when applied to novel domains. We bridge this gap by training a single model on diverse data from indoor, outdoor, and object domains. A central challenge is the severe geometric discrepancy across domains, i.e., differences in scene scale, sensor noise, point density, and structural patterns, which hinders processing with a unified point-based model. To address this, we introduce a geometry-aware normalization strategy that jointly voxelizes and normalizes point clouds into a standardized geometric space, adaptively based on their geometric properties to preserve salient local structures while standardizing resolution. Built on this normalization, RAM follows a hierarchical coarse-to-fine paradigm, and employs an efficient geometric transformer that models local geometric consistency instead of globally over all points. This design mitigates discretization noise introduced by voxelization, and improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of inlier ratio and registration recall. Notably, our method outperforms the counterparts trained on each separate domain, showing superior generalization capability.

title: Multilingual Brain Decoding Reveals Shared Cortical Semantic Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.26927v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Human languages differ markedly in lexical and syntactic form yet can convey similar semantic content. The neural basis of this cross-language semantic commonality remains unclear. Here we developed a multilingual brain decoding framework and analysed brain recordings from 227 participants spanning Chinese, English and French. We found that cortical semantic representations exhibited consistent semantic geometry relationships across languages and individuals, revealing a shared cortical semantic geometry. Importantly, the cross-language consistency of cortical semantic geometry increased from sensorimotor to higher-order association cortex, forming a shared semantic geometry gradient closely aligned with the principal cortical functional gradient. Our work establishes generalizable multilingual brain decoding and identifies stable cortical semantic geometry as a neural basis for semantic commonality across languages.

title: RiO-DETRv2: Geometry-Aware Uncertainty Modeling Meets Real-Time Oriented Object Detection Transformer
description:
arXiv:2610.29159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RiO-DETR is the first real-time end-to-end transformer for oriented object detection, yet further localization gains require a more expressive box representation. Although distributional regression has succeeded in horizontal DETRs, extending it to oriented detection introduces geometry-misaligned boundary modeling and topology-inconsistent orientation refinement. We present RiO-DETRv2, a geometry-aware uncertainty modeling framework for real-time oriented object detection. To resolve the geometry mismatch, Object-Aligned Boundary Distribution Refinement represents box boundaries as probability distributions in an object-aligned coordinate system and progressively refines them across decoder layers. For better orientation topology consistency, we introduce Circular-to-Local Angular Residual Refinement that transitions from global periodic search to local fine-grained estimation. Unified OBB Quality-Aligned Learning further aligns classification, boundary and angular refinement with complete-OBB localization quality. Together, these designs improve localization without compromising efficiency, achieving a better balance between speed and accuracy. Specifically, RiO-DETRv2-l/x achieves 53.7/54.1 mAP50-95 on DOTA, outperforming RiO-DETR-l/x by 1.2/1.5 points with nearly unchanged computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/RicePasteM/RiO-DETRv2.

title: Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026
description:
Screen Sizes & Viewport Cheat Sheet for 2026

Every responsive bug report starts the same way: "it looks broken on my phone." Then you spend ten minutes hunting for that phone's viewport width — one site lists the panel resolution, another lists a viewport from two generations ago, and a third just says "various."

This is the cheat sheet I keep coming back to: the device viewports worth testing in 2026, the framework breakpoints next to them, and the three numbers — resolution, viewport, DPR — that developers constantly mix up. All values below are portrait CSS-pixel references. Treat heights as references, not guarantees: mobile browser bars, keyboards and zoom change the visible height, while width stays comparatively stable.

Phone viewports worth testing

Eleven models cover nearly every width your layout will meet in production, from the narrow 360px Android baseline to the 440px Pro Max class. The full model-by-model reference lives in the iPhone viewport sizes table and the device screen sizes index.

Device CSS viewport Panel resolution DPR
Galaxy S25 360 × 780 1080 × 2340 3
iPhone SE (3rd gen) 375 × 667 750 × 1334 2
Galaxy S25 Ultra 384 × 832 1440 × 3120 3.75
iPhone 14 390 × 844 1170 × 2532 3
iPhone 16 393 × 852 1179 × 2556 3
iPhone 17 402 × 874 1206 × 2622 3
Pixel 10 412 × 923 1080 × 2424 2.625
iPhone Air 420 × 912 1260 × 2736 3
Pixel 10 Pro 427 × 952 1280 × 2856 3
iPhone 16 Plus 430 × 932 1290 × 2796 3
iPhone 17 Pro Max 440 × 956 1320 × 2868 3

Patterns worth internalizing:

  • Modern iPhones cluster tightly. Everything from the iPhone 14 to the 17 sits between 390 and 440 CSS pixels wide, all at DPR 3. If your layout survives 390, 402 and 430, it survives the current iPhone line.
  • Android is wider at the edges. The base Galaxy line still reports 360px — the narrowest mainstream target, and the one that exposes cramped toolbars and rigid dialogs first.
  • DPR is not always a whole number. The Pixel 10 ships at 2.625 and the S25 Ultra at 3.75. Hard-coding "retina = 2x or 3x" assumptions into image pipelines is how blurry hero images happen; serve srcset steps and let the browser pick.
  • Shared widths hide differences. Several models share a viewport width while differing in height, DPR and safe areas. A matching reference is a starting point for testing, not proof two devices render identically.

Tablets and laptops, briefly

Tablet viewports overlap small-laptop widths, which is why "tablet layout" and "small desktop layout" so often collide around 1024px.

Device / class CSS viewport / workspace Panel resolution
iPad mini (A17 Pro) 744 × 1133 1488 × 2266
Classic iPad reference 768 × 1024 —
iPad (10th gen) / iPad Air 11" 820 × 1180 1640 × 2360
iPad Pro 11" (M4) 834 × 1210 1668 × 2420
iPad Pro 13" (M4) 1032 × 1376 2064 × 2752
Budget laptop (WXGA) 1366 × 768 1366 × 768
MacBook Air 13" (M3) 1470 × 956 2560 × 1664
MacBook Pro 14" (M4) 1512 × 982 3024 × 1964
1080p panel at 125% scaling 1536 × 864 1920 × 1080

Two things to notice. First, laptop "workspace" values are scaled: a 2560 × 1664 MacBook Air panel gives CSS a 1470 × 956 layout space, and OS scaling — not the panel — decides what your media queries see. Second, the classic 768 × 1024 iPad reference refuses to die; it is still a useful portrait test width even though current iPads report larger viewports.

Tailwind vs. Bootstrap breakpoints

Both frameworks are mobile-first min-width systems, but their thresholds only agree at 768px. The side-by-side reference, with a live checker that tracks your current width against both systems, is the responsive breakpoint checker.

Tier Tailwind Bootstrap
Base 0–639px (base) 0–575px (xs)
Small sm 640px sm 576px
Medium md 768px md 768px
Large lg 1024px lg 992px
Extra large xl 1280px xl 1200px
Largest 2xl 1536px xxl 1400px

Practical consequences:

  • A layout that switches to two columns at Bootstrap lg (992px) does so 32px earlier than the same layout at Tailwind lg (1024px). Porting components between the two without adjusting expectations shifts every boundary.
  • Tailwind expresses its thresholds in rem (640px = 40rem at the default root size), Bootstrap in px. If a user changes their browser's root font size, rem-based breakpoints move and px-based ones don't — a classic source of "works on my machine."
  • Test the pixel below each threshold, not just the threshold itself: 639, 767, 1023, 1279 and 1535 are where the old layout makes its last stand.

If you only keep one testing set, make it 360, 393, 430, 768, 1024, 1366, 1536 and 1920 — narrow Android, common iPhone, large phone, tablet portrait, tablet landscape, small laptop, large laptop and desktop. The reasoning behind that set is laid out in the common screen resolutions reference.

Check your own device, live

Tables tell you what a device should report. Your actual browser may disagree — because of zoom, OS display scaling, an installed web app shell, or a keyboard eating half the screen. When a bug is on your desk, measure the real thing:

  1. Open the viewport size checker on the device in question.
  2. Read three values: viewport (window.innerWidth × innerHeight), DPR (window.devicePixelRatio), and the active Tailwind/Bootstrap range.
  3. Resize or rotate and watch the values update; then paste the report straight into the bug ticket, so QA reproduces at your width instead of guessing.

For screenshot and image bugs, multiply the CSS slot by the live DPR: a 360px-wide slot on a DPR 3 phone needs a 1080px asset to stay sharp, and exporting at the panel resolution "to be safe" just ships megabytes nobody asked for.

The three numbers everyone confuses

Most screen-size confusion is one paragraph away from disappearing:

Physical resolution is the panel's pixel grid — 1179 × 2556 on an iPhone 16. It describes hardware. Your CSS never sees it directly. CSS viewport is the area the page renders into, in CSS pixels — 393 × 852 on that same phone. Media queries, breakpoints and layout respond to this number and only this number. DPR is the ratio between them: how many physical pixels paint one CSS pixel. It drives image sharpness (and screenshot dimensions), but it does not change which breakpoint is active.

So when a spec sheet brags about a huge resolution, divide by DPR before you panic: what lands in your stylesheet is the viewport. And when a user reports a "tiny" screen, ask for their viewport and DPR — not their panel resolution — before you touch a single media query.

TL;DR

Test widths, not devices: 360–440px covers current phones, 768–1032px covers tablets, and scaled laptop workspaces matter more than panel resolutions. Keep resolution, viewport and DPR in separate mental buckets, verify your own browser live instead of trusting spec sheets, and always check the pixel just below the breakpoint.

title: AI Found This CVE in 6 Hours. Your Team Would Have Taken 6 Weeks.
description:
Security research has a discovery problem. Most critical vulnerabilities sit dormant in codebases for months or years before anyone finds them — not because they're hidden, but because manual code review doesn't scale.

The PHP2Shell disclosure changed that calculus.

What the Numbers Actually Mean

When Wiz Research used AI to find CVE-2026-109618 in roughly one week, the real story isn't the CVE — it's the time compression. A team of three senior security researchers, working manually, would typically spend 4–8 weeks to reach the same result. AI didn't replace the researcher. It multiplied their output by 10x.

How the Triage-Pattern-Exploit Loop Works

The methodology Wiz used isn't proprietary magic. It's a reproducible loop:

  1. Ingest the entire codebase — not just the files you think matter, but everything
  2. Apply historical CVE patterns — use prior bugs in the same codebase as fingerprints for similar flaws
  3. Rank by exploitability — not all memory bugs are equal; AI sorts them by proximity to input surfaces
  4. Generate a candidate exploit chain — let the model show the attack path before a human validates it

This loop works because most CVEs in mature codebases share structural DNA with prior CVEs in the same project. PHP's zend engine has had multiple use-after-free bugs. Each one is a training signal.

The Gap This Creates

Organizations that adopt AI-assisted security discovery don't just find bugs faster — they find bugs their competitors haven't found yet. In the current threat environment, that asymmetry is everything.

The attacker community is already using these tools. The question is whether defenders will close that gap or continue relying on annual pen tests and manual code reviews that can't keep up.

What Autonomous Remediation Adds

Discovery is only half the problem. The other half is remediation velocity. When a CVSS 9.2 CVE drops with active exploits in the wild, the organization with autonomous patching deployed wins. The one that kicks off a two-week change management process loses.

Cognitive Daniel is built on exactly this principle — autonomous AI that doesn't just find vulnerabilities but patches them across entire fleets, with zero manual intervention per server.

Full writeup: cognitivedaniel.com

title: Delayed Webhook Queue Publish Explained 7 Nightly Cron Trigger Batch Worker (Latency/Cost)
description:
For a fintech shipment update fanout, the least complex reliable choice is a nightly cron trigger that batches pending webhooks into a durable queue, then lets workers publish with idempotency and backoff. Keep the trigger boring. Put the cleverness in observability and recovery.

Short answer: use a queue when delayed webhook delivery can tolerate seconds or minutes of waiting; use a direct publish path only when the subscriber contract demands sub-second latency and you can absorb its cost.

The dispatch decision in one table

Pattern Pick this when Main cost Failure to watch
Direct publish from the transaction One or two subscribers, strict latency, short request budgets Coupled availability and request time A slow endpoint delays the database request
Transactional outbox plus queue Events must not disappear when a commit succeeds A relay and queue to operate Duplicate delivery after a retry
Nightly cron batch into a queue Pending work is acceptable overnight and spend is the primary constraint Delivery is intentionally delayed A growing backlog hides until morning
Workflow scheduler Delays, branches, and human review are part of the process More state and operational surface State-machine complexity exceeds the job

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. A hosted task service, BullMQ backed by Redis, and Temporal-style workflows all solve different slices of the same problem. Their APIs and durability guarantees differ, so compare the contract you need rather than the logo on the dashboard.

How should a cron trigger queue pending webhooks for a nightly batch?

Start with a durable record. When the shipment status changes, write an outbox row in the same database transaction as the status update. A separate publisher claims rows that are ready, creates a queue message, and marks the row as enqueued. This is the transactional outbox pattern: the business write and the intent to publish commit together, while delivery happens later.

The cron trigger is only a nudge. It should select a bounded batch, such as 500 rows, and enqueue work with a stable message key. It must be safe to run twice. A lock or lease prevents two schedulers from claiming the same rows, but the worker still needs idempotency because queues commonly provide at-least-once delivery.

Here is a small Node.js example. It uses generic interfaces so the same shape can sit over a cloud task queue, Redis-backed queue, or an internal broker.

type PendingWebhook = {
  id: string;
  shipmentId: string;
  endpoint: string;
  payload: unknown;
  attempts: number;
};

interface PendingStore {
  claimReady(limit: number, leaseSeconds: number): Promise<PendingWebhook[]>;
  markEnqueued(id: string, messageId: string): Promise<void>;
  markDelivered(id: string): Promise<void>;
  reschedule(id: string, nextAttempt: Date): Promise<void>;
}

interface Queue {
  enqueue(messageId: string, body: PendingWebhook): Promise<void>;
}

export async function nightlyEnqueue(store: PendingStore, queue: Queue) {
  const batch = await store.claimReady(500, 300);
  for (const item of batch) {
    const messageId = `shipment-webhook:${item.id}`;
    await queue.enqueue(messageId, item);
    await store.markEnqueued(item.id, messageId);
  }
}

One small detail matters: the message ID comes from the outbox ID, not from the current time. That gives you a deduplication key you can inspect in logs. If enqueue succeeds and the process dies before markEnqueued, the next cron run may publish the same item again. That is expected. Make the receiver—or your delivery ledger—treat item.id as an idempotency key.

What does the worker publish, retry, and measure?

The worker owns the network call. It sets a bounded timeout, sends an idempotency key, and records the response class. A 2xx response marks delivery. A timeout or 5xx response gets exponential backoff with jitter. A 4xx response usually needs quarantine and an operator decision; retrying a permanently invalid signature forever just burns queue capacity.

export async function deliver(
  item: PendingWebhook,
  store: PendingStore,
  fetcher: typeof fetch,
) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 8_000);
  try {
    const response = await fetcher(item.endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        "idempotency-key": item.id,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(item.payload),
      signal: controller.signal,
    });

    if (response.ok) {
      await store.markDelivered(item.id);
      return;
    }

    if (response.status >= 400 && response.status < 500) {
      await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date("2099-01-01T00:00:00Z"));
      return;
    }

    const delaySeconds = Math.min(3_600, 2 ** item.attempts * 30);
    await store.reschedule(item.id, new Date(Date.now() + delaySeconds * 1000));
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

The 2099 date is a readable quarantine sentinel for this example; production code should use an explicit dead-letter state. Do not hide that distinction in a generic retry helper.

Measure the path as a timeline: outbox_created, queue_enqueued, worker_started, request_finished, and delivered. The useful metrics are age of the oldest pending row, batch size, enqueue lag, delivery latency, retry count, and dead-letter count. Alert on age and error rate, not on a single slow request. Logs should carry shipment ID, webhook ID, message ID, attempt, and a trace ID. That lets an on-call engineer answer “where did this update stop?” without replaying the entire night.

Which queue shape fits latency versus cost?

If customers watch a shipment screen in real time, a nightly batch is the wrong shape. Use the outbox relay continuously and let workers drain small messages; the extra queue operations buy lower latency. If the webhook is a reconciliation hint consumed by a back-office job, a 15-minute or nightly batch can be rational. Your mileage may vary when subscribers are spread across time zones or have contractual delivery windows.

A queue service usually charges for requests and retained work; Redis-backed queues shift cost toward always-on capacity and operations; workflow engines charge for state transitions and add visibility for multi-step processes. I’m not sure which line item dominates for your traffic until you chart messages per shipment, retry probability, and retention hours. Cost belongs beside latency in the design review, never in place of a delivery guarantee.

The catch is operational ownership. A cron plus queue is not suitable when each webhook needs human approval, calendar-aware waits, or a long saga; stick with a workflow engine then. Conversely, a workflow engine is excessive for one POST and one retry policy. Keep the state model proportional to the failure modes you can actually explain.

Limits and a practical rollout

Begin in shadow mode: enqueue copies, measure lag, and compare the worker's result with the existing publisher. Then enable one subscriber group, cap concurrency, and document the replay command. Test duplicate messages, a full queue, a rotated signing key, and a database lease that expires halfway through a batch. These are ordinary paths, not exotic chaos tests.

Measure twice.

For a useful rehearsal, freeze the subscriber endpoint for ten minutes while a batch is in flight. The queue should retain the messages, the worker should record timeouts without losing payloads, and the age-of-oldest metric should climb. Restore the endpoint, watch retries drain, and verify that the delivery ledger contains one terminal result per webhook ID even if the same message was attempted several times. Run that exercise with 50 records first, then with the largest batch your database lease can hold; the point is to validate the handoff and the alert, not to manufacture a benchmark.

There is no exactly-once network delivery. There is only an idempotent receiver, a durable intent, and enough evidence to replay safely. If the business cannot accept delayed updates at all, move the decision earlier: publish from the committed outbox continuously and design the subscriber contract around bounded latency.

References

Further reading:

  • https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.temporal.io/

title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.24806v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven.
  Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $\alpha$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $\alpha$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $\alpha$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ \mu$M).
  We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.

title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
description:
arXiv:2610.28699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.

title: The Data Differentiator Framework (DDF): Quantifying Marginal Data Value with Information-Theoretic and Game-Theoretic Measures in an Agentic Evaluation Pipeline (SDSAE)
description:
arXiv:2610.28933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In data-rich enterprises the hard question is not whether a candidate dataset is good in isolation, but whether it adds information beyond what the organization already holds, and whether that increment is worth its price. We present the Data Differentiator Framework (DDF), a composite scoring method for candidate data assets that combines (i) a mutual-information-based redundancy penalty against the existing portfolio, (ii) a cost-normalized, significance-gated marginal utility score derived from an ablation study, and (iii) explicit governance inputs (trust, identity resolution quality, strategic weights) set by the business. The framework is executed by a staged pipeline, the Strategic Data Sourcing Agent Ecosystem (SDSAE), that short-circuits expensive model-retraining steps for assets failing governance or redundancy gates. Conceptually, the DDF extends the relevance-minus-redundancy principle of mRMR feature selection from the feature level to the asset level, and adds cost normalization, a statistical significance gate, and governance terms that per-sample valuation methods such as Data Shapley do not model. We validate the framework on the public credit-card fraud benchmark (284,807 transactions) with five constructed candidate assets spanning the redundancy spectrum. Only the genuinely differentiated asset passes the significance gate ($\Delta$AUC = +0.0029, DeLong $p = 1.4\times 10^{-9}$, Holm-corrected $p = 7.2\times 10^{-9}$) and receives an acquire recommendation (DDS = +0.663); the fully redundant asset scores lowest (DDS = -0.135). The recommendation is stable across 19 of 22 admissible strategic-weight configurations and across all decision thresholds in [0.15, 0.66]. We state clearly which quantities in the case study are computed from data and which are simulated governance inputs, and we discuss the design limits of a single-dataset evaluation.
