title: I let Stripe grade my tests: building a billing simulator where no expected value comes from my own code
description:
Built for the TestSprite Hackathon, Season 4. Live: tera-orpin-three.vercel.app · Code: github.com/PugarHuda/tera

Founders are afraid to touch pricing, and they are right to be. Move a customer from $29 to $79 on day 17 of a 31-day month and Stripe writes two proration lines you have probably never computed by hand: an "Unused time" credit of −$14.03 and a "Remaining time" charge of $38.23, on top of the $79 renewal. Add a coupon that was applied once, a tax rate that is inclusive, a trial, or a subscription in Stripe's new flexible billing mode, and the invoice your customer sees is no longer something you can predict from the pricing page.

Tera simulates it first. You give it a customer timeline (subscribe, change seats, upgrade, apply a coupon, pause, cancel) and it returns every invoice to the cent, plus the webhook events Stripe will send for it. This post is not really about the simulator, though. It is about the question every test suite eventually has to answer: who decides what the right answer is?

The rule: the engine never writes its own expectations

The easiest way to get a green test suite for a billing engine is to run the engine, save its output, and assert that it does not change. That suite is worthless the day the engine is wrong, because it was wrong when the snapshot was taken too.

So Tera has one rule. Every expected value is derived by hand from the billing rules, written next to its arithmetic, and then replayed in a real Stripe test-mode account with test clocks. Scenario S05 in golden/scenarios.json looks like this:

"math": "remaining 15/31: -round(2900*15/31)=-1403, +round(7900*15/31)=3823",
"expect": [{ "date": "2027-02-01", "lines": [-1403, 3823, 7900], "total": 10320 }]

A script creates the same customer in Stripe, advances a test clock through the timeline, reads back Stripe's invoices and diffs them line by line against both the hand-derived values and Tera's engine. Only when all three agree is the scenario marked verified, and the evidence (invoice ids, test clock id) is committed to the repo. Today there are 130 golden scenarios and all 127 timelines among them match Stripe to the cent. The other three are migration scenarios with no invoices to replay.

When Stripe disagreed with my hand derivation, Stripe won, and I kept the receipts. A coupon applied in the same second as subscribing discounts the next invoice, because Stripe finalizes the first one at creation. A repeating coupon for 3 months lasts three calendar months, not three invoices. A percent discount on a proration comes off the rounded gross. None of those were in my head when I started.

Letting Stripe find the cases I did not think of

Hand-written scenarios only cover what you already suspect. So Tera also runs differential fuzzing: a seeded generator produces random customer timelines, with month-end anchors, Feb 29, random times of day, trials, seat and plan changes, coupons and both tax behaviours. Each one runs through Tera and through Stripe, and any difference is a finding.

Every finding goes through the same pipeline: a targeted Stripe probe to isolate the rule, a new hand-derived golden scenario that pins it, then the engine fix. The fuzzer runs nightly in CI with fresh seeds, in both of Stripe's billing modes. The rules it surfaced are some of the most interesting in the repo. Stripe prorates the unit price to 12 decimals before multiplying by seats, so a credit of exactly 11257.5 lands a cent under the tie. In flexible mode every credit refunds its original debit with the gross and the discount rounded separately.

This week the same approach caught a real gap in usage-based billing. A code audit found the engine silently dropping metered usage on an immediate cancellation. Seven live probes gave the rules: tier lines run only up to the tier the usage reaches, a metered item has no unused-time line, and cancelling with invoice_now bills the usage so far. A follow-up fuzz batch for metered prices then found that Stripe still sends a $0 final invoice after an unused last period. It also found a stale usage window in my own replay script.

Where TestSprite fits

Stripe is the oracle for the engine. TestSprite is the gate for everything a user actually touches.

  • 28 UI tests on every pull request, run by the TestSprite GitHub App against that PR's own Vercel preview. Branch protection requires the TestSprite V3 check. Each test asserts hand-derived amounts in the browser: "Invoice 2 totals $103.20", not "an invoice is shown".
  • The tests live in the repo. Every plan is a JSON file in testsprite/plans/ and every test has hand-written Playwright code in testsprite/code/. A CI check compares both with the cloud project and fails on drift. That matters because an auto-healing run can quietly rewrite stored code, for example pinning a preview URL or loosening an assertion to two words.
  • API tests against the preview, too. TestSprite gives backend tests no target URL, so a small script stores each API test with its base URL pointing at the PR's preview, runs it with auto-heal off, and puts production back.
  • Triage that uses the oracle. When TestSprite V3 fails, a workflow downloads the failure bundle, replays the golden scenarios behind that test on the same preview, and compares them with Stripe's recorded invoices. One PR comment then says either "engine still matches Stripe, so this is a UI regression" or which invoice the engine now gets wrong.
  • A nightly money-math canary on production, plus Playwright user journeys, Schemathesis fuzzing of the OpenAPI spec, Arazzo workflows, Lighthouse budgets and Stryker mutation testing on every PR.

TestSprite caught a real bug before merge on PR #18. A price added in the builder billed $0.00 instead of ¥4,500, because the builder put a metered price first. The fix went in, and the check went green.

What went wrong, honestly

The workspace ran out of TestSprite credits twice during the hackathon. When that happens the check reports "Not enough credits" without running a single test. Nine pull requests hit that wall; the ones that shipped were merged by the repository admin after every other check had passed. They are not hidden: docs/LOOP.md is generated from the GitHub API and lists every PR and every commit's TestSprite verdict. Five went red on real test results, all fixed in the same PR, and nine were blocked by credits. A credit shortfall is not a test verdict, and treating it as one in either direction would make the ledger lie.

A second lesson: every new test layer I added found something about the previous layers. Schemathesis found the OpenAPI spec looser than the validator. Redocly Respect's strict schema checks found my conditional schemas rejecting properties their parent declared. Then my fix for that made Schemathesis unable to generate requests at all. Each layer is cheap. Not running the next one is what gets expensive.

If you build something similar

  1. Pick an oracle that is not your code. For billing it is Stripe's test clocks. For tax it could be a published calculator. For physics, a reference implementation.
  2. Derive expectations by hand and write the arithmetic next to them. Future you will need it when the oracle disagrees.
  3. Let the oracle generate the questions too (differential fuzzing), and turn every disagreement into a pinned example.
  4. Keep your end-to-end tests in the repo and check the cloud copy against it.

Try it: open the simulator on S05, change the upgrade date, and press Verify in Stripe. Your own timeline gets replayed in a fresh test clock and diffed to the cent.

AI disclosure: this post was drafted by an AI agent (Claude Code) from the project's own repository, evidence files and CI history, and published at the author's request. The project itself was built with the same agent.

title: Vercel Connect adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

Here's how access works:

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

If your app uses Vercel Passport, you can request a token for Slack’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with the signed-in user’s identity:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1T9cFkjaRDDmRFQ5bWVmD6

Connect supports Cross-App Access (XAA), including its use for MCP authorization through EMA. Follow the Vercel Connect EMA setup guide to configure your identity provider and services and enable EMA on their Connect connectors.

title: Beyond the Sequentiality Bottleneck: A Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.28584v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.

title: How to Build Zero-Dependency Single-Binary CLI Tools with AI Agents: A Deterministic Go Scaffolder MCP Server
description:
How to Build Zero-Dependency Single-Binary CLI Tools with AI Agents: A Deterministic Go Scaffolder MCP Server

Autonomous coding swarms (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Devin, Roo-Code) are increasingly tasked with generating backend utilities, system micro-tools, and automation CLIs.

However, when agents default to Python or Node.js, the developer experience degrades rapidly:

  1. Runtime Dependency Friction: Distributing Python CLI scripts requires handling virtual environments (venv, pipx, poetry), Python version mismatches, and C-extension compilation errors. Node.js scripts carry bloated node_modules folders and heavy V8 engine startup times (200ms–800ms).
  2. Third-Party Bloat in Go (Cobra/Viper): When asked to write Go, agents frequently scaffold massive Cobra/Viper boilerplates with dozens of transitive dependencies that slow down compilation and introduce software supply-chain vulnerabilities.
  3. Cross-Compilation Headaches: Cross-compiling for Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon / Intel), and Windows with proper linker flags (-ldflags="-s -w") and static linking (CGO_ENABLED=0) is difficult for agents to orchestrate without deterministic tooling.

In this tutorial, we will explore GoCLIForge MCP, an open-source and enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that empowers AI agents to generate, validate, cross-compile, and distribute zero-dependency, single-binary Go CLI tools with sub-millisecond execution.

🏗️ Architecture: Standard Library vs. Heavy CLI Frameworks

Go's standard library includes flag.FlagSet, which provides isolated, thread-safe subcommand argument parsing without importing external packages.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   AI Coding Agents                     │
│        (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Devin, Roo-Code)       │
└───────────────────────────▲────────────────────────────┘
                            │ JSON-RPC 2.0 (stdio)
┌───────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
│                GoCLIForge Pro MCP Engine               │
├───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Zero-Dep CLI Scaffolder│ 4. Binary Symbol Optimizer │
│    (flag.FlagSet POSIX)   │    (strip, dead-code elim) │
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Cross-Compiler Matrix  │ 5. Embedded Asset Engine   │
│    (Linux, Darwin, Windows│    (//go:embed SQLite/docs)│
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Checksum & Tarballer   │ 6. GitHub Actions Workflow │
│    (SHA-256 manifest gen) │    (Automated multi-arch CI│
└───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

1. Zero-Dependency Subcommand Routing

Here is the clean, idiomatic pattern generated by GoCLIForge for modular subcommands:

package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

func ExecuteRun(args []string) int {
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet("run", flag.ExitOnError)
    fs.Usage = func() {
        fmt.Printf("Usage: myapp run [options]\n\nOptions:\n")
        fs.PrintDefaults()
    }

    inputFile := fs.String("file", "", "Path to input file")
    verbose := fs.Bool("verbose", false, "Enable verbose logging")

    if err := fs.Parse(args); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error parsing flags: %v\n", err)
        return 1
    }

    fmt.Printf("[OK] Running task with file=%s, verbose=%v\n", *inputFile, *verbose)
    return 0
}

And the primary dispatcher in main.go:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

var version = "1.0.0"

func main() {
    args := os.Args[1:]
    if len(args) == 0 {
        fmt.Println("Usage: myapp <command> [arguments]")
        os.Exit(0)
    }

    switch args[0] {
    case "-v", "--version", "version":
        fmt.Printf("myapp version %s\n", version)
    case "run":
        os.Exit(ExecuteRun(args[1:]))
    default:
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Unknown command: %s\n", args[0])
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Key Advantages:

  • Zero Third-Party Imports: The entire tool compiles in <1 second with go build.
  • Static Binary: Does not require Go, libc, Python, or Node.js on the user's host.
  • POSIX Compliant: Accepts standard --flag=value and -flag value syntax.

2. Embedding Static Assets with //go:embed

Often, a CLI tool requires templates, documentation, or an embedded database schema. Go's native embed package packs files directly into the compiled binary:

package assets

import (
    "embed"
    "fmt"
)

//go:embed *
var EmbeddedFS embed.FS

// ReadAsset reads a file from the embedded filesystem
func ReadAsset(name string) ([]byte, error) {
    data, err := EmbeddedFS.ReadFile(name)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("embedded asset %s not found: %w", name, err)
    }
    return data, nil
}

3. Deterministic Cross-Compilation Matrix

Go has native cross-compilation built into the toolchain. By setting CGO_ENABLED=0, GOOS, and GOARCH, Go generates standalone static executables for all major operating systems:

# Linux x86_64
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/mycli-linux-amd64 .

# Linux ARM64 (Raspberry Pi, AWS Graviton)
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/mycli-linux-arm64 .

# macOS Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4)
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/mycli-darwin-arm64 .

# Windows x86_64
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o dist/mycli-windows-amd64.exe .

Why -ldflags="-s -w"?

  • -s: Strips the symbol table.
  • -w: Strips DWARF debug information.
  • Result: Reduces binary size by 35% to 50% with zero impact on runtime performance.

4. Configuring Claude Desktop & Cursor

Integrating GoCLIForge MCP into your local agent environment takes less than 30 seconds.

In Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json): 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "gocliforge": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "gocliforge.cli", "--stdio"]
    }
  }
}

In Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json): 

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "gocliforge": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "gocliforge.cli", "--stdio"]
    }
  }
}

5. Live Agent Demo Prompts

Once connected, your AI agents can perform automated tooling tasks:

  1. Scaffold a Complete CLI Project:

    "Scaffold a zero-dependency Go CLI named 'logpipe' with subcommands 'tail' (flags: --file, --follow) and 'filter' (flags: --pattern, --regex)."

  2. Audit Codebase Purity:

    "Validate our Go codebase structure and verify that zero third-party dependencies have been introduced."

  3. Cross-Compile for Release:

    "Compile static release binaries for Linux amd64, macOS Apple Silicon, and Windows for this project with stripped symbols."

  4. Generate CI/CD Release Automation:

    "Generate a GitHub Actions release pipeline that compiles all 5 target binaries and publishes them with SHA-256 checksums."

📦 Open-Source & Enterprise Editions

  • Open-Source (Lite): Includes project scaffolding, standard library flag generation, structure validation, and target matrix inspection.

    👉 GitHub Repository

  • Enterprise Pro ($14.99 USD): Unlocks automated cross-compilation matrix builds, //go:embed asset bundling, binary footprint optimization, and turnkey GitHub Actions release workflows with SHA-256 checksum generation.

    👉 Get GoCLIForge Pro on Gumroad

title: Virtual DOM
description:
In the previous post, we discussed what React really is, the meaning of declarative UI, and its tree-like structure. Now, let’s continue that discussion further.

If you have worked with React, you have probably heard about state, how and why it is used. Don’t worry if you don’t know about it yet.

What is State in React?

State is information that can change over time and affects what a component renders.

Now, assume React renders the component and the user clicks a button. The information about whether the button is clicked or not is stored in this state.

Whenever the user clicks the button, the information in the state changes from its default value to clicked.

The state changes, so React schedules an update. The component is evaluated again. React compares the previous UI and the new UI to determine what needs to change in the actual DOM.

Previous UI vs. New UI

Here, you can see the two UIs: the previous UI and the new UI. So, what is the difference between them?

Understanding the Virtual DOM

To understand the difference, we need to discuss the Virtual DOM.

Assume you already have a UI. Now, you perform some action, and the UI changes.

To track the changes in the UI, React uses an in-memory representation of the updated UI.

To perform reconciliation, React compares both UIs: the previous UI that needs to be updated and the new UI created by React. This is commonly described as the Virtual DOM.

Note: I know this is an oversimplification, but to understand the idea of the Virtual DOM, this mental model is useful.

Using the Virtual DOM, React can determine the required changes instead of rebuilding the entire browser DOM every time the state updates.

The new UI we talked about is the Virtual DOM. Using reconciliation and the Virtual DOM, React updates the specific changes.

What is Reconciliation?

Now, I have used the word reconciliation many times. So, what is reconciliation?

Reconciliation is the process React uses to determine how the current rendered tree, which is the host tree, should change when new data or state produces a new tree, which is commonly referred to as the Virtual DOM.

In a web application, the host environment is generally the browser DOM. React is responsible for the UI programming model and reconciliation.

title: Agentic Ensemble with Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.28560v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual anomaly detection aims to detect abnormal objects, while anomaly samples are often scarce during model training. Assembling multiple pretrained detectors can help by leveraging their transferable image scores and anomaly maps. However, most existing ensemble methods apply fixed fusion rules over saved predictions which struggle when pretrained detectors clearly disagree due to different training objectives, priors, and visual representations. To this end, we design AnomalyAgent, a post-training fusion framework for accurate visual anomaly detection. AnomalyAgent aligns heterogeneous scores and maps, summarizes score- and region-level disagreement, and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. It implements two types of actions: 1) score actions that determine how to fuse image-level detector confidence via consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, or score-map consistency; 2) map actions that fuse dense anomaly responses via consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, or disagreement correction. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) is introduced to inspect high-conflict samples and select valid score action and map action to produce the final prediction. We evaluate AnomalyAgent on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, together with seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation. Across these benchmarks, AnomalyAgent consistently improves over equal-weight fusion and achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among the compared fusion methods on MVTec AD and VisA, while demonstrating robust transfer across additional anomaly domains.

title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
description:
arXiv:2610.28385v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.

title: Policy Central: Detecting Conflicts, Redundancy, and Similarity in Deployed Police Policy
description:
arXiv:2610.29338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Policy Central is a deployed system that helps police departments find relationships between sections of their written policy: whether two sections conflict, are redundant, are merely similar, or are different. We describe the system and compare two architectures. Retrieve-Judge, a retrieve-then-classify pipeline, runs as a cheap library-wide health signal; Screen-Confirm, a screen-then-confirm cascade, is a selective audit of the documents a reviewer chooses, checking them exhaustively against one another. On a 302-pair benchmark drawn from one department's ~84 real policy documents, given each pair Screen-Confirm reaches 0.795 aggregate recall and 0.885 on Conflict, so current models judge well. Finding the pair is the hard part: Retrieve-Judge's composed recall falls to 0.457, and Screen-Confirm recovers 0.472 (0.615 on Conflict). Today these pairs are found by reading the whole library, nearly 20,000 sections, checked against one another and re-checked after every revision. A scan that returns half of them in minutes, at low cost, and can be re-run on demand changes the economics of policy review even before recall improves.

title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.28467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.

title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.28798v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative ML agents develop models by editing code, running experiments, reading a validation score, and choosing what to try next. In current harnesses this loop is served by an exact validation score returned after every attempt, which leaves the validation split open to adaptive selection. In this work, we introduce an explicit feedback contract for ML-agent harnesses, which specifies what an agent may observe, when iteration should stop, and when the test split may be touched. The contract releases a validation score only when a submission clears a noise threshold computed from the paired standard error, so no margin has to be tuned. We ran experiments on click-through-rate prediction, learning to rank, and a control task with no signal to find. The control is the sharpest case, because the true gain there is zero by construction: an agent reading exact scores ended by reporting a gain of 0.0157, while under the contract it reported 0.0033. On both real tasks the contract narrows the validation-test gap, and test performance is slightly higher rather than lower. The largest difference is in when the agents stop. Exact feedback used its entire budget of thirty submissions on two of the three tasks, including the one where nothing can be learned, while the contract halted after four to twelve. A run that exhausts its budget is usually read as diligence. It is better read as a symptom: when the feedback channel is unbounded, noise keeps supplying improvements to chase.

title: Different Defects, Different Effects: A Controlled Audit of Face Recognition Training Data
description:
arXiv:2610.28766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of face recognition has been strongly supported by the availability of large-scale training datasets. Among them, MS-Celeb-1M has played an important role by providing millions of facial images from nearly 100K identities. However, the size and heterogeneity of such datasets increase the likelihood of annotation errors, redundant samples, and other forms of data inconsistency. This motivated the introduction of refined versions, such as MS1MV2 and MS1MV3, aimed at improving the quality of the training data. Despite these cleaning efforts, we show that several types of training-data defects remain in MS1MV3. By proposing complementary data-auditing strategies, we identify five defect categories: exact and near-duplicate images, split identities, crop errors, multiple-face ambiguity, and invalid content. We then assess the effect of correcting these defects under a controlled face-recognition training protocol based on IResNet-50 and ArcFace. The results show that targeted interventions can preserve, and in some cases improve, recognition performance while requiring fewer optimization steps to reach the performance of the original training set. Duplicate removal provides the clearest overall benefit, while split-identity merging and invalid-content removal also improve training efficiency. Overall, the results indicate that the effect of dataset cleaning depends strongly on the type of defect being addressed and provide further evidence that training-data quality remains an important and comparatively underexplored factor in large-scale face recognition. The training manifests and code used in this work will be released upon acceptance.

title: My login page shows the demo credentials — a starter kit has to be runnable in 60 seconds
description:
Every starter kit I've bought died in the same place: the login screen. Not because the auth was broken — because I couldn't find a single valid credential to try it with. Buried in the README, step 9, between the queue worker and the mail config. I gave up and closed the tab.

So when I built my own kit, I made one rule: the login page ships the demo credentials in the open.

Here's the relevant part of my Login.jsx:

{import.meta.env.VITE_DEMO_MODE === 'true' && (
  <p className="mt-3 rounded-lg bg-indigo-50 px-4 py-2 text-xs text-indigo-700">
    Interactive preview — sign in with the demo credentials below. Data is simulated.
  </p>
)}

{/* ... the form ... */}

<div className="mt-6 rounded-lg bg-slate-50 px-4 py-3 text-xs text-slate-600">
  <p className="font-semibold text-slate-700">Demo credentials</p>
  <p className="mt-1">
    Email: <span className="font-mono">admin@demo.io</span>
  </p>
  <p>
    Password: <span className="font-mono">password</span>
  </p>
</div>

Two pieces. The box under the form is always there: email admin@demo.io, password password. The banner above the form only renders when the build sets VITE_DEMO_MODE=true, because it makes a claim that's only true in the public preview — "data is simulated", since the demo build runs against an in-memory mock axios client instead of Laravel.

The credentials box isn't gated, because in a real local run those credentials are real. My DatabaseSeeder creates them with firstOrCreate, idempotent, so it works whether you seeded once or five times:

User::firstOrCreate(
    ['email' => 'admin@demo.io'],
    ['name' => 'Admin', 'password' => 'password', 'role' => 'admin']
);

Is printing credentials on a login page a security smell? In a production app, yes. In a starter kit, it's documentation that can't be skipped. Nobody reads README step 4; everybody stares at the login page. The credentials box is the fastest path from git clone to seeing the dashboard.

Two smaller details I kept: the submit button disables and switches to "Signing in…" while the request is in flight (no double submits), and a failed login renders a rose-coloured box above the form with the API's message — deliberately generic, never saying which half was wrong.

If you're building a kit: make the login page teach the login. The README is for the 10% who read it.

This login page is from my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit — the whole auth loop (Sanctum tokens, roles, seeded demo admin) ships in it: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling with Uncertain Forward Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion posterior samplers reconstruct signals by combining a pretrained diffusion prior with a measurement likelihood specified by a forward model and a noise model. Calibration and reference data can characterize uncertainty in the forward model's parameters, such as blur kernels or detector responses. Fixing these parameters at estimated values leaves their uncertainty out of the likelihood, and parameter errors are thus absorbed into the reconstruction. We introduce an uncertainty-aware likelihood (UAL), a Gaussian approximation to the marginal likelihood obtained by integrating over the uncertain parameters. For each candidate signal, UAL propagates parameter uncertainty into a structured measurement covariance, reducing the quadratic penalty along residual directions that parameter variation can explain. Existing samplers can use UAL in their data updates while retaining their pretrained diffusion priors and sampling schedules. Under a fixed Gaussian nuisance model, we bound likelihood error from linearization and average divergence between the exact marginal and UAL posteriors. We compare samplers with and without UAL across six inverse problems spanning Gaussian and motion deblurring, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and fluorescence microscopy, and find improvements in reconstruction and ensemble prediction. UAL reduces geometric mean MSE by 9% to 20% across samplers in the main Gaussian-deblurring setting and by 51% to 92% in motion deblurring when non-blind samplers use the population-mean kernel. In motion deblurring, DAPS and PnP-DM with UAL also give 6.2 to 6.4 dB higher ensemble-mean PSNR than published BlindDPS and Fast Diffusion EM. On the ablation set, UAL outperforms trace-matched isotropic inflation for PnP-DM in both deblurring tasks; in motion deblurring, it also exceeds the best-tested fixed scalar data weighting by 3.3 dB for PnP-DM and 4.2 dB for DAPS in average PSNR.

title: Amazon Cognito extends multi-Region replication to AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
description:
Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication (MRR) now supports AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, extending the resilience benefits of MRR to more workloads. MRR lets you synchronize user and machine identity data, including credentials, user pool configurations, and federation setups, to a secondary user pool in a standby Region you designate, in near real-time. With user data in the standby Region, you can redirect traffic and keep authentication available if there is a disruption in your primary Region.

Previously, MRR was available in 16 commercial Regions. You can now also use MRR to replicate between additional AWS Regions, helping you meet resilience, data residency, and compliance requirements in the Regions that best align with your business needs.

MRR is available as an add-on for user pools in the Essentials or Plus feature tiers, and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). For the full list of AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region. To get started, visit the developer guide for instructions and the pricing page for pricing details.

title: Reflection AI's Beam now available on AI Gateway for free
description:
Beam from Reflection AI, previously available in stealth as stealth/cat-jam, is now available on AI Gateway. Beam is free to use for a limited time during the launch period when serviced by Reflection AI.

Beam is an low latency US open-weight reasoning model for coding and agentic tasks, with weights released under Apache 2.0. Beam supports tool calling and structured outputs, with a 1M-token context window for code, documents, and conversation history. Reasoning effort is adjustable. Beam is designed for speed, activating only 23B of its 501B parameters per token and avoiding tokens a task doesn't need, so it tends to reach answers sooner than larger open models.

title: Caching Is Easy. Cache Invalidation Is Where Systems Break: A Practical Guide
description:
Adding a cache takes ten minutes. Debugging the bug it causes six months later takes a week.

Caching trades correctness for speed. The senior move is deciding how much correctness you're willing to give up, and making that decision explicit.

Start with the question, not the tool

Before you reach for Redis, answer three things:

  1. How stale can this data be? (seconds, minutes, never)
  2. What does a wrong answer cost? (a flicker, or a wrong invoice)
  3. What's the read-to-write ratio? (caches pay off on read-heavy data)

If you can't answer #1, you're not ready to cache it.

The four patterns 

CACHE-ASIDE (lazy)            WRITE-THROUGH
App -> Cache: hit? return     App -> Cache -> DB
      miss -> DB -> fill      (write both, in order)

WRITE-BEHIND                  READ-THROUGH
App -> Cache -> (async) DB    App -> Cache (cache loads DB itself)
Pattern Good for Risk
Cache-aside Most apps, default choice Stale reads, stampedes
Write-through Data read right after write Slower writes
Write-behind Write-heavy, loss-tolerant Data loss if cache dies
Read-through Simplifying app code Provider lock-in

My default: cache-aside with a TTL. It's simple, and failure is safe because the DB stays the source of truth.

Cache-aside in code 

async function getUser(id) {
  const key = `user:${id}`;

  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const user = await db.users.findById(id);
  if (user) {
    // TTL + jitter so keys don't all expire together
    const ttl = 300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60);
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(user), "EX", ttl);
  }
  return user;
}

async function updateUser(id, data) {
  await db.users.update(id, data);
  await redis.del(`user:${id}`); // invalidate, don't update
}

Delete on write, don't update. Updating the cache invites race conditions where an older write lands after a newer one.

The three failure modes

1. Cache stampede

A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once.

t=0   key expires
t=0+  [req][req][req][req][req] -> all miss -> all hit DB -> DB falls over

Fixes:

  • Request coalescing (single flight): one request rebuilds, the rest wait.
  • Lock on rebuild with a short timeout.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: serve the old value while one worker refreshes.
  • TTL jitter, as in the code above. 
const inflight = new Map();

function singleFlight(key, loader) {
  if (inflight.has(key)) return inflight.get(key);
  const p = loader().finally(() => inflight.delete(key));
  inflight.set(key, p);
  return p;
}

2. Cache penetration

Requests for keys that don't exist always miss and always hit the DB (bots love this).

Fix: cache the negative result briefly (null with a 30-60s TTL), or put a Bloom filter in front.

3. Stale data after writes 

Thread A: reads DB (old)  ............  writes cache (old)
Thread B:        updates DB (new), deletes cache
Result: cache now holds OLD data until TTL

Fixes: short TTLs as a safety net, versioned keys (user:42:v7), or event-driven invalidation from the write path.

Layers matter 

Browser cache -> CDN -> API gateway -> App memory -> Redis -> DB
   (fastest, least control) ------------------> (slowest, most control)

Push caching as close to the user as correctness allows. For public, static-ish data, HTTP headers do more than any Redis cluster:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

What to measure

  • Hit ratio (below ~80% on a hot path means rethink the key design)
  • p99 latency with and without cache
  • Eviction rate and memory pressure
  • DB load during cold start: can you survive an empty cache?

That last one is the real test. If a cache flush takes you down, your cache isn't an optimization, it's a dependency.

Rules I follow

  • The database is the source of truth, always.
  • Every key has a TTL. No exceptions.
  • Invalidate by deleting, not by updating.
  • Design for a cold cache on day one.
  • Don't cache what you can't afford to be wrong.

Takeaway

There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Treat invalidation as a design problem up front, and your cache stays a speed boost instead of becoming a source of mysterious bugs.

What's the nastiest caching bug you've shipped? Share it in the comments. 👇

title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
description:
arXiv:2610.29174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.

title: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.29210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next-token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first-token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRows.

title: TIL: Reinstalling GBase Database? Check Installation Leftovers First
description:
Reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s) only to encounter an "instance already exists" message or another initialization error? Before rerunning the installer, check whether files from the previous installation are still present.

Old installation files, temporary files, and existing instance configuration can interfere with a reinstall. But the right cleanup procedure depends on what remains and how the previous installation was configured.

Here's a safer way to investigate.

1. Check Whether the Old Instance Is Still Running

Before removing anything, inspect the current instance status:

onstat -

If the instance is running and you intend to shut it down, use the appropriate shutdown procedure for your environment. For example:

onmode -ky

Important: onmode -ky shuts down the instance. Use it only when stopping that instance is appropriate, and make sure no active workload depends on it.

2. Inspect the Previous Installation Directory

Check whether the old installation directory still exists:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase

Before removing or replacing it, verify that this is the correct path and determine whether it contains files you need to preserve.

Do not assume that deleting the installation directory is always necessary. Confirm the previous installation layout and follow the supported uninstall or cleanup procedure for your GBase Database version.

3. Check for Leftover Temporary Files

Installation and initialization processes may create temporary files under /tmp or another temporary directory.

Inspect relevant files and directories before cleaning them up:

ls -la /tmp

Remove only files that you can confidently identify as leftovers from the previous installation. Avoid broad deletion commands that could remove unrelated temporary files used by other applications or active database processes.

4. Reinstall After Verifying the Environment

Once the previous installation has been handled and any confirmed leftovers have been cleaned up, retry the installation.

If the same error persists, check the exact error message and the installation logs rather than repeatedly deleting files. The cause may be an existing instance configuration, an incorrect installation path, permissions, or another issue unrelated to temporary files.

TIL Takeaway

When reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s), don't assume the latest installation attempt is responsible for every error.

Check the previous instance, inspect the installation directory, and identify relevant temporary files before making changes. Careful cleanup is safer than blindly deleting directories—and it makes the next troubleshooting step much easier.

The rule I follow: verify what is left, confirm what is safe to remove, and only then reinstall.

title: Dynamic Dual-Feedback Conformal Inference for Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.26987v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Quantifying uncertainty in time series forecasting is particularly demanding because sequential data exhibit temporal dependence and are prone to distributional changes. Conformal inference has emerged as a powerful uncertainty quantification approach through the construction of prediction sets. Recent advances have introduced online conformal methods that adaptively adjust prediction thresholds through feedback mechanisms. However, the existing feedback mechanism typically relies solely on miscoverage indicators (actual feedback), whether the true label falls within the interval at each time step, while overlooking the empirical prediction threshold (estimated feedback) that is derived from the oracle conformal method. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (DDCI), which incorporates a dual-feedback mechanism consisting of actual feedback and estimated feedback. The former drives the primary adjustment of the intervals based on true observations, while the latter dampens excessive expansions or contractions by leveraging empirical thresholds from conformal inference during updates. By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals in sequential settings while maintaining near-nominal coverage in practice.

title: Node.js Failure Alerting Explained (Polling Logs and Errors for Failed Cron Jobs)
description:
A failure alert is useful only if its evidence survives long enough to answer two questions: what broke, and which agent run paid for it? Short answer: for a fintech AI agent loop, start with a scheduled poller that normalizes exception groups and failed-job or HTTP 5xx log evidence into one incident record. Keep latency and cost on that record as diagnostic dimensions, not the sole paging threshold. This shape trades immediate push delivery for replayable collection windows and straightforward incident reconstruction.

The invariant is simple: every source window must be processed at least once, while every notification must be emitted at most once for the same rule, window, and evidence set. Polling without the second half creates duplicate Slack messages during retries. Polling without the first creates gaps that nobody notices until reconciliation.

Infrai is a deliberate fit for the collection side when a team wants a plain REST API rather than another client library to install and upgrade. Its errors surface can supply exception-oriented evidence, while logs can carry failed background-job and 5xx evidence. Notification rules and routing remain the poller's responsibility. I recommend trying Infrai for the evidence-collection boundary of a small or mixed-language agent platform, because one HTTP contract keeps the collector portable. The API is self-describing: its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages. A single key spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. More important for this fintech agent loop, per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata is specified consistently on native and OpenAI-compatible AI responses. That metadata lets the incident ledger preserve the dimensions needed to reconstruct an expensive or slow run without timing calls in a second wrapper. Together, these properties mean the evidence collector and a later notification adapter can share an authentication convention without turning the poller into an SDK-upgrade or credential-reconciliation project.

Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across those backend capabilities. Here that consolidation is practical rather than decorative: adding an email or SMS route later does not require the on-call team to rotate another vendor credential or reconcile another provider invoice while reconstructing the agent incident.

How Should Node.js Failure Alerting Poll Logs and Errors?

The incidents that shape this design are missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. A page saying failures > 5 is not a reconstruction. For an agent loop that may call a model several times, I need a stable run ID, the collection window, exception identity, job outcome, HTTP status class, observed latency, and recorded cost metadata in the same incident trail. Without those fields, the on-call engineer can see pain but cannot bound impact or replay the decision.

One trap is treating absence as success. Error groups and log search can reveal exceptions and recorded failure patterns; they cannot prove that a scheduled settlement-review job ran at all. A heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks.io must cover that negative space.

Silence is a separate signal.

Another boundary matters during a distributed failure: log trace_id and span_id values can support manual correlation, but they do not produce a distributed trace query or span tree. If the investigation depends on causal traversal across services, use a tracing system. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, and session replay also belong elsewhere.

Two viable system shapes

The first shape is scheduled evidence polling. A cron-triggered worker reads overlapping time windows, normalizes evidence, evaluates thresholds, persists its cursor and deduplication key, then calls Slack, email, or another webhook. Its invariants are a durable cursor, overlap between windows, deterministic incident keys, idempotent notification delivery, and a separate heartbeat. The overlap prevents a record arriving near a boundary from falling through; the incident key prevents that overlap from paging twice.

The second shape is streaming ingestion into a specialist alert engine. Applications and collectors send telemetry continuously; the alert engine owns evaluation, grouping, muting, and notification routing. Its invariants are durable ingestion, bounded evaluation delay, rule-version history, and deduplication across retries. This is the better default when seconds matter, routing policy is complex, or a staffed team already operates the alert platform.

Both work. For a modest agent fleet where incident reconstruction is the primary decision axis, I choose polling first: a five-minute evidence window is easy to replay, audit, and compare against the agent run ledger. I would choose streaming for fraud controls or payment authorization paths where waiting for the next schedule is itself unacceptable.

The polling worker should use error groups or events for exception alerts and log search for failed jobs and 5xx patterns. Exact log-search filters are not declared in the discovery parameters, so the adapter must validate its query shape against the live discovery contract and representative staging data before production use. Do not bury guessed filter fields in the evaluator. Keep that uncertainty at the adapter boundary.

Fair comparison by operating boundary

Option Natural operating shape Strong fit here Boundary to keep visible
Infrai REST evidence source plus a team-owned scheduled evaluator Portable collection across mixed services, with public discovery for contract inspection No native alert rules, push channels, heartbeat monitoring, or span-tree queries
Sentry Specialist error monitoring Exception grouping and workflows when application errors dominate A separate heartbeat is still needed for work that never starts
Datadog Managed observability and alerting platform Central rules and routing when logs, metrics, and traces already live there Broader platform ownership and instrumentation are part of the decision
Grafana Cloud Hosted observability around telemetry backends Alert evaluation close to existing metrics and logs Rule and data-source operations replace the small poller's simplicity
Healthchecks.io Dead-man's-switch monitoring for scheduled work Detecting job never ran or job never finished It complements exception and log evidence rather than replacing them

This is not a feature-score exercise. Sentry is a stronger choice when exception triage is the center of gravity. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is more appropriate when native alert evaluation, routing, and distributed telemetry are already organizational standards. Healthchecks.io fills the blind spot every error-query design has: nothing was emitted because nothing ran. Infrai fits when the desired system shape is a thin, language-neutral evidence boundary and the team is comfortable owning the rule engine.

A small evaluator that will not double-page

The preventative path below intentionally starts after vendor-specific retrieval. Adapters translate their responses into Observation; the evaluator owns the policy. That split keeps undeclared search filters out of business logic and makes recorded incident fixtures replayable in tests.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    ID, AgentRun, Kind string
    LatencyMS          int64
    CostUSD            float64
}

type Incident struct {
    Key       string
    WindowEnd time.Time
    Count     int
    RunIDs    []string
    CostUSD   float64
    MaxMS     int64
}

func fetchEvidence(client *http.Client, key, url string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status %d: %s", url, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: rate limit persisted after retries", url)
}

func evaluate(end time.Time, threshold int, observations []Observation) (Incident, bool) {
    unique := make(map[string]Observation)
    for _, o := range observations {
        if o.ID != "" && (o.Kind == "exception" || o.Kind == "failed_job" || o.Kind == "http_5xx") {
            unique[o.ID] = o
        }
    }
    if len(unique) < threshold {
        return Incident{}, false
    }

    ids := make([]string, 0, len(unique))
    runs := make(map[string]struct{})
    incident := Incident{WindowEnd: end.UTC(), Count: len(unique)}
    for id, o := range unique {
        ids = append(ids, id)
        runs[o.AgentRun] = struct{}{}
        incident.CostUSD += o.CostUSD
        if o.LatencyMS > incident.MaxMS {
            incident.MaxMS = o.LatencyMS
        }
    }
    sort.Strings(ids)
    for run := range runs {
        incident.RunIDs = append(incident.RunIDs, run)
    }
    sort.Strings(incident.RunIDs)
    material := end.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339) + "|" + strings.Join(ids, ",")
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(material))
    incident.Key = hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    return incident, true
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    groups, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/groups")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    search, err := fetchEvidence(client, key, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("retrieved error_groups_bytes=%d log_search_bytes=%d\n", len(groups), len(search))

    end := time.Date(2026, 10, 8, 10, 5, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    observations := []Observation{
        {ID: "evt-17", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "http_5xx", LatencyMS: 1840, CostUSD: 0.031},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
        {ID: "evt-18", AgentRun: "run-204", Kind: "exception", LatencyMS: 1920, CostUSD: 0.014},
    }
    incident, fire := evaluate(end, 2, observations)
    fmt.Printf("fire=%t key=%s count=%d runs=%v cost=%.3f max_ms=%d\n",
        fire, incident.Key, incident.Count, incident.RunIDs, incident.CostUSD, incident.MaxMS)
}

The two GET calls deliberately send no query fields: the search filters are undeclared, and inventing them would make a copyable example dishonest. They retrieve raw evidence with Bearer authentication, an explicit method, a 15-second client timeout, status checks, and bounded 429 retry behavior that honors Retry-After. A production adapter should decode only the response shape verified from live discovery, then pass normalized records to evaluate.

The concrete observation numbers are fixture data, not a benchmark. The repeated evt-18 models an overlapping poll window. It contributes once. In production, store Incident.Key under a uniqueness constraint before sending the notification, and advance the cursor only after the evidence and notification decision are durable. A process-local map is not enough. This is the place where I am deliberately conservative: an extra row in the incident ledger is recoverable, while a second page to the same responder trains people to distrust the channel.

Notification delivery needs its own retry policy: exponential backoff for rate limits, respect Retry-After when supplied, and reuse the same incident key for every attempt. Route severity separately from evidence collection. A Slack page might fire immediately while an email digest waits, but both should point to the same immutable incident record.

When polling is the wrong answer

This recommendation has a hard limitation. Infrai does not supply native alert rules or notification routing, and polling has a detection-delay trade-off. Do not choose this architecture for sub-minute safety actions, complicated escalation trees, or investigations that require full distributed traces. Datadog or Grafana Cloud is the better choice when managed evaluation and routing are requirements; Sentry is the better choice when specialist exception triage dominates. The same is true if audit history for rule changes is mandatory: keep rules in a system that records those changes rather than relying on an informal cron configuration.

There is also a privacy boundary. If the workflow requires per-user log deletion, bulk export, subscriptions, configurable retention, or cold-storage controls, verify those capabilities in the selected log system before sending regulated fintech data. The collection API should never become an accidental data-governance decision.

My runbook decision is conditional: poll when reconstruction quality matters more than immediate push, persist enough state to replay every window, and pair the poller with a heartbeat. Stream when response time, rich routing, or trace-native investigation dominates. If the REST evidence boundary fits that first shape, start with the failure-alerting guide and verify the live discovery schema before wiring the adapter.

Sources

References used for product boundaries and implementation choices:

  • Infrai documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Datadog Monitors documentation
  • Grafana Cloud Alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • OpenTelemetry tracing specification

title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.29223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

title: How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)
description:
How to Track SEC EDGAR Filings as JSON (Without Maintaining a Scraper)

If you are building filing alerts, compliance checks or equity-research workflows, SEC EDGAR is the
source: every filing from every US issuer, published minutes after acceptance. The official EDGAR
APIs are free and return JSON — but wiring them up yourself still means declaring a User-Agent the
SEC accepts, staying under its published limit of 10 requests per second, paginating full-text
search results, and handling fields that one endpoint returns while another does not.

Here is how to get the data in two ways, with a real sample of the output.

The official API, in a nutshell

  • Endpoints: the EDGAR application programming interfaces (submissions by CIK, filing metadata, full-text search).
  • No API key: EDGAR's endpoints are anonymous.
  • Politeness rules: send a declared User-Agent with your contact information and stay under the published limit of 10 requests per second; requests that ignore this are rejected.
  • Scope: filing metadata and issuer organisations only. There is no officer or contact data here — personal data stays out of scope, by design.

Option A — call the official API directly 

curl -sS -A "your-app your@email.com" \
  "https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000320193.json" | jq '.filings.recent | .accessionNumber[0:3]'

That works fine for one issuer. The moment you watch a shortlist of companies or run a full-text
search, you are maintaining pagination, date filtering and field reconciliation for every endpoint
you touch.

Option B — run a ready-made Actor

steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor wraps those endpoints on the Apify platform: it handles the declared
User-Agent, the 10 req/s budget, pagination, retries and an output schema check on every run. No SEC
key needed (an optional proxy of your own token keeps your run budget isolated).

Input — by issuer, or by full-text query:

{ "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"], "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10 }

{ "query": "supply agreement", "startDate": "2026-10-01", "endDate": "2026-10-17", "maxResults": 25 }

At least one of cik or query is required.

Run it with one API call:

curl -sS -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/steadfetch~sec-edgar-monitor/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cik":"0000320193","formTypes":["10-Q"],"startDate":"2026-07-01","maxResults":5}'

Real output sample (a genuine filing record, as published in the Actor's docs):

{
    "accession_no": "0000320193-26-000020",
    "cik": "0000320193",
    "company_name": "Apple Inc.",
    "form_type": "10-Q",
    "filing_date": "2026-07-31",
    "report_date": "2026-06-27",
    "acceptance_datetime": "2026-07-31T14:01:02.000Z",
    "primary_document_url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "is_amendment": false,
    "url": "https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/000032019326000020/aapl-20260627.htm",
    "scrapedAt": "2026-10-19T12:00:00.000Z"
}

One dataset item per filing, validated against the published dataset schema on every run — if a field
type changes upstream, the run fails loudly instead of writing bad rows.

JavaScript and Python

Node.js, with apify-client:

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });

const { defaultDatasetId } = await client.actor('steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor').call({
  cik: '0000320193',
  formTypes: ['10-K', '10-Q', '8-K'],
  startDate: '2026-01-01',
  maxResults: 10,
});

const { items } = await client.dataset(defaultDatasetId).listItems();
console.log(JSON.stringify(items, null, 2));

Python, with apify-client:

import json, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("steadfetch/sec-edgar-monitor").call(run_input={
    "cik": "0000320193", "formTypes": ["10-K", "10-Q", "8-K"],
    "startDate": "2026-01-01", "maxResults": 10,
})
items = client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).list_items().items
print(json.dumps(items, indent=2))

Runnable versions of all three (curl, Node, Python) plus the sample output live in
steadfetch/examples/sec-edgar-monitor.

What it costs

Pay-per-result pricing on Apify: 5.00 USD per 1,000 filings (0.005 USD per filing) plus a
0.00005 USD run-start fee. Failed requests, retries and empty searches are not charged per result,
and no proxy is billed — EDGAR answers with structured JSON, so no browser is involved.

Fields you get

Field Meaning
accession_no Official accession number of the filing
cik / company_name Issuer identity
form_type 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and the rest of the EDGAR form taxonomy
filing_date / report_date When it was filed and the period it covers
acceptance_datetime EDGAR acceptance timestamp — null when the full-text endpoint omits it; never invented
primary_document_url / url Direct link to the filing document
is_amendment Whether the filing amends an earlier one
scrapedAt Extraction timestamp, on every record

Getting started

Open the Actor page in the Apify Store, run it
from the console or with the API snippets above, and pull the dataset into whatever you already use.

Steadfetch builds public-data Actors that don't break: schema-validated output, official sources
only. More at apify.com/steadfetch.

title: Every Step Runs Inside poll(): The Kafka Consumer Flow, End to End
description:
Every Kafka consumer application calls poll(). Very few developers can list what happens inside it.

That gap shows up at the worst time: a consumer that hangs, a group that rebalances in a loop, a commit that keeps failing. Each of those failures lives in a specific step of the flow below. The flow is seven steps. The first is setup, the next four are a handshake, and the last two are the steady state the consumer spends its life in.

Step 1: Create consumer and subscribe

Application code builds a KafkaConsumer with bootstrap.servers and a group.id, then calls subscribe() with the topic list.

subscribe() only registers interest. Nothing is fetched, nothing is assigned, no broker knows the consumer exists yet. Every step that follows is driven by poll() — it is the engine of the entire client, and the handshake below unfolds across its first calls.

Step 2: FindCoordinator

The consumer asks any bootstrap broker a simple question: which broker coordinates this group.

The answer is the broker that leads the __consumer_offsets partition assigned to the group. In this walkthrough that is Broker 3, coordinating the group payments-group. From this point, all group traffic — joins, heartbeats, offset commits — goes to Broker 3. None of it goes to the brokers holding the actual data.

Step 3: JoinGroup

The consumer sends a JoinGroup request carrying its protocol preferences and timeouts:

group.id=payments-group
session.timeout.ms=45000
rebalance.timeout.ms=300000

assignment protocols offered: range, cooperative-sticky

The coordinator starts a rebalance and elects a group leader from the members. It issues a generation number — generation 17 in this walkthrough — plus a member ID for each consumer. The generation matters later: it is how the coordinator detects members acting on a stale view of the group.

Step 4: SyncGroup

The elected leader computes the partition assignment for every member and sends it back through the coordinator. SyncGroup returns this consumer's share: partitions payments-0 and payments-1.

Only now does the consumer know what it owns. Everything before this step was negotiation.

Step 5: OffsetFetch

The consumer asks the coordinator — not the partition leaders — where the group left off. The committed offsets come back: payments-0 → 100, payments-1 → 250.

Position starts from the committed offset. If a partition has no committed offset at all, auto.offset.reset decides where to start. That one configuration quietly determines whether a brand-new group reads a topic from the beginning or only sees new records.

Step 6: Fetch

Fetch requests go to each partition's leader broker — this is the data path, separate from the coordinator path. payments-0 is fetched from Broker 1, payments-1 from Broker 2.

Each fetch starts at the consumer's position, and record batches stream back per poll(). Fetch is a long poll: the broker holds the request, waiting up to fetch.max.wait.ms to accumulate at least fetch.min.bytes of data. An idle topic does not mean a stuck consumer. It usually means the broker is patiently waiting to send a batch worth sending.

Step 7: Process and commit

Application code processes the records, then commits. The commit carries the next offset: after processing through offset 109 on payments-0, the committed offset is 110. The coordinator writes it into __consumer_offsets, and that write is the group's durable progress.

A commit can fail on a stale generation. That failure means a rebalance happened mid-processing — the correct response is to rejoin and retry, not to hammer the commit. After a successful commit, the flow loops back to Fetch. Steps 6 and 7 repeat for the life of the consumer. The handshake in steps 2 through 5 only reruns when a rebalance forces it.

Under the hood

The Java client splits this flow across a few key classes:

  • KafkaConsumer — the API application code touches.
  • ConsumerCoordinator — group management: FindCoordinator, JoinGroup, SyncGroup, OffsetFetch, OffsetCommit, and heartbeats.
  • Fetcher — records from the partition leaders.
  • SubscriptionState — the current assignment and position.
  • NetworkClient — everything on the wire.

The split explains the two network paths. Group management runs through the coordinator, Broker 3. The data path runs to the leaders, Broker 1 and Broker 2. Committed progress at the end of this walkthrough: payments-0 → 110, payments-1 → 260, stored in __consumer_offsets where the next generation of the group will find it.

Rule of thumb

When a consumer hangs, the useful move is naming the step that broke: the handshake (steps 2–5), the fetch (step 6), or the commit (step 7).

It is almost never the process() code.

Takeaways

  • subscribe() registers interest and nothing more. poll() drives every step that follows.
  • Group traffic and data traffic take different paths: coordination to one broker, fetches to the partition leaders.
  • A rebalance is the handshake rerunning. Generation numbers are how stale members get caught.
  • A commit stores the next offset to read, and committed offsets in __consumer_offsets are the group's only durable memory.
  • Consumer problems debug fastest by step: handshake, fetch, or commit.
