title: HorizonComposer: Spatiotemporally Consistent Driving Video Editing with Enriched Traffic Semantics
description:
arXiv:2610.28829v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Instruction-guided video generative models offer a scalable solution for stress-testing autonomous driving systems by simulating diverse environmental conditions. However, driving scenes operate within a dense Operational Design Domain (ODD) governed by strict traffic semantics. When applied to global driving-condition edits, general-purpose instruction-guided video editors frequently corrupt these semantics, leading to structural hallucinations and ``temporal shock.'' This work distills and protects traffic semantics during video editing at three levels. First, we construct a hybrid dataset by combining temporally aligned real-world videos with synthetic edits, balancing foundational scene structure with unambiguous appearance signals. Second, during training, we adapt advantage conditioning from offline reinforcement learning to align the model using dense rewards. We extract dense, pixel-level rewards from the hybrid data to serve as a localized signal and actively steer generation toward structurally reliable pixels. Finally, our model mitigates temporal shock by introducing thinking frames, a transition mechanism that seamlessly reconciles static image conditioning with dynamic video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method prevents the corruption of multi-actor dynamics, establishing state-of-the-art spatiotemporal consistency, yielding consistent user preference (39% relative improvement in content preservation and 12% in temporal consistency), and achieving a significant 5% gain in downstream road line segmentation and 7% gain in downstream multi-object detection.

title: A Client Stole My Proposal and Hired Someone Cheaper to Build It — Here's the Paid-Scoping Fix
description:
A pattern that comes up constantly in freelance communities: you spend real hours on a detailed proposal (architecture, scope, pricing) to win a client, they go quiet after the call, and a few weeks later their project ships — built exactly on top of what you sent them, just by someone cheaper.

The usual advice is "charge for the proposal." True, but it's incomplete — the part that actually determines whether a client says yes or walks is how you structure that paid step. Three things that made the difference for me:

1. Split the pitch into two documents, not one

Most people send a single combined doc: why-us and the exact technical plan, in one file. That's exactly what makes it easy to lift — the client has everything they need to brief a cheaper freelancer the moment you hit send.

Instead, split it:

  • Capability pitch (free to share): who you are, the expected outcome, rough timeline and price range. No architecture, no step-by-step plan.
  • Execution blueprint (gated): the actual "how we'd build it" — only exists after a paid scoping step.

A client who ghosts after the free pitch never had the material to hand to someone else in the first place.

2. Make the paid step a real invoice, not a verbal policy

"We charge for scoping" said out loud on a call is not the same as a dated invoice for a named deliverable ("Technical scope & architecture document — Project X"). If a dispute ever happens, "here's the signed quote and the paid invoice for this specific document" is a real paper trail. "We had a call and I mentioned we charge for that" is not.

I use my own invoice generator for this — a scoping fee is a line item like any other, it just happens to be deliverable #0.

3. Frame the fee as creditable, not an extra cost

State up front: this fee becomes a credit toward the project if you hire me. This kills the "why would I pay for a proposal" objection, because the honest answer becomes "you're paying for this research either way — this way you keep the value if we move forward." It reduces a scoping fee from "extra friction" to "you were always going to pay for this, I'm just making it explicit and fair."

The part people skip: put it in writing before the blueprint goes out

None of this works as a verbal understanding. Before I send the gated blueprint, the client has signed something — doesn't need to be a lawyer-drafted contract, a one-page mutual agreement covering confidentiality and the credit terms is enough to make the paid-scoping step mean something if it's ever tested. I use a free NDA generator for exactly this — fill in two names, done in under a minute, no account needed.

And if you're scoping a full services contract (not just an NDA) after the paid phase converts into real work, a contract checklist scanner catches the clauses people forget — payment terms with a real late fee, IP assignment tied to a specific moment, an acceptance deadline. I wrote about the 6 clauses that actually matter in more detail previously.

What this doesn't fix

A bad-faith client who's willing to pay a small scoping fee and still shop your blueprint around afterward isn't stopped by any of this — nothing short of a strong contract and a lawyer stops that. What this does fix is the much more common case: the tire-kicker who was never going to pay for anything, filtered out before you've sunk two unpaid days into their "quick proposal."

title: A Single SQL Constraint Can Save Your Database From Bad Data — Do You Know Which One?
description:
Imagine you are building an order management system.

Your "customers" table contains 10,000 customers. Your "orders" table contains 500,000 orders.

Everything works perfectly.

Then one day, an application inserts an order for "customer_id = 99999".

The problem? Customer 99999 does not exist.

Your database now contains an order that cannot be linked to a valid customer.

Your reports may become unreliable. Your joins may not return the expected information. Your team may spend hours investigating a data-quality problem that could have been prevented.

The solution is not another SQL query. It is a database constraint.

Let's explore how SQL developers prevent these problems and learn some common SQL interview traps along the way.

  1. CREATE TABLE: Start With the Right Structure

First, create a customer table.

CREATE TABLE customers (
customer_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_name VARCHAR2(100) NOT NULL
);

Notice two important constraints:

  • "PRIMARY KEY" ensures that every customer has a unique, non-NULL identifier.
  • "NOT NULL" prevents a customer record from being inserted without a name.

Now create an orders table.

CREATE TABLE orders (
order_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
customer_id NUMBER,
order_amount NUMBER(10,2)
);

At first glance, everything looks fine.

But there is a hidden problem.

Nothing in this table definition prevents an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

How do we fix it?

  1. FOREIGN KEY: Protect Table Relationships

Add a foreign key.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
REFERENCES customers(customer_id);

Now the database enforces the relationship.

If someone tries to insert an order with a non-NULL customer ID that does not exist in "customers", the database rejects the operation.

Why is this important?

Because your database should not depend entirely on every application developer remembering to validate every relationship correctly.

Interview takeaway: A foreign key enforces referential integrity at the database level.

One important detail: a nullable foreign key can contain "NULL" unless the column is also defined as "NOT NULL".

  1. ALTER TABLE: Change Structure Without Recreating the Table

Business requirements rarely remain the same forever.

Suppose you now need to store customer email addresses.

Do you need to drop the table and create it again?

No.

ALTER TABLE customers
ADD email VARCHAR2(150);

The new column is added to the existing table, and existing rows are retained.

You can also use "ALTER TABLE" to add or remove constraints and modify columns, subject to database-specific rules and existing data.

In production, always review dependencies before changing a schema. A column modification or removal can affect reports, stored procedures, applications, and downstream data pipelines.

  1. DROP vs TRUNCATE vs DELETE: The SQL Interview Trap

An interviewer asks:

"You have a table containing 10 lakh records. You want to remove all records but retain the table structure. Which command would you use?"

Many candidates immediately answer "DELETE".

But let's understand the differences.

DROP — Remove the Table

DROP TABLE orders;

This removes the table itself, including its data and associated table objects such as indexes and constraints.

Use it only when the table is no longer needed.

TRUNCATE — Remove All Rows

TRUNCATE TABLE orders;

This removes all rows while retaining the table structure.

There is no "WHERE" clause, so you cannot use it to remove only selected records.

DELETE — Remove Selected Rows

DELETE FROM orders
WHERE order_amount < 1000;

This removes only rows matching the specified condition.

You can also delete all rows by omitting the "WHERE" clause.

Important Oracle interview tip: DDL statements such as "DROP" and "TRUNCATE" have implicit-commit implications. Do not assume you can roll them back like an ordinary uncommitted "DELETE".

Always verify the target table and understand the transaction behavior before running destructive commands.

  1. COMPOSITE PRIMARY KEY: When One Column Is Not Enough

Consider an order-items table.

A single order can contain several products, and the same product can appear in different orders.

CREATE TABLE order_items (
order_id NUMBER,
product_id NUMBER,
quantity NUMBER,
unit_price NUMBER(10,2),

PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)

);

Why use two columns in the primary key?

Because the combination of "order_id" and "product_id" identifies each row.

For example:

  • "(101, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 101.
  • "(101, 20)" identifies product 20 in order 101.
  • "(102, 10)" identifies product 10 in order 102.

These combinations are different.

But inserting "(101, 10)" a second time would violate the composite primary key.

This concept is useful when designing junction tables, order details, and many-to-many relationships.

  1. CHECK CONSTRAINT: Prevent Invalid Values

Suppose an order amount must never be negative.

You can enforce that rule at the database level.

ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_order_amount
CHECK (order_amount >= 0);

Now an insert or update that violates the constraint is rejected.

One subtle detail: a "CHECK" constraint alone does not reject "NULL" values. If the amount must also be present, define the column as "NOT NULL" or add an appropriate constraint.

This is the kind of detail that separates memorizing SQL syntax from understanding how database rules actually work.

Your SQL Interview Challenge

Before you leave, try this question without looking up the answer.

You have two tables:

  • "customers", containing customer information.
  • "orders", containing customer orders.

You must prevent an order from referencing a customer who does not exist.

Which solution is best?

A. Create an index on "orders.customer_id".

B. Add a foreign key referencing "customers.customer_id".

C. Use "ORDER BY customer_id".

D. Add a "CHECK" constraint requiring "customer_id > 0".

Pause and decide before reading further.

Correct answer: B — Add a foreign key.

An index can improve access performance, but it does not enforce the relationship. Sorting rows does not enforce data integrity, and checking that an ID is positive does not establish that the customer exists.

A foreign key directly enforces the required relationship.

The key principle is simple:

Good database design makes invalid data harder to create.

Want to Master SQL DDL for Interviews?

We've covered the fundamentals, but there is much more to learn.

What happens when you need a many-to-many relationship? When should you use "ON DELETE CASCADE"? How do you modify existing constraints safely? What mistakes do interviewers expect SQL developers to avoid?

I've brought these topics together in a detailed guide on Sankalan Data Tech.

The complete tutorial covers:

  • "CREATE", "ALTER", "DROP", and "TRUNCATE" with practical examples
  • Primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints
  • One-to-many and many-to-many relationships
  • Composite primary keys and junction tables
  • Constraints versus triggers
  • Common interview mistakes and follow-up questions
  • 21 SQL interview questions with answers

👉 Continue learning with the complete SQL DDL guide:

https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/ddl-manage-tables-relationships-sql-faq.html

If you are preparing for a SQL developer, Oracle PL/SQL, or data engineering interview, work through the examples and understand the reasoning behind each constraint instead of simply memorizing syntax.

Save this post for revision, and test yourself on the interview questions in the full guide.

title: CRAB: Cuboid-based Representation for As-built BIM from Point Clouds
description:
arXiv:2610.29257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions. Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on handcrafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure. We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters. CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing. To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes. Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization. For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm. The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.

title: Robust Representation Learning for Spiking Neural Networks based on Conditional Information Bottleneck
description:
arXiv:2610.28110v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have shown great potential for low-power neuromorphic computing due to their event-driven processing and spatiotemporal sparsity, but they remain vulnerable to input perturbations, hardware-intrinsic noise, and adversarial attacks in real-world deployment. We attribute this vulnerability partly to input-specific hidden representations learned by standard SNNs trained with conventional cross-entropy loss, as our information-plane analysis empirically shows that substantial input-related information can still be retained after label-predictive information becomes stable. To address this issue, we propose SCIB, a simple yet effective robust learning objective for SNNs based on the Conditional Information Bottleneck. Different from conventional variational IB methods, SCIB replaces the mutual information compression term $I(X;S)$ with the conditional mutual information $I(X;S|Y)$ and derives a tractable variational upper bound. Moreover, it introduces a learnable class-conditional prior instead of a label-agnostic isotropic Gaussian prior, improving the expressiveness of variational compression and encouraging class-structured representations when combined with the supervised classification objective. Systematic experiments on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under external environmental noise, neuromorphic hardware noise, and adversarial attacks show that SCIB improves robustness over standard SNNs and IB-based baselines under most evaluated noise conditions, improves adversarial accuracy under the evaluated attacks without using adversarial training, and reduces the SynOps-based single-sample inference energy consumption by 24.9% relative to an unconstrained SNN baseline.

title: Pair-Free Coarse-to-Real Video Generation via Real-to-Coarse Image Supervision
description:
arXiv:2610.28954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coarse-to-real (C2R) video generation converts coarse animation, simulation, or game-rendered videos into photorealistic videos while preserving scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics. Training such models requires aligned (coarse, realistic) video pairs, which are expensive to create and confine prior systems to narrow synthetic domains. We exploit a simple asymmetry: paired videos are hard to obtain, but paired real-to-coarse images are easy to construct with existing editing and 3D reconstruction tools. Using these image pairs, we train the DINO-R2C model to transfer realistic images to coarse images in DINO feature space, and apply it frame-wise to ordinary real videos to synthesize pseudo-coarse videos. The C2R# model then learns to generate each real video from its pseudo-coarse counterpart, free from needing (coarse, realistic) video pairs. At inference, the DINO-R2C model is discarded and actual coarse videos drive the C2R# model directly. Thus, our pair-free training scales with any real-video corpora rather than with paired synthetic videos. We will release the model and project webpage at https://gonzalognogales.github.io/coarse2real-sharp/.

title: Statewave Guide — Day 5: We taught it to speak. Then realized it still doesn't finish the job
description:
Built 27 Aug 2026 · written up 21 Oct 2026

Yesterday's question:

Can we turn verified product truth into human guidance without inventing anything new?

Yes.

At least linguistically.

Task-wise…

not so much. 😅

We added Guidance Compilation.

Instead of rendering the Product Model directly:

What the app does → What we should tell the user → How we should say it

Then we ran the same 21-feature review again.

Same instrument as yesterday: one model, one fixture, and the language and usefulness scores come from a separate model against a fixed rubric, not from people.

The language result was almost absurdly clear.

Too technical                 14      → 0
Natural-language quality      1.14/2  → 1.95/2
Clarity                       1.43/2  → 1.86/2
Malformed identifier soup     gone
Incorrect factual claims      still 0

And for the first time:

two features scored a full 3/3 usefulness.

And, also for the first time, one scored 0.

A feature with nothing verified to say, which produced a title and a question.

Round 2's spread had neither end.

And the capability split moved: measured again after the language fix, features with a verified capability scored 2.00 against 1.07 for those without. Yesterday's "barely a difference" was bad presentation, not a missing signal.

Nice.

Except the overall usefulness gate still failed.

1 / 3   median
33%     useful outputs

Why?

Because we'd taught the system how to speak…

but it kept stopping halfway through the task.

Rotate API key?

Open Settings.

That's it.

Delete client?

Open Client Detail.

Upgrade client?

Open Client Detail.

Export CSV?

Open Clients.

Perfectly readable English.

Almost impressively unhelpful. 😂

The metrics made the bug obvious.

missing_workflow    5     → 16
Actionability       1.24  → 1.14

And 10 of our 14 low-scoring examples had the same root cause.

Their verified workflow referred to:

feature:<id>

The compiler expected a graph node.

Couldn't classify it.

Quietly dropped the action.

Then proudly called:

Open Clients.

"actionable guidance."

Narrator:

it was not actionable guidance.

That gave us another rule:

Correct language is not the same as complete guidance.

So we're now separating:

Entry → Task action → Terminal action → Complete path

And another rule:

Every dropped verified action needs a reason.

No more silent disappearing acts.

The bottleneck keeps moving.

First prove truth.

Then prove ownership.

Then make it human.

Now make sure it actually finishes the job.

Still no chat UI.

And I'm increasingly happy about that.

Because a beautiful chatbot answering:

Open Settings.

when you ask how to rotate an API key…

is still just a very expensive tooltip.

Statewave Guide — Day 5.

Next question:

Can verified product knowledge become a complete user task — without giving the model any new authority?

This day in the repo: PR #5 · Previous: Day 4 — We passed the safety test. Then failed the product test

Statewave Guide is built on Statewave — an open-source, self-hosted memory runtime for AI agents. Governance and provenance, not just retrieval. Apache 2.0.

→ statewave.ai · github.com/smaramwbc/statewave

title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
description:
arXiv:2610.28998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL) requires both efficient rollout generation and training on long sequences. However, the memory requirements and model-specific operators of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next make this difficult with existing open-source implementations. To resolve these limitations, we introduce FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework based on prime-rl, with vLLM for software engineering (SWE) rollout generation. Our main focus is BF16 training of the full 48-layer model on a single 8xB200 node, with the first two layers, the n-gram table, the sparse-attention indexer and the multi-token prediction head frozen. We optimize host offload, gradient accumulation and the kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. In the full-model development study, non-padding training throughput increases from approximately 395 tokens/s/GPU in the initial 32K-token configuration to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU in the optimized 131K-token configuration, with hardware matmul throughput (aka without considering the cost of attention components) increasing from approximately 20 to 213 TFLOPs/GPU. A controlled cumulative study on an 8-layer model further quantifies the contributions of individual optimizations. Together with three inference nodes, the system supports a live SWE RL run with a target batch of 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit. Over steps 5-15, an iteration takes 22.4 minutes on average, with bounded entropy and trainer-sampler mismatch KL. These results highlight the importance of tailoring RL training to the model's architecture, memory layout and kernel requirements, rather than relying only on general-purpose RL infrastructure.

title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.29357v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.

title: How to Redeem a Muse Invite Code (and Get 1 Billion Tokens) — Step-by-Step
description:
If you just created a Muse account and heard there is a free token bonus for new users, here is exactly how to claim it. It takes about a minute — but only if you do it in time.

What is Muse?

Muse is Meta's personal AI assistant. You can chat with it, ask questions, draft and summarize text, brainstorm ideas, and much more. Muse runs on a token-based usage system, so extra tokens mean a lot more room to explore what it can do.

The new-user invite bonus

Muse has an invite program: when a new user redeems an invite code in Settings within 48 hours of joining, both the new user and the person who shared the code receive 1 billion Muse tokens. It is a two-sided reward — you get tokens, and so does the inviter.

Invite code: 07YNX6

Enter it exactly as shown: all uppercase, no spaces.

Step-by-step: how to redeem

On mobile (the app)

  1. Create your Muse account and sign in.
  2. Open Settings.
  3. Tap Redeem token.
  4. Enter the code 07YNX6 and confirm.

On the web

  1. Create your Muse account and sign in.
  2. Open Settings.
  3. Go to General → Usage.
  4. Click Redeem invite code, enter 07YNX6, and confirm.

Once the code is accepted, the bonus tokens are credited to your account — and the same amount goes to the inviter.

Important rules (read before you redeem)

  • The 48-hour window. You can only redeem a code within 48 hours of creating your account. The clock starts when the account is created, not when you first hear about the program. If you are new, redeem first and explore later.
  • One redemption per account. Each account can redeem an invite code only once, so codes cannot be stacked.
  • Each code has a usage cap. An invite code can only be redeemed a limited number of times in total, so a widely shared code may eventually stop working.
  • It is completely free. Redeeming a code costs nothing and requires no payment method.
  • Protect your account. You redeem the code inside Muse's own Settings. You never need to give your password (or any verification code) to any person or third-party website to claim this bonus. If someone asks for your password in exchange for tokens, that is a scam — walk away.

FAQ

I created my account three days ago. Can I still redeem?
No. Redemption is only available within the first 48 hours after account creation.

The code did not work. Why?
The usual reasons: the 48-hour window has passed, your account already redeemed a code, the code was typed with lowercase letters or extra spaces (it must be 07YNX6, all caps, no spaces), or the code has reached its total usage limit.

Do I need to pay anything?
No. Redeeming is free.

Disclosure

Full transparency: 07YNX6 is my personal invite code. If you redeem it, we both receive 1 billion Muse tokens — that is exactly why I am sharing it. If a friend of yours already uses Muse, feel free to use their code instead; the steps above are identical either way.

Happy prompting — and if you are brand new to Muse, go redeem that code before your 48-hour window closes!

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Point your agent at our Python guides in the Knowledge Base

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
description:
arXiv:2610.29054v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.

title: Attention-based Classification for Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.28988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.

title: ROCOCO: Robust Outline Completion of Occluded Curvilinear Objects
description:
arXiv:2610.29177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a learning-based generative model for completing curvilinear features under occlusion by environmental obstacles. To this end, we adopt a flow matching-based approach that supports the inpainting of occluded regions with the appropriate curvilinear features. To eliminate the reliance on privileged information about the occlusion a priori, we also train a UNet-based mask prediction model, which can identify regions for inpainting given only the occluded observation. The components of our approach are validated via experiments using procedurally-generated test cases, and the complete pipeline is validated using large public datasets for curvilinear objects. Against off-the-shelf inpainting baselines, ROCOCO is the strongest method by a wide margin when no occlusion mask is given, and is competitive with mask-supervised inpainting when one is, achieving best on full-image error and second only to LaMa on the occluded region, while using a completer of $7.7$M parameters against LaMa's $51$M and Stable Diffusion's $860$M.

title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors
description:
arXiv:2610.29241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.

title: Dirty flash vs clean flash: when your Galaxy actually needs a full wipe
description:
When people talk about flashing Samsung firmware with Odin, one question comes up in almost every thread: "Do I need to wipe my phone first?" The answer most people give — always wipe — is wrong as often as it's right. There's a real distinction between a dirty flash and a clean flash, and knowing which one your situation needs saves you from both data loss and pointless re-setup.

What the terms mean

A "dirty flash" is flashing new firmware over your existing installation without wiping user data — the phone keeps your apps, settings, and files, and the new system replaces the old one underneath. A "clean flash" wipes everything (the data partition) and starts the phone from a blank state, like it just came out of the box.

When a dirty flash is fine

If you're upgrading or reinstalling the same Android version family — say, moving from one build to a newer build of the same One UI version — a dirty flash usually works perfectly. The system partition gets replaced, your data partition stays untouched, and the phone boots with everything where you left it. This is also the right choice when you're re-flashing the same firmware to fix a boot problem: wiping data rarely fixes a corrupted system partition, and it costs you everything.

When you actually need a clean flash

There are three cases where wiping is the correct move. First, downgrading: going from a newer Android version back to an older one almost always needs a clean flash, because the newer version's data format can confuse the older system. Second, switching regions or carriers: moving between firmware variants with different CSC configurations can leave conflicting carrier settings behind. Third, persistent crashes or strange behavior after an update: if you've flashed and the phone still misbehaves, leftover data from the old system is the most likely cause, and a clean flash is the definitive test.

The part people get wrong

The wipe in Odin is controlled by the CSC file you load. A HOME_CSC preserves your data; a regular CSC wipes it. The mistake isn't choosing one or the other — it's choosing without backing up first. Phone storage is cheap to back up and expensive to lose: even when you're planning a dirty flash, back up your data before you start, because a flash can fail in ways that force a wipe afterward.

The safe workflow

One: back up everything you care about. Two: match the firmware to your model and CSC, exactly. Three: decide dirty or clean based on the three cases above — not on habit. Four: use HOME_CSC for dirty, CSC for clean, and don't toggle anything else you don't understand. Five: flash, then let the first boot take its time; it's building caches from scratch and interrupting it causes more problems than patience does.

Most flashing disasters aren't technical failures. They're people wiping a phone they didn't need to wipe, or not wiping one they should have — usually with no backup either way. Decide before you click Start.

For the firmware side of the process — finding the exact build for your model and region before you decide which kind of flash you need — SamFware keeps a library of official stock firmware organized by model and CSC code, with guides that walk through the whole flash from backup to first boot. SamFware is free to use, with no registration required.

title: I Migrated a Cloudflare Agents Workspace and Measured Everything: What Changes When the Storage Format Changes?
description:
The difference was not the table names.

TL;DR

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare Agents switched its Workspace implementation from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer. The change is not just a new API name. It changes how files are stored. The old implementation stored one row per path, with the file contents base64-encoded in that same row. The new one separates inodes and chunks, storing content-addressed blobs in 512 KiB pieces.

I ran the old and new implementations in the same Durable Object and compared the data before and after migration.

  • The tables are different, so old files are invisible after switching without migration. They are still there, though.
  • Storing a whole file in one row changes the size limit and performance. The old implementation hit a limit at about 6 MiB, and its 1 MB read/write cycle was 13.5 times slower.
  • The schema is versioned, so it migrates forward automatically but cannot go backward.
Aspect Old @cloudflare/shell New @cloudflare/computer
Tables cf_workspace_<namespace> vfs_* / _vfs_*
Representation of one file One row (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY) Inode + 512 KiB chunks
Where content lives Base64 in the same row's content column Blob addressed by SHA-256
Observed file-size limit About 6 MiB without R2 No single-row limit; content is chunked
1 MB write + read 87.25 ms 6.45 ms
Same content at two paths Stored twice Both paths share one blob row
Reopen with old implementation Works Fails with EIO

Test code: GitHub repository

Here is the main point upfront.

The old and new implementations differ in storage format, not API. Once you understand that, the reason files disappear after switching without a migration, why the file-size limit changes, why the new implementation is faster, and why you cannot switch back all follow from the same underlying change. The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The deeper difference is their structure, not their names.

This article expands on my talk about migrating a Cloudflare Agents Workspace with measurements I could not fit into the presentation. It is for people using Cloudflare Agents who are preparing to move to @cloudflare/computer.

1. The announcement

On October 20, 2026, Cloudflare posted this changelog:

Think and Agent Skills now use the workspace from @cloudflare/computer as well as the filesystem tools.
@cloudflare/shell is deprecated, and so is Think's createExecuteTool. These will no longer be developed nor supported from today onwards.

On the same day, Cloudflare published @cloudflare/think@0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer@0.6.0, and agents@0.29.0. @cloudflare/shell also received version 0.5.0 that day to announce its deprecation. npm's deprecated flag applies retroactively to earlier versions too, so 0.4.3 shows the same warning.

The migration guide itself had landed earlier, in PR #2564 on October 14. It did not arrive at the same time as the announcement.

The Changelog also says:

This is a breaking change. @cloudflare/computer stores files in different tables from @cloudflare/shell, and there is no automatic data migration between workspace formats.

“Different tables.” That is where I started. Let's see how different they are.

2. The old Workspace stored one file per row

A Workspace is where an agent stores its files. A model interacts with them through read, write, edit, and ls; the files themselves live in Durable Object SQLite.

The old @cloudflare/shell schema is included in the migration guide:

CREATE TABLE cf_workspace_default (
  path             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_path      TEXT NOT NULL,
  name             TEXT NOT NULL,
  type             TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('file','directory','symlink')),
  mime_type        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'text/plain',
  size             INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  storage_backend  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'inline' CHECK(storage_backend IN ('inline','r2')),
  r2_key           TEXT,
  target           TEXT,
  content_encoding TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'utf8',
  content          TEXT,
  created_at       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch()),
  modified_at      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch())
);

It is straightforward: the path is the primary key, and the metadata and content live in the same row. The content column holds file contents, base64-encoded for binary files.

Large files are handled separately. The default threshold is 1,500,000 bytes. Files above that threshold are moved to R2, leaving only an r2_key in the row. If no R2 bucket is provided, the implementation logs a warning and keeps the file inline:

if (size >= this.threshold && !r2)
  console.warn(`[Workspace] File ${path} is ${size} bytes but no R2 bucket was provided. Storing inline.`);

This “put everything in one row” design matters later.

3. The new Workspace separates inodes and chunks

The new @cloudflare/computer uses several tables:

Table Stores
vfs_dirents Parent inode + name → child inode
vfs_nodes Inode metadata (type / mode / mtime / size / link_target)
vfs_chunks Inode + chunk index → blob SHA-256
vfs_blobs SHA-256 → size and last-reference time
vfs_blob_bytes SHA-256 → actual bytes
vfs_meta schema_version and revision counter

Path resolution walks vfs_dirents from the root (inode = 1). File contents are split into 512 KiB chunks, each stored in vfs_blob_bytes as a blob keyed by SHA-256:

const CHUNK_SIZE = 524288;

The tables start with vfs_ or _vfs_, so they do not collide with cf_workspace_*. Both formats can coexist during migration.

From here, I measured what follows from the structural difference.

4. Consequence #1: switching does not make old files visible

I put both implementations on the same Durable Object. Splitting them across two DO namespaces would not test migration on the same storage. I switched between them inside one class.

I wrote 13 items with the old implementation, initialized the new one, and tried reading them:

Read through old Workspace before switch → {found: true, length: 23}
Initialize new Workspace
Read /workspace/notes.md through new     → ENOENT no such file
Read /notes.md through new               → ENOENT no such file
New-side tree                            → [{path: "/workspace", type: "dir"}]

The new implementation could not see the files.

If I stopped here, the article would say “the data is gone.” That would be quick—and wrong.

Add two controls

“Not visible through the new implementation” does not tell us whether the original write failed. In the same run, I verified that the old Workspace could still read the file both before and after switching:

Read through old before switch        → {found: true, length: 23}
Read through old after switch         → {found: true, length: 23}
Rows in cf_workspace_default          → 14 (same as before)

The old implementation could still read the file after the switch. The row count had not changed either.

The data was not gone. The new implementation was looking somewhere else. A table listing showed both formats coexisting:

cf_workspace_default
computer_execution_runtime
sqlite_sequence
vfs_blob_bytes   vfs_blobs    vfs_changes   vfs_chunks
vfs_dirents      vfs_manifests  vfs_meta    vfs_nodes
_vfs_fetch_cursor  _vfs_mounts  _vfs_push_cursor
_vfs_sync_operations  _vfs_sync_skips  _vfs_watermark

I also learned that all vfs_* tables are created as soon as you call new Workspace(). They do not wait for the first filesystem operation. The schema_version was 10.

5. Consequence #2: the size limit changes when everything fits in one row

The old implementation base64-encodes file contents and puts them in one cell. A 4 MB file becomes 5,592,408 base64 characters.

Meanwhile, the Durable Objects Limits page says:

Item Documented limit
Maximum string, BLOB, or table row size 2 MB
KV key size Key and value combined cannot exceed 2 MB

A 4 MB file should not fit in the old Shell. I predicted that while designing the benchmark and prepared files of 1 KB, 100 KB, 1 MB, and 4 MB.

They all worked.

My prediction was wrong.

4 MB → storage_backend=inline, content_encoding=base64,
       content_len=5,592,408 → read-back SHA-256 matches
8 MB → Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG

I got the same result in local Miniflare and a deployed production Durable Object.

Measurement: where is the actual limit?

Stepping through the library would only reveal its implementation constant, not the underlying limit, so I called ctx.storage.sql and ctx.storage.kv directly to find the boundary. Each probe used a new Durable Object.

Largest accepted  8,388,627 bytes
Smallest rejected 8,388,628 bytes

8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes. TEXT, BLOB, and a KV value all failed at the same boundary.

That is four times the documented 2 MB. I repeated probes around the boundary on a new Durable Object and got the same result. I reported it in cloudflare-docs#34502. Since I could not rule out 2 MB being the guaranteed limit and 8 MiB merely an implementation allowance, I did not open a PR asserting a new limit; I attached a reference branch instead.

Why does the old implementation stop at 6 MiB?

The old Shell hit its own boundary below the raw SQL limit:

Largest file accepted by shell.writeFileBytes  6,291,408 bytes (8,388,544 base64 chars)
Smallest rejected                             6,291,409 bytes (8,388,548 base64 chars)

Base64 expands the content by about 4/3, so that works out to roughly 6 MiB of file data.

I could not explain why the Shell fails earlier than raw SQL at 8,388,627 bytes. I reproduced its DDL, indexes, INSERT statement, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause, and base64 string, then ran them against the same Durable Object. Raw SQL accepted the value. I also suspected that UPSERT might duplicate the value through excluded, but an UPSERT against an existing row accepted the same size.

The stack trace points to the Shell's INSERT:

Error: string or blob too big: SQLITE_TOOBIG
  at Object.run (index.js:367:17)
  at Workspace.writeFileBytes (index.js:652:22)

I stopped there. For practical purposes, remember that “without R2, the old Shell's file-size limit is about 6 MiB.”

The new Computer splits content into 512 KiB chunks, so this particular wall is gone. Files of 8 MB, 16 MB, and 32 MB all worked. Chunking may look like a performance design, but it also changes the size limit.

6. Consequence #3: base64 conversion on every operation is slower

I hit an oddity here: Date.now() does not advance inside a Worker. In production, even a 4 MB write was recorded as 0ms. It advanced in local Miniflare, so at first I thought I was misreading the production logs.

I measured from outside instead. I sent one request that repeated the operation 60 times and a control request that did nothing, then divided the difference by 60. The table shows the median of seven runs:

Size Old Shell New Computer
1 KB 1.58 ms -0.75 ms
100 KB 4.92 ms 0.80 ms
1 MB 87.25 ms 6.45 ms

I cannot draw conclusions from the 1 KB and 100 KB results. As the negative value shows, the differences are buried in HTTP round-trip variance.

At 1 MB, the gap was clear: 13.5×. The old Shell base64-encodes a 1 MB file into one row on every write and decodes it on every read, adding overhead. My measurement includes the write and the read together, so I cannot say which one is slower on its own.

7. Consequence #4: content addressing enables deduplication

The new implementation uses the blob's SHA-256 as its primary key. The same bytes can be shared by files anywhere in the tree.

I wrote the same 512 KiB of content to two paths and counted rows in vfs_blobs:

Initial blob count                 → 0
Write identical content to path 1  → 1
Write identical content to path 2  → 1  (no increase)
Control: write different content  → 2  (increases)

Without the control, I could not distinguish deduplication from an implementation that never added a blob at all. The different byte sequence confirmed that a second row is created when the content differs.

The old implementation stores content per path, so putting the same file in two places uses storage twice.

8. Consequence #5: there is nowhere to put some metadata

The old FileInfo has mimeType, createdAt, and updatedAt. The new WorkspaceStatResult has only these fields:

{ name, inode, mode, mtime, size, isFile, isDirectory, isSymbolicLink }

There is no API in workspace.fs to read or write MIME types. There is only one timestamp, mtime.

The migration guide also says this metadata is not retained:

Things the copy does not keep:

  • created_at and modified_at. Computer stamps the time of the copy.
  • mime_type. Computer does not store a MIME type per file.

In my measurements, every migrated file's mtime was the time the copy ran. It is not just that the data is “not retained”; the new schema has nowhere to store it.

9. Consequence #6: you can move forward, but not backward

The new implementation versions its schema. Its initialization code looks like this:

const onDiskVersion = db.one("SELECT v FROM vfs_meta WHERE k = ?", "schema_version")?.v ?? 0;
if (onDiskVersion > 10) throw createWorkspaceError("EIO", `Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version ${onDiskVersion}`);
if (onDiskVersion > 0 && onDiskVersion < 10) runMigrations(db, onDiskVersion, 10);

Migrations run forward automatically. There are nine registered migrations, from v1 to v10.

There is no migration backward.

Rather than deploying an old version, I changed the on-disk schema_version to 11 to simulate a database newer than the binary, then ran the same initialization path:

Current schema_version                 → 10
Control: reconstruct with same version → {read: "hello"}
Set schema_version to 11
Open again with older binary            → EIO Unsupported workspace filesystem schema version 11
Set schema_version back to 10
Can it open now?                        → {read: "hello"}

What I measured is that the binary cannot open a database whose on-disk schema_version is newer than the version it supports. This means “you cannot roll back” only if a new release raises the schema version. It has already been raised nine times, so it is reasonable to expect that it could happen again.

Neither the migration guide nor the Changelog mentions this. There is one sentence in the implementation document 03_filesystem_schema.md:

Open() refuses to run if the binary is older than the on-disk schema_version.

The old data remains, so if migration fails you can still read from the old tables. The inability to roll back is the less recoverable part.

10. Running the migration guide's script

Now that I understood the structural difference, I ran the migration.

The guide provides a copy function named copyShellWorkspace(). It walks the old Workspace with glob("/**") and writes the files through the new fs API. The destination is under /workspace, which Think also uses as its working directory.

I ran the script without changing it. My test data included UTF-8 Japanese text, TypeScript in a nested directory, JSON for exact-content comparison, 64 KB of binary data generated with a deterministic pseudorandom sequence, an empty directory, and four symlinks covering relative, absolute, and root-escaping targets.

comparison → {
  total: 13, missing: [], typeChanged: [],
  contentMismatch: [], extra: []
}

All 13 items existed after migration, their types had not changed, and the 64 KB binary's SHA-256 matched. The empty directory remained too. I got the same result in local wrangler dev and in a deployed production environment.

I also verified that the hash comparison could actually detect a mismatch. I changed one bit in a byte sequence and confirmed that it produced a different hash: af2ba40f… versus 73734ea1…. A comparison that cannot detect a mismatch does not prove that two files match.

I checked one assumption the script relies on as well. A comment says, “glob returns rows ordered by path, so parents come before children.” If that were false, writeFile could run before mkdir. In my tests, results were sorted lexicographically, so each parent appeared before its children.

Symlinks need one extra check

When I followed each link individually, one of them failed:

Link Target in Shell Target after migration Can follow it?
/links/rel.md ../notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/abs.md /notes.md /workspace/notes.md Yes
/links/dotdot.md /src/../notes.md /workspace/src/../notes.md Yes
/links/esc.md /../notes.md /workspace/../notes.md ENOENT

/workspace/../notes.md resolves to /notes.md, which is outside the migration destination /workspace.

The cause is in the script's resolveTarget():

// Shell resolves a relative target against the link's directory and never
// goes above `/`.
function resolveTarget(link: string, target: string): string {
  if (target.startsWith("/")) return target;   // Absolute paths pass through
  const parts = link.split("/").slice(1, -1);
  for (const part of target.split("/")) {
    if (part === "..") parts.pop();
    else if (part !== "" && part !== ".") parts.push(part);
  }
  return `/${parts.join("/")}`;
}

The @cloudflare/shell implementation (resolveSymlink) also sends absolute paths through normalizePath. normalizePath stops .. at the root, so /../notes.md becomes /notes.md in Shell. The migration script passes the path through unchanged. When it prefixes /workspace, the target escapes that directory.

The conditions are narrow. Relative paths all migrate correctly. Absolute paths containing ., //, or .. that does not go above the root also work. The only failure is an absolute path containing .. that goes above the root.

The script does not report an error. symlink() saves the target without validating it, and following it stops at the root rather than throwing. This is like a legal dangling link on POSIX. The copy completes successfully.

A path/type/hash comparison will not catch this. The link exists, so it is not missing. Its type is still symlink, so the type matches. It has no file content, so it is not included in the hash comparison. My own comparison script reported missing: [], contentMismatch: []. To catch this, you have to follow and read the link:

await to.fs.readFile(linkPath, "utf8");   // ENOENT if the target cannot be followed

A second issue is that the migration is not safe to rerun:

First migration  → ok
Second migration → EEXIST path exists: /workspace/links/abs.md

mkdir({ recursive: true }) silently succeeds for an existing directory. writeFile overwrites unless exclusive is specified. symlink(target, path) has no equivalent of a force option; if the path already exists, it always throws EEXIST. That matches Node's fs.symlink behavior and is not a library bug.

The guide's onStart example sets a flag after copying completes. If the copy fails partway through, the flag is never set and the next startup fails again on the same link. Remove the link before recreating it:

const link = at(entry.path);
if (await to.fs.readlink(link).then(() => true, () => false)) {
  await to.fs.rm(link);
}
await to.fs.symlink(at(target), link);

I reported these two issues in cloudflare/agents#2645. Before filing, I checked for duplicates and found that both had been raised in earlier reviews. One did not survive a PR replacement; the other had been marked resolved based on the incorrect assumption that absolute paths were already rebased. Checking first meant I did not present either as a new discovery.

If your Workspace has no symlinks, you will not hit this part.

11. Persistence survives hibernation

The storage format changed, but the files still live in Durable Object SQLite. I checked whether they survive restarts.

“Readable from another request” is not enough evidence. The same instance might still be in memory and return the file from there. I generated a crypto.randomUUID() in the constructor and included it in the response. If that value changes, the Durable Object is a new incarnation.

                     bootId                                  Read
1. Write             1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok
2. Read immediately  1cadfbdd-7595-4879-94c1-43abca4688c0   ok   (same)
3. After 15 seconds  e4f5f2ab-3d7d-4389-8e2d-ee32fdd97b02   ok   (changed)
4. After 150 seconds c602f7f1-c9f6-465e-9b36-0c3259706d64   ok   (changed again)

Reads 3 and 4 came from different incarnations. The file content included the old bootId from when it was written, showing it was the same data.

I decided which fields to record before running the test: a case number for writing back the verdict, bootId to show whether a restart happened, env to distinguish local from production, sha256 and size to identify the file, the operation's elapsed time, and ok and error fields that hold results instead of throwing exceptions.

This control proved useful. After redeploying, my first immediate read succeeded, but the bootId was unchanged. The DO was still in memory and running the old code; it had not restarted. Without the control, I might have concluded that the file persisted across a restart. I waited 15 seconds and tried again, then confirmed that the bootId changed and the file was still readable.

How long until hibernation?

I varied the wait time and checked bootId. The zero-second wait was the control:

Wait (s)  Restarted  Read
      0   No         ok   (control)
      3   No         ok
      6   No         ok
      9   No         ok
     11   Yes        ok
     13   Yes        ok
     15   Yes        ok

The boundary is between 9 and 11 seconds, matching the documentation's “hibernate after 10 seconds of inactivity.”

12. Before you migrate

  • Count your symlinks. Run glob("/**") and count entries with type === "symlink". If there are none, the official script should work as-is.
  • If you have links, follow and read them after migration. Path/type/hash comparisons will not catch the issue.
  • Check for files larger than 6 MiB. If the old implementation stored them in R2, pass the same r2 bucket and name during migration.
  • Deploy assuming you cannot roll back. Once the new schema has been written, an older @cloudflare/computer cannot open that Durable Object.
  • Do not delete the old data immediately. The old tables remain, so wait to DROP TABLE until your comparison is done.

The dependency arrangement changes too. In @cloudflare/think@0.20.2, @cloudflare/shell was a direct dependency; you did not install it yourself. In 0.21.0, @cloudflare/computer is a peer dependency. The mechanism behind “I upgraded and my Workspace is empty” is right there.

13. Conclusion

The storage format changed, and the rest followed from it:

  • Different tables → files are invisible after switching without a migration, but the old tables remain and the old Workspace can still read them.
  • One row versus chunks → the old implementation hits a limit at about 6 MiB; the new one accepts files of 32 MB.
  • Base64 conversion on every operation → a 13.5× difference in the 1 MB read/write test.
  • Content-addressed blobs → the same content at two paths takes one blob row.
  • Fewer metadata columns → there is nowhere to store mime_type or created_at.
  • A versioned schema → it migrates forward automatically and cannot be opened by an older implementation after the version changes.

The migration guide says to copy files manually because the tables differ. The difference is not just the table names; it is the structure. Understanding that structure tells you what to verify before you migrate.

I also found two mismatches with the documentation. The Durable Object SQLite value limit I tested was 8 MiB, not 2 MB, and the user-facing docs do not mention that an older implementation cannot open a Durable Object after its schema has been upgraded.

The most surprising result was that a 4 MB file worked. I had predicted the result from the official limit and got it wrong. Because I had trusted the documented number, I no longer trusted my other predictions once it failed. I ended up measuring both the size limit and performance myself. That took more time than the migration itself.

References

  • Think agents now use a @cloudflare/computer workspace — The announcement, the lack of automatic migration, and deprecation of createExecuteTool.
  • Migrating from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer — Both schemas and the copy script discussed in §10.
  • cloudflare/computer docs/03_filesystem_schema.md — All vfs_* table definitions, chunk size, and schema version behavior.
  • Durable Objects — Limits — The documented 2 MB row-size limit tested in §5.
  • Durable Objects — Lifecycle — Sources for the 10-second hibernation and 70–140-second eviction behavior.
  • cloudflare/computer#217 / #219 — Acknowledgment that writing to R2 and namespaces are not supported yet.
  • cloudflare/agents#2645 — Report about the symlink migration script in §10.

title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
description:
arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.
